t-e-lawrence: Thomas Edward Lawrence was born on 16 August 1888 in Tremadog, Wales, the illegitimate son of Sir Thomas Chapman, an Anglo-Irish landowner, and Sarah Lawrence, a governess in Chapman's household. His parents did not marry but lived together under the name Lawrence. In 1896 the family moved to Oxford, where he attended the City of Oxford High School for Boys and read history at Jesus College from 1907 to 1910. Before the war he worked as an archaeologist for the British Museum, chiefly at Carchemish in Ottoman Syria.

After the outbreak of war in 1914 he was commissioned in October and sent to the Arab Bureau, a military intelligence unit in Cairo, arriving on 15 December. The Arab Revolt began in June 1916, and in October he was sent to the Hejaz, where he interviewed the sons of Sharif Hussein and concluded that Faisal was the best candidate to lead it. With Faisal he developed a strategy of avoiding the capture of Medina and extending northwards towards Damascus. In 1917 he proposed a joint attack on Aqaba, led by Sharif Nasir of Medina.

Lawrence arrived in Damascus around 9 am on 1 October 1918, several hours after it had fallen, and helped establish a provisional Arab government under Faisal. After the war he joined the Foreign Office and attended the Paris Peace Conference as a member of Faisal's delegation. In 1922 he withdrew from public life and served as an enlisted man in the Army and the Royal Air Force until 1935. King George V offered him a knighthood in October 1918, but he declined, because he thought British policy had betrayed the Arab cause.

His major work is Seven Pillars of Wisdom, his account of the Arab Revolt, which he rewrote three times and published in 1926. An abridged version, Revolt in the Desert, appeared in March 1927 and was a best-seller. He also translated Homer's Odyssey and wrote The Mint, on his service in the RAF, which was published after his death. Some alleged embellishments in Seven Pillars have been disproved, but his own notebooks refute his claim to have crossed Sinai from Aqaba to the Suez Canal in 49 hours without sleep; the ride lasted more than 70 hours. Richard Aldington attacked his veracity in 1955. Lawrence died in 1935 at the age of 46 after a motorcycle crash in Dorset.
tabasco: Tabasco, officially the Free and Sovereign State of Tabasco, is one of the 32 federal entities of Mexico. It covers 24,731 square kilometres and is divided into seventeen municipalities. It borders Campeche to the northeast, Veracruz to the west and Chiapas to the south, and the Petén department of Guatemala lies to the southeast. The northwest lies on the coastal plain of the Gulf of Mexico. Rain falls plentifully all year, and most of the state is covered in rainforest. Since 1994 it has been divided for documentation into two regions named after the Grijalva and Usumacinta rivers.

The Olmec civilisation dominated much of what is now Tabasco about 3,000 years ago, and its main site there is La Venta, surrounded by swamps and marshes about 15 km from the Gulf. The Maya began to dominate part of the state around 300 CE; their sites include Comalcalco, Pomoná, El Tortuguero and Jonuta. At Comalcalco they built in adobe brick because the area lacked building stone, using clay and lime extracted from shells.

The first Spanish contact came in 1518, when Juan de Grijalva landed at the mouth of the river that now bears his name. Hernán Cortés came the next year and fought the natives at the Battle of Centla; among the twenty female slaves he received as conqueror was La Malinche. The territory was never fully subjugated because of its climate, terrain and lack of minerals, and the Franciscans who arrived in the 16th century did not stay. European diseases decimated the local population, and the Spanish brought African slaves to work plantations. Significant agricultural production, chiefly cacao and cattle, came only in the 18th century.

Tabasco became one of the first fourteen states under the 1824 Constitution. During the Mexican–American War troops under Matthew C. Perry took the port of Frontera in 1846 and later Villahermosa, but guerrilla groups and the climate forced the United States to withdraw. Its forces returned in 1847 and occupied the capital for thirty-five days, causing great destruction.

Villahermosa is the capital. The state produces petroleum and natural gas, and its farming includes cacao, coconut, bananas, sugar cane and cattle. Most speakers of indigenous languages use the Tabascan dialect of Chontal Maya. The Parque Museo de La Venta in Villahermosa, created in the 1950s by the writer Carlos Pellicer, shelters major pieces from La Venta, and Comalcalco is the Maya site open to the public. The state seal was granted in 1598 by Philip II of Spain to the town of Villahermosa, then called San Juan Bautista.
tabriz: Tabriz lies in the valley of the Quru River in Iran's historic Azerbaijan region, between the Sahand and Eynali mountains, at an elevation of between 1,350 and 1,600 metres. The valley opens into a plain that slopes gently down to the eastern shore of Lake Urmia, 60 kilometres to the west. The area is prone to earthquakes, and the city has been devastated and rebuilt several times; earthquakes are recorded in 858, 1041 and 1721. According to some sources the name derives from tap-riz, meaning flowing hot, in reference to the area's thermal springs.

Early history is poorly documented. An Iron Age graveyard of the first millennium BCE was found beside the Blue Mosque, and the city appears as Tarui or Tauris in an inscription of the Assyrian king Sargon II dated 714 BCE. After the Muslim conquest the Azd tribe from Yemen settled there. In 791 Zubaidah, wife of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, rebuilt the city after a devastating earthquake and beautified it so much that she was credited as its founder.

Tabriz was the capital of the Ilkhanate from 1265, and under Ghazan Khan, who came to power in 1295, it reached its highest splendour. It was again a capital under the Qara Qoyunlu from 1375 to 1468 and the Aq Qoyunlu from 1468 to 1500. Ismail I was crowned there in 1501 and announced Twelver Shia Islam as the official religion of the Safavid Empire, and the largely Sunni population was forced to convert. After the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 Selim I sacked the city, and in 1555 Tahmasp I moved the capital to Qazvin to escape the growing Ottoman threat.

Its closeness to the West made Tabriz the centre of the Iranian Constitutional Revolution between 1905 and 1911, led locally by Sattar Khan and Bagher Khan. Russian forces occupied it in 1909 and again from December 1911, executing about 1,200 residents, and held it until 1917.

Tabriz is the capital of East Azerbaijan province and the largest economic centre of north-western Iran, with a population of over 1.7 million in 2016. Most of its people speak Iranian Azerbaijani as their first language and Persian as their second. Its Bazaar is a World Heritage Site, and most preserved monuments date from the Ilkhanid, Safavid and Qajar periods. The city is known for hand-woven carpets, and the University of Tabriz was established in 1947.
tachira: Táchira is one of the three Venezuelan Andean states, with Mérida and Trujillo. It covers 11,100 square kilometres and had 1,168,908 inhabitants at the 2011 census. It borders Zulia to the north, Barinas and Mérida to the east, Apure and Barinas to the south, and the Colombian department of Norte de Santander to the west. Its mountains are the southern continuation of the Mérida range, and its highest point, the Páramo El Pulpito, is about 3,995 m above sea level. The Andes of Táchira rose during the Eocene, when the Nazca and Caribbean plates began to slide under the South American plate.

The territory was inhabited by Timote, Cuica and Chibcha groups such as the Machirí, Umuquena and Táriba, and was colonised extensively in the 16th century. Captain Juan Maldonado Ordoñez y Villaquirán founded San Cristóbal in 1561 and Francisco de Cáceres founded La Grita in 1576, which began the farming of the area. La Grita was the capital of its province until European trading companies arrived and settled mainly in the more accessible San Cristóbal. The Dominican Friar Alonso de Andrada said the first mass in the territory on 25 July 1558.

For over two hundred years Táchira was Venezuela's main coffee producer. Important European trading houses arrived in the 19th century, but the region stayed relatively isolated from the rest of the country, and received more cultural influence from Colombia. At the end of the 19th century the national oil industry was born at the place now called La Petrolia, where Venezuela's first oil wells were drilled. Táchira became a state in 1863 and in 1864 joined the United States of Venezuela as an independent state. In 1881 it joined Guzmán (Mérida) and Trujillo in the Great State of Los Andes, and when that was dissolved in 1899 it recovered its status as a separate state.

The capital, San Cristóbal, lies at 825 metres above sea level on a succession of river terraces and is one of the oldest cities in Venezuela. Its position on the border with Colombia makes it a commercial city. Táchira's economy rests on coffee, pineapple, cattle and food processing, and the state is connected to Colombia by three international bridges. Its protected areas include El Tamá National Park, Chorro El Indio National Park and the Páramo El Zumbador.
tacitus: Little is known of the personal life of Tacitus. What is known comes from scattered hints in his own works, the letters of his friend Pliny the Younger and an inscription found at Mylasa in Caria. He was born in 56 or 57 into an equestrian family. His place of birth and his first name are not known: the letters of Sidonius Apollinaris call him Gaius, and the major manuscript of his work gives Publius. His marriage to the daughter of a senator from Gallia Narbonensis suggests that he came from that province. He owed his rank to the Flavian emperors, as he says himself.

Tacitus studied rhetoric in Rome to prepare for a career in law and politics. In 77 or 78 he married Julia Agricola, daughter of the general Gnaeus Julius Agricola. He entered political life as a quaestor in 81 or 82 under Titus, became praetor in 88 and served in the provinces from about 89 to about 93. He gained acclaim as an orator, which sits ironically with his cognomen, Tacitus, meaning silent.

He and his property survived the reign of Domitian, but the experience left him jaded and perhaps ashamed of his own complicity, and instilled in him the hatred of tyranny evident in his works. In 97, under Nerva, he became suffect consul, the first of his family to do so. In 100 he and Pliny prosecuted Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa, for corruption. In 112 to 113 he held the governorship of the province of Asia.

Five works ascribed to Tacitus survive, with gaps. The Life of Agricola and the Germania date to about 98. The Germania is an ethnographic work on the Germanic tribes outside the empire. The Dialogue on Oratory followed about 102, the Histories about 105 and the Annals about 117. The Histories and the Annals were meant to form a single work of thirty books, a continuous narrative from the death of Augustus in 14 to the death of Domitian in 96.

Of the Histories only the first four books and part of the fifth survive, covering the year 69 and part of 70. Of the Annals, books 7 to 10 and parts of others are missing. The first half survives in a single manuscript from Corvey Abbey and the second half in one from Monte Cassino.
tacna: Tacna, officially San Pedro de Tacna, lies in the Caplina River valley in southern Peru, about 35 km north of the border with Chile, and is the capital of the department of Tacna. The surrounding area is generally desert, with a few fertile spots near the mountains. The name is derived from the Quechua words taka, meaning to hit, and na, meaning place. At the time of the Spanish conquest the region was multiethnic, with local sedentary populations making up about 66% of the people, settlers from the Altiplano about 25% and fishing people known as Camanchacos about 9%. The encomienda system was established there in 1540.

In 1811 the royal accountant Francisco Antonio de Zela started the push for Peruvian independence from Spain at Tacna, and in 1828 President José de La Mar declared it the Heroic City. It was the capital of the short-lived Peru–Bolivian Confederation from 1836 to 1839. Sodium nitrate and other resources brought prosperity and a wave of Italian immigrants. The War of the Pacific ended this: a large Peruvian and Bolivian army was quartered in the city in poor sanitary conditions, which cost it much of its population to infectious diseases, and Chile captured it in May 1880 after defeating the allied army outside the city under General Manuel Baquedano.

Under the Treaty of Ancón of 1883, Chile was to administer the provinces of Tacna and Arica for ten years, after which a plebiscite would decide their sovereignty. When the ten years ended, the two sides could not agree whether to include a large number of imported Chilean labourers in the vote. Chilean authorities pursued a campaign of Chilenization, which Peruvian nationalists defeated, and the plebiscite was never held. Peruvian historiography calls the period the cautiverio. Tacna's patriotic Paseo de la Bandera began in 1901 when a group of its people defied a Chilean ban on showing Peruvian flags.

The Treaty of Lima of 1929 gave Chile Arica, while Peru recovered Tacna and received an indemnity of 6 million dollars and other concessions; the treaty took effect on 28 August 1929. Each year on 28 August a large Peruvian flag is carried through the city in the Paseo de la Bandera, which celebrates the return of Tacna to Peru. Tacna is a commercial city, with trade based on links with northern Chile, and it has monuments commemorating Peruvian independence and the War of the Pacific, among them the arch of the Alto de la Alianza complex and the Tacna Parabolic Arch. The Toquepala caves nearby have yielded some of the oldest human remains in Peru.
tadeusz-kosciuszko: Tadeusz Kościuszko was born in February 1746 on the Mereczowszczyzna estate in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, now in Belarus; his exact birthdate is unknown. He was the youngest son of Ludwik Tadeusz Kościuszko, an officer and member of the szlachta, whose family held modest lands worked by 31 peasant families. After graduating from the Corps of Cadets in Warsaw, he went to Paris in 1769 on a royal scholarship. As a foreigner he could not enter the French military academies, so he enrolled in the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture, studied architecture privately, and audited military lectures for five years. The French Enlightenment and the economic theory of physiocracy left a strong impression on him.

In 1776 Kościuszko sailed for America and, with Benjamin Franklin's recommendation, was commissioned a colonel of engineers in the Continental Army. He built fortifications including those at West Point, and as chief engineer to General Nathanael Greene he helped the Continental Army cross the rivers in the Race to the Dan in 1781. In 1783 the Continental Congress promoted him to brigadier general.

He returned to Poland in 1784 and became a major general in the Commonwealth army in 1789. In the Polish-Russian War of 1792 he commanded a division, and although he lost no battle, the king capitulated and the Second Partition followed. In March 1794, in Kraków's Main Square, he announced an uprising and took the title Naczelnik. He won at Racławice on 4 April by leading a charge of peasant volunteers armed with scythes, and at Połaniec he issued a proclamation granting serfs civil rights and reducing their labour obligations. He was captured at the Battle of Maciejowice in October 1794, and the uprising's defeat in November led to the Third Partition of 1795.

After Catherine II died, Tsar Paul I pardoned Kościuszko in 1796 and he left for the United States. A friend of Thomas Jefferson, he wrote a will in 1798 dedicating his American assets to the education and freedom of enslaved people in the United States, but its execution proved difficult and the funds were never used as he intended. He eventually returned to Europe and lived in Switzerland until his death on 15 October 1817. He is a national hero in Poland, the United States, Lithuania and Belarus.
tagalog-language: Tagalog is a Central Philippine language within the Austronesian family, and so related to Malagasy, Javanese, Indonesian, Malay and Tetum. It is closely related to the languages of the Bicol Region and the Visayas, including Waray, Hiligaynon and Cebuano. It differs from them in its treatment of the Proto-Philippine schwa vowel, which merged with one vowel in most Bikol and Visayan languages and with another in Tagalog. The word Tagalog is possibly derived from taga-ilog, meaning river dweller. The linguists David Zorc and Robert Blust speculate that the Tagalogs and other Central Philippine groups originated in northeastern Mindanao or the Eastern Visayas.

Before the Spanish arrived in 1521 and began colonisation in 1565, Tagalog was written in an abugida called Baybayin, with symbols for three vowels and 14 consonants. It belongs to the Brahmic family of scripts and is believed to descend from the script used by the Bugis in Sulawesi. It gradually gave way to the Latin alphabet taught by the Spaniards. Until the first half of the 20th century Tagalog was written in various ways based on Spanish orthography, in a 32-letter alphabet called the abecedario. In 1940 the grammarian Lope K. Santos introduced a 20-letter alphabet called the Abakada, and in 1971 the alphabet was expanded to make room for loans, especially Spanish and English family names.

Tagalog was declared the official language by the first revolutionary constitution of the Philippines, the Constitution of Biak-na-Bato, in 1897. The selection of a Tagalog-based national language in 1937 caused controversy, with speakers of Cebuano and Ilocano mainly regarding it as a cultural imposition. President Manuel L. Quezon signed Executive Order No. 263 in 1939, designating the language the Wikang Pambansâ, and on 12 April 1940 the teaching of the national language was ordered in all public and private schools. The first Tagalog Bible, Ang Biblia, was published in 1905.

Tagalog is spoken as a first language by the ethnic Tagalog people, a quarter of the population of the Philippines, and as a second language by the majority. Its standardised form, Filipino, is the national language and one of the two official languages with English. The Tagalog homeland, Katagalugan, covers much of central and southern Luzon, and Tagalog is also spoken natively on Marinduque and Mindoro.

The language commonly uses verb-subject-object order and is agglutinative, with verbs that take many prefixes, infixes and suffixes. Its vocabulary is mostly native Austronesian, with many Spanish and English loanwords and, from the precolonial use of Trade Malay, many Malay words. Words from Sanskrit, Tamil, Hokkien and other Chinese languages, Japanese, Arabic and Persian also appear. The polite particles pô and hô express respect to elders and others.
tagus: The Tagus, called the Tajo in Spanish and the Tejo in Portuguese, is 1,007 km long. It rises at an elevation of 1,593 metres in the municipality of Frías de Albarracín in Teruel, in the Sierra de Albarracín, part of the Montes Universales. It flows 816 km through Spain, then forms a border of 47 km between Spain and Portugal before running 145 km through Portugal. Aranjuez, Toledo and Talavera de la Reina are its main Spanish cities, and Abrantes, Santarém and Lisbon its main Portuguese ones. Its basin covers 80,600 square kilometres.

The river's Latin name was Tagus, and its most probable origin is an Indo-European root meaning to drip. Its history is bound up with Toledo and Lisbon, two cities of great historical weight in the Iberian Peninsula. Toledo was built on a hill about 100 m high around the meander known as the Torno del Tajo, which protected it from attack. From the Late Middle Ages the mouth of the Tagus carried intense commercial activity between northern Europe and the Mediterranean, and from the Renaissance it was the main communications hub of the Portuguese Empire, which extended through America, Africa and Asia. The lower Tagus is seismically active, with major earthquakes recorded in 1309, 1531, 1755 and 1909.

The basin is the most populated in the Iberian Peninsula, with more than ten million inhabitants, and includes the Madrid metropolitan area and the Lisbon region. The river's estuary is one of the few inverted deltas in the world: about 15 km wide and 25 km long, it exits to the sea through an opening only 2 km wide and forms a large lagoon with shallow sand banks. In the second half of the 20th century engineering works regulated the flow for drinking water, irrigation, electricity and the cooling of nuclear power plants. Protected areas include the Alto Tajo Nature Park, Monfragüe National Park and the Tagus Estuary Natural Reserve.
taha-hussein: Taha Hussein was born in Izbet el Kilo, a village in the Minya Governorate in central Upper Egypt, the seventh of thirteen children of lower middle class Muslim parents. He contracted ophthalmia at the age of two and became blind through the malpractice of an unskilled physician. After a kuttab he studied religion and Arabic literature at El Azhar University, but from an early age he was dissatisfied with the traditional education system.

When the secular Cairo University was founded in 1908 he was keen to be admitted, and despite being poor and blind he won a place. He then went to Montpellier, where he enrolled in the university and attended courses in literature, history, French and Latin. After his MA he continued at the Sorbonne, where he hired Suzanne Bresseau to read to him and later married her.

In 1919 Hussein returned to Egypt with Suzanne and was appointed professor of history at Cairo University. He went on to become a professor of Arabic literature and of Semitic languages. At the Academy of the Arabic Language in Cairo he was made responsible for completing Al-Mu'jam al-Kabir, The Great Dictionary, and he also served as the academy's president. He was the founding Rector of the University of Alexandria.

In 1950 he became Minister of Education and led a call for free education and for the right of everyone to be educated. He turned many Quranic schools into primary schools and converted a number of high schools into colleges, such as the Graduate Schools of Medicine and Agriculture. He is credited with establishing several new universities. In 1955, after his time as minister, he proposed that Al-Azhar University be closed down.

Hussein wrote more than sixty books, including six novels, and about 1,300 articles, and worked as a journalist, often writing daily. His autobiography Al-Ayyam, The Days, appeared in English as An Egyptian Childhood in 1932 and The Stream of Days in 1943. He also translated works by Racine, Voltaire and Sophocles. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature twenty-one times.

On Pre-Islamic Poetry (1926) claimed that much early Arabic poetry had been falsified in ancient times through tribal pride and rivalries, and hinted that the Qur'an should not be taken as an objective source of history. Religious scholars at Al Azhar were angered and accused him of insulting Islam. The public prosecutor said the book was the opinion of an academic researcher and took no action, but the book was banned and republished with slight changes as On Pre-Islamic Literature. In The Future of Culture in Egypt he argued that most Egyptians descended from the ancient Egyptians, and he rejected pan-Arabism.
tahirid-dynasty: The Tahirids were a culturally Arabized, Sunni Muslim dynasty of Persian dehqan origin. Their founder, Tahir ibn Husayn, played a major military role in the civil war between the rival caliphs al-Amin and al-Ma'mun, and he and his ancestors had earlier been given minor governorships in eastern Khorasan for their service to the Abbasids. In 821 Tahir was made governor of Khorasan, but he died soon afterwards, and the caliph appointed his son Talha. Another son, Abdallah, was sent to Egypt to retake the province from a rebel and was made governor there.

Talha failed to remove the Kharijites from Sistan, and the Tahirids occupied Zarang without ever collecting taxes in the surrounding countryside. Abdallah took over Khorasan when Talha died in 828. His reign saw a flourishing of agriculture in Khorasan, and he was a noted poet. The historian Hugh Kennedy rejects the view that the Tahirids were the first independent Iranian dynasty and calls the arrangement a partnership between the Abbasids and the Tahirids.

Under Muhammad ibn Tahir the dynasty declined. Oppressive policies in Tabaristan led its people to revolt and declare allegiance to the Zaydi ruler Hasan ibn Zayd in 864, and Sistan had already been lost to rebels. In 873 the Saffarid dynasty overthrew Muhammad and annexed Khorasan. The Tahirids also served as military governors of Baghdad from 820. Ishaq ibn Ibrahim held the city for over twenty-five years and carried out the Mihna there. In the 860s Abdallah, a later governor of the city, gave refuge to the caliph al-Musta'in during the Anarchy at Samarra and commanded Baghdad's defence when al-Mu'tazz besieged it in 865. In 891 Badr al-Mu'tadidi took charge of the city's security in place of the Tahirids.

Although Persian, the Tahirids were eager to be accepted in the caliphal world, where Arabic culture carried prestige. They patronised Arabic poetry and did not take part in the renaissance of Early New Persian, which the Saffarids helped lead. Later writers such as Daulatshah said that Abdallah ibn Tahir ordered Persian works destroyed. The historian Shivan Mahendrarajah credits the Tahirids with starting the process by which Persian came to be written in the Perso-Arabic script.

They supported Sunni orthodoxy and suppressed sectarian movements in Khorasan and Transoxiana, and their coins and sermons acknowledged the Abbasid caliphs. The religious scholar Abu Ubayd dedicated his Garibu'l-Hadis to Abdallah. Mansur ibn Talha rebuilt the minaret of the congregational mosque in Nishapur.
tahlequah: Tahlequah lies in Cherokee County, Oklahoma, at the foothills of the Ozark Mountains, about 40 miles west of the Arkansas state line, and is the county seat. Many linguists believe the name comes from the Cherokee word di li gwa, meaning grain, which described a native grain with a red hue that grew on the open flats of east Tennessee. A local legend that the name means two is enough, from two elders who waited for a third, began to circulate only in the 1930s. The settlement existed as early as 1832.

The first capital of the Cherokee Nation-West was Tahlonteeskee, established in 1828. When new arrivals from the Trail of Tears flooded the area in 1839, the Western Cherokee, who had agreed in 1834 to let the newer migrants settle near them, joined their government with that of the Eastern Cherokee at Tahlequah. The seat of government was officially moved there by mid-1840.

The town grew quickly. By 1842 it had four stores, and in 1843 its 160-acre town site was surveyed and an intertribal council drew ten thousand participants from 21 tribes. The National Hotel was built in 1844, and the newspaper Cherokee Advocate issued its first edition on a press installed in the new Supreme Court building.

The first school opened in 1845 and the Cherokee Male Seminary in 1851. Most of the government buildings were destroyed in the Civil War, during which the Cherokee became divided into two bitterly opposing sides. A brick capitol was first occupied in 1870, and in 1907, at Oklahoma statehood, it became the county courthouse. It was returned to the Cherokee Nation in 1970.

The Cherokee Supreme Court Building, built in 1844, is the oldest public building in Oklahoma. Northeastern State University has its main campus in the city and descends from the Cherokee Female Seminary, which burned at Park Hill in 1887, was rebuilt in Tahlequah, and was taken over by the state after statehood. Street and business signs appear in both Cherokee and English, in the syllabary created by Sequoyah. The 2020 census counted 16,209 people. The capital of the modern Cherokee Nation lies in nearby Park Hill, with a Tahlequah postal address.
tahmasp-i: Abu'l-Fath Tahmasp Mirza was born on 22 February 1514 in Shahabad, a village near Isfahan, the eldest son of Ismail I and his principal consort, the Mawsillu princess Tajlu Khanum. The Safavids were a family of Kurdish origin who were sheikhs of a Sufi order centred in Ardabil.

Tahmasp took the throne as a ten-year-old under the guardianship of Div Sultan Rumlu, his lala and the de facto ruler. Other Qizilbash tribes, especially the Ostajlu and Takkalu, would not accept Rumlu rule. In the spring of 1526 battles in the northwest grew into a civil war, in which the Ostajlu leader Kopek Sultan was killed on the order of Chuha Sultan. Uzbek raiders temporarily seized Tus and Astarabad, and Div Sultan Rumlu was blamed and executed by Tahmasp himself.

In 1528, aged fourteen, Tahmasp defeated the Uzbeks at the Battle of Jam by using artillery. In 1532 the Ottomans sent troops to Iran; they seized Tabriz and Kurdistan, and Tahmasp drove them out, but another Uzbek invasion prevented a decisive victory. The Ottoman grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha occupied Tabriz in July 1534, and the sultan peacefully conquered Baghdad and Shia cities such as Najaf. Between 1540 and 1553 Tahmasp led four campaigns against the Georgian kingdoms, looting Tbilisi in the first.

In 1544 the Mughal emperor Humayun, fleeing his brothers' rebellions, met Tahmasp at Soltaniyeh. Tahmasp honoured him as a guest but refused political help unless he converted to Shia Islam; Humayun reluctantly agreed and reverted to Sunni Islam on his return. In 1555 Tahmasp moved the capital from Tabriz to Qazvin, farther from the Ottomans, and in 1556 he issued an Edict of Sincere Repentance, renouncing dancing, music, wine and painting.

Tahmasp governed by personal rule, seeking to reduce Turkoman influence by empowering the Persian bureaucracy. He built up military slaves, taken from Caucasus prisoners, who commanded the gunners and musketeers. Until 1533 the Qizilbash urged him to continue as the successor of Ismail I, whom they worshipped as the promised Mahdi; that year he had a spiritual rebirth and outlawed irreligious behaviour, presenting himself as a pious Shia king.

He patronised miniature painting during the first half of his reign, and the Shahnameh begun for his father around 1522 and completed in the mid-1530s bears his name. Around 1555 he lost interest and disbanded the royal workshop, and some artists moved to the Mughal court. Western accounts portrayed him as a miser and a bigot, but modern historians describe a capable commander who preserved his father's empire.
taichung: Taichung lies in the Taichung Basin on the main western coastal plain of Taiwan, with the Central Mountain Range just to the east. The plains were populated by the Atayal and by Plains peoples including the Taokas, Papora, Pazeh, Hoanya and Babuza, who were hunter gatherers and later cultivated millet and taro. In the 17th century the Papora, Babuza, Pazeh and Hoanya established the Kingdom of Middag in the western part of the present city.

Zhuluo County was established in 1684, and Taichung traces its beginnings to a settlement named Toatun, meaning large mound, in 1705. An aboriginal revolt broke out on the Dajia River in 1731 after Chinese officials compelled the people to provide labour, and it spread as far south as Changhua County before the rebels were chased into the mountains. In 1786 the Lin Shuangwen rebellion began as an attempt to restore the Ming dynasty. When Taiwan became a province in 1887, Toatun was chosen as capital and took the title Taiwan-fu, which Tainan had held for more than 200 years. Liu Ming-chuan oversaw its development, including a railway, but the provincial capital was ultimately moved to Taipei.

After Taiwan was ceded to Japan in 1895 the city was renamed Taichū. The Japanese wanted it to be the first modern area of Taiwan and invested in roads, dams and levees. Taichū Park was completed in 1903, the railway station opened in 1917, and the city hall was completed in 1924 after 11 years of construction. Taichū Middle School was founded in 1915 by local gentry, including Lin Hsien-tang, and the Taiwanese Cultural Association moved to the city in 1927. On 25 December 2010 the city merged with Taichung County to create a special municipality.

Taichung is a special municipality in central Taiwan and the largest city of the central region, with more than 2.8 million residents. Its main industries are machinery and retail, and it is known for bicycle manufacturing and for suncakes. The Chun Shui Tang teahouse is where bubble tea was invented. The city houses the National Museum of Natural Science, the Lin Family Gardens and Taichung Park.
taif: Taif lies at an elevation of 1,879 metres on a raised valley surrounded by the Hejaz Mountains, part of the Sarat range. Its climate set it apart from the dry and barren country closer to the Red Sea, and wheat, vines and fruit orchards were grown around it, which earned it the title Garden of the Hejaz. Its older name was Wajj. The present name comes from an Arabic root related to circulation, and the city was named for the wall that the Banu Thaqif built around it, so that it means the encircled city.

In the 6th century the city was dominated by the Thaqif tribe, whose descendants still live in and around it. The walled city was a religious centre because it housed the idol of the goddess Lāt, called the lady of Ta'if, and its people traded closely with Mecca. In 630 a battle took place at Hunayn, close to the city, and shortly after it came the unsuccessful siege of Ta'if. After the Battle of Tabuk in 631 left it isolated, members of Thaqif went to Mecca to negotiate its conversion to Islam, and the idol of Lāt was destroyed.

In 1517 Sultan Selim I took the Hijaz, and Taif stayed Ottoman until 1802, when rebels allied with the House of Saud took it. Muhammad Ali of Egypt reconquered it in 1813. The traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt visited that year and found most buildings still in ruins. In the Arab Revolt, Abdullah, son of Husayn ibn Ali, came to Taif in July 1916 with seventy men, built his force up to 5,000, and after a siege the Ottoman garrison surrendered on 22 September. In September 1924 the Saudi-sponsored Ikhwan militia attacked, and killed three hundred of the king's son's men in what became known as the Taif massacre. Ibn Saud died there on 9 November 1953.

Taif is a city and governorate in Mecca Province, with a population of 563,282 in 2022. It remains a centre of agriculture, known for grapes, pomegranates, figs, roses and honey, and for the making of attar from the Damask rose. The Taif rose was included in UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2024. Nearby is the site of Souk 'Okaz, the best known of the pre-Islamic markets, where tribes held annual gatherings and competitive recitations of poetry.
taifa: The word taifa comes from the Arabic ṭā'ifa, meaning party, band or faction. Muslim historians first used the phrase kings of the factions for the regional rulers who followed Alexander the Great and ruled in the Parthian period. In the 11th century Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī applied it to the rulers who appeared after Umayyad power collapsed in Spain, a usage that implied cultural decline.

The taifas emerged between 1009 and 1031 from the fall of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba, which had suffered a civil war known as the Fitna of al-Andalus. Their roots lay in the caliphate's provinces and in the divisions of its elite among Arabs, Berbers, Muladíes, who were indigenous converts, and the Saqaliba, former slaves from Eastern Europe. The most secure rulers were the governors of frontier provinces such as the Farthest Frontier of Zaragoza, whose families had ruled for generations.

After 1031 about 33 independent taifas arose, though the weaker ones were soon taken over by stronger neighbours. The largest were Zaragoza, Toledo, Badajoz and Seville. Seville, under the Abbadid dynasty, conquered most of its neighbours. Wars between taifas were common, and some rulers allied with Christian kingdoms or hired Christian mercenaries. Eventually Badajoz, Toledo, Zaragoza and Seville paid tribute, known as parias, to Alfonso VI of Castile.

After the fall of Toledo in 1085 the taifa princes invited the Almoravid dynasty from North Africa, and after the fall of Lisbon in 1147 they invited the Almohad Caliphate. Taifa warriors fought at the Battle of Sagrajas. Yet the Almoravids and Almohads annexed the taifas rather than helping them, and Seville was the first of the major taifas to fall. Taifas reappeared in the middle of the 12th century as Almoravid rule declined. By the end of the 13th century only the Emirate of Granada remained.

Taifa rulers were wary of calling themselves kings and took the title hajib, presenting themselves as representatives of a temporarily absent caliph. They competed for cultural prestige and tried to recruit the best poets and artisans, and the larger courts were centres where poets, scientists and other scholars thrived. By the 1090s, accusations by the ulama against the taifa kings made a popular revolt a real possibility.
tainan: Tainan faces the Taiwan Strait on the island's western coast. Archaeological excavations in Zuojhen District suggest the region has been inhabited for at least 20,000 to 31,000 years. By the 16th century the indigenous Siraya dominated it, and the Sakam people of the Sinkan sub-tribe lived where the city stands. The area later called Tayouan, on a sandy peninsula in modern Anping, is claimed to be the origin of the name Taiwan.

In 1622 the Dutch East India Company merchant Cornelis Reyersz sailed to Taiwan to find a site for a trading post. In 1624 he built a small fort named Orange, which was expanded and renamed Fort Zeelandia. It became the centre of Dutch trade between China, Japan and Europe. Between 1640 and 1661 the Chinese population grew from 5,000 to 35,000.

Koxinga attacked the Dutch in 1661, and after a nine-month siege Governor Frederik Coyett surrendered Fort Zeelandia on 1 February 1662, ending 38 years of Dutch rule. In 1665 Zheng Jing built the Taiwan Confucian Temple, the first in Taiwan. On 17 July 1683 the Qing commander Shi Lang defeated the Tungning fleet at the Battle of Penghu, and Taiwan Prefecture was set up in 1684 with its seat at Tainan. When Taiwan was ceded to Japan in 1895 the Republic of Formosa was proclaimed at Tainan. Its leader Liu Yongfu fled in October, and the missionary Thomas Barclay negotiated the Japanese entry, so the city was taken without resistance. In 1904 Tainan was Taiwan's most populous city, with about 50,000 people.

Tainan is a special municipality, formed in 2010 by the merger of the city with Tainan County. It is known for its temples, with 1,613 registered by 2015, and for the National Cheng Kung University, founded in 1931 as Tainan Technical College. Its monuments include the Confucian temple, remains of the old city's eastern and southern gates and Fort Provintia, built by the Dutch in 1653 and known since 1945 as Chihkan Tower. The Southern Taiwan Science Park, founded in 1995, made it a centre of electronics manufacturing.
taino: Taíno is not a name the Indigenous peoples of the Greater Antilles used for themselves. Constantine Samuel Rafinesque first applied it to them in 1836. It derives from nitaino, which referred to an elite social class, and has been translated as men of the good. Historians disagree whether the peoples now called Taíno were one group or several. They spoke an Arawakan language, which Julian Granberry and Gary Vescelius divide into Classical Taíno and Ciboney Taíno.

Scholars offer two theories of their origin. One holds that their ancestors were Arawak speakers from the Amazon Basin who reached the Caribbean by way of the Orinoco Valley and the Lesser Antilles. The other, the circum-Caribbean theory first put forward by Julian H. Steward, derives them from the Colombian Andes.

The Taíno lived in villages called yucayeques, around a central plaza used for games, festivals and rituals, including the areitos, ceremonies celebrating the deeds of ancestors. Their chiefdoms, the cacicazgos, were led by caciques, and Spanish chroniclers described four classes: the cacique, the nitaínos, the bohíques and the naborias. Kinship and inheritance were matrilineal, and women could hold the rank of cazica.

The staple crop was yuca, grown on heaped mounds of soil called conucos and ground into flour for bread after women had squeezed out its poisonous juice. Sweet potato was the next most important root, and tobacco was used in medicine and ritual. The Taíno also fished from dugout canoes and hunted with bows and arrows. Their religion centred on the worship of zemis, spirits or ancestors, among them Atabey, associated with the moon, fresh water and fertility, and her son Yúcahu, the spirit of cassava and the sea.

Christopher Columbus landed on Guanahaní in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492, and about 24 Taíno were abducted to travel with him to Spain in 1494. Estimates of the population of Hispaniola range from 10,000 to 1,000,000. Bartolomé de las Casas wrote that over three million people had perished from war, slavery and the mines between 1494 and 1508. Many Spanish colonists married Taíno women, and Spanish documents declared the Taíno extinct as early as 1550.

Histories of the Caribbean have long called the Taíno extinct, but scholars now accept that part of their heritage survives. Many people in Puerto Rico, Cuba and the Dominican Republic have Indigenous mitochondrial DNA, and some communities identify as Taíno or as descendants. Their words, such as tabaco, also survive in everyday speech.
taipei: Taipei lies in northern Taiwan, mostly on the Taipei Basin, an ancient lakebed. The basin is bounded by the narrow valleys of the Keelung and Xindian rivers, which join to form the Tamsui River along the city's western border. The city is an enclave of the municipality of New Taipei City and sits about 25 kilometres southwest of the port city of Keelung. In the north the terrain rises to Qixing Mountain, 1,120 metres high, the highest dormant volcano in Taiwan, in Yangmingshan National Park.

The spellings Taipei and Tʻai-pei derive from the Wade–Giles romanisation, and the name means the north of Taiwan in Chinese. During Japanese rule from 1895 to 1945 the city was known as Taihoku, the Japanese reading of the same two characters.

Before the influx of Han Chinese colonists, the Taipei Basin was inhabited mainly by the Ketagalan, a Plains Indigenous people. The number of Han colonists grew gradually from the early 18th century under Qing rule, after the government began permitting development in the area. In 1875 the northern part of the island was incorporated into the new Taipeh Prefecture. Taipeh-fu was the temporary capital of the island in 1887, when it was declared a province, Fukien-Taiwan Province, and it was formally made the provincial capital in 1894.

When the Empire of Japan annexed Taiwan in 1895, the name was changed to Taihoku and the city was administered under Taihoku Prefecture. The Japanese rulers embarked on an extensive programme of urban planning that featured extensive railway links, and a number of landmarks and cultural institutions date from this period. The National Taiwan Museum, the island's oldest, was founded by the colonial government on 24 October 1908. Taipei has been the national seat of the central government of the Republic of China since 1949, and in 1967 it became a special municipality under the Executive Yuan.

Taipei is the capital of Taiwan, and the municipality had an estimated population of 2,494,813 in March 2023. It forms the core of the Taipei–Keelung metropolitan area, with New Taipei and Keelung, which has 7,047,559 inhabitants. The city is the political, economic, educational and cultural centre of Taiwan.

Its landmarks include the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall, the Lungshan Temple of Manka, the Zhinan Temple, the National Palace Museum and the Presidential Office Building, around which stands Ketagalan Boulevard, a site of parades and public gatherings. Natural features include Maokong, Yangmingshan and hot springs. Because of the island's ambiguous political status, the name Chinese Taipei is used for Taiwan in international organisations and sporting events such as the Olympics.
taiping-rebellion: In the 19th century the Qing dynasty suffered famines, natural disasters, economic troubles and defeats by foreign powers. The Qing military had recently lost the First Opium War, and large-scale illicit imports of opium upset the economy. Farmers were heavily overtaxed and rents rose, and many peasants deserted their lands. China's population nearly doubled between 1766 and 1833 while the cultivated land stayed the same. Banditry spread, and secret societies and self-defence units formed. The government, commanded by Manchus, was increasingly corrupt and weak in the south, where local clans dominated, and anti-Manchu feeling was strongest among the Hakka, a Han Chinese subgroup, to which Hong Xiuquan belonged.

The rebellion began in Guangxi when local officials persecuted the God Worshipping Society. In early January 1851 a rebel army of about 10,000, organised by Feng Yunshan and Wei Changhui, routed Qing forces at Jintian. On 11 January 1851 Hong declared himself Heavenly King of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. The Taiping marched north into Hunan, took Wuchang in December 1852 and moved down the Yangtze, capturing Anqing in February 1853 and Nanjing on 19 March 1853. Hong renamed it Tianjing. The Taiping killed the Manchu men there and burned Manchu women to death. Their Northern expedition failed, and the Western expedition had limited success.

Hong withdrew from active administration in 1853. His clash with Yang Xiuqing led to the Tianjing Incident of 1856, in which Yang and his followers were slaughtered on Hong's orders, and the bloodshed split the leadership. Provincial armies such as Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army then did what the dynasty's own troops could not. The Taiping failed to take Shanghai, which a Qing army with European officers, the Ever Victorious Army, helped defend. Zeng's forces besieged Nanjing from May 1862. Hong died during the siege on 1 June 1864, and the city fell barely a month later.

The war was fought without mercy on both sides. Taiping soldiers massacred Manchus, and the Qing government massacred the civilians of Nanjing. Both sides destroyed farmland and slaughtered the people of captured cities.

Taiping armies continued the fight after Nanjing fell, and the last of them was wiped out in August 1871. Estimates of the dead range from 20 to 30 million, mostly from plague and famine, to as many as 100 million, since no reliable census existed. Thirty million people fled the conquered regions. The Qing court had to rely on gentry-led militias, power became partly decentralised, and Han officials held more high posts. Franz H. Michael argued that these militias evolved into the private armies of the warlords who dominated China after the Qing, though Diana Lary cited studies sceptical of this. The Nian Rebellion and Muslim rebellions in the southwest and northwest continued to trouble the dynasty.
taisho-period: On 30 July 1912 Emperor Meiji died and Crown Prince Yoshihito succeeded him. In his coronation address the new emperor announced the era name Taishō, meaning great righteousness, taken from a passage of the I Ching. The end of the Meiji period had left heavy government and defence spending, nearly exhausted credit and a lack of foreign reserves, and a new intellectual ferment, with growing interest in socialism and communism and an urban proletariat. The Japan Socialist Party had been dissolved a year after its founding.

The era opened with the Taishō political crisis of 1912 and 1913. When Saionji Kinmochi tried to cut the military budget, the army minister resigned and the cabinet fell, and the genrō could find no solution. Public anger at military manipulation of the cabinet and at the recall of Katsura Tarō strengthened demands for an end to genrō politics.

Japan declared war on Germany on 23 August 1914 and quickly occupied German-leased territories in Shandong and the north Pacific islands. In January 1915 it presented the Twenty-One Demands to China, which would have reduced China to a protectorate; after widespread anti-Japanese feeling in China and international condemnation Japan withdrew the final group. The war turned Japan from a debtor into a creditor nation. In 1918 more than 70,000 Japanese troops joined the Allied intervention in Siberia, and rice riots that summer brought down the cabinet of Terauchi Masatake.

In 1918 Hara Takashi became the first commoner to serve as prime minister. Students, professors and journalists held large, orderly demonstrations for universal male suffrage in 1919 and 1920. Hara was assassinated in 1921 and nonparty and coalition cabinets followed. The General Election Law of 1925 gave the vote to men over 25, but the Peace Preservation Law of the same year forbade any change in the political structure or the abolition of private property. Japan took part in the Washington Naval Conference of 1921 and 1922, which set a 5:5:3 capital ship ratio for the United States, Britain and Japan.

The Great Kantō Earthquake of September 1923 is described as a turning point: martial law gave the military a greater role and was used to suppress leftist movements. The Japanese Communist Party, founded in July 1922, was forced underground by 1926. From 1927 the Seiyūkai and the Rikken Minseitō alternated in power until 1932.

Parliamentary government was not rooted deeply enough to withstand the pressures of the 1930s, and the ambiguity of the Meiji Constitution about the emperor's position made the shift to military influence possible. The army's unauthorised invasion of Manchuria in 1931 marked the end of civilian control. Emperor Taishō died on 25 December 1926 and was succeeded by Crown Prince Hirohito, who had been regent since 1921.
taiwan-semiconductor-manufacturing-compa: In 1986 Li Kwoh-ting, representing the Executive Yuan, invited Morris Chang to become president of the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) and offered him a blank cheque to build Taiwan's chip industry. Investors were hard to find because of the cost and risk. Texas Instruments and Intel turned Chang down, and only Philips agreed to a joint venture, putting up 58 million dollars and transferring its production technology in exchange for 27.6 per cent of the company. The government's National Development Fund supplied another 48.3 per cent. Eight private companies, asked directly by the government to invest, provided 20 per cent, and the Kuomintang's investment arm 4.1 per cent. TSMC was established in 1987 and became the first dedicated semiconductor foundry.

The company has been listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange since 1993, and in 1997 it became the first Taiwanese company listed on the New York Stock Exchange. Chang led it for 31 years. TSMC was the first foundry to offer 7-nanometre and 5-nanometre production and the first to bring ASML's extreme ultraviolet lithography into high-volume use.

In August 2019 GlobalFoundries sued TSMC for patent infringement in the United States and Germany, and TSMC countersued in October. On 29 October 2019 the two announced a settlement, a cross-licence of all their existing patents and those filed over the next ten years.

TSMC makes chips designed by other companies. Most fabless semiconductor companies, among them AMD, Apple, Broadcom, MediaTek, Qualcomm and Nvidia, are its customers, and some manufacturers with their own factories, such as Intel and Texas Instruments, outsource part of their production to it. Its business follows the cycles of the semiconductor industry: it must secure capacity for the upturns, and in downturns it carries excess capacity and high fixed costs, so its results tend to fluctuate over a few years. The company is headquartered in Hsinchu Science Park, and its operations use a large amount of power and water.
taiwan-strait: The strait connects the South China Sea in the south with the East China Sea in the north. It has also been called the Formosa Strait, the Strait of Fuchien, and the Black Ditch, a calque of its name in Hokkien and Hakka. The whole strait lies on Asia's continental shelf and is almost entirely less than 150 metres deep, so it holds many islands. The largest and most important off the coast of Fujian are Xiamen, Gulangyu, Pingtan, Kinmen and Matsu, of which the last two are controlled by the Republic of China, as are the Penghu Islands, or Pescadores, in the middle of the strait. All of Fujian's rivers except the Ting flow into it, the largest being the Min and the Jiulong.

A theoretical median line down the middle, known as the Davis line, was defined in 1955 by the US Air Force general Benjamin O. Davis Jr., after which the United States pressured both sides not to cross it. It never gained official or legal status, and the People's Republic of China has never recognised it.

For millennia the strait mostly separated the Han culture of the mainland from the indigenous peoples of Taiwan, although Hakka and Hoklo people traded and migrated across it. Portuguese, Spanish and Dutch traders used it in the Ming period to set up forward bases, which were also used for raiding the Chinese coast and rival ships. Widespread Chinese migration across the strait began in the late Ming.

During the Qing conquest, Zheng Chenggong, known as Koxinga, expelled the Dutch and established the Kingdom of Tungning in 1661, planning to reconquer the mainland in the name of the Southern Ming. Limited to raiding across the strait, he was succeeded by his grandson Zheng Keshuang, who surrendered to the Qing after his admiral lost the Battle of the Penghu Islands in 1683. Japan seized the Penghu Islands in the First Sino-Japanese War and gained Taiwan in 1895; the strait protected its bases there until aerial warfare reached the island by 1943. The advance of the Communist People's Liberation Army in 1949 drove the government of the Republic of China to retreat across the strait.

After the Chinese Civil War the two governments fought several brief armed conflicts there, known as the First, Second and Third Taiwan Strait Crisis, none of which became a large-scale war. The Three Links of direct flights, shipping and post across the strait were established on 15 December 2008.
taiyuan: Taiyuan lies roughly in the centre of Shanxi, where the Fen River leaves the mountains and enters a relatively flat plain; the name combines the characters for great and plain. It commands the north–south route through the province and natural routes through the Taihang Mountains to Hebei in the east and to northern Shaanxi in the west. Through history it was also called Bingzhou, Jinyang and Longcheng, the city of the dragon.

The first city of Jinyang was built in 497 BCE by Dong Anyu, a steward of Zhao Jianzi of the state of Jin. In the Battle of Jinyang in 453 BCE the Zhao broke the dams of the Fen River and flooded the Zhi armies, with help from Wei and Han. In 248 BCE Qin took the area and set up the Commandery of Taiyuan, the first official use of the name for the present site. Under the Tang, Taiyuan expanded greatly as the military base of the founding emperors Li Yuan and Li Shimin, and in 690 Wu Zetian made it the Northern Capital, one of three in the empire.

After the Tang it was the provisional capital of Later Tang and, from 936, of Later Jin. The Song besieged it in 968 and 969, but heavy rains, disease and supply problems lifted the siege. In 979 Emperor Taizong of Song defeated the Liao relief force, and the Northern Han resisted for only fifteen days. Taizong dealt harshly with the city, flooding it by releasing the Fen River and setting it on fire, and the former capital was reduced from prefecture to county town. A new city was founded in 982 on the banks of the Fen.

A Mongol army took Taiyuan in 1218, and the Ming took it from the Yuan in 1368. In the Qing period Shanxi's banks and its tea trade with Russia made the central Shanxi basin the financial centre of the empire. The warlord Yan Xishan held Shanxi from 1911 to 1949, and Taiyuan was not taken by an invader until the Japanese occupied it in 1937. Communist forces took the city on 22 April 1949.

Taiyuan is the capital of Shanxi, with 5,304,061 inhabitants in the prefecture at the 2020 census. The oldest existing building is the Temple of the Goddess in the Jinci complex, built in 1023 and rebuilt in 1102. The Tianlongshan Grottoes, begun under the Northern Qi, hold Buddhist sculpture, and the Taoist Longshan Grottoes were carved in 1234–1239.
taiz: Taiz lies in the Yemeni highlands near the Red Sea port of Mokha, at about 1,400 metres above sea level, and is the capital of Taiz Governorate. Its old quarters have houses built of brown bricks and mostly whitewashed mosques. The citadel, called Cairo Citadel, stands above the city to the south, and the governor's palace rests on a mountain spur 450 m above the centre. Mount Sabir is one of the best-known mountains in Yemen.

The first reference to Taiz in historical sources dates from the first half of the 12th century, when the Sulayhid sultan Abdullah bin Muhammad al-Sulayhi built the Al-Qahira Castle. It first became an urban area under his brother Ali bin Muhammad al-Sulayhi. Turan-Shah, the older brother of Saladin, conquered Yemen in 1173, built the citadel on the hill above the old town, and made Taiz the capital in 1175 as it became part of the Ayyubid dominions.

The city expanded faster under the Rasulid dynasty, which ruled Yemen from 1229 to 1454. The second Rasulid king moved the capital from Sanaa to Taiz because it was closer to Aden. Its golden age came under the Rasulid sultans, who spent lavishly on palaces, mosques and madrasas, and it became a centre for the study of the Shafi'i school of Islamic jurisprudence. Ibn Battuta, who visited in 1332, described it as one of the finest and largest towns of Yemen, made up of three quarters: the king's residence, the military station called ʽUdayna and the commoners' quarter, al-Mahálib, with the principal market.

Ottoman forces took Aden in 1538 and Sanaa in 1547, and faced repeated revolts from the Zaidi imams. Osman Pasha besieged the Al-Qahira Castle in 1569 without taking it, and Sinan Pasha then recaptured Taiz from the followers of al-Mutahhar. Yahya Muhammad Hamid ed-Din founded the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen in 1918. Taiz stayed a walled city until 1948, when Imam Ahmed made it the second capital, allowing it to grow beyond its walls. State administrations moved back to Sanaa in 1962.

Taiz is among the largest cities of Yemen. Its best-known mosques are the Ashrafiya, the Mua'tabiya and the Mudhaffar. Taiz was known for coffee, and the Mocha coffee of the region was considered among the finest in the early 20th century. Fruit, vegetables, cereals and qat are also grown around it, and the town is known for its cheese. Cotton weaving, tanning and jewellery are among its industries.
taj-mahal: Shah Jahan, the fifth Mughal emperor, commissioned the Taj Mahal in 1631 as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died on 17 June that year giving birth to their 14th child. Court historians record that he avoided royal affairs for a week in his grief and for two years gave up music and lavish dress. He chose land south of Agra on which stood a mansion of Raja Jai Singh I, who agreed to give it in exchange for a large palace in the centre of the city.

Construction began in 1632. The mausoleum was completed in 1648 and the rest of the complex in 1653. More than 20,000 workers and artisans took part under a board of architects led by the court architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori. The white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, and 28 kinds of precious and semi-precious stone, from China, Tibet, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Arabia among other places, were inlaid in it.

The mausoleum stands on the right bank of the Yamuna at the centre of a complex of 17 hectares, with a mosque, a guest house and formal gardens enclosed by a crenellated red sandstone wall on three sides. It draws on Timurid and Mughal models, including the Gur-e Amir in Samarkand, the tomb of Timur, and Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, which inspired its charbagh garden.

The marble building stands on a square plinth with four identical sides, each with an iwan, a vaulted arched doorway, and is topped by an onion-shaped marble dome 23 metres high with a gilded finial. Shah Jahan himself was later buried beside his wife. The plan is symmetrical and aligned north to south, and the marble appears to change colour with the hour and the weather.

Shah Jahan, deposed by his son Aurangzeb in 1658, was held at Agra Fort, from where he could see the Taj Mahal, and died in 1666. By the late 19th century parts were in disrepair, and Lord Curzon ordered a restoration completed in 1908. The Archaeological Survey of India has maintained it since 1947.

UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1983 as the jewel of Muslim art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage. A longstanding story that he planned a black marble twin across the river comes from the writings of the traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, and excavations in the 1990s showed that the blackened stones at Mehtab Bagh had been white.
tajiks: The Tajiks are a group of Persianate Eastern Iranian peoples native to Central Asia, living mainly in Afghanistan and Tajikistan, with substantial minorities in Pakistan and Uzbekistan. They are of mixed origin, and descend chiefly from Bactrians, Sogdians and Scythians, but also from Persians, Greeks and Turkic peoples. They are therefore mainly Eastern Iranian in ancestry while speaking a form of Persian, a Western Iranian language, which they likely adopted in the seventh century CE after the Islamic conquest of Persia, when Persian spread east and the Bactrian and Sogdian languages gradually died out. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes them as direct descendants of Iranian peoples attested in Central Asia from the middle of the 1st millennium BCE.

Before the Arab conquest the ancient Tajiks were chiefly farmers. After the conquest Islamization brought rapid urbanisation to Khorasan and Transoxiana, which lasted until the Mongol invasion. Samarkand, Bukhara, Khujand and Termez are surviving ancient urban centres of the Tajik people.

The word Tajik is most plausibly traced to the Middle Persian tāzīk, meaning Arab. In the 8th century Turks of Central Asia used a variant for their Muslim adversaries in general, and by the 11th century the Qarakhanid Turks applied it to the Persian Muslims of the Oxus basin and Khorasan. Persian writers of the Ghaznavid and Seljuq periods took the word over, and Iranians soon accepted it as a name for themselves. The terms Fārsīwān, Persian speaker, and Dīhgān, settled villager, were also used. The Tajik term was once used with a pejorative sense for eastern Persians, but it has become acceptable in recent decades.

The language of the Tajiks is an eastern variety of Persian called Dari, from darbārī, of the royal courts. In Tajikistan, where it is written in Cyrillic, it is called Tajiki; in Afghanistan it is written in the Perso-Arabic script. The Soviet Union introduced the Latin script in 1928 and later Cyrillic, and the Persian of Tajikistan came to be treated as a separate Tajik language. Many Tajik authors have lamented this separation.

Zoroastrian and Buddhist heritage is recorded among the Tajiks, and fire temples have been found at Balkh and in Bactria. Today the great majority are Sunni Muslims, with small Twelver and Ismaili Shia minorities. Their culture is predominantly Persianate but contains strong elements of Turkic cultures and is infused with Islamic traditions. The Tajiks are the largest ethnic group in Tajikistan, and the term does not refer to a cohesive transnational ethnic group.
takamatsu: Takamatsu is the capital of Kagawa Prefecture, on the island of Shikoku. It lies on the Takamatsu Plain, part of the Sanuki Plain, and its northern part faces the Seto Inland Sea, forming a semicircular urban area centred on Takamatsu Port and Takamatsu New Port. The western part of the city is an alluvial fan formed by the Koto River, and the eastern part is a flood plain of the Kasuga and Shinkawa rivers.

In the north-east, Yashima is a table-shaped plateau protruding into the sea, the site of the Battle of Yashima in the Genpei War, and Cape Takei is the northernmost tip of the main island of Shikoku. Parts of the city lie within the Setonaikai National Park, and it includes a number of small inhabited islands.

The area belonged to the ancient Sanuki Province. During the Heian and Kamakura periods it was the closest port to Honshu from Shikoku, a transportation centre and a gateway for pilgrims to the Kotohira Shrine. In the Sengoku period Ikoma Chikamasa built the first Takamatsu Castle in 1588.

In 1642 Matsudaira Yorishige, the son of Tokugawa Yorifusa of Mito Domain and a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu, was awarded the Takamatsu Domain, assessed at 120,000 koku, which his descendants ruled until the Meiji restoration.

The city was created on 15 February 1890, when the modern municipal system was established, and the castle tower that had been its symbol was destroyed during the Meiji period. In World War II the XXI Bomber Command of the United States chose Takamatsu as a target because it was a focal point of Shikoku's rail and road transport and held some industry vital to the war effort.

On 3 July 1945, 128 B-29 bombers dropped over 800 tons of incendiary bombs, destroying 78 percent of the built-up area and killing 1,359 people. The city recovered quickly after the war and was designated a core city with greater local autonomy on 1 April 1999. In 2005 and 2006 it absorbed several neighbouring towns.

Takamatsu is the largest municipality in Shikoku. It holds most of the national government's branch offices for the island and many companies' regional offices, and it is the home of the Shikoku Railway Company. The Seto-Ōhashi Bridge links its rail line to Okayama on Honshu. Kagawa University and Takamatsu University are in the city. The 2020 census counted 417,496 people.
takht-e-soleyman: Takht-e Soleymān, Persian for Throne of Solomon, lies midway between Urmia and Hamadan, very near the present-day town of Takab and 400 km west of Tehran. The fortified site stands on a hill created by the outflow of a calcium-rich spring pond. It appears on the Peutinger Map. The biblical name came after the Muslim conquest of Persia in the 7th century. Folk legend says King Solomon imprisoned monsters in a nearby crater about 100 m deep, called Zendan-e Soleyman, the Prison of Solomon, and that he created the flowing pond.

Excavations have revealed traces of an occupation of the 5th century BCE in the Achaemenid era and later Parthian settlements in the citadel. Coins of the Sasanian shahs and of the Byzantine emperor Theodosius II have also been found. The citadel holds the remains of Adur Gushnasp, a Zoroastrian fire temple of the Sasanian era. It housed one of the three Great Fires, or Royal Fires, before which Sasanian rulers humbled themselves in order to take the throne, and was dedicated to the warrior class.

The Ilkhanid ruler Abaqa (r. 1265-82), a son of Hülagü, chose the site for a summer and hunting palace, partly because of the large ruins of the old temple and palace, whose layout he could use. Building probably began in 1271 and was completed by his son Arghun. The choice also helped the Ilkhanids, who had not been Muslim at first, to present themselves as part of Iran's history. The palace stood within an oval fortified wall, around a courtyard with an artificial lake, with four iwans and polygonal chambers. An audience hall with a large dome stood on the site of the fire temple.

The Ilkhanid complex is the only surviving secular structure of that period. Its walls carried painted stucco and lustre tiles in the lajvardina technique. Tiles show dragons and phoenixes alongside scenes from the Shahnameh, such as Fereydun defeating Zahhak, and quotations from the Qur'an. A stucco plate found in the southern octagonal chamber, now in the National Museum of Iran, carries a 42 cm muqarnas plan, one of the earliest known Islamic architectural plans of its kind.
The British explorers Theodore and Mabel Bent dug at the site in early May 1889. Takht-e Soleymān was recognised as a World Heritage Site in July 2003, and a small museum shows finds from it.
talal-of-jordan: Talal was born in Mecca on 26 February 1909, the eldest son of Abdullah bin Hussein and Musbah bint Nasser. Abdullah, a son of Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca, founded the Emirate of Transjordan in 1921. Talal was educated privately in Amman, graduated from the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, in 1929 and was commissioned in the cavalry of the Arab Legion. He became aide to his grandfather, the ousted King of the Hejaz, in exile in Cyprus, and by 1948 he was a general. In November 1934 he married Zein al-Sharaf bint Jamil, and their son Hussein was born in 1935.

Transjordan became the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan after it sought independence in 1946, and Talal became crown prince. On 20 July 1951 Abdullah I was assassinated at the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem by a Palestinian, amid rumours that he planned a peace treaty with Israel. Prince Hussein, aged fifteen and at his grandfather's side, survived. Talal became king.

His main achievement was the constitution ratified on 1 January 1952, which made the government collectively, and the ministers individually, responsible to the Jordanian Parliament. He is also judged to have eased relations with Egypt and Saudi Arabia. Historians differ on his attitude to Britain. A British resident called him deeply anti-British at heart, while Avi Shlaim argues that his resentment of British interference was genuine. A set of stamps issued for his accession was withdrawn and burned after he left the throne.

In 1952 the British resident, Queen Zein al-Sharaf and Prime Minister Tawfik Abu al-Huda reported that Talal was mentally ill, and he was flown to Paris for treatment. Abu al-Huda summoned both houses of parliament, which on 11 August 1952 unanimously deposed him on medical grounds, citing schizophrenia. Abu al-Huda governed until Hussein came of age on 2 May 1953. Talal had wished to live in the Hejaz but was sent to a sanatorium in Istanbul, where he died on 7 July 1972.
tallahassee: Indigenous peoples occupied the Tallahassee area for thousands of years before European contact. Around 1200 the large and complex Mississippian culture built earthwork mounds near Lake Jackson, which survive today and are preserved in the Lake Jackson Archaeological State Park. The city covers 254.3 square kilometres, of which 247.9 are land, and lies in a humid subtropical climate with long summers and short, mild winters.

Florida became an American territory in September 1821, in accordance with the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819, and Tallahassee became its capital in 1824. According to the city's heritage account, most of its original founders were settlers from North Carolina, descended from Scots or from Scots Presbyterians from County Down and County Antrim. Florida State University, founded in 1851, stands on the oldest continuous site of higher education in the state. Frenchtown is the oldest historically black neighbourhood in Florida.

Until the Second World War Tallahassee remained a small Southern town, with virtually the whole population within one mile of the Capitol. Its main economic drivers were the colleges and state government. The first plan to consolidate government buildings in one downtown area was the Taylor Plan of 1947, and in 1974 the Capitol Center Planning Commission produced a plan for expanding the centre, projecting 2.3 million square feet of new government facilities. In the Jim Crow period, laws passed by Democrats in Florida disenfranchised most African Americans until the late 1960s, which kept the Republican Party uncompetitive in the area for decades.

Tallahassee is the capital of Florida, the county seat of Leon County and its only incorporated municipality, with 196,169 residents at the 2020 census. It holds the Florida State Capitol, the Supreme Court of Florida and the Governor's Mansion, and is a college town, home to Florida State University, Florida A&M University and Tallahassee State College. Its museums include the Museum of Florida History, the Old Capitol Museum, the Knott House Museum and Mission San Luis de Apalachee.
talmud: Talmudic tradition emerged and was compiled between the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE and the Arab conquest in the early seventh century. In antiquity the two major centres of Jewish scholarship were the academies of Syria Palaestina and of Babylonia, and each produced a Talmud. The earlier, the Jerusalem Talmud, was compiled in Galilee between the late fourth century and the first half of the fifth. It is also called the Palestinian Talmud, which is more accurate, since it was not compiled in Jerusalem, and it draws on the teachings of rabbis at Tiberias, Sepphoris and Caesarea.

The Babylonian Talmud consists of documents compiled over late antiquity, from the 3rd to the 6th centuries. Babylonian centres of learning included Nehardea, Nisibis, Mahoza, Pumbedita and the Sura Academy. Tradition holds that Rav Ashi and Ravina II compiled it around 500 CE, but it is more likely to have been compiled in the middle of the sixth century.

The Talmud follows the structure of the Mishnah, a compilation of legal opinions and debates by the Tannaim, rabbis of the second century CE. It is divided into six orders, abbreviated as Shas, and 63 tractates, with 517 chapters in all. The Gemara is a commentary on the Mishnah, produced by the Amoraim, rabbis of the third to fifth centuries, through a process of debate called shakla v'tarya, or taking and throwing. It also comments on baraitot, traditions of the Oral Torah that are not in the Mishnah. Short later treatises, the minor tractates, are printed at the end of the order of damages.

The Babylonian Talmud is much longer, at about 2.5 million words, and a third of its material is non-legal Aggadah, against a sixth in the Jerusalem Talmud. It is written mostly in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, with quotations of the Mishnah, baraitot and Hebrew scripture in Hebrew. The Jerusalem Talmud is written in a Western Aramaic dialect and is more fragmentary because its redaction was incomplete.

The only complete manuscript of the Talmud, Munich Codex Hebraica 95, dates from 1342. The earliest manuscript fragments, from the Cairo Genizah, date from the late seventh or eighth century, and Ms. Oxford 2673, with much of tractate Keritot, is the earliest manuscript with a known date, 1123.

Until the Haskalah of the 18th and 19th centuries the Talmud was the centrepiece of Jewish culture in nearly all communities and served as the guide for daily life. The word Talmud means study or learning, from the Semitic root lmd. When used without qualification it refers to the Babylonian Talmud, which has received far more attention from commentators and is held to be the more authoritative.
tamale: Tamale lies in the Tamale Metropolitan District, which covers about 647 km2. The district borders the Sagnarigu District to the west and north, the Mion District to the east, the East Gonja District to the south and the Central Gonja District to the southwest. The city stands within the Kingdom of Dagbon, and is traditionally inhabited by the Dagombas. Gonja, Mamprusi, Nanumba, Konkomba and Akan people also live there.

The climate is tropical savanna (Köppen Aw), with a single rainy season each year. Mean monthly rainfall is about 89 mm, spread over some 95 days of showers, and mean monthly temperatures are around 34 °C, with minimums near 23 °C. Humidity is lowest between December and March, at about 30 percent, and highest around August, at about 70 percent.

The area of Tamale once consisted of small villages under the Kingdom of Dagbon, and it was a popular destination of cattle trails in the region. In 1907 the British decided to establish administrative headquarters there, with help from the Dakpema, after German officials had taken over Yendi. A road added in 1920, nicknamed the Great North Road, helped make Tamale an important centre of business in the Northern Territories.

Through the 20th century the population grew rapidly, as people looked for water and electricity, and land taken for infrastructure threatened residents' ability to farm. A series of disputes between the Gulkpe Na and the Dakpema over power in the town arose in part because British indirect rule created an imbalance between the chiefs. Local councils were later introduced and indirect rule was discontinued, but tension between the chiefs has continued. In 1960 Tamale became the capital of the Northern Region, after the region had separated from the rest of the north.

Tamale is the capital of the Northern Region and Ghana's third largest city, with 374,744 people at the 2021 census. Its economy rests on agriculture, trading, teaching and manufacturing. The first educational institution was a teacher training college of 1944, followed by a secondary school in 1951; British wishes to keep the Northern Territories agricultural and pastoral held education back, but the city has since become the educational hub of northern Ghana. It has the Tamale Teaching Hospital and Tamale International Airport, about 11 km from the centre.

Most residents are Muslim: 90.5 percent at the 2010 census. Annual festivals include the Damba festival, Bugum chugu, Eid ul-Fitr and Eid Adha, and the Dagbamba perform dances such as the Baamaya and Tora. The Aliu Mahama Sports Stadium hosted some matches of the 2008 African Cup of Nations.
tamanrasset: Tamanrasset, also known as Tamanghasset or Tamenghest, stands in the Ahaggar Mountains at an altitude of 1,320 metres. It is an oasis, where citrus fruits, apricots, dates, almonds, cereals, corn and figs are grown despite the difficult climate. The climate is a hot desert one with very little rain, although the altitude moderates the summer heat. The name is said to derive from Imanrassaten, a noble tribe now associated with the Ajjers, which reportedly once lived in the wadi region or used it to mark the boundaries of its grazing lands.

The place originated as the centre of a network of camel caravan routes that ran from Kano, Lake Chad, Gao, Agades and Zinder. Under French rule in Algeria the Catholic priest Charles de Foucauld built his hermitage here in 1905, and the fort was established by 1915. Foucauld was shot to death outside his compound on 1 December 1916 by Sermi ag Thora, acting under the command of El Madani ag Soba.
