As a military post the settlement was named Fort Laperrine, after General François-Henry Laperrine, who died in the desert nearby in 1922. On 1 May 1962, near Ecker, 150 km north of Tamanrasset, a French underground nuclear test was accidentally vented. The shaft had been improperly sealed, a flame burst through the concrete cap, and radioactive gases and dust rose in a plume up to 2,600 metres high. Radiation was detected hundreds of kilometres away. About a hundred French soldiers and officials, including two ministers, were irradiated; the number of Algerians contaminated is unknown.

Tamanrasset is the capital of Tamanrasset Province and the chief city of the Algerian Tuareg. Its population was 92,635 at the 2008 census, up from 72,741 in 1998. It is a centre of trade across the Sahara and into neighbouring countries, and it is served by Tamanrasset Airport and the Trans-Sahara Highway. The Museum of the Hoggar holds exhibits on Tuareg life and culture, and the commune includes the locality of Assekrem among its fourteen.
tamar-of-georgia: Tamar belonged to the Bagrationi dynasty and was the daughter of George III of Georgia and his consort Burdukhan, a daughter of the king of Alania. Her name is of Hebrew origin, and like other biblical names it was favoured by the Bagrationi, who claimed descent from David, the second king of Israel. Her father proclaimed her heir and co-ruler in 1178. Medieval Georgian sources gave her the title mepe, meaning king, which stressed that she was the first woman to rule Georgia in her own right.

Tamar was crowned a second time at Gelati cathedral near Kutaisi after her father's death in 1184. Part of the aristocracy questioned the legitimacy of a woman ruler, and others tried to use her youth to gain autonomy, so that she needed the support of her aunt Rusudan and the Catholicos-Patriarch Michael IV and had to make him chancellor. She married Yury Bogolyubsky, son of Andrey Bogolyubsky of Vladimir-Suzdal, in 1185, but divorced him and expelled him two years later, and she defeated his later coup attempts. In 1191 she married the Alan prince David Soslan, with whom she had two children, George and Rusudan, who both became monarchs.

Tamar then revived Georgia's expansion. In the 1190s Georgia reduced Shirvan to a tributary state, and David Soslan defeated the Eldiguzid atabeg Abu Bakr at the Battle of Shamkor. Armenian generals, Zakare and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli, took fortresses towards the Ararat Plain. In 1204 Alexios I Megas Komnenos and his brother David, her nephews, founded the Empire of Trebizond with Georgian troops. By the end of her reign Georgia stretched from the crest of the Greater Caucasus to Erzurum and near Ganja, and Tamar issued coins with Georgian and Arabic inscriptions.

Tamar crowned her son Lasha-Giorgi coregent and became ill while discussing state affairs at the Nacharmagevi castle near Gori. She was taken to Tbilisi and then to the castle of Agarani, where she died, and she was buried at Gelati. Her reign saw a flowering of Georgian culture, with domed cathedrals and Shota Rustaveli's epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin, revered in Georgia as the finest achievement of its native literature. Medieval chroniclers called her a protector of the widowed, and the Georgian Orthodox Church later canonised her, commemorating her on 14 May (1 May in the Julian calendar). The Georgian state she left collapsed under Mongol attacks within two decades.
tamaulipas: Tamaulipas, officially the Free and Sovereign State of Tamaulipas, is one of the 32 federated entities of Mexico and is divided into 43 municipalities. It borders Nuevo León, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz, and has a 370 km stretch of the border with Texas along the Río Bravo, known in the United States as the Rio Grande. Its largest cities include Reynosa, Matamoros, Nuevo Laredo, Tampico and Mante. The name derives from Tamaholipa, a Huastec term whose prefix tam- means place where; the meaning of holipa is not agreed, though high hills is a common interpretation.

The area has been inhabited for at least 8,000 years, originally by the nomadic Chichimec and the sedentary Huastec, together with hunter-gatherer and fishing peoples. Spain subjugated its inhabitants only gradually; the first permanent Spanish settlement was Tampico in 1554. Franciscan missionaries and widespread ranching followed, forcing native peoples from their lands. In the mid-18th century the region became a separate province of New Spain called Nuevo Santander, and towns along the Rio Grande, among them Laredo, Mier, Camargo and Reynosa, were founded under Escandón as a defensive line.

In 1824 Tamaulipas was one of the 19 founder states of the United Mexican States. The Republic of Texas, created in 1836, claimed northern Tamaulipas, and after the Mexican–American War the state lost more than a quarter of its territory in 1848 through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Its capital, Aguayo, was renamed Ciudad Victoria in honour of Guadalupe Victoria, the first president of Mexico. The last French soldiers left the state in 1866, before the fall of Emperor Maximilian's empire in 1867. Growth followed, especially after the railroad reached Tampico.

Ciudad Victoria is the capital and a significant educational centre. In the north the economy shares much with that of Texas and includes many maquiladoras, while the south rests on petrochemical industries around Altamira and Ciudad Madero and on the ports of Tampico and Altamira. The Tropic of Cancer crosses the southern part of the municipality of Victoria. The state anthem, Himno a Tamaulipas, was composed in 1926.
tamil-nadu: Tamil Nadu covers 130,058 square kilometres on the southeastern coast of the Indian peninsula. The Western Ghats and the Deccan Plateau lie to the west, the Eastern Ghats to the north and the Bay of Bengal to the east, with the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait to the southeast and the Laccadive Sea at the southern cape. The river Kaveri crosses the state. The name means the land of the Tamils.

Excavations at Keezhadi have revealed a large urban settlement, with the earliest artefact dated to 580 BCE. Inscriptions at Adichanallur use Tamil Brahmi, dated to the 5th century BCE. In the Sangam period, from about 500 BCE to 300 CE, Tamilakam was ruled by three monarchical states: the Cheras in the west, the Pandyas in the south and the Cholas in the Kaveri delta. Their kings patronised the Vedic religion, Buddhism and Jainism and sponsored some of the earliest Tamil literature. The oldest surviving work is the Tolkāppiyam, a Tamil grammar.

The Pallavas, with Kanchipuram as their capital, were noted for their patronage of architecture, and the gopuram, the tower at the entrance of a temple, originated with them. They built the rock-cut monuments of Mahabalipuram and temples at Kanchipuram, and were in constant conflict with the Cholas and Pandyas until the Chola prince Aditya I defeated them in the 9th century. The Vijayanagara kingdom, founded in 1336, conquered the entire Tamil country by about 1370 and ruled for almost two centuries, until its defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565. Its military governors, the Nayaks of Madurai and Thanjavur, then took control and rebuilt temples such as the Meenakshi Temple at Madurai.

European colonisation began with trading ports in the 17th century, and the British controlled much of the state as part of the Madras Presidency for two centuries. After 1947 it became Madras State, which lost Andhra in 1953 and took its present shape when states were redrawn on linguistic lines in 1956. It was renamed Tamil Nadu on 14 January 1969.

Tamil Nadu is the southernmost state of India, with its capital at Chennai, and 72.1 million people at the census of 2011. Tamil, the first language recognised as classical in India, is its official language, and 87.6 per cent of its people follow Hinduism. It has four World Heritage Sites and is known for its great temples and its classical Tamil literature.
tamils: The Tamils are a Dravidian ethnic group who natively speak Tamil and trace their ancestry mainly to the south of the Indian subcontinent. Archaeological evidence from Tamil Nadu indicates continuous human occupation for more than 3,800 years. Megalithic urn burials at Adichanallur date back to 1500 BCE, and excavations at Keezhadi have revealed a large urban settlement, with its earliest artefact dated to 580 BCE. Inscriptions and potsherds from these sites use Tamil Brahmi, a rudimentary script dated to the 6th century BCE. The meaning of the name Tamil is unclear, and scholars have proposed several derivations, among them 'self-speak' or 'our own speech'.

In the Sangam period, between about 300 BCE and 300 CE, the Tamil country, Tamilakam, was ruled by the three crowned kings, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, with smaller Velir chieftains beside them. Coastal towns grew with trade across the Indian Ocean, and excavated artefacts indicate early trade with the Romans. The Pallavas later ruled from the 3rd to the 9th century CE, and the Vijayanagara Empire from the 14th to the 17th century.

In the 10th century the Cholas established their influence across Sri Lanka and parts of Southeast Asia, and scripts carried by Tamil traders, such as Grantha and Pallava, shaped the development of many Southeast Asian scripts. The Jaffna Kingdom controlled the Tamil territory in the north of Sri Lanka from the 13th to the 17th century. European colonisation began in the 17th century.

Tamils have migrated worldwide since the 19th century. Many went as indentured labourers or traders to British territories such as Malaya, Burma, South Africa, Fiji and Mauritius, and a large emigration of Sri Lankan Tamils began in the 1980s.

In India Tamils form about 5.7 per cent of the population and the majority in Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, and they are a significant share of the populations of Sri Lanka, Malaysia and Singapore. Sri Lanka's government counts Sri Lankan Tamils, descended from the old Jaffna Kingdom and the eastern Vannimai chiefdoms, separately from Indian Origin Tamils, descendants of 19th-century plantation labourers in the central highlands.

Tamil literature has an antiquity of more than two thousand years, beginning with the Sangam anthologies. Hinduism is the major religion, with smaller numbers of Christians and Muslims. Pongal, a harvest festival in January, and Puthandu, the new year in April, are major festivals, and Bharatanatyam is among the classical performing arts.
tampere: Tampere lies in the Finnish Lakeland, between Lake Näsijärvi and Lake Pyhäjärvi, which differ in water level by 18 m. The Tammerkoski rapids that connect them have been an important source of power throughout history, most recently for generating electricity. The Pyynikki Ridge, a large esker formed from moraine during the Weichselian glaciation, rises 160 m above sea level. The name derives from the rapids, and the explanation most accepted traces it to a Proto-Samic phrase for a deep, slow part of a stream followed by the word for rapids.

The earliest known permanent settlements around Tammerkoski date from the 7th century, when settlers from the west began to farm land in an area largely inhabited by Tavastian tribes. The population stayed small for centuries, and in 1638 Governor-General Per Brahe the Younger ordered two markets a year at Tammerkoski. The first industries in the 17th century were watermills and sawmills.

The neighbouring parish of Pirkkala had been the most important parish in the area through the Middle Ages. In 1771 and 1772 the pastor Erik Edner proposed a town on the banks of the rapids, Gustav III of Sweden made it a market town, and on 1 October 1779 Tampere received full town rights. Farming was forbidden within the city limits, so its inhabitants lived mainly by trade and crafts, and when the Grand Duchy of Finland was formed in 1809 the town still had fewer than a thousand inhabitants.

Tampere became known as the Manchester of the North for its past as a centre of Finnish industry, and the red-brick factories along the Tammerkoski, such as Finlayson and Tampella, left a strong mark on the city. It was also the scene of political events in the early 20th century. In 1905 the conference of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, led by Vladimir Lenin, met in the Tampere Workers' Hall and decided to launch an armed insurrection. On 1 November 1905, during the General Strike, the Red Declaration was proclaimed in Keskustori.

Tampere is the regional capital of Pirkanmaa and the most populous inland city in the Nordic countries, with about 263,000 inhabitants. Finnish is the first language of most of them. Its buildings range from the Old Stone Church of Messukylä, the only medieval one, to Tampere Cathedral. Pispala, a ridge between the two lakes, housed much of the industrial labour in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and joined the city in 1937.
tampico: Tampico lies on the north bank of the Pánuco River, about 10 kilometres inland from the Gulf of Mexico, in the south-east of the state of Tamaulipas and directly north of Veracruz. The name comes from the Huastec tam-piko, meaning place of otters or water dogs, a reference to the otters that lived in the rivers and lagoons of the Pánuco delta. The area had several Huastec settlements, among them the important site at Las Flores, which flourished between 1000 and 1250 CE.

In 1532 the Franciscan priest Andrés de Olmos established a mission and monastery over a former Huastec village, and at his request Spanish officials founded San Luis de Tampico in 1554. That site was abandoned in 1684 because of frequent pirate attacks, and the area stayed empty for nearly 150 years. The present city was founded on 13 April 1823, after Mexican independence. It lived at first from exporting silver and from trade as a market town for an agricultural region. In 1829 Spain sent troops from Cuba to regain the region, but General Antonio López de Santa Anna forced them to surrender in September.

The first oil well in Mexico was drilled near Tampico, at Ébano, in 1901 by the Californian Edward Doheny, who founded the Mexican Petroleum Company. American investment and a large American community followed, and the Chijol Canal, begun in 1901, carried oil 120 km south through the fields to Tuxpan. The city became the chief oil-exporting port of the Americas and the second busiest in the world. On 9 April 1914, during the Mexican Revolution, a confrontation between Mexican soldiers and sailors of the USS Dolphin, the Tampico Affair, led the United States to occupy Veracruz for seven months and helped bring down General Victoriano Huerta. Mexico nationalized its oil industry in 1938.

The oil boom paid for the grand buildings of the downtown, often compared with those of Venice and New Orleans. Wrought-iron balconies, some bearing the plaques of the Derbyshire forge of Andrew Handyside and Company, line the Plaza de la Libertad, and the neoclassical Town Hall and the English redbrick Customs House stand nearby. The cathedral on the Plaza de Armas dates from the late 19th century, and Doheny gave large sums for its construction after 1902. In 1895 snow was reported to have fallen in Tampico, the farthest south at a coastal location in North America.
tancredo-neves: Tancredo de Almeida Neves was born on 4 March 1910 in São João del-Rei, Minas Gerais, of mostly Portuguese descent. After his schooling in his home town he moved to Belo Horizonte, took a law degree at the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais in 1932 and served as a public prosecutor in 1933. He sympathised with the Liberal Alliance that brought Getúlio Vargas to power in 1930.

He was elected city councilman of São João del-Rei in 1935 and became president of the council. After the New State was instituted in November 1937 he returned to law, acted for his city's railway union and for a time worked in the textile business.

In 1947 he was elected to the Minas Gerais state legislature for the Social Democratic Party (PSD) and was one of the spokesmen for the state constitution. He became a federal deputy in 1950, and on 26 June 1953 President Vargas appointed him Minister of Justice, a post he held until Vargas's suicide in 1954.

On 25 August 1961 he announced the installation of parliamentarism, which let João Goulart take the presidency after the resignation of Jânio Quadros and so avoided a military coup. Congress approved the amendment on 2 September, and Goulart named him President of the Council of Ministers on 8 September. After the military coup of 1964 he was among the few who saw Goulart off into exile, and he did not vote for Castelo Branco.

A moderate critic of the regime, he joined the Brazilian Democratic Movement, was re-elected deputy several times and became a senator in 1978. He founded the Popular Party in 1980 and in 1982 was elected governor of Minas Gerais, serving from 1983.

When the Dante de Oliveira amendment for direct presidential elections was defeated in 1984, after the Diretas Já campaign, Neves became the candidate of the Democratic Alliance of opposition parties. He was elected by the electoral college on 15 January 1985. Suffering abdominal pain, he delayed announcing his illness until the heads of state had arrived, since he feared that military hardliners would refuse to hand power to the vice-president. He was taken to hospital during the inauguration events and died on 21 April 1985. The official explanation was diverticulitis, but twenty years later doctors at the Hospital da Base in Brasília said it had been a benign tumour.
José Sarney took office as president. Law 7.465 of 21 April 1986 placed Neves among the former presidents of Brazil. The Tancredo Neves Memorial opened in São João del-Rei in 1990.
tang-dynasty: The Tang dynasty was founded by Emperor Gaozu, born Li Yuan, who had been Duke of Tang and governor of Taiyuan during the collapse of the Sui dynasty. The Li family were of ethnic Han origin and belonged to the north-western military aristocracy; Gaozu's mother was part Xianbei. Official Tang records trace the family's descent from Laozi, and Li Yuan used the claim to attract a following. The Tang took advantage of Sui decline and precipitated its final collapse in 618, and the first half of the dynasty was a period of progress and stability. The territory won by the military campaigns of its early rulers surpassed that of the Han dynasty.

The dynasty was formally interrupted from 690 to 705, when Empress Wu Zetian seized the throne and proclaimed the Wu Zhou dynasty, becoming the only legitimate Chinese female emperor. Emperor Xuanzong, who reigned from 712 to 756, ruled when the dynasty was at the height of its power.

The An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 ended its prosperity: An Lushan, a Tang commander, rebelled in Hebei with more than 100,000 troops, took Luoyang and named himself emperor of a new Yan state, and the court fled Chang'an. The Uyghur Khaganate helped recapture the capital, but demanded an enormous tribute in silk, and the Tang were never again able to reconquer Central Asia.

Regional military governors, the jiedushi, rose in the ninth century and weakened civil order. In the 840s Emperor Wuzong suppressed Buddhism. The rebellion of Huang Chao from 874 to 884 devastated northern and southern China and sacked both Chang'an and Luoyang; the Tang never recovered, and the dynasty ended in 907. It was followed by the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.

The dynasty kept a civil service recruited by examinations and recommendations. Emperor Taizong issued a legal code that later Chinese dynasties and neighbouring polities in Vietnam, Korea and Japan took as a model; the earliest surviving code, of 653, has 500 articles. Candidates sat the mingjing, on the Confucian classics, or the jinshi, which tested essays and poetry. An official census of 609 counted about 50 million people.

By 742 the armies had about 500,000 men, and in 668 Tang and Silla forces destroyed the kingdom of Goguryeo. Chang'an, the capital, was laid out in 108 walled wards, and its checkerboard plan was copied in Heian-kyō. Over 48,900 Tang poems by more than 2,200 authors survive, among them those of Li Bai and Du Fu, and woodblock printing produced the Diamond Sutra of 868, the first full-length book printed at regular size.
tangerang: Tangerang lies on the north side of Java, on the western border of Jakarta, and is crossed by the Cisadane River, whose headwaters are on the slopes of Mount Salak and Mount Pangrango near Bogor. The river is described as an inseparable part of the city's identity. The land is lowland, mostly 10 to 30 metres above sea level, and the climate is tropical rainforest bordering on tropical monsoon. The city covers 164.55 square kilometres. It was once part of the province of West Java, whose western and north-western cities and regencies were separated in 2000 to form Banten Province.

The archives of the VOC, as read by F. de Haan, report that the Sultanate of Banten created a large territory west of the Untung Jawa River and moved 5,000 to 6,000 inhabitants to fill it. In 1668 the Sultan appointed Raden Sena Pati and Kyai Demang as rulers, then dismissed them on suspicion of seizing the kingdom. By 1680 the ruler was Kyai Dipati Soera Dielaga, who with his son Subraja asked for VOC protection. He later received the title Raden Aria Suryamanggala and became the first regent of Tangerang. An agreement signed on 17 April 1684 made Tangerang part of the VOC's territory and denied Banten any right to intervene there.

Because the Bantenese often attacked suddenly, guard posts were built along the river. In 1705 Governor-General Hendrick Zwaardecroon agreed to replace a bamboo-walled post with a fort having walls 20 feet thick or more, garrisoned by Europeans and Makassarese, with bricks supplied by the regent. The fort became the Company's base against rebellion from Banten, and the town became known as the Citadel. It was repaired in 1801 but no longer maintained after 1812.

During the Indonesian revolution a Muslim militia, Laskar Hitam, was formed in Tangerang in October 1945. It kidnapped the Republic's Minister of State, Otto Iskandardinata, on 31 October 1945, and he is presumed to have been murdered on 20 December 1945. Tangerang became an autonomous city on 27 February 1993, having been an administrative city within Tangerang Regency.

Tangerang is the most populous city of Banten Province. Its 2020 census population was 1,895,486. It is a manufacturing hub for Java with more than 1,000 factories, and many residents commute to Jakarta. It holds Soekarno–Hatta International Airport, the main airport serving the Jakarta metropolitan area. It has a long-established Chinese Indonesian community, the Cina Benteng, whose roots in the Tangerang area go back centuries.
tangier: Tangier lies in north-western Morocco, on the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. The centre sits about 23 kilometres east of Cape Spartel between two hills at the north-west end of the Bay of Tangier, so that the city rises like an amphitheatre with the commercial district in the middle. The western hill holds the citadel, or kasbah, and the eastern hill forms Cape Malabata. The bay was historically the best natural harbour on the Moroccan coast. The old Berber name Tingi is linked to a word for marsh, and the Greeks claimed that the city was named for Tinjis, a daughter of the Titan Atlas.

Tangier was founded as a Phoenician colony, possibly as early as the 10th century BCE and almost certainly by the 8th century BCE. Berber tombs around it held Punic jewellery by the 6th century BCE, and the Carthaginians made it an important port by the 5th. It probably took part in the expeditions of Hanno the Navigator. Vandals under Gaiseric occupied Tingis in 429 CE, and Belisarius reconquered it in 533 for Justinian I, although the provincial administration moved to Septem, now Ceuta.

The Portuguese failed to take Tangier in 1437, 1458 and 1464 but occupied it unopposed on 28 August 1471, after its garrison fled on learning that Asilah had fallen. They turned the chief mosque into a cathedral and built houses, chapels and monasteries. The Wattasids attacked in 1508, 1511 and 1515 without success. In the 17th century it passed with Portugal's other domains into Spanish control while keeping a Portuguese garrison. The United States opened its first consulate there, and in 1821 Slimane of Morocco gave the United States a mansion, now the Tangier American Legation Museum. The French under the Prince of Joinville bombarded Tangier on 6 August 1844.

In 1923 Tangier became an international zone managed by colonial powers, attracting diplomats, spies, writers and businessmen. Its legal status let nationalists meet there, and in 1951 the National Front, a pact of four nationalist parties, was created in Tangier. The powers agreed in 1952 to abolish the zone, and Tangier rejoined Morocco on the restoration of full sovereignty in 1956, with phases lasting to 1960. It is the capital of the Tangier-Tetouan-Al Hoceima region and a major industrial centre. Its economy has benefited from the Tanger-Med port.
tanguts: The early Tanguts lived on the steppes and mountains of south-east Qinghai and north-west Sichuan, regions that correspond to Amdo and Kham on the Tibetan plateau. They first lived under Tuyuhun authority and later submitted to the Tang dynasty. Their leader Tuoba Chici, probably of mixed Xianbei and Qiang heritage, was given the title Captain General of Western-Rong and the surname Li. In the early 8th century pressure from the Tibetan Empire forced them north to the eastern Ordos. By the time of the An Lushan Rebellion (755-763) they were the predominant local power in what is now eastern Gansu, Ningxia and northern Shaanxi.

In 881 the Tanguts helped the Tang suppress the Huang Chao rebellion, and the general Li Sigong received the prefectures of Xia, Sui and Yin as hereditary titles. After the Tang collapsed they expanded south-west. In 1002 they conquered Ling Prefecture and set up a first capital at Xiping. By 1036 they had annexed the Guiyi Circuit and the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom and had conquered Xining. The state of Western Xia was proclaimed in 1038.

Li Yuanhao, who took the throne as Emperor Jingzong, sought to set his state apart from Song China. He ordered an official Tangut script, required traditional dress and short or shaved hair for men, and took the Tangut surname Weiming in place of Li and Zhao. His capital was Xingqing, modern Yinchuan. Genghis Khan attacked Western Xia in six campaigns between 1205 and 1227 and died in its territory during the last. In 1227 the Mongols overran the capital, burnt its buildings and records, killed the last emperor and massacred tens of thousands of civilians.

Tangut society was divided into the Red Faced, who were commoners, and the Black Headed, an elite priestly caste named for the black caps of Root West shamans. According to myth the Black Headed descended from a heavenly white crane and the Red Faced from a monkey. The Tanguts were primarily Buddhists. The Chinese Buddhist canon was translated into Tangut over about fifty years and published around 1090 in about 3,700 fascicles. The state supervised teachers, required government approval for monks and allowed women to serve as nuns, though only if widowed or unmarried.

The Tangut language, also called Fan, is a tonal Tibeto-Burman language, and later research places it in the Gyalrongic branch of Qiangic. Both it and its script are extinct. Tangut families joined the Mongol Empire after 1227, and under the Yuan the Tanguts were counted as Semu. Small communities survived in Anhui and Henan into the Ming dynasty, and Tanguts in central China kept their language until at least the 16th century.
tanintharyi-region: Tanintharyi Region covers the long narrow southern part of Myanmar on the northern Malay Peninsula, reaching to the Kra Isthmus. The Andaman Sea lies to its west and the Tenasserim Hills, beyond which is Thailand, to its east. Mon State lies to the north. Many islands lie off the coast, among them the large Mergui Archipelago and the smaller Moscos Islands. The region covers 43,344.9 square kilometres, and its capital is Dawei. It has also been known as Tenasserim, and in 1989 the Burmese government officially changed its English name to Tanintharyi.

In the first millennium the southern coast formed part of the ancient emporium of Takkola, named by Ptolemy and in Buddhist texts, and one of the five kingdoms of the confederative polity of Tun Sun. The north belonged to the Thaton Kingdom before 1057, and the whole coast then became part of King Anawrahta's Pagan Empire. After the fall of Bagan in 1287 the area fell to the Siamese kingdom of Sukhothai and later to Ayutthaya. King Bayinnaung of the Toungoo Dynasty conquered it in 1564, but Ayutthaya had regained independence by 1587 and held the whole peninsula by 1599.

In 1614 King Anaukpetlun recovered the northern half of the coast to Dawei. Myeik was a principal centre of trade between the Siamese and Europeans. From the middle of the 18th century to the early 19th, Burma and Siam fought for nearly seven decades over the coastline. King Hsinbyushin conquered all of it in 1765. Burma ceded the region south of the Salween River to the British after the First Anglo-Burmese War under the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826. The British and the Siamese signed a boundary treaty on 20 June 1826, and Mawlamyine became the first capital of British Burma.

After independence in 1948 the north-eastern districts went to the newly created Karen State, and in 1974 the northern part of what remained became Mon State. The capital moved from Mawlamyine to Dawei. The region had 1,406,434 people at the 2014 census. The Dawei, or Tavoyans, are a subgroup of the Bamar and speak the Tavoyan dialect of Burmese, and the Karen form the largest minority. Buddhists were 87.5 per cent of the population in 2014. Other main towns are Myeik and Kawthaung.
tanis: Tanis, the Greek name of the ancient Egyptian ḏꜥn.t, is also known as San al-Hagar. It is an important archaeological site in the north-eastern Nile Delta, on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, which has long since silted up. The city was the capital of Egypt in the 21st and 22nd Dynasties.

Tanis is unattested before the 19th Dynasty, when it was the capital of the 14th nome of Lower Egypt. It is securely attested in two documents of the 20th Dynasty, the Onomasticon of Amenope and the Story of Wenamun, as the home of the future pharaoh Smendes. The earliest known buildings there date to the 21st Dynasty. Monuments of earlier date were mostly brought from nearby cities, above all from Pi-Ramesses, the royal residence that was abandoned at the end of the New Kingdom when the Pelusiac branch of the Nile silted up and its harbour became unusable.

The kings of the 21st Dynasty and later the 22nd, along with Bubastis, ruled from Tanis. They supported their legitimacy with traditional titles and building, though the works are modest beside those of the New Kingdom. They built and enlarged the Great Temple of Amun-Ra, with minor temples to Mut and Khonsu, and scholars call Tanis the northern Thebes. The royal necropolis at Tanis replaced the one in the Valley of the Kings.

After the 22nd Dynasty Tanis lost its royal status and became capital of the 19th nome. Building revived from the 30th Dynasty through the Ptolemaic period. The city was populated until it was abandoned in Roman times. In Late Antiquity it was the seat of bishops of the Coptic Orthodox Church.

Excavation began in 1825 with Jean-Jacques Rifaud, who found two pink granite sphinxes now in the Louvre. Auguste Mariette dug there from 1860 to 1864 and Flinders Petrie from 1883 to 1886. In 1866 Karl Richard Lepsius found a copy of the Canopus Decree, whose full hieroglyphic text allowed a direct comparison with the Greek and confirmed Champollion's approach to deciphering hieroglyphs. Pierre Montet worked at the site from 1929 to 1956. In 1939 and 1940 he found the intact burials of Psusennes I, Amenemope and Shoshenq II, with gold jewellery, precious stones and funerary masks. They are the only intact royal pharaonic burials known.

Because so many monuments bore the names of Ramesses II, archaeologists long believed Tanis was Pi-Ramesses, and the Year 400 Stela led some to identify it with Avaris. The later discovery of Qantir and Tell el-Dab'a showed that these were separate sites. More than twenty fallen obelisks mark the Great Temple of Amun-Ra.
tank: The tank is the 20th-century realisation of an ancient concept, that of giving troops mobile protection and firepower. At the Battle of Mobei in 119 BCE the Han general Wei Qing used armoured heavy wagons, drawn up in rings, to shelter archers, crossbowmen and infantry from the Xiongnu cavalry. In the 15th century Jan Žižka built armoured wagons carrying cannon, used effectively in several battles of the Hussite wars. The internal combustion engine, armour plate and the continuous track were the key innovations leading to the modern tank.

The word tank was first applied in a military context in 1915 to keep the nature of the British landships secret. According to Albert Gerald Stern, secretary of the Landship Committee, at a conference on 24 December 1915 Thomas J. Macnamara suggested changing the committee's title for secrecy, and Mr d'Eyncourt proposed water carriers. Stern, who thought the initials of that title unsuitable, changed the word to tank, and the committee became the Tank Supply Committee. In France Colonel J. B. E. Estienne had the word char d'assaut preferred.

A tank is an armoured fighting vehicle meant as a primary offensive weapon in front-line ground combat. Its capability rests on firepower, protection and mobility, and designs differ in how they blend them. In the First World War the first designs, such as the British Mark I, were long and large in order to cross wide trenches and were classed as heavy tanks, while smaller vehicles such as the French Renault FT were classed as light tanks or tankettes. Improved suspension in the Second World War, such as the Christie system and the torsion-bar suspension of Ferdinand Porsche, greatly improved cross-country performance. Japan was the first to begin moving from petrol to diesel engines, with the Type 89B in 1934.

The British and French built thousands of tanks in the First World War, while Germany, unconvinced of their potential and short of resources, built only twenty. Commanding tanks in the field was difficult. Armoured bulkheads, engine noise, dust and smoke hindered communication, and radios were not portable or robust enough to be mounted in a tank, although Morse code transmitters were installed in some Mark IVs at Cambrai as messaging vehicles. Crews sometimes sent reports back by releasing carrier pigeons, and vehicles signalled to one another by hand or by semaphore flags, which the Red Army and Soviet Army kept in use through the Second World War and the Cold War.
tanzimat: Through the 1700s structural problems in Ottoman governance led to defeats in the Russo-Turkish Wars and the Greek War of Independence, and showed that the empire could not compete with European armies. Provincial governors, the ayans, and local leaders such as Muhammad Ali of Egypt increasingly defied the centre. Mahmud II, a reform-minded sultan, waited until the Auspicious Incident of 1826 to destroy the Janissaries, and after that his reign was a period of Western reform and centralisation. In 1838 the Treaty of Balta Liman with Britain dismantled Ottoman trade monopolies.

Mahmud II died suddenly on 1 July 1839 and was succeeded by his son Abdul Mejid I. Reformists such as Mustafa Reşid Pasha, who had been ambassador in London and Paris, argued that European institutions could restore imperial power. Their ideas took shape in the Gülhane Edict, issued on 3 November 1839.

The edict promised security of life, property and honour for all subjects, fair taxation and conscription, public trials and the end of tax farming, the iltizam. It guaranteed the rule of law to non-Muslims as well and put an end to the kul system, under which a ruler's servants could be executed or lose their property at his will. Statutes followed that created new ministries, the first paper banknotes in 1840, a regular method of army recruitment in 1843-44 and the first nationwide census in 1844. Telegraph networks began in 1847 and railways in 1856.

The Reform Edict of 1856 promised full legal equality to citizens of all religions and abolished the jizya, though it was replaced with an exemption payment for military service. Secular Nizamiye Courts were set up in 1864, a Nationality Law of 1869 created a common Ottoman citizenship, and the Mecelle, a civil code, was published between 1869 and 1876. The reforms peaked in 1876 with an Ottoman constitution, written by Midhat Pasha.

The reforms met resistance from conservative clerics who feared secular courts and schools, from officials who defended their privileges, and from Muslim artisans and peasants who lost tax exemptions and faced European competition. Christians in the Balkans often wanted autonomy that was harder to obtain under a centralised state, and the 1875 Herzegovina Uprising was partly fuelled by tax grievances. Foreign borrowing led to bankruptcy in 1875, and in 1881 European powers set up the Ottoman Public Debt Administration to control revenues.

Sultan Abdul Hamid II signed the 1876 constitution but soon turned against it. The period is held to have ended with the Great Eastern Crisis of 1875-1878, although reform continued. Historians disagree about its effect: some credit it with building a powerful national government, while others argue that it speeded the empire's fragmentation.
taoiseach: The words taoiseach and tánaiste, the title of the deputy prime minister, are both Irish and of ancient origin. Tánaiste refers to tanistry, the Gaelic system in which a leader named an heir apparent while still living. In Scottish Gaelic tòiseach means clan chief, and the Welsh tywysog, now meaning prince, has a similar origin.

When the draft Constitution of 1937 was debated in the Dáil, the opposition politician Frank MacDermot moved to put Prime Minister in the English text, keeping Taoiseach only in Irish. He argued that the word would be mispronounced by most people. Éamon de Valera, then President of the Executive Council, gave its meaning as chieftain or captain and declined to support the change. The amendment was defeated. Some later observers remarked that the sense of leader made the title resemble Führer, Duce and Caudillo.

The Constitution describes the taoiseach as the head of the Government or Prime Minister. A simple majority of the voting members of Dáil Éireann nominates one of its members, and the president must then appoint whomever the Dáil designates. A taoiseach who loses the support of a majority of the Dáil must resign or ask for a general election.

The taoiseach nominates the other members of the government, who are appointed by the president with the Dáil's consent, and may advise the president to dismiss ministers. The taoiseach also appoints eleven of the sixty members of the Seanad. The Department of the Taoiseach supports the office.

The office replaced the President of the Executive Council of the Irish Free State, which existed from 1922 to 1937. Under the Free State constitution that president was largely the chairman of the cabinet and could not dismiss a minister on his own authority. The taoiseach created in 1937 can advise the president to dismiss ministers and dissolve parliament, advice that by convention the president almost always follows.

W. T. Cosgrave held the earlier office from 1922 to 1932 and de Valera from 1932 to 1937. By convention taoisigh are numbered to include Cosgrave. An unusual choice was John A. Costello, an agreed candidate because the other parties refused to accept the Fine Gael leader Richard Mulcahy.
taoism: The core of Taoist thought crystallised during the early Warring States period, c. 450 to c. 300 BCE, when the Tao Te Ching and the Zhuangzi, widely regarded as the fundamental texts of Taoist philosophy, were largely compiled. Early Taoism drew on diverse influences, among them the Shang and Zhou state religions, Mohism, Confucianism and Legalist theories. Scholars disagree about its beginnings: Harold Roth argues that it began as inner-cultivation lineages of master and disciple, while Russell Kirkland holds that before the Han dynasty there were no real Taoists or Taoism, only sets of practices and ideas that were later synthesised.

By the Han dynasty, 202 BCE to 220 CE, the sources had coalesced into a coherent tradition of ritualists in the state of Shu, modern Sichuan. The Huang–Lao movement of the 2nd century BCE was an influential school, and the earliest surviving commentaries on the Tao Te Ching date from the Han. Taoist secret societies precipitated the Yellow Turban Rebellion in the late Han, attempting to create what has been characterised as a Taoist theocracy.

Taoism is a philosophical and religious tradition indigenous to China, emphasising harmony with the Tao, translated as way, road, path or technique. The opening line of the Tao Te Ching, that the Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao, is generally read to mean that the Tao is on an ultimate level indescribable. De, often translated virtue or power, is the active expression of the Tao, and the central values include ziran, naturalness, and wu wei, effortless action or non-interference. A common goal of practice is self-cultivation, which in religious forms includes longevity and immortality.

Religious Taoism has its own scriptures, priestly lineages, rites and ritual systems, and it has long been intertwined with Chinese folk religion, so that the boundary is often blurred. Its practices include offerings, the recitation of scriptures, purification rites, divination, meditation, and longevity methods related to Chinese medicine.

Monks assembled the Daozang canon from the 5th century CE onward. The alchemist Ge Hong wrote the Baopuzi in the 4th century. A united Taoist identity, called daojiao, gained official status in the Tang dynasty, which was the height of Taoist influence. Taoism was combined with Confucianism and Buddhism in the Three Teachings discourse by the 6th century. In the 19th and 20th centuries it suffered much destruction from persecution and wars, and by the 20th century only one complete copy of the Daozang survived intact, at the White Cloud Monastery in Beijing. It recovered after 1979, with temples restored and Taoist literature published.
taormina: The town occupies the ancient site, on a hill that forms the last projecting point of the mountain ridge running along the coast from Cape Pelorus. The old town stands about 250 metres above the sea. A very steep and almost isolated rock, crowned by a Norman castle, rises about 150 metres higher and is the likely site of the ancient citadel, which ancient writers describe as inaccessible. Portions of the ancient walls can be traced round the brow of the hill, and fragments of ancient buildings lie across its surface, including large water reservoirs, tombs and tessellated pavements.

The Greek name of the city was Tauroménion, later Tauromenium in Latin. The 3rd-century BCE historian Timaeus came from it, and the 4th-century BCE ruler Andromachus and the tyrant Tyndarion, in 278 BCE, governed it. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it remained one of the island's more important towns. The Arabs built the Saracen Castle on the rock of Monte Tauro, which controlled the valley of the river Alcantara, and an Arab necropolis, probably built between the ninth and eleventh centuries, lay outside the walls.

After Italian unification Taormina began to attract well-off visitors from northern Europe, and it became a welcoming haven for artists. The German photographer Wilhelm von Gloeden lived there from 1880. During the Second World War it was the headquarters of the German command, and on 9 July 1943, the feast day of its patron Saint Pancras, Allied aircraft bombed it twice, destroying part of its southern section and a wing of the San Domenico Hotel.

Taormina is a comune in the Metropolitan City of Messina and a tourist destination. Its ancient theatre has a diameter of 109 metres after an expansion in the 2nd century, making it the second largest of its kind in Sicily after that of Syracuse. It is brick, probably of Roman date, though its plan follows Greek theatres, and it is still used for concerts and opera. Other sights include the 13th-century cathedral, the Palazzo Corvaja and a Baroque fountain of 1635.
tapa-estonia: Tapa lies in Tapa Parish, Lääne-Viru County, at the junction of the Tallinn–Narva and Tallinn–Tartu–Valga railway lines. The Valgejõgi River passes on its northeastern side. Tapa Army Base is on the southern outskirts, and the Estonian Defence Forces' central training area, Keskpolügoon, lies north-west of the town. The origin of the name is uncertain. It may come from an older form of the personal name Tabbe, from the Estonian words tapu or tappo, or from the Karelian tapos. In Estonian tapa is also an imperative of the verb meaning to kill, which is considered a folk etymology.

Tapa developed as a village in the 13th and 14th centuries and was first mentioned in 1482. The Tapa knight manor, Taps, is recorded in 1629. The Baltic Railway Company opened its tracks there on 24 October 1870, the Tapa–Tartu branch followed in 1876, and a repair shop opened the same year. The three white bars on the town's flag stand for the three branches of the railway. Tapa was officially recognised as a town in 1926.

An armoured train regiment was formed there on 1 August 1923, and an airfield has stood on the southern edge since 1932. Soviet forces dissolved the regiment in January 1941, and German troops took over the town on 14 August 1941. The Soviets built a large military airfield from 1952, which came under the Estonian Defence Ministry in 1993. As Soviet troops and families left, the population fell from 10,395 in 1989 to 6,800 in 2000. In 2005 the town merged with three neighbouring parishes to form Tapa Parish.

Tapa has been known as both a railway and a military town throughout its history. Since 2002 it has been home to a military base, the Northeast Defence District, with an army training centre and artillery, anti-aircraft and engineer battalions. A bronze plaque on the railway station commemorates the Estonian War of Independence.

On 30 May 1908 delegates from Tallinn and Tartu met in Tapa in the first of four conferences, held until 1911, on how the Estonian language should be written. The Lutheran St. Jacob's Church was dedicated there in 1932. The station also appears as the Tallinn station in the 2008 film Detsembrikuumus.
taraba-state: Taraba State is named after the Taraba River, which traverses its southern part, and is nicknamed Nature's Gift to the Nation. It is bordered on the west by Nasarawa and Benue states, on the northwest by Plateau State, on the north by Bauchi and Gombe states, on the northeast by Adamawa State and on the south by the Northwest Region of Cameroon, along a frontier of about 525 km. The Benue, Donga and Taraba are its main rivers. They rise in the Cameroonian mountains, drain almost the whole length of the state on their way north, and then turn west to join the Niger River.

The state has an annual average temperature of 33 °C and is hottest in March and April, when the average high is about 40 °C. Rainfall is heaviest around August. The state also holds part of the Mambilla Region, which is described as the Bantu cradle and as an area occupied for about five millennia.

Taraba State was created out of the former Gongola State on 27 August 1991 by the military government of General Ibrahim Badamasi Babangida. It is an amalgamation of three former divisions: Wukari, Mambilla and Muri.

Its population includes about 80 distinct ethnic groups and languages. The northern part is mostly Fulani, Mumuye and Sho, and the southern part primarily Jukun, Wurkum, Tiv, Chamba, Kuteb and Ichen. The central region is mainly occupied by the Fulani, Mambilla, Ndola, Tigon, Jibu, Wurbo and Daka.

The capital is Jalingo, and the state has sixteen local government areas, among them Bali, Takum, Wukari, Zing and Ibi. Agriculture is the main occupation. Coffee, tea, groundnuts and cotton are grown as cash crops, and maize, rice, sorghum, millet, cassava and yam are produced in commercial quantity. Cattle, sheep and goats are reared in large numbers, especially on the Mambilla Plateau and along the Benue and Taraba valleys, and communities on the three rivers fish all year. Pottery, weaving, dyeing, mat-making, carving and blacksmithing are practised in many parts of the state.

Visitors go to the Mambilla Tourist Center and to Gumpti Park and game reserve in Gashaka. The Karimjo Abedahh festival and the Nwunyu fishing festival at Ibi are usually held in April, with canoe racing, swimming and dances. Other festivals include the Purma of the Chamba, the Tagba of the Acha at Takum and the Kuchecheb of the Kuteb.
taras-shevchenko: Taras Shevchenko was born on 9 March 1814 (25 February in the old style) in Morintsy, a village in Kiev Governorate, about 20 years after the third partition of Poland brought the territory under Russian rule. His parents were serf peasants who worked land owned by Vasily Engelhardt. When Engelhardt died in 1828, his son Pavel became the family's landlord and trained the 14-year-old Taras as a servant. In 1829 Taras travelled in Engelhardt's retinue to Warsaw and Vilno. When Engelhardt caught him painting a portrait of the Cossack general Matvei Platov at night, he had the boy whipped, but later apprenticed him to a painter-decorator, who recommended lessons from the Polish painter Franciszek Ksawery Lampi.

In Saint Petersburg the young Ukrainian artist Ivan Soshenko gave Shevchenko lessons and introduced him around June 1832 to the painter Karl Briullov. Briullov asked Engelhardt for Shevchenko's freedom and was refused. Shevchenko later became a student of the Imperial Academy of Arts with Briullov as his mentor. He travelled to Ukraine in 1843, 1845 and 1846, and in October 1843 wrote the poem The Dug Grave. In 1845 he became a drawing teacher at Kiev University and met members of the Brotherhood of Saints Cyril and Methodius.

He was arrested on 5 April 1847 and exiled to Central Asia for his association with the Brotherhood; he continued to create art and poetry despite prohibitions. He received an amnesty from the new emperor in 1857 but was not permitted to settle in Saint Petersburg until 1858. In June 1859 he visited Ukraine for the last time.

Shevchenko composed his last poem, left unfinished, on 14 February 1861 and died in Saint Petersburg on 10 March 1861. His friends carried out the wish he expressed in his poem Testament: his remains were taken to Ukraine, and on 22 May 1861 he was reburied on Monk's Hill, now Taras Hill, in Kaniv. Of 237 poems he wrote, only 28 were published in the Russian Empire during his life. He wrote his poetry in Ukrainian and his prose in Russian. His poetry, above all the Kobzar, is regarded as the foundation of modern Ukrainian literature.
taraz: Finds of chest ornaments, bronze statues of kings and ceramics in the Talas valley show settlement in the bronze age, and tribal unions of Saka Scythians had formed there by the 7th and 8th centuries BCE. The claim to a history of 2,000 years rests on a fortress built on the Talas River by the Xiongnu chanyu Zhizhi, described in the Hanshu, and on the Battle of Zhizhi in 36 BCE. The city is first recorded under the name Talas in 568 CE by Menander Protector.

At that time it lay within the First Turkic Kaganate, and in 568 an embassy from Byzantium led by Zemarchus reached Taraz, to the court of Istemi Yabgu, who allied with Byzantium rather than with a Persian envoy who arrived at the same time.

The medieval city was a fortified trading town on the Silk Road, and the Sogdian merchants who controlled the caravan route in Central Asia were important to its commerce. The monk Xuanzang, who passed in 629, called it Daluosi and wrote that merchants from various nations had settled it. The Talas alphabet, a variant of the Orkhon script, takes its name from the town. The Battle of Talas in 751, between the Tang dynasty and the Abbasid Caliphate, was fought somewhere in the Talas valley, and one indirect result was the introduction of paper to the West through the capture of Chinese papermakers. The medieval city declined in the 13th century.

At the end of the 18th century a fortress of the Khanate of Kokand was built on the ruins, and a new town grew around it, named Aulie-Ata in 1856. Colonel Chernyev's detachment took it for the Russian Empire in 1864, and the Semirechensky railway reached the town in 1917.

In 1936 the city was renamed Mirzoyan after Levon Mirzoyan, and in 1938 Dzhambul after the Kazakh folk singer Zhambyl Zhabayev. Many deported peoples settled there during the Soviet period. It took the name Taraz in 1997. The city lies on the Talas River in southern Kazakhstan, near the border with Kyrgyzstan, and is the administrative centre of Jambyl Region. Its 2,000th anniversary was marked in 2001, with recognition from UNESCO.
tarbes: Tarbes lies in the rich agricultural plain of the river Adour, at the foot of the Pyrenees, about 155 kilometres south-west of Toulouse and 20 kilometres north-east of Lourdes. It stands at an average elevation of 304 metres. A fifth-century record gives its name as Civitas Turba ubi castrum Bigòrra, the town of Turba, possibly of the crowd, where the castle of Bigòrra stands. Gregory of Tours called it Talvam vicum in the 6th century. A legend holds that Tarbis, queen of Ethiopia, rejected by Moses, wandered to Bigorre and founded the town on the Adour.

The foundations of Tarbes began to emerge in the 3rd century BCE, according to buried remains. Merchants, probably Aquitanians, carrying salt across the Pyrenean foothills had to ford the Adour and pause to split their loads, and a sandy rise in the valley bottom prompted people to settle. It was an important town of Novempopulania, a Roman province. In the 5th and 6th centuries, under successive barbarian invasions, the city shrank around its castrum.

In the 17th century, after the plague, the town revived. The Episcopal Palace was rebuilt in 1652, a third hospital was founded in 1690, and two new convents were established. From 1800 Tarbes was the chef-lieu and prefecture, and in 1806 Napoleon re-established the National Stud there, where the Anglo-Arabian horse breed was born. Rail linked it to Paris in 1859, and an arsenal begun in 1871 produced artillery in the First World War. Ferdinand Foch, who commanded the Allied armies, was born there in 1851.

Tarbes is the capital of the Hautes-Pyrénées department and of the historical region of Bigorre, and the seat of the diocese of Tarbes-et-Lourdes. It had 44,399 inhabitants in 2023. Its cathedral has a classical façade of the 17th century, with a transept dating from the 12th century, and Saint Vincent de Paul was ordained deacon there in 1598. The Haras de Tarbes, created by Napoleon in 1806, stands in a park of Empire buildings, and the Massey Museum houses the International Museum of the Hussars.
tarim-basin: The Tarim Basin is an endorheic basin of about 888,000 square kilometres, bounded by the Tian Shan to the north and the Kunlun Mountains to the south. The Taklamakan Desert fills much of it and is too dry for permanent habitation. The Yarkand, Kashgar and Aksu rivers join to form the Tarim River, which runs along the north side and ends at Lop Nur, a marshy saline depression.

Meltwater from the mountains feeds the oases along which the Silk Road routes ran: one route north of the desert, one south, and a shorter middle route across the Lop Nur region, which became uninhabitable in the 4th century and has been deserted since the 6th. The historical Uyghur name for the basin is Altishahr, meaning six cities.

Bronze appeared in the basin from about 2000 BCE, in six cultural zones. Mummies found at Loulan, the Xiaohe tomb complex and Qäwrighul were once suggested to be Tocharian, but recent evidence points to a distinct population. The Han dynasty came to influence the basin in the reign of Emperor Wu, and General Ban Chao (32–102 CE) wrested control from the Xiongnu at the end of the 1st century. The Chinese administered it as the Protectorate of the Western Regions.

The Kushans expanded into it in the 1st and 2nd centuries and established a kingdom at Kashgar. Kingdoms such as Kucha and Khotan passed Buddhism and other influences between India, Central Asia and China; the monk Kumārajīva came from Kucha.

Under Emperor Taizong the Tang dynasty campaigned against the oasis states, then vassals of the Western Turkic Khaganate: Gaochang was annexed in 640, Karasahr taken in 644 and Kucha conquered in 649. From the late 8th to 9th centuries the region changed hands between the Tang and the Tibetan Empire. Satuq Bughra Khan of the Kara-Khanid Khanate converted to Islam in 966, and Khotan fell to the Kara-Khanid Khanate around 1006; the basin became Islamic over the following centuries. In the early 14th century its eastern parts belonged to the Chagatai Khanate, and the Dughlat tribe held the western basin and raised Tughlugh Timur to the throne in 1347.

The basin lies in the Xinjiang region of north-western China, and Uyghurs form the majority in cities such as Kashgar and Hotan. Xinjiang as a single province dates from 1884, after the Qing conquest of 1759, when the Tarim Basin and Dzungaria had been governed separately. Excavations have found wooden tablets in the Kharosthi script of the 3rd and 4th centuries at Niya, and Buddhist murals at Miran that show links with Central Asia and northern India.
tariq-ibn-ziyad: Medieval Arabic historians give contradictory accounts of Tariq's origins and ethnicity, and details of his personality are uncertain. Many modern scholars hold that he was a Berber mawla, a freedman client, of Musa ibn Nusayr, the Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya. According to David Nicolle he came from a Berber tribe native to the Tafna in what is now Algeria, and he first appears in the record as governor of Tangier. Ibn Abd al-Hakam (803–871) says Musa appointed him governor of Tangier after its conquest in 710–711.

An unconquered Visigothic outpost remained at Ceuta, held by a nobleman named Julian, Count of Ceuta. In the story told by Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Julian was enraged because King Roderic had raped his daughter, Florinda la Cava, at the Visigothic court, and so he made a treaty with Tariq and used his merchant ships to carry the Muslim army across the straits. Tariq's army, which landed on or about 26 April 711, consisted of about 7,000 soldiers, largely of Berber stock but with Arab troops, and it gathered at the mountain that became known as Jabal Tariq, or Gibraltar.

Roderic assembled an army said to number 100,000, though the real figure may have been much lower. Most of it was commanded by the sons of Wittiza, whom Roderic had deposed, and it was defeated at the Battle of Guadalete on 19 July, where Roderic was killed. Tariq then divided his army into four. One division took Córdoba under Mughith al-Rumi, others took Granada and further places, and Tariq's own took Toledo before he advanced north to Guadalajara and Astorga. He was de facto governor until Musa arrived a year later, and within a few years the two had taken two-thirds of the peninsula.

In 714 the caliph al-Walid I ordered both Tariq and Musa back to Damascus, where they spent the rest of their lives. Arabic sources differ on their relationship: some tell of Musa's anger and envy at a freedman's conquest, while al-Baladhuri says only that Musa wrote him a severe letter and the two were later reconciled. The historians Ibn Khallikan, in 1274, and al-Maqqari, in the 16th century, attribute to him a long speech to his troops before Guadalete. He also appears in a story of the One Thousand and One Nights.
tarnowskie-gory: Tarnowskie Góry, in German Tarnowitz, lies in Silesia in the Silesian Highlands near Katowice. Its name comes from Tarnowice, a local village, and góry, which in Old Polish meant mines. The German name was introduced in the late 18th century, after the Third Silesian War. In the Middle Ages the region was inhabited by Lechitic Polish tribes, and in the 10th century it became part of the emerging Polish state under Mieszko I.

An outbreak of plague in 1676-77 decimated the population. The Prussian army entered the town on 16 December 1740 during the first of the Silesian Wars, and in 1742 Austrian rule ended and Tarnowskie Góry fell under Prussia. Around 1780 Friedrich Wilhelm von Reden opened a government-controlled mine and a silver and lead foundry. Salomon Isaac, a Jewish trade agent and mining entrepreneur, contributed greatly to Silesian mining and metallurgy, although Jews were restricted or banned from the area.

In 1788 a Newcomen atmospheric engine was imported from Wales to drain the mines, and eventually eight steam engines were used. Drainage tunnels were later cut to replace them, and a 600-metre part of the Fryderyk adit is now a tourist route, the Black Trout Adit. A school of mining was begun in 1803, and the Upper-Silesian Brotherhood Cooperative, an insurance society for miners, had its headquarters in the town. The first railway, to Opole, arrived in 1857, and by the end of the century the town was becoming one of the largest marshalling yards in Europe.

Early in the 20th century the silver ore ran out and mining stopped. After the plebiscite that followed three Silesian uprisings of 1919-1921, the Tarnowitz district voted 61.7 percent to join Poland, although the city itself voted 82 percent for Germany, and in 1922 the town was returned to Poland.

The town, with 61,842 inhabitants in 2021, is in the Silesian Voivodeship. The Historic Silver Mine of Tarnowskie Góry is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Black Trout Adit has been a national Historic Monument since 2004, and the town has a museum opened in 1958 and the 16th-century Gwareks' bell-tower, named for the old Polish word for miners. The Gwarki Tarnogórskie festival has marked mining culture each September since 1957.
tarquinius-priscus: According to Livy, Tarquinius came from the Etruscan city of Tarquinii and was first named Lucumo. Modern scholars note that lucumo was a title of political rank among the Etruscans, meaning king, so the tradition may have mistaken a title for a personal name. His father Demaratus was a Greek merchant from Corinth, who according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus belonged to the Bacchiadae and left the city when Cypselus overthrew them.

After inheriting his father's fortune, Lucumo was denied office at Tarquinii because his father was Greek-born. His wife Tanaquil, gifted in prophecy, persuaded him to move to Rome, where foreigners were said to be readily made citizens. Tradition tells that an eagle took his cap on the Janiculum and replaced it, an omen she read as a sign of kingship. In Rome he took the name Lucius Tarquinius and became the trusted adviser of King Ancus Marcius.

When Ancus died his sons were still boys. Tarquinius sent them off on a hunting trip and then won the Comitia Curiata with a speech, becoming the first king in Roman history to canvass for the throne. He is said to have fought the Latins, the Sabines and the Etruscans, held Rome's first triumph in Etruscan style, and added a hundred men from lesser noble families to the Senate, bringing it to two hundred.

The sources also credit him with building. He is said to have laid permanent seating for the Circus Maximus and to have built the Cloaca Maxima to drain the low ground for the Forum. He began the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill and a stone wall around the city, though neither was finished in his reign; the temple was dedicated under Tarquinius Superbus in 509 BCE. Tradition also gives Rome the fasces, the curule chair and the toga praetexta from him.

According to tradition, assassins organised by the sons of Ancus Marcius killed him with a blow of an axe to the head. Tanaquil is said to have managed the transfer of power so that Servius Tullius took the throne. Modern historians treat most of the account as foundation legend shaped in a later age. Livy and Dionysius wrote about five hundred years after the events, relying on annalists who survive only in fragments. The 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica noted that the story of his Corinthian origins is chronologically impossible. Excavations beneath the Forum have found channels thought to belong to an early Cloaca Maxima.
tarquinius-superbus: Ancient accounts of the regal period mingle history and legend. Tarquin was said to be the son or grandson of Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of Rome. The oldest sources make him Priscus's son, but modern historians think that impossible under the traditional chronology. His mother was supposedly Tanaquil, who placed Servius Tullius on the throne after the sons of Ancus Marcius had Priscus assassinated.

Servius married his daughters to Tarquin and his brother Arruns. According to the tradition, the ambitious Tullia Minor and Tarquin conspired to bring about the deaths of her sister and of Arruns, and then married. Tarquin courted the patrician senators with presents, seated himself on the throne in the senate house, denounced Servius, and threw the aged king down the steps; Servius was murdered in the street by Tarquin's assassins.

Tarquin began by refusing to bury Servius and putting to death senators he suspected of loyalty to him. By not replacing them and not consulting the senate he reduced its size and authority. He made an ally of Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum, one of the most eminent Latin chiefs, by betrothing his daughter to him, and persuaded the Latins to renew their treaty with Rome.

He took the wealthy town of Suessa Pometia and with its spoils began the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill. When he could not take Gabii by arms, his son Sextus fled there, pretending to have been beaten, won command of its troops and, on a sign from his father, killed or banished its leading men. Tarquin is said to have ordered the excavation of the cloaca maxima, and, by one story, to have bought three of nine Sibylline Books from the Cumaean Sibyl after she burned the others.

In 509 BCE the pace and burden of his building had angered the Roman populace, and Tarquin marched against the Rutuli to besiege Ardea. In the story, his son Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, the wife of Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, and she stabbed herself after telling her husband and father. Lucius Junius Brutus persuaded the comitia to revoke the king's imperium and send him into exile, and two consuls were elected in his place.

Tarquin sought help from Etruscan cities and from Lars Porsena of Clusium. In 499 or 496 BCE he joined Octavius Mamilius's Latin army, which Rome defeated. He then went to the court of Aristodemus at Cumae, where he died in 495 BCE. The expression tall poppy syndrome takes its name from Livy's tale of Gabii.
tarragona: Tarragona stands on the Costa Daurada on the Mediterranean shore, around the mouth of the river Francolí. The Romans developed it on a coastal hill, some 75 to 90 metres above sea level, near an earlier Iberian settlement. Its position atop a high rock gave it the epithet arce potens Tarraco. The real founding date is unknown. One Catalan legend says it was named for Tarraho, eldest son of Tubal, and another attributes the name to Tearcon the Ethiopian, a pharaoh of the seventh century BCE.

During the Second Punic War the brothers Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus fortified Tarraco and made it a fortress and arsenal against the Carthaginians. It became the capital of Hispania Citerior and then of Hispania Tarraconensis, and also a bishopric seat. Augustus wintered there after his Cantabrian campaign and gave the city honorary titles. Its Jewish community, established in the Roman era, is among the oldest in Spain.

After the end of the Western Roman Empire the Vandals and the Visigoths took the city, and Visigothic rule ended with the Umayyad conquest of Hispania in 714. It was an important border city of the Caliphate of Córdoba between 750 and 1013. The County of Barcelona took it in 1117, and from 1129 to 1173 it was the capital of the short-lived Principality of Tarragona. It later belonged to the Principality of Catalonia within the Crown of Aragon until 1714.

In the Peninsular War the army of Louis-Gabriel Suchet besieged it from 5 May to 29 June 1811 and stormed the defences, killing or capturing almost all the Spanish garrison. In the Spanish Civil War it stayed with the Republic until Nationalist troops captured it on 15 January 1939.

The Archaeological Complex of Tàrraco is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The remains include parts of the Roman walls, the circus, the second-century amphitheatre and Les Ferreres Aqueduct, 217 metres long. Tarragona Cathedral dates from the 12th and 13th centuries and combines Romanesque and Gothic elements. The Santa Tecla Festival, held from 15 to 24 September, has been held since 1321, and the castells, human towers, are a living tradition there.
tartu: Tartu lies about 186 kilometres southeast of Tallinn on the Emajõgi river, which connects Lake Võrtsjärv with Lake Peipus. Archaeological evidence of permanent settlement on the site dates to as early as the 5th century CE. By the 7th century local inhabitants had built a wooden fortification on the east side of Toome Hill, and around the 9th and 10th centuries the settlement became an inland trading centre. The name is thought to derive from the Estonian word for aurochs, tarvas.

From the 13th century until the end of the 19th, the town was known in most of the world by variants of Dorpat. In 1262 the army of Prince Dmitri of Pereslavl captured and destroyed it but could not take the bishop's fortress on Toome Hill. In the 1280s Dorpat joined the Hanseatic League. In 1558 Tsar Ivan the Terrible began the Livonian War by besieging it, and the local bishop was imprisoned in Moscow, which ended local self-government. The city then passed between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Sweden, which held it for good from 1625.

In 1708 Russian forces blew up the remaining fortifications and houses and deported the citizens to Russia, and with the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 the city became part of the Russian Empire. The Great Fire of 1775 destroyed most of the buildings in the centre, and the town hall was built between 1782 and 1789. In the second half of the 19th century Tartu was the cultural centre of the Estonians: it hosted the first song festival in 1869, the founding of the Vanemuine theatre in 1870 and of the Society of Estonian Literati in 1872. Much of the city was destroyed in the Second World War, and under Soviet rule the population almost doubled from 57,000 to over 100,000 between 1944 and 1991.

Tartu is often called the intellectual capital of Estonia. It is the seat of the Supreme Court of Estonia, the Estonian National Museum, whose new main building opened in 2016, and the Vanemuine theatre, the oldest Estonian-language theatre, and it is the birthplace of the Estonian Song Festivals. After independence was regained in 1991 the old town was renovated and St. John's Church, in ruins since the war, was restored.
tartus: Tartus lies on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean, on a coastal plain bordered to the east by the Syrian Coastal Mountain Range, whose limestone hills in places give way to basalt. Arwad, the only inhabited island on the Syrian coast, lies a few kilometres off the shore. The name derives from the Ancient Greek Antaradus, meaning the town facing Aradus, which became Tortosa in Latin and Ṭarṭūs in Arabic. It has a Mediterranean climate with mild, wet winters and hot, humid summers. The city was governed from Latakia until the 1970s, when Tartus Governorate was created.

Tartus was founded as a Phoenician colony of Aradus, the larger settlement on the island, and was called Antaradus. Little remains of it. In the Greco-Roman and Byzantine periods it had its own bishops, and bishops of Antaradus and of Aradus appear at councils from Chalcedon in 451 onward. The first chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary is said to have been built there in the 3rd century, and the city was favoured by Constantine for its devotion to her cult. Caliphate armies under Ubadah ibn al-Samit conquered it in 636, and Mu'awiya I built an amsar complex there.

Frankish forces captured the city in 1099 during the First Crusade. Raymond of Saint-Gilles recaptured it in February 1102 after a two-week siege, and in 1123 the Crusaders built the semi-fortified Cathedral of Our Lady of Tortosa over a Byzantine church popular with pilgrims.

In 1152 Tortosa was handed to the Knights Templar, who made it a military headquarters and about 1165 built a castle with a large chapel, an elaborate keep and thick double concentric walls. Nur ad-Din Zangi held it briefly. Saladin recaptured it in 1188, but some Templars kept the keep for another hundred years until it fell in 1291, the last Templar outpost on the Syrian mainland. They then held the island of Arwad for another decade. Under the Mamluks the city lost its prestige, which it regained under Ottoman rule through trade with Cyprus and Europe.

Muhammad Ali Pasha of Egypt conquered Tartus in 1832. The Ottomans regained it in 1839, and in 1840 British frigates and marines attacked the citadel without capturing it. Ottoman rule lasted until 1918.

Tartus is a major port and the second largest port city in Syria after Latakia, with a 2023 population estimated at 458,327. The historic centre is built on and inside the walls of the Templar fortress, whose moat still separates the old town from the modern city. The former cathedral, the Romanesque-Gothic Notre-Dame of Tartus of the 12th century, has housed the National Museum of Tartus since 1956.
tashkent: Tashkent is in northeastern Uzbekistan, on a well-watered plain on the road between Samarkand and Shymkent, just across the border in Kazakhstan. It sits at the confluence of the Chirchiq River and several of its tributaries and is built on deep alluvial deposits up to 15 m deep. The city lies in an active tectonic area and suffers numerous tremors and occasional earthquakes. Its climate is Mediterranean with some humid continental influences: winters are cold and often snowy, and summers are long, hot and dry.

Abu Rayhan Biruni wrote that the name comes from the Turkic tash and the Persian kent, Stone City or City of Stones. The older name Chach has been traced by Ilya Gershevitch to an Old Iranian word for an area of water or lake, though Ünal criticizes that derivation as based on too many assumptions and derives Čač from a Proto-Turkic word for stone.

Tashkent's history stretches back centuries as part of the ancient Silk Road. Before the influence of Islam in the mid-8th century, Sogdian and Turkic culture was predominant. Genghis Khan destroyed the city in 1219, after which it was rebuilt and profited from its place on the Silk Road. From the 18th to the 19th centuries it was an independent city-state, before being re-conquered by the Khanate of Kokand. The Russian Empire took Tashkent in 1865, and it became the capital of Russian Turkestan. In 1868 the Samarkand Kufic Quran was taken as a war trophy from Samarkand to Saint Petersburg, and the Bolsheviks returned it to Tashkent in 1923.

In Soviet times the city grew greatly and its population changed because of forced deportations from throughout the Soviet Union. Thousands of Pontic Greeks were displaced in the early 1940s, and about 11,000 refugees of the Greek Civil War were sent to Tashkent after 1949. Its population was 1,902,000 in 1983 and about 2,136,600 in 1991. The 1966 earthquake destroyed much of the city, which was rebuilt as a model Soviet city and was then the fourth-largest in the Soviet Union, after Moscow, Leningrad and Kiev. The Tashkent Metro, the first in Central Asia, opened in 1977.

Tashkent is the most populous city in Central Asia. Ethnic Uzbeks form the majority, and Uzbek is the main language, with Russian used as a lingua franca. Most of the ancient city was destroyed in the 1917 revolution and the 1966 earthquake. Surviving landmarks include the Kukeldash Madrasah, dating from the reign of Abdullah Khan II (1557-1598), Chorsu Bazaar, the Hazrati Imam Complex and the mausoleum of Qaffol Shoshi, built in 1542. The city marked 2,200 years of written history in 2009.
tassili-najjer: Tassili n'Ajjer, meaning plateau of rivers, is a mountain range and plateau in south-eastern Algeria at the borders of Libya and Niger, covering more than 72,000 square kilometres. Its highest point is Adrar Afao, at 2,158 metres, and the nearest towns are Djanet and Illizi. The range is mostly sandstone stained by desert varnish, and erosion has formed rock forests resembling a lunar landscape, nearly 300 natural rock arches in the south-east, deep gorges and permanent pools in the north.

Because of its height and the water-retaining sandstone, vegetation is more lush than in the surrounding desert, with open woodland of endangered Saharan cypress and Saharan myrtle. It is a national park and Biosphere Reserve and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1982.

The highlands show occupation from 5500 to 1500 BCE, mainly by transhumant pastoralists of the Neolithic who camped there in the dry season, while hearths and stone tumuli in the lowlands date between 6000 and 4000 BCE. Hunter-gatherers lived in the region between about 10,000 and 7500 years ago, and after 7500 years ago people organised into pastoral groups in response to an increasingly unpredictable climate.
Cattle were herded across wide areas as early as 3000 to 2000 BCE, followed by horses before 1000 BCE and then camels, whose arrival reflects the growth of trans-Saharan trade.

European study of Algerian rock art began in 1863. Westerners were widely introduced to Tassili through sketches by French legionnaires, particularly Lieutenant Charles Brenans in the 1930s, who brought the archaeologist Henri Lhote. Lhote returned several times between 1956 and 1970. His expeditions have been heavily criticised, his team being accused of faking images and of damaging paintings by brightening them for tracing and photography.

The rock art, first reported in 1910, includes about 15,000 engravings so far identified. The earliest pieces are presumed to be around 12,000 years old, although sources vary considerably, and most date to between 9,000 and 10,000 years ago or later. The subjects are large wild animals such as antelopes and crocodiles, cattle herds, and humans hunting and dancing. The art falls into five traditions: Archaic, Round Head, Bovidian or Pastoral, Horse and Camel. The Round Head paintings include some of the oldest and largest exposed rock paintings in Africa, with figures over five metres tall, and their concentration in particular places suggests ritual centres.
