The Horse period shows chariots and riders beside Libyan-Berber inscriptions that remain undeciphered. The Camel period coincides with caravan routes that carried salt, goods and enslaved people across the Sahara.
tatars: The name Tatar possibly referred first to the Tatar confederation, which Genghis Khan incorporated into the Mongol Empire. Western cartographers later applied the term, often spelled Tartar, to anyone from the northern and central Asian landmass then known as Tartary. The name became that of populations of the former Golden Horde in Europe, such as those of the Kazan, Crimean, Astrakhan, Qasim and Siberian Khanates. The Persian word is first recorded in the 13th century in reference to the hordes of Genghis Khan. Studies of ancestry suggest that the three main groups, the Volga, Crimean and Siberian Tatars, formed independently of one another.

The Volga Tatars descend from Kipchaks of the Golden Horde or from Volga Bulgars who survived the Mongol conquest of 1236 to 1237. About 40 thousand Tatars arrived with Khan Uluk-Muhammad in 1438 to 1445 when the Kazan Khanate was formed. Its conquest by Ivan IV in 1552 followed a six-month siege.

The Crimean Tatars formed between the 13th and 17th centuries, mainly from Kipchaks and Ottoman Turks. Crimea passed to the Giray dynasty, founded by Hacı Giray after an embassy invited him from Lithuania in 1441.

In 1502 the Crimean Khanate defeated the Great Horde, and it was among the strongest powers in Eastern Europe until the early 18th century, formally a vassal of the Ottoman Empire. A major source of income was frequent raids into Eastern Europe and the Caucasus for slaves.

Russia annexed it in 1783, and at least 800 thousand Tatars left Crimea by the early 20th century. In May 1944 the Soviet State Defense Committee ordered the deportation of all Crimean Tatars to Central Asia, and 46 per cent of them are said to have died during the deportation and the first years of exile.

Tatars settled in the Polish-Lithuanian lands between the 13th and 17th centuries. The Lipka Tatars first settled in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania at the beginning of the 14th century, and Grand Duke Vytautas invited a further, Muslim wave towards the end of it. The grand dukes encouraged the migrations because of the Tatars' reputation as skilled warriors, and the settlers were granted szlachta (noble) status. Estimates for the 17th century put their number at about 15,000, in about 60 villages with mosques.

They kept their religion and culture through royal privileges and internal autonomy, and were allowed to marry Christians, which was uncommon in Europe at the time. By the 18th century they had adopted the local language. The May Constitution of 1791 gave them a seat in the Sejm. Henryk Sienkiewicz's historical novels made their role well known in Poland.
tatarstan: Tatarstan lies in the centre of the East European Plain, about 800 kilometres east of Moscow, between the Volga and the Kama rivers. It covers 68,000 square kilometres and borders Kirov, Ulyanovsk, Samara and Orenburg oblasts and the republics of Mari El, Udmurtia, Chuvashia and Bashkortostan. Its capital and largest city is Kazan. Oil, natural gas and gypsum are its main natural resources.

The earliest known organised state within its present boundaries was Volga Bulgaria (c. 700 to 1238), a mercantile state with trade contacts across Inner Eurasia, the Middle East and the Baltic. Islam was introduced by missionaries from Baghdad around the time of Ibn Fadlan's journey in 922. The Golden Horde and the Khanate of Kazan followed, until Russia conquered the khanate in 1552. In the 19th century the region became a centre of Jadidism, an Islamic movement that preached tolerance of other religions.

During the Civil War of 1918 to 1920 Tatar nationalists tried to found an independent Idel-Ural State with the neighbouring Bashkirs. The Bolsheviks, who had at first supported it, arrested members of its parliament in March 1918. The Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was established on 27 May 1920, with boundaries that did not include a majority of the Volga Tatars. On 30 August 1990 Tatarstan declared its sovereignty. A constitution approved by about 62 per cent of voters in 1992 defined it as a sovereign state, but the Russian Constitutional Court declared the referendum and constitution unconstitutional. Since the 2002 text, the constitution defines Tatarstan as part of the Russian Federation.

Tatarstan is a republic of the Russian Federation. Its two state languages are Tatar and Russian, and the official script is Cyrillic. The 2021 census counted 4,004,809 inhabitants, among them about 2 million Tatars and 1.5 million Russians, with Chuvash, Mari and Udmurts in smaller numbers. Most Tatars are Sunni Muslims, and a minority, the Keräşen Tatars, are Orthodox Christians. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the republic: the Kazan Kremlin, the Bulgarian State Museum-Reserve, and the Assumption Cathedral and Monastery of the town-island of Sviyazhsk.
taunus: The Taunus is the southeastern part of the Rhenish Slate Mountains. This low mountain range is about 75 kilometres long from south-west to north-east and about 35 kilometres wide, and covers some 2,700 square kilometres. The Rhine and the valley of the Lahn bound it on the west and north, the Main and the Rheingau on the south, and the plain of the Wetterau on the east. It is divided into the Vordertaunus, the Hohe Taunus, the Hintertaunus and the Idstein Depression. The highest parts, in the Feldberg massif, are wooded, colder and wetter than the lowlands around them.

Its rocks are mostly slates, phyllites and sandstones laid down in the Ordovician to Devonian periods. Taunus quartzite, a very weather-resistant rock, forms many summits, among them the Altkönig and the Kleiner Feldberg. Iron ore, silver ore and roofing slate were mined in the Lahn area from the 17th to the 20th century, and between Idstein and Usingen pits were worked from the late Middle Ages. The last active lead and silver mine, at Heftrich, closed around 1924.

The Roman frontier, the Limes, was built across the Taunus, and the Saalburg, a restored Roman fort, now houses a museum. After the fall of the Limes in 259 or 260 CE the Alamanni settled in the range, and Alemannic cemeteries survive in its southern foothills. Around 500 CE, after the Battle of Tolbiac, the area passed to the Frankish confederation. The Celtic ring walls on the Altkönig are built of Taunus quartzite.

Until the late 18th century the range was known simply as die Höhe, the height, a name kept in Bad Homburg vor der Höhe and Rosbach vor der Höhe. The name Taunus comes from the Annals of Tacitus, which mention a fort in monte Tauno, probably near present-day Friedberg. In past centuries the Taunus became known among aristocrats for its hot springs.

Several spa towns lie in the Taunus. Bad Schwalbach is mentioned in documents from the 16th century, and Bad Ems has been one of the most reputed therapeutic spas in Germany since the 17th century. By the 19th century the best-known spa towns were Wiesbaden, Bad Homburg vor der Höhe, Bad Nauheim and Bad Soden am Taunus. Groundwater from the quartzite, pumped through four tunnels, contributes much to the water supply of Wiesbaden. The Ford Taunus car line is named after the range.
taurus-mountains: The Taurus Mountains are a mountain complex in southern Turkey, extending in a curve from Lake Eğirdir in the west to the upper reaches of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers in the east. They form part of the Alpide belt of Eurasia and were known in antiquity also as Mons Masius. They are divided into three chains. The Western Taurus arcs around the Gulf of Antalya, with peaks above 3,000 metres; the highest is Kizlarsivrisi, at 3,086 metres, in the Bey Mountains. The Central Taurus includes Mount Demirkazık, at 3,756 metres, and the Bolkar and Aladağlar ranges. The Southeastern Taurus forms the northern boundary of the Southeastern Anatolia Region and North Mesopotamia.

The mountains were formed by the collision of the African and Eurasian tectonic plates and rest mainly on limestone. In the Aladağlar and Bolkar ranges the eroded limestone has formed karst landscapes with waterfalls, underground rivers and some of the largest caves in Asia. The climate is Mediterranean, and at lower elevations evergreen oak and Turkish pine grow, with black pine, Lebanon cedar and Taurus fir above 1,200 metres.

The name appears in the Histories of Polybius as Taûros. According to the scholar Heinrich Kiepert, it was borrowed into Greek from an Old Aramaic root meaning mountain. The bull was a common symbol of the storm gods of the ancient Near East, and the mountains held many storm-god temples. The ancient Syrians held that the thunderstorms of these mountains were the work of the storm god Adad, who made the Tigris and Euphrates rise and flood and so fertilise their land. Modern scholars place the Hurrians, probably the originators of the various storm gods, in the Taurus at their probable earliest origins. At Kestel there is a Bronze Age site where early evidence of tin mining has been found.

The Cilician Gates, or Gülek Pass, crossed the range north of Tarsus and has been the principal route through it since ancient times, linking the coastal plain of Cilicia with central Anatolia. In the Amanus range, a natural frontier with Cilicia to the west and Syria to the east, the passes such as the Amanian Gate were of great strategic importance. In 333 BCE Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at the Battle of Issus in the foothills between two of them. In World War I, the German and Turkish railway through the Taurus was a major objective of the Allies.
tavira: Tavira lies in the east of the Algarve on the south coast of Portugal, 28 kilometres east of Faro and 75 kilometres west of Huelva across the Guadiana into Spain. The Gilão River meets the Atlantic here. The municipality had 26,167 inhabitants in 2011 and covers 606.97 square kilometres. Tavira is the Portuguese representative community for the inscription of the Mediterranean Diet as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity of UNESCO.

The settlement's origins go back to the late Bronze Age. In the 8th century BCE it became one of the first Phoenician settlements in the west of Iberia, with massive walls, at least one sanctuary, two harbours and a regular urban plan, which lasted until the end of the 6th century BCE. Excavations on the hill of Santa Maria found part of a casemate fortification wall and ritual deposits. The site was later revived in the so-called Tartessian period and abandoned again by the end of the 4th century BCE. Under Caesar the Romans built a new port about 7 kilometres from modern Tavira, which prospered and declined with the empire.

The Moorish period, from the 8th to the 13th century, shaped the area's agriculture, culture and architecture, with whitewashed buildings and Moorish style doors. The Moors built Tavira Castle, two mosques and palaces, and the seven-arched bridge once thought Roman proves to be a 12th-century Moorish work. The area stayed mostly rural until the 11th century, when the town grew rapidly into one of the important settlements of the Gharb al-Andalus. In 1242 Dom Paio Peres Correia retook Tavira after seven of his principal knights were killed during a truce. His troops killed most of the population, and the few survivors were confined to a small quarter known as the Mouraria.

In the 18th century the river port shipped salt, dried fish and wine, but the earthquake of 1755 destroyed almost all the town's buildings. It was rebuilt with many 18th-century buildings and has 37 churches. The church of Santa Maria do Castelo, built on the ruins of a mosque and dating to the 13th century, holds the tombs of Paio Peres Correia, who died in Tavira in 1275, and his knights. Fishing was once the main industry but declined, partly because of the changing migration of tuna and the silting of the Gilão. The sand-bar island of Ilha de Tavira forms part of the Ria Formosa wetlands.
tawhid: The word tawhid, an assertion or declaration of oneness, comes from the Arabic verb wahhada, which can mean to make one or to consider to be one. In Islam it holds that God is indivisibly one and single. The first part of the declaration of faith, the shahada, is the declaration of belief in the oneness of God, and Muslims believe that the whole of Islamic teaching rests on it. Chapter 112 of the Quran, al-Ikhlas, states that God is One, never had offspring and was not born, and has no equal. The Quran uses 99 terms, the Excellent Names of God, to express the complexity of the divine nature.

Its opposite is shirk, associating partners with God, a term usually translated as polytheism but understood to be more complex. It is classed as greater shirk, open and apparent, and hidden shirk, such as performing rituals for social recognition. The Quran says that God does not forgive associating others with Him but forgives anything else of whoever He wills.

Muslim theologians have argued for the oneness of God by reason. Against the polytheism of pre-Islamic Arabia, the Quran argues that God as creator of everything excludes lesser gods, who would themselves have to be created, and that the order of the universe shows a single administrator. Verse 21:22 says that had there been gods besides God in the heavens and earth, both would have been ruined. Later theologians reasoned that two gods would sooner or later have conflicting wills, and one would be powerless, which is incompatible with being God. Avicenna (965–1037) proposed an ontological argument in the Metaphysics of The Book of Healing, distinguishing essence from existence.

Scholars have understood tawhid in different ways. Some theologians use it for the whole discussion of God and his attributes, and sometimes for the whole of kalam, Islamic theology. Philosophers such as al-Farabi, al-Razi and Avicenna interpreted it by reason, under the influence of Plotinus's emphasis on divine simplicity. In Sufism it is both an affirmation in speech and a practical realisation of God's unity, through purification from worldliness.

Tawhid shaped Muslim culture widely. Early Muslims understood religion to cover the state, law and society, since God's rule extends to all creatures and to all aspects of life. A single raised index finger is used as a symbol of tawhid. The wish to preserve God's transcendence led to the prohibition of visual depictions of God and of any prophet, and the dominant forms of Islamic art became calligraphy and arabesque. The medieval scholar al-Ghazali held that a believer who thinks himself better than another through wealth or colour adopts the hierarchical principle of Iblis and so falls into shirk.
taxila: Taxila, known in Sanskrit as Takṣaśilā, lies on the Pothohar Plateau in Punjab, Pakistan, about 25 kilometres north-west of the Islamabad and Rawalpindi area, near the Indus. The Sanskrit name is translated as City of Cut Stone or Rock of Taksha. According to the Ramayana the city was founded by Bharata, brother of Rama, and named for his son Taksha. The modern name derives from the Greek rendering recorded in Ptolemy's Geography.

Settlement in the Taxila valley goes back to the late 4th or early 3rd millennium BCE at Sarai Khola, and the first major settlement, on the Hathial mound, was established around 1000 BCE. Taxila was a capital of the Gandhara kingdom, together with Puṣkalāvatī, though at times it formed its own district or city-state. It may have grown considerably by the time of the Achaemenid conquest of the 6th century BCE. In 326 BCE its king Taxiles, called Āmbhi, surrendered to Alexander the Great without a battle; Greek historians described the city as wealthy, prosperous and well governed, and Alexander kept Taxiles as satrap.

Within about a decade of Alexander's departure Chandragupta Maurya captured the city. Buddhist texts say Chanakya came from Taxila, and under Ashoka, the grandson of Chandragupta, it became a great seat of Buddhist learning. It lay on the ancient Grand Trunk Road linking Pataliputra to Central Asia. In the 2nd century BCE the Indo-Greeks built a new capital, Sirkap, across the river, and Maues overthrew the last Greek king of Taxila around 90 BCE. Inscriptions of 76 CE show Kushan rule, and Kanishka later founded Sirsukh, the latest of the ancient settlements, when the city was known for trade in silk, sandalwood, horses, cotton, pearls and spices.

The invading Hunas devastated Taxila in the 5th century, and by the time the monk Xuanzang described it in the 7th century it was in decline. Its ruins were rediscovered in the mid-19th century by Alexander Cunningham and extensively excavated by Sir John Marshall. UNESCO designated Taxila a World Heritage Site in 1980. Some scholars regard the so-called university of ancient Taxila as one of the earliest centres of education in Asia.
tbilisi: Tbilisi stands on the banks of the Kura River. Its name comes from the Old Georgian tpili, meaning warm, because of the area's numerous sulfuric hot springs. Until 1936 the name in English and most other languages followed the Persian pronunciation, Tiflis. On 17 August 1936, by order of the Soviet leadership, the official Russian names of various cities were changed to match the local language, and the Georgian form was modernised from Ṭpilisi to Tbilisi on the proposal of Georgian linguists. Some languages, among them Turkish, Persian, Greek, Spanish and German, have kept a form of Tiflis. Its position at the crossroads between Europe and Asia, near the Silk Road, made it a point of contention among powers.

Archaeologists found evidence of continuous habitation of the suburb of Dighomi since the early Bronze Age, and stone artifacts from the Paleolithic. In the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age it was the largest settlement in the Caucasus. According to legend the site was covered by forest as late as 458. One widely accepted variant of the foundation myth says that King Vakhtang I of Iberia (r. c. 447/49 - 502/22) went hunting with a falcon, which caught or injured a pheasant, and both birds fell into a hot spring and died of burns. The king was so impressed by the springs that he had the forest cleared and built a city there.

King Dachi of Iberia (r. 522-534), Vakhtang's successor, moved the capital of Iberia from Mtskheta to Tbilisi and began building the fortress wall that marked the city's new boundaries. From the sixth century Tbilisi grew steadily because of its strategic position on trade and travel routes between Europe and Asia. It served as the capital of various Georgian kingdoms and republics.

Between 1801 and 1917, as part of the Russian Empire, it was the seat of the Caucasus Viceroyalty, which governed both the northern and southern sides of the Caucasus. Its population has always been diverse in culture, ethnicity and religion, though overwhelmingly Eastern Orthodox Christian.

Tbilisi is the capital and largest city of Georgia, with more than 1.3 million inhabitants, almost one third of the country's population. Its architecture mixes medieval, neoclassical, Beaux Arts, Art Nouveau, Stalinist and modern buildings. Among its landmarks are the Sameba and Sioni cathedrals, the medieval Narikala Fortress and the Georgian National Museum.
teanum-sidicinum: Teano, the ancient Teanum Sidicinum, is a town in the province of Caserta in Campania, about 30 kilometres northwest of Caserta on the main railway line from Naples to Rome. It stands at the southeast foot of an extinct volcano, Rocca Monfina. Strabo calls Teanum the most important town on the Via Latina, joined by a branch road from Suessa.

Teanum Sidicinum was the capital of the Oscan tribe of the Sidicini, who drove the Aurunci from Roccamonfina. They probably submitted to Rome in 334 BCE, and their troops were grouped with those of Campania in the Roman army. Like Cales, Teanum kept the right of coinage, and like Suessa and Cales it remained faithful to Rome in both the Hannibalic and the Social wars. It was apparently made a colony by Claudius, not by Augustus.

In the 4th century Teano became the seat of a diocese, and it was later an important Lombard county, part of the Duchy of Benevento. Monks from Montecassino took refuge there when their abbey was destroyed in 883, and one of the first documents in the vernacular Italian was issued there in 963. On 26 October 1860 Teano was the site of the Handshake of Teano, when Giuseppe Garibaldi, having wrested the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies from the Neapolitan Bourbons, shook hands with Victor Emanuel II, King of Sardinia, and hailed him as King of Italy.

Roman remains include a theatre of the 2nd century BCE, rebuilt in the 2nd century CE, once one of the largest in Italy at 85 metres in diameter, and extensive baths known as Le Caldarelle. The cathedral of St Clement, begun around 1050 and finished in 1116, uses Corinthian columns taken from the ancient town. The castle, built by the dukes of Sessa in the 15th century on a fortress of the 4th century BCE, served as a prison in the Bourbon era. The cathedral is the see of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Teano-Calvi.
tecumseh: Tecumseh was born in Shawnee territory in what is now Ohio, probably at the town of Chillicothe on the Scioto River, into the Panther clan of the Kispoko division. His father, the war chief Puckeshinwau, was killed in the 1774 Battle of Point Pleasant, after which the Shawnees ceded Kentucky to the colonists. His older brother Cheeseekau, a noted war chief, taught him.

At the age of fifteen Tecumseh attended an intertribal conference at Lower Sandusky, where speakers such as Joseph Brant argued that Indian lands were held in common and that no more should be ceded without the consent of all the tribes. As a young war leader he joined Chief Blue Jacket's armed struggle, which ended in defeat at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794 and the loss of most of Ohio in the 1795 Treaty of Greenville.

In 1805 his younger brother Lalawéthika, later known as Tenskwatawa, began preaching that Native Americans should reject European influences, stop drinking alcohol and return to a traditional way of life. Tecumseh followed his teachings. In 1808 the brothers established Prophetstown in present-day Indiana, which grew into a large multi-tribal community.

After the Treaty of Fort Wayne Tecumseh became prominent and tried to build a confederacy from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico. In August 1810 he met William Henry Harrison at Vincennes and demanded that the treaty be rescinded, saying that otherwise they would have to fight it out. In 1811, while he was in the South seeking allies, Harrison defeated Tenskwatawa at the Battle of Tippecanoe and destroyed Prophetstown.

In June 1812 Tecumseh joined the British at Fort Malden. He took part in the Siege of Detroit under Major-General Isaac Brock, where he led about 530 warriors, and General William Hull surrendered on 16 August 1812. At Fort Meigs in 1813 he is said to have stopped the killing of American prisoners.

After the American naval victory in the Battle of Lake Erie on 10 September 1813, General Henry Procter decided to retreat from Amherstburg. Tecumseh reluctantly agreed and retreated with him up the Thames River. At the Battle of the Thames on 5 October he held the right with about 500 warriors while Procter's left collapsed, and he was killed in the fighting led by Colonel Richard Mentor Johnson. His confederacy collapsed after his death.

He was admired even by Americans who had fought him, and Harrison called him one of those uncommon geniuses who produce revolutions. He became a folk hero in American, Indigenous and Canadian history.
tegucigalpa: Tegucigalpa lies in the southern-central highlands of Honduras, in a valley ringed by mountains, in the department of Francisco Morazán, of which it is also the departmental capital. The city stands on a chain of mountains, at elevations of 975 metres at its lowest points and 1,463 metres in its highest suburbs, and is hilly with few flat areas. The Choluteca River separates it from its sister city Comayagüela. The surrounding country was open woodland of pine and oak, and the climate is a tropical savanna one, tempered by the altitude, with a rainy and a dry season.

The Spaniards claimed the site on 29 September 1578 and founded it as the Real de Minas de San Miguel de Tegucigalpa, on the site of an existing settlement of the Lenca and the Tolupans. Juan de la Cueva became its first mayor in 1579. Among its first important buildings were the Dolores Church (1735), the San Miguel Cathedral (1765), the Casa de la Moneda (1780) and the Immaculate Conception Church (1788). The origin of the name is uncertain: the most widely accepted version derives it from a Nahuatl phrase meaning 'hills of silver', although the local people are said to have been unaware of the mineral deposits, and other proposals include 'painted rocks'.

On 30 October 1880 President Marco Aurelio Soto moved the seat of government from Comayagua to Tegucigalpa. The constitution of 1936 made Tegucigalpa and Comayagüela a single Central District, formed on 30 January 1937, and the constitution of 1982 keeps that arrangement as the permanent national capital. In late October and early November 1998 Hurricane Mitch stayed over Honduras for five days; on saturated ground and deforested slopes the rain caused catastrophic flooding, especially in Tegucigalpa, and destroyed parts of the city along the banks of the Choluteca.

Tegucigalpa is the largest city of Honduras and its political and administrative centre, seat of the national government and of the National Autonomous University of Honduras, founded in 1847. Legally the capital is the Municipality of the Central District, though nearly all government institutions stand on the Tegucigalpa side of the river, while Comayagüela on the western bank is largely made up of lower-income neighbourhoods. The census of 2013 counted 1,157,509 people in the Central District. Roman Catholicism has been the leading religion since the Mercedarian missions of about 1548, and the Diocese of Comayagua was moved to the city and renamed the Diocese of Tegucigalpa by 1916.
tehran: Tehran is bounded in the north by the southern end of the Alborz range, whose highest point near the city is Tochal Peak at 3,963 metres. The northern districts begin at about 1,800 metres, with houses and streets on steep slopes, while Rey at the southern end lies at about 1,100 metres beside the single mountain of Raga. Fertile meadows and villages, fed by the Karaj and Jajrud rivers, lie to the west and south-west. Mount Damavand, Iran's highest peak, stands near the city and figures in Ferdowsi's Šāhnāme as the homeland of Keyumars and the place where King Fereydun bound the dragon fiend Zahhak.

The origin of the name is disputed. The city's own account derives it from the Persian words for 'bottom' and 'slope', the foot of the mountain, while the linguist Zana Kamrani proposes that it means 'the warm place', in contrast to Shemiran, 'the cool place'.

Archaeological remains from the ancient city of Ray suggest that settlement in the area is more than 6,000 years old. In the Median period part of present-day Tehran was a suburb of the prominent city of Rhages, which appears in the Avesta and in Old Persian inscriptions as a province; from there Darius I sent reinforcements to his father Hystaspes in Parthia. In 641 the last Sasanian king, Yazdgerd III, issued his final appeal to the nation from Rhages before fleeing to Khorasan. Because the city resisted the Muslim invasion, the Arabs ordered it destroyed and rebuilt by the aristocrat Farrukhzad.

In the ninth century Tehran was a well-known village, though less so than the flourishing Rhages nearby. Agha Mohammad Khan of the Qajar dynasty first chose it as the capital of Iran in 1786, because of its closeness to Iran's contested territories in the Caucasus and to avoid the rival factions of earlier dynasties. Under Reza Shah the city gained Iran's first institute of higher learning, bank, railway line and museum. Large-scale construction began in the 1920s, and Tehran became a destination for mass migration from all over Iran, especially in the 20th century.

Tehran is the capital and largest city of Iran, with 8,693,706 inhabitants at the 2016 census. Persians are the majority, with Azeris the second-largest ethnic group at about 10 to 15 per cent. Its historical sites include the Golestan Palace of the Qajar dynasty, a World Heritage Site, and the Sa'dabad and Niavaran palace complexes; the Azadi Tower was built in 1971 to mark 2,500 years of the Persian Empire.
telangana: Telangana lies on the Deccan Plateau, in the central stretch of the eastern seaboard of the Indian Peninsula, and covers 112,077 square kilometres. It borders Maharashtra and Chhattisgarh to the north and Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka to the south. The Godavari and Krishna rivers drain it, along with smaller rivers such as the Bhima, the Manjira and the Musi, but most of the land is arid. The name comes from Telinga, and was used to set the predominantly Telugu region of the old Hyderabad State apart from Marathwada and Kalyana-Karnataka.

One of the earliest known political formations here was the Aśmaka Mahajanapada, which flourished roughly between 700 and 400 BCE and was the only southern kingdom among the sixteen great Mahajanapadas. Its capital, Podana, is identified by most scholars with present-day Bodhan. The region later belonged to many empires, among them the Maurya, Satavahana, Chalukya, Chola, Rashtrakuta, Delhi Sultanate, Bahmani Sultanate and Golconda Sultanate. The region experienced a golden age under the Kakatiya dynasty, which ruled most of present-day Andhra Pradesh and Telangana from 1083 to 1323; Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra II were prominent rulers. It weakened after the attack of Malik Kafur in 1309 and was dissolved when Muhammad bin Tughluq's forces defeated Prataparudra in 1323.

From the seventeenth to the nineteenth century the Mughals and the Nizams of Hyderabad ruled the region. In 1823 the Nizams ceded the Northern Circars and the Ceded Districts to British India, which left Hyderabad a landlocked princely state. When India became independent in 1947 the Nizam wished to stay independent, and the Government of India annexed Hyderabad State on 17 September 1948 in a military operation called Operation Polo. After decades of protest by the Telangana movement, the state of Telangana was created in 2014 from the Telugu regions of the former Hyderabad State.

Telangana has Hyderabad as its capital. Telugu is the primary official language and Urdu the second; about 75 per cent of people speak Telugu and 12 per cent Urdu. Before 1948 Urdu was the official language of Hyderabad State and the language of the educated elite. At the 2011 census Hindus formed 85.1 per cent of the population and Muslims 12.7 per cent. Warangal Fort, the Kakatiya capital, has the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, which appears on the state emblem, and the Ramappa Temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The state is divided into 33 districts.
telavi: Telavi is the main city and administrative centre of the province of Kakheti. It lies on the foothills of the Tsiv-Gombori Range, 500 to 800 m above sea level, facing the range to the south and south-west and bordering the Alazani Valley to the north and east. The Greater Caucasus Mountain Range, which runs to the north of the valley, can be seen from most of the city.

The first archaeological finds from Telavi date from the Bronze Age. In the 2nd century CE the Greek geographer Claudius Ptolemaeus mentions a name, Teleda, that refers to it. From the 8th century it grew into a fairly important political and administrative centre. The Arab geographer Al-Muqaddasi in the 10th century listed it beside Tbilisi, Ganja, Shamkhor, Shemakha and Shirvan, and noted that most of its population was Christian.

From the 10th to the 12th centuries Telavi was the capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti and later of Kakheti-Hereti. During the Georgian state's 12th and 13th centuries it became one of its most important political and economic centres. After the united Georgian Kingdom disintegrated in the 15th century its role declined and it became an ordinary town of trade and crafts. It regained importance in the 17th century as the capital of the Kingdom of Kakheti, and by 1762 it was the second capital, after Tbilisi, of the united eastern Georgian Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti.

King Erekle II, who was born and died in Telavi, reigned from 1744 to 1798, and the period was a special epoch for the town. He founded a theological seminary and a theatre there, and Georgians remember him affectionately as Patara Kakhi, the Little Kakhetian. In 1801 Kartli-Kakheti was annexed by the Russian Empire and Telavi lost its status as a capital. In the 19th century it was the centre of the Telavi uezd in the Tiflis Governorate, with small industries such as pottery, leather painting and wine-making. About 12,000 people lived there at the end of the century, around 9,000 of them Armenians and 2,000 Georgians.

Telavi has about 16,800 inhabitants. It keeps four fortification monuments from four periods, which leads scholars to call it the most medieval city in Georgia. They include Batonis Tsikhe, a 17th-century fortress that is one of the few well-preserved medieval royal palaces in the country, and Dzveli Galavani, the fortress of the first Kakhetian kings. Nearby are the 11th-century Alaverdi Cathedral, the Ikalto Academy, where Shota Rustaveli studied, the ruins of Gremi and the Tsinandali Gardens. The Armenian churches of the old town were mostly closed in 1923.
telegraph: Signalling over distance is ancient. The signal towers of the Great Wall of China are among the oldest examples, and by 400 BCE signals could be sent by beacon fires or drum beats. These ancient systems, including Chinese ones, could send only predetermined messages and so were not true telegraphs. The first true telegraph in widespread use was the optical telegraph of Claude Chappe, which operated in France from 1793; its stations signalled to each other with shutters or paddles. The word telegraph, from the Greek for writing at a distance, was coined by Chappe himself.

Early electric telegraphs were electrostatic, with a system over a substantial distance by Ronalds in 1816, which the British Admiralty rejected as unnecessary because its optical telegraph to Portsmouth seemed adequate. Electromagnetic systems replaced the electrostatic ones. The first operative electric telegraph, by Gauss and Weber in 1833, linked Göttingen Observatory to the Institute of Physics about a kilometre away.

Cooke and Wheatstone received a patent for an electric telegraph on 12 June 1837, and the world's first permanent railway telegraph, between London Paddington and West Drayton, was completed in July 1839. Railway companies installed lines first in Germany and Britain, and private companies then offered a public service along them. Samuel Morse developed a rival system in the United States, and the Morse system was adopted as the international standard in 1865, using a modified code developed in Germany in 1848.

Ocean cables needed a flexible insulator that resisted seawater. Gutta-percha, a natural rubber sent to London from Singapore by William Montgomerie in 1843, proved suitable, and a cable between Dover and Calais was laid in 1850, though a French fishing vessel severed it almost at once. It was relaid the next year, and connections to Ireland and the Low Countries followed. Telegrams became popular once prices fell, and at their peak in 1929 an estimated 200 million were sent.

The electric telegraph freed communication from the time constraints of the postal service and revolutionised society and the global economy. Earlier optical lines had been installed by governments, often for military purposes, and reserved for official use. By the end of the 19th century the telegraph was increasingly common among ordinary people. Some feared that it would erode public discourse by carrying irrelevant, context-free news; Henry David Thoreau imagined that the first news over the Atlantic cable would be that Princess Adelaide had the whooping cough.

Use began to decline around 1920 with the growth of the telephone, which grew out of work on the harmonic telegraph. Teleprinters, punched tape and the Baudot code automated transmission, and telex, a switched network of teleprinters, became operational in Germany in 1933.
telemark: Telemark lies in south-eastern Norway, extending from the Hardangervidda mountain plateau in the north to the Skagerrak coast in the south. Its landscape includes a rugged coastline, valleys, lakes, hills and mountain plateaus. The name means the mark of the Thelir, the ancient North Germanic tribe that inhabited what is now Upper Telemark in the Migration Period and the Viking Age. The Norse form was Þelamǫrk, whose last element means woodland or borderland. Traditional Telemark, now called Upper Telemark, lies inland and makes up more than two thirds of the county by its traditional definition. The south, Grenland, is flatter, closer to the coast and more urban.

Upper Telemark had more self-owning farmers than any other region of Norway, in the Middle Ages and later. It kept Norse culture to a greater degree, in its more egalitarian society, religion, values and language, and the people were often described as the most violent in Norway. Its farmers held on to aspects of Old Norse religion and later of Catholicism longer than other regions and often defied the central authorities of Denmark-Norway. Its dialects are the closest to Old Norse, and it has more buildings from medieval times than any other Norwegian region. Upper Telemark traditionally lacks cities entirely.

Grenland and the Skien fjord were marked by cities, seafaring, trade and industry, with more contact with continental Europe. Skien was in the early modern period one of Norway's most important cities, ahead of Christiania, though its importance declined after the Napoleonic Wars. The playwright Henrik Ibsen was born there. During the union with Denmark the two regions became the fief of Bratsberg, named after the farm where the governor had his seat. With the introduction of absolute monarchy in 1662 it became a county, and it was renamed Telemark in 1919.

Kviteseid in Upper Telemark is known as the birthplace of skiing as a modern sport. The Telemark style of skiing, invented by Sondre Norheim, and the Telemark landing of ski jumping are named after it. Telemark has also been a major industrial region for centuries, with paper mills in Grenland and heavy water and fertilizer production by Norsk Hydro in Upper Telemark.

Telemark merged with Vestfold in 2020, and on 1 January 2024 the county of Telemark was re-established. Its largest population centres are Skien, Porsgrunn, Notodden, Rjukan and Kragerø. The international road E134, the fastest route between Oslo and Bergen, runs through its inland municipalities. The Gea Norvegica Geopark, established in 2006 in the south, is the first UNESCO Global Geopark in Scandinavia.
telescope: The word telescope was coined in 1611 by the Greek mathematician Giovanni Demisiani for one of Galileo Galilei's instruments, presented at a banquet of the Accademia dei Lincei. In the Starry Messenger Galileo had used the Latin term perspicillum. The Greek roots are tele, far, and skopein, to look or see, giving teleskopos, far-seeing. The first practical instruments were refracting telescopes with glass lenses, used both on land and for astronomy. Word of the invention spread through Europe, and Galileo heard of it before building his own version.

Originally the telescope was an optical instrument that used lenses, curved mirrors or both to observe distant objects. The word now covers a wide range of instruments that detect different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum. There are three main optical types: the refracting telescope, which forms an image with lenses; the reflecting telescope, which uses mirrors; and the catadioptric telescope, which combines mirrors with lenses. A place holding one or more telescopes or other instruments is called an observatory.

Radio telescopes are directional antennas that usually employ a large dish. By correlating the signals received by several dishes, astronomers compute high-resolution images, a technique called aperture synthesis. X-rays are harder to focus, and X-ray telescopes use ring-shaped mirrors of heavy metals that reflect the rays at a glancing angle; Hans Wolter outlined three ways of building such a telescope in 1952. Because the atmosphere is opaque to most of the spectrum, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray instruments are carried on balloons or satellites.

The idea that the light-gathering element could be a mirror instead of a lens was investigated soon after the refracting telescope appeared. Parabolic mirrors promised less spherical aberration and no chromatic aberration. In 1668 Isaac Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope, of the design now called the Newtonian reflector. The achromatic lens of 1733 partly corrected the colour fringes of simple lenses and allowed shorter, more useful refractors.

Reflectors were long hampered by mirrors of speculum metal, which tarnished quickly in the 18th and early 19th centuries. Silver-coated glass mirrors, introduced in 1857, and aluminized mirrors, from 1932, eased the problem. Refractors cannot grow beyond about one metre across, so most large research telescopes built since the turn of the 20th century are reflectors. John Dobson invented the Dobsonian telescope in 1956. The first purpose-built radio telescope began operating in 1937, and infrared telescopes followed in the 1960s.
telugu-language: Telugu descends from Proto-Dravidian, which linguistic reconstruction places around the fourth millennium BCE. It belongs to the South Dravidian-II, or South-Central Dravidian, subgroup, with Gondi, Kuvi, Koya, Pengo, Konda and Manda. The philologist Mikhail S. Andronov places its separation from Proto-Dravidian at about 1000 BCE. The name is explained as a form of Tenugu, from the Proto-Dravidian word for south, meaning the people who lived to the south of the speakers of Sanskrit and Prakrit; Telugu results from an alternation of n and l.

Its history is divided into phases. Telugu words appear early in Prakrit inscriptions, and one early word, nāgabu, found at the Amaravati Stupa, is dated to about 200 BCE. The first long inscription entirely in Telugu, dated to 575 CE, is attributed to the Renati Choda king Dhanunjaya and was found in the Kadapa district. Titles of Mahendravarman I in Telugu, from about 600 CE, are inscribed in caves in Tamil Nadu. About 10,000 pre-colonial inscriptions survive in Telugu.

Telugu is a Dravidian language native to the Indian states of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, where it is the official language, and is also official in the Yanam district of Puducherry. It is spoken by about 100 million people and is the most widely spoken member of its family. Words generally end in vowels. Its grammar has suffixes only, with three noun classes, seven cases and a basic subject-object-verb order. Most of its vocabulary is inherited from Proto-Dravidian, with many borrowings from Sanskrit. There are Telangana, Rayalaseema, Coastal Andhra and North Andhra dialects, and standard Telugu is based on the speech of educated speakers of the central dialect.

Telugu has an unbroken literary tradition of over a thousand years. The Vijayanagara Empire dominated from 1336 to the late 17th century, and Telugu literature had what is considered its Golden Age in the 16th century under Krishnadevaraya. The Venetian explorer Niccolò de' Conti, visiting in the 15th century, noted that its words end in vowels, as in Italian, and called it the Italian of the East. In the precolonial era it became the language of high culture throughout South India, which Vijaya Ramaswamy compared to the dominance of French in Europe. Telugu also predominates in Carnatic music.

Persian and Arabic influence produced a distinct variant around Hyderabad, beginning with the Delhi Sultanate in the 14th century. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries English influence and the printing press, especially in the Madras Presidency, shaped writers such as Kandukuri Veeresalingam and Gurajada Apparao. The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act of 1966 declared Telugu the official language of the state, later divided into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
temple-in-jerusalem: According to the Hebrew Bible, the First Temple was built by King Solomon in the 10th century BCE, completed in 957 BCE. As the sole place of Israelite sacrifice, according to Deuteronomy, it replaced the Tabernacle built in the Sinai under Moses. The Bible says it was sacked a few decades later by Shishak, identified as the pharaoh Shoshenq I. It was destroyed c. 587 BCE in the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations have not found remnants of it.

According to the Book of Ezra, Cyrus the Great called for the Second Temple to be built, and work began in 538 BCE. Some 19th-century calculations place completion on 21 February 515 BCE, though some modern researchers consider these dates unreliable. The governor Zerubbabel dedicated the new temple, and Herod the Great later renovated it.

The First Temple had an outer court where people assembled, an inner court of the priests and the temple building, with the larger Holy Place and the smaller inner sanctum, the Holy of Holies. The Herodian Temple was the most elaborate, with a wide precinct including the Court of the Gentiles, the Court of the Women and the Court of the Israelites for ritually pure Jewish men. Two surviving pieces of Herod's expansion are the Temple Warning inscriptions, which forbade pagans to enter the courtyard, and the Trumpeting Place inscription.

Daily morning and afternoon offerings were made there, with special offerings on festivals, while Levites recited Psalms. The daily service included the Shema and the Priestly Blessing, which still form the basis of the traditional morning service.

The destruction of the Temple is mourned on the fast day of Tisha B'Av, and weddings traditionally end with the groom breaking a glass in remembrance. Daily prayer contains petitions for its rebuilding. In the Middle Ages the Temple appeared in illuminated manuscripts, marriage contracts and wedding rings.

For Muslims the site is the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, or Haram al-Sharif, regarded as the third-holiest site in Islam and the destination of Muhammad's Night Journey. According to tradition, Umar cleared the site after the Muslim conquest, and the Dome of the Rock was built on the mount under Abd al-Malik. In Christianity, Matthew 24:2 records Jesus predicting the destruction of the Second Temple.
temple-of-artemis: The temple stood near the ancient city of Ephesus, near modern Selçuk in Turkey. The sacred site was older than the temple itself: excavations in 1987–1988 confirmed that it was occupied as early as the Bronze Age, and a peripteral temple with a floor of hard-packed clay was built in the second half of the 8th century BCE, perhaps the earliest Greek temple surrounded by colonnades anywhere. In the 7th century BCE a flood destroyed it. The ancient accounts differ on the older history: Pausanias believed the temple pre-dated the Amazons, while Callimachus attributed the first sanctuary to them.

The second temple was sponsored at least in part by Croesus, who founded Lydia's empire and was overlord of Ephesus. Designed from around 550 BCE by the Cretan architect Chersiphron and his son Metagenes, it was 115 metres long and 46 metres wide and supposedly the first Greek temple built of marble. A rich foundation deposit yielded more than a thousand items, including what may be the earliest coins of electrum. The temple attracted merchants, kings and sightseers.

In 356 BCE it burned down. Ancient sources describe an arson by Herostratus, who sought fame; the Ephesians sentenced him to death and forbade anyone to mention his name. Modern scholars have questioned his part. Alexander the Great offered to pay for the rebuilding, but the Ephesians refused, saying it would be improper for one god to build a temple to another, and after his death they rebuilt it at their own expense from 323 BCE. The third temple measured 137 by 69 metres, with more than 127 columns. The cult of Artemis was closely tied to the civic identity of Ephesus, and large crowds came each year for the main procession.

According to Jordanes, a raid by the Goths in the 3rd century CE set fire to the temple, though the extent of the damage is unknown, and Christian authors refer to its closure in the 5th century. Some of its stone was reused in other buildings. The site was rediscovered in 1869 by an expedition led by John Turtle Wood and sponsored by the British Museum, after six years of searching; excavations continued until 1874, and David George Hogarth excavated in 1904–1906. Sculpted fragments are displayed in the British Museum. Today a single column built from fragments marks the site.
ten-commandments: The phrase Ten Commandments comes from Exodus 34:28, Deuteronomy 4:13 and Deuteronomy 10:4, and in each case can be translated as the ten words, sayings or matters. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, rendered it as dekalogos, which became Latin decalogus and English Decalogue.

In the biblical narrative the revelation begins in Exodus 19, when the Israelites reach Mount Sinai, also called Horeb. On the third morning there are thunders, lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain, and in Exodus 20 God speaks the words of the covenant to all the people. Scholars have proposed three main datings: early Mosaic authorship, a pre-exilic monarchic origin, or a postexilic composition. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman argue for the seventh century BCE, and David H. Aaron for a date after 586 BCE.

The seventeen verses of Exodus 20:1 to 17 and Deuteronomy 5:4 to 21 are divided into ten commandments in different ways, although they contain more than ten imperatives. One approach separates the prohibition of other gods from that of images, as in the Septuagint and among Eastern Orthodox and Reformed Christians following Calvin. Another joins them, as Augustine did in the 4th century, dividing the prohibition on coveting into two. The Samaritan Pentateuch adds an instruction to sacrifice to Yahweh, which Samaritans count as the tenth.

Exodus 34:28 itself names the passage of Exodus 34:11 to 27 as the Ten Commandments, and since it concerns proper worship rather than murder or theft, some scholars call it the Ritual Decalogue and the better known text the Ethical Decalogue.

In Judaism the commandments are the foundation of rabbinic law, held to state God's universal and timeless standard, unlike the rest of the 613 commandments the tradition finds in the Torah. Most Christian traditions hold that they remain valid and divinely authoritative. In the New Testament, Jesus refers to the prohibitions of murder and adultery in the Sermon on the Mount and repeats five of them in Matthew 19. In Islam the receiving of the tablets by Moses is described in Surah A'raf, and Surah An'am 6:151 to 153 is widely taken as a reinstatement of the commandments.

After the Reformation, European Protestants replaced some visual art in churches with plaques of the Ten Commandments. In England such Decalogue boards also represented the monarch's emphasis on royal law within the churches. In 1980 the United States Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional a Kentucky statute requiring a copy in every public classroom. Hundreds of monuments were placed as publicity for Cecil B. DeMille's 1956 film The Ten Commandments.
tengrism: The name Tengri is first recorded in Chinese chronicles, in the 4th century BCE, as the sky god of the Xiongnu. Tengrism formed from Turkic and Mongolic folk religions that had many deities, spirits and gods and resembled the religious traditions of Siberia, Central Asia and Northeast Asia; ancestor worship played an important part. The cult of Heaven-Tengri is fixed in the Old Turkic script of the Göktürks in inscriptions of the 8th to 10th centuries. The word Tengrism itself is recent: it was brought into scholarly use in 1956 by the French scholar Jean-Paul Roux.

Tengrism is an animistic belief system that includes medicine, reverence of nature and ancestor worship. It centres on the sky god Gök Tengri, who stays abstract and is never shown in human or animal form, while other deities are often personified. Itugen, an earth or fertility deity, often accompanies Tengri; Umay is the goddess of children, and Kayra and Ülgen are other gods. Its cosmology divides the world into the heavens, the Earth and an underworld, joined by a world tree, and a shaman, called a kam, can communicate with the spirits of these worlds. People and animals are believed to have several souls.

Old Turkic inscriptions describe humans as the product of Heaven above and Earth beneath, so that mankind is part of nature and holds no special rank over it. Scholars disagree on its character: many hold it to have been mainly polytheistic and shamanistic, first touched by monotheism in the imperial period, while the Turkish historian Ahmet Taşağıl argues that it had a distinct theological structure around an abstract deity in heaven.

Tengrism was the prevailing religion of the Göktürk, Hun, Xiongnu, Bulgar and Mongolic peoples and the state religion of several medieval states, among them the First Turkic Khaganate, Khazaria and the Mongol Empire. The Orkhon inscriptions say that Tengri had a large part in the choice of the khagan and in guiding his acts, many of which were done because Heaven so ordained. The Secret History of the Mongols, written in 1240, traces Genghis Khan's ancestry to Borte Chino, the Blue Wolf, born with destiny from Tengri. Khans also held religious debates, whose outcomes were viewed as guided by heavenly support.

Tengrism was assimilated into Mongolian Buddhism, surviving unassimilated only in far-northern Mongolia, and Turkic and Mongolic peoples in Central Asia largely converted to Islam during the 14th century, often through Sufism, in which both Gök Tengri and Allah appear as names of God. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 a revival has taken place in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Mongolia and parts of Russia such as Buryatia and Sakha. Related movements include Altaian Burkhanism and the Chuvash Vattisen Yaly.
tennessee: Tennessee is a landlocked state that borders eight others: Kentucky and Virginia to the north, North Carolina to the east, Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi to the south, and Arkansas and Missouri to the west. It is divided into three Grand Divisions, East, Middle and West Tennessee. The Blue Ridge Mountains along the eastern border reach some of the highest elevations in eastern North America, the Cumberland Plateau has scenic valleys and waterfalls, and West Tennessee has level, fertile plains. The Tennessee River crosses the state twice and the Mississippi River forms its western border.

The first inhabitants were Paleo-Indians who arrived about 12,000 years ago, at the end of the Last Glacial Period. Archaeologists name the Archaic (8000–1000 BCE), Woodland (1000 BCE–1000 CE) and Mississippian (1000–1600 CE) periods. Squash, corn, gourds and sunflowers were first grown in Tennessee during the Woodland period, when the first mounds were built, and Mississippian peoples developed organised chiefdoms and built many ceremonial structures. The state's name comes most directly from the Cherokee town of Tanasi. A Spanish party under Juan Pardo met a village called Tanasqui in 1567, and Governor James Glen of South Carolina is credited with the modern spelling in the 1750s.

The Watauga Association of 1772, a frontier pact, is generally regarded as the first constitutional government west of the Appalachian Mountains. The area was first part of North Carolina and then of the Southwest Territory, and it became the 16th state on 1 June 1796. Its constitutions date from 1796, 1834 and 1870. The capital moved among Knoxville, Nashville and Murfreesboro before Nashville became the permanent capital in 1843. The nickname The Volunteer State reflects a strong tradition of military service.

Tennessee was a slave state until the Civil War and was politically divided: most of the west and middle supported the Confederacy, while the east was largely pro-Union. It was the last state to secede and the first former Confederate state readmitted to the Union. In the 20th century it moved from an agrarian society to a more diversified economy, helped by the Tennessee Valley Authority and by Oak Ridge, established in the Second World War to house the Manhattan Project's uranium enrichment facilities.

Nashville is the capital and largest city; Memphis, Knoxville, Chattanooga and Clarksville follow. The state has 95 counties and about 7.2 million people. Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the most visited national park in the United States, lies in the east. Tennessee has played a major role in the development of country, blues, rock and roll, soul and gospel music, and the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville has broadcast continuously since 1925.
tenochtitlan: Tenochtitlan, also called Mexico-Tenochtitlan, was a Mexica altepetl, or city-state, on an island in Lake Texcoco. The exact date of its founding is unclear; 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 to mark the 600th anniversary. Tradition held that the Mexica were to settle where an eagle with a snake in its beak perched on a cactus, and they saw this vision on a small swampy island. The city covered an estimated 8 to 13.5 square kilometres and was linked to the mainland by causeways to the north, south and west, broken by bridges that could be pulled away. Canals ran through it, so that every part could be reached on foot or by canoe.

Lake Texcoco was brackish. The levee of Nezahualcoyotl, reputedly designed by him and completed around 1453, kept fresh spring water around the city. Two double aqueducts of terracotta, each more than 4 kilometres long, brought water from the springs at Chapultepec. The city was divided into four zones, each of 20 districts called calpullis.

Using the chinampa system, the Mexica built up and expanded the island, and Tenochtitlan became the capital of the expanding Aztec Empire in the 15th century. After a flood of the lake the city was rebuilt under Ahuitzotl, who ruled between 1486 and 1502. Its population has been estimated at between 200,000 and 400,000, and one academic survey arrived at 212,500 people on 13.5 square kilometres. In the ceremonial centre, a walled square 500 metres to a side, stood about 45 public buildings, among them the Templo Mayor, dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. The marketplace of its sister city Tlatelolco drew, by Hernán Cortés's estimate, about 60,000 people daily.

Cortés arrived on 8 November 1519, and the ruler Moctezuma II received him as an ambassador. Cortés later besieged the city, causing famine, while disease spread among its people. Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521. Cortés then directed its systematic destruction and founded Mexico City on its ruins, with a Spanish zone, the traza, at the centre. Indigenous people were settled in San Juan Tenochtitlan and Santiago Tlatelolco, each with its own council.

The ruins lie in the historic centre of Mexico City. The Templo Mayor was dismantled and built over by the Spanish, and its site was rediscovered in the early 20th century; major excavations took place from 1978 to 1982 after workers found a stone disc of the goddess Coyolxauhqui, 3.25 metres across. Mexico City's Zócalo stands on the original central plaza, and many of the old causeways correspond to modern streets. The World Heritage Site of Xochimilco contains what remains of the Mexica capital's waters, boats and floating gardens.
tenzing-norgay: Accounts of Tenzing's early life conflict. In his autobiography he wrote that he was a Sherpa born and raised at Tengboche in Khumbu, in north-eastern Nepal; many later accounts say he was born in Tibet, in the Kama Valley, and grew up at Thame. He was born Namgyal Wangdi, and his name was changed on the advice of the head lama of Rongbuk Monastery. His exact date of birth is unknown, but the Tibetan calendar year and Hunt's statement that he was 39 in 1953 make 1914 likely. After the ascent of Everest he decided to celebrate his birthday on 29 May.

As a teenager he ran away from home twice, to Kathmandu and then to Darjeeling, where he settled among the Sherpas and eventually acquired Indian citizenship. He once went to Tengboche Monastery to become a monk, but decided that was not for him and left.

At 20 he joined Eric Shipton's 1935 British reconnaissance expedition to Everest, and he went on three official British attempts from the Tibetan side in the 1930s as a high-altitude porter. In 1952 he took part in the two Swiss expeditions, the first serious attempts from the Nepalese side; on 28 May he and Raymond Lambert reached about 8,595 metres on the south-east ridge, a new altitude record.

In 1953 he joined John Hunt's expedition of over 400 people. After Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans turned back from the South Summit on 26 May, Hunt directed Tenzing and Edmund Hillary to go for the summit. They reached the summit at 11:30 on 29 May and stayed about 15 minutes. Journalists asked which of them was first; Hunt answered that they reached it together, as a team, and in his 1955 autobiography Tenzing wrote that Hillary stepped on top first. Hillary and Hunt were knighted, while Tenzing, who was not a British subject, received the George Medal.

In 1954 Tenzing became the first Director of Field Training of the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute in Darjeeling. In 1959 the Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan. He died of a cerebral haemorrhage in Darjeeling on 9 May 1986, at the age of 71, and was cremated at the Institute. In 2003 the Indian government renamed its highest adventure sports award after him, and in 2008 Lukla Airport became Tenzing–Hillary Airport.
tepelene: Tepelenë is a town and municipality in Gjirokastër County in southern Albania. It lies on the left bank of the Vjosa River, on a plateau about three kilometres downstream from the river's union with the Drino. North of the town the Bënça flows into the Vjosa. Its location at the confluence of two valleys has made it an important traffic hub in southern Albania. A ruined citadel stands on a point 300 metres above the river.

The name has been explained in three ways: from the Turkish word Tepedelen, meaning head-piercing; from Tepe e Lenes, the hill of Lenes; or, the version regarded as most convincing, from an Illyrian word Antibylyne, meaning in front of the Bylynes.

The Byzantines built a defensive tower there, which was developed under the Ottoman Empire in the 15th century and again by Ali Pasha in the early 19th century. Tepelenë and Ioannina were Ali Pasha's headquarters. The British writer Edward Lear visited in 1847 and noted devastated buildings. In July 1833 the inhabitants rose in revolt against Emin Pasha, and in February 1909 the Young Turk revolutionaries met there to try to persuade Albanian nationalists to join them.

An earthquake in 1920 severely damaged the town, which was rebuilt completely. Italian forces landed in Albania on 7 April 1939 and took Tepelenë. After the failed Italian invasion of Greece in 1940 the Greek army advanced towards the town but could not take it, and withdrew in late April 1941 after the German invasion of Yugoslavia. After the war the socialist government turned the Italian army camp into a labour camp, where influential Albanian families of earlier governments were held. The camp closed in 1954. In March 1997 a people's committee took charge of the town during the unrest and released the opposition politician Fatos Nano from the local prison.

The municipality was formed in the 2015 local government reform by merging Kurvelesh, Lopës, Qendër Tepelenë and Tepelenë. Until districts were abolished in 2000 the town was the seat of Tepelenë District. The municipality had 8,949 inhabitants at the 2011 census, on an area of 431.50 square kilometres. The National Road 4 from Fier to Gjirokastër runs through it, and a mineral water plant is an important local enterprise.
terceira: Terceira lies 1,181 kilometres due west of Lisbon and covers 396.75 square kilometres. It consists of four overlapping stratovolcanoes built over the Terceira Rift, a triple junction between the Eurasian, African and North American tectonic plates, and rising from more than 1,500 metres of ocean depth. The oldest, the Cinco Picos complex, finished its main activity some 370,000 years ago, and its caldera has largely been refilled to form a fertile plain. The only historical eruptions were in 1761, along a fissure on the Santa Bárbara volcano, and in 1867 and 1998 to 2000 from vents off the west coast.

The island first appears on the Venetian map of Andrea Bianco in 1436 as the Insula de Brasil. It may have been discovered on 1 January 1445 by Vicente de Lagos, pilot of Gonçalo Velho Cabral, and was first called the Island of Jesus Christ before the colloquial Terceira, meaning third, took over. Colonisation began by decree of Henry the Navigator on 21 March 1450, with the Fleming Jácome de Bruges as administrator. After he disappeared in 1474 the island was divided into the captaincies of Angra and Praia. Settlers from Madeira, enslaved people, New Christians and Jews developed wheat, sugar-cane and woad.

In the Portuguese succession crisis of 1580 the Azores were the only part of the Portuguese overseas empire to resist the Spanish, until the summer of 1583. The Azores welcomed the restoration of Portuguese independence under John IV in 1640. In the 1820s constitutionalists on Terceira set up a Junta Provisória in the name of Queen Maria II in 1828, and hostilities broke out at the Battle of Praia da Vitória in 1829. On 15 March 1830 the constitutionalist forces named Angra the Portuguese capital, and in 1832 Pedro I arrived to form a government in opposition to the absolutist regime in Lisbon.

Terceira has a population of 53,311. Its main town, Angra do Heroísmo, is the oldest city of the Azores, the historical capital of the archipelago and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is also the seat of the archipelago's Supreme Court. The island has two main seaports, at Angra do Heroísmo and Praia da Vitória, and the Lajes air base, which Portugal opened to the United States by an agreement signed in 1944. Portuguese bullfighting is popular, including the street version called tourada à corda.
terek-river: The Terek rises in the Mtskheta-Mtianeti region of Georgia, near the juncture of the Greater Caucasus range and the Khokh Range, south-west of Mount Kazbek. It winds north in a white torrent between the town of Stepantsminda and the village of Gergeti toward North Ossetia and Vladikavkaz, then turns east through Chechnya and Dagestan. Below Kizlyar it divides into two branches and forms a swampy delta about 100 kilometres wide where it enters the Caspian Sea. The Terek drains most of the north-eastern Caucasus, as its sister river the Kuban drains the north-western Caucasus into the Black Sea.

Its tributaries include the Malka, Ardon, Sunzha and, from the Darial Pass, the Kistinka and Armkhi. The main cities on the river are Vladikavkaz, Mozdok and Kizlyar, and small hydroelectric stations on its upper course provide power as well as irrigation.

In the Georgian Royal Annals the river is called Lomeki, from the Ingush name for its upper reaches, meaning mountain water. The Khazar capital Samandar may have stood on its banks. In 1262 the army of Hulagu, khan of the Ilkhanate, was defeated on the Terek by the army of Berke, khan of the Golden Horde, led by Berke's nephew Nogai Khan, in the Berke-Hulagu war, the first civil war of the Mongol Empire. In 1395 Timur defeated Tokhtamysh on the river.

The Terek Cossack Host, which existed from 1577 to 1832 and again from 1860, had its base in the Terek basin, and during the Russian conquest of the Caucasus it was part of the North Caucasus Line. Leo Tolstoy's novel The Cossacks is set on the river among its Cossacks. In late August 1942 German forces reached the Terek near Mozdok, the furthest extent of their conquests in the Soviet Union, but were unable to advance beyond a small bridgehead toward the Baku oil fields.
terence: Ancient authors say that Terence was born in Carthage and came to Rome as a slave in the household of an otherwise unknown senator, P. Terentius Lucanus, who educated and freed him, after which he took the name Terentius. He is said to have become a member of the Scipionic Circle. This biography derives from the Vita Terenti preserved in the commentary of Aelius Donatus and attributed to Suetonius, and it is often construed as conjecture based on the plays and their production notices. His cognomen Afer, meaning the African, may be the source of the report of African birth, since such names did not necessarily denote origin.

Terence wrote six comedies based on Greek originals by Menander or Apollodorus of Carystus, and all six survive complete. According to the production notices, each was staged by the company of Lucius Ambivius Turpio, with music by a tibicen named Flaccus. Andria was produced in 166 BCE, Heauton timorumenos in 163, Eunuchus and Phormio in 161, and Adelphoe and Hecyra in 160, the last after two abortive productions. Rome had no permanent theatre before 55 BCE, so the plays were staged on temporary wooden stages for audiences of fewer than 2,000.

Unlike Plautus, Terence favoured simple, conversational Latin over visual humour. Five of the six plays centre on a pair of young men in love. In his prologues he abandoned the traditional explanation of the plot and instead answered criticism, aimed at an old and spiteful poet whom Donatus identified as Luscius Lanuvinus.

According to tradition, Terence sailed east around the age of 25 and died either of disease in Greece or in a shipwreck on the return. His plays quickly became school texts, and by the end of the 2nd century BCE he was a literary classic. By the late 4th century CE he was one of four canonical school authors, with Cicero, Sallust and Vergil, and he kept a central place in the European curriculum until the 19th century, influencing William Shakespeare and Molière. The Codex Bembinus, kept in the Vatican library, dates to the 4th or early 5th century.
teresa-of-avila: Teresa Sánchez de Cepeda Dávila y Ahumada was born on 28 March 1515, either in Ávila or in Gotarrendura. Her paternal grandfather, Juan Sánchez de Toledo, was a converso, a Jew forced to convert to Christianity or emigrate; the Spanish Inquisition condemned him for allegedly returning to Judaism, but he later assumed a Catholic identity. Her father, Alonso Sánchez de Cepeda, was a successful wool merchant and one of the wealthiest men in Ávila.

Her mother raised her as a dedicated Christian. Fascinated by accounts of the lives of the saints, she ran away at seven with her brother Rodrigo to seek martyrdom in the fight against the Moors, until an uncle brought them home. After first resisting a religious vocation, she entered the Carmelite Convent of the Incarnation in 1534, at the age of 20, to the disappointment of her father.

Teresa wrote her autobiography, The Life of Teresa of Jesus, at Ávila between 1562 and 1565, as a defence of her ecstatic experiences; it was published after her death. The Way of Perfection appeared in 1566 and taught her nuns how to progress through prayer. The Interior Castle, written in 1577 and published in 1588, compares the soul to a castle with seven successive mansions, the innermost holding God, and treats the journey of faith as a passage through them to union with God.

In the autobiography she describes four stages of prayer, using the image of watering a garden: mental prayer and meditation, a prayer of quiet, absorption in God, and an ecstatic state. Commentators note that she wrote from her own experience and did not compose a systematic theology of prayer. Her other writings include poems and 342 surviving letters.

Teresa fell ill on a journey from Burgos to Alba de Tormes and died in 1582, just as Catholic Europe changed from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar and the dates of 5 to 14 October were removed. She died either before midnight on 4 October or early on 15 October, which is her feast day. She was buried at the Convento de la Anunciación in Alba de Tormes. Her body was moved to Ávila in 1585 and returned to Alba de Tormes in 1586, when Pope Sixtus V ordered that it remain there on pain of excommunication.
teresa-teng: Teresa Teng was the only daughter among five children of waishengren parents who had fled to Taiwan after the communist takeover of mainland China in 1949. Her father was a soldier in the Republic of China Armed Forces, and the family lived in military dependents' villages, first in Yunlin and then in Pingtung. Her father retired in 1957 and sold cakes to make ends meet. He loved Peking opera and her mother Huangmei opera, and both took her to theatres. At six she began voice lessons through an acquaintance of her father who instructed an Air Force band, and her first mentor introduced her to singing before military audiences, a practice she kept up throughout her life.

Her professional career began in 1967, when she hosted the television programme One Star a Day. At fourteen she left school to focus on music and signed with Yeu Jow Records, releasing albums of dance tunes, Western covers and folk tunes. She sang in nightclubs and set a record at Paris Night in Taipei with 70 consecutive days of 90-minute shows. In Hong Kong she worked with Polydor from 1975, and her album Island Love Songs: Goodbye My Love won the Ten-Star Prize. Her first Cantonese album, in 1980, was the year's best-seller.

She entered the Japanese market in 1973. Her first Japanese single, released on 1 March 1974, sold about 30,000 copies, but her second, Airport, released on 1 July 1974, sold 700,000. In 1979 she was caught entering Japan with a fake Indonesian passport and barred for a year. In 1983 she signed with Taurus Records and released Light Exquisite Feeling, which set twelve Tang and Song poems to music and was her first album of entirely new songs. In Taiwan her songs were also used in the Kuomintang's psychological war against the Chinese Communist Party, and were blasted from speakers on Kinmen Island towards the mainland.

Teng died on 8 May 1995, at the age of 42, while on holiday in Chiang Mai, Thailand. Several sources reported a severe asthma attack, while Thai doctors attributed her death to heart failure. No autopsy was performed, because the families of Teng and of her fiancé Paul Quilery declined it, and the police closed the case for lack of evidence.

She is credited as the first pop superstar of the Far East and a pioneer of modern Chinese popular music. Her songs were recorded in Mandarin, Hokkien, Cantonese, Shanghainese, Japanese, Indonesian, English and Italian. In 2007 she was inducted into the Popular Music Hall of Fame at the Koga Masao Museum of Music in Tokyo, the only non-Japanese person so honoured.
termez: Old Termez, a few kilometres west of the modern city on the Amu Darya, was founded sometime before the 3rd century BCE, making it one of the oldest towns of Central Asia. Most recent scholarship holds that it is the site of Alexander the Great's Alexandria on the Oxus, though some identify that city with Ai-Khanoum. After Seleucid rule it became part of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. Under the Kushan Empire Greek gave way to Bactrian in administration, and Termez, called Ta-li-mi in Chinese sources, became an important centre of Mahāsāṃghika Buddhism. In the 7th century the monk Xuanzang reported about ten monasteries with about a thousand monks.

The Umayyad Caliphate conquered the city in 676. It again became a religious centre under the Abbasid and Samanid empires, and produced the hadith scholar al-Tirmidhi and the Sufi theologian al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi. From the 11th to the 13th centuries it passed through the hands of the Ghaznavid, Seljuk, Karakhanid and Khorezmshah kingdoms. After a two-day siege in 1220 Genghis Khan's troops destroyed it, and one account says that the people were driven onto the plain and killed. Ibn Battuta found a new town, built two miles from the river. It later came under the Timurids and the Emirate of Bukhara, but by the second half of the 18th century it was again abandoned.

A village called Pattakesar stood near the ruins. The Russian Empire stationed a river fleet on the Amu Darya from 1887, and in 1900 the Emirate of Bukhara gave it over 9,000 acres. In 1928, under Soviet rule, Pattakesar was renamed Termez, and it became a town in 1929. During the Soviet–Afghan War of 1979 to 1989 over 100,000 Soviet troops were stationed there, and the Afghanistan–Uzbekistan Friendship Bridge was built. Soviet forces withdrew across it in 1989.

Termez is the capital of Surxondaryo Region in southern Uzbekistan and has about 182,800 inhabitants. The bridge at Hairatan, about 12 km east, is the only border crossing between Uzbekistan and Afghanistan. Its Archaeological Museum, opened in 2002, holds about 27,000 items, many of them Buddhist. Surviving sites include the Zurmala Stupa of the 1st to 2nd centuries, Fayaz Tepe, Kara Tepe and the Sultan Saodat necropolis of the Termez Sayyids, built between the 10th and 17th centuries.
ternopil: Ternopil, known until 1944 mostly as Tarnopol, stands on the banks of the Seret River in western Ukraine and belongs to the historical regions of Galicia and Podolia. Its Polish name, Tarnopol, means Tarnowski's city. The city began as a military stronghold and castle protecting the eastern borders of the Polish kingdom from Tatar raids. On 15 April 1540 King Sigismund I the Old, in Kraków, gave Jan Amor Tarnowski permission to establish it near Sopilche.

In 1570 the city passed to the Ostrogski family and in 1623 to the Zamoyski family. Turkish forces under Ibrahim Shishman Pasha almost completely destroyed it in 1675, during the Polish–Ottoman War, and Aleksander Koniecpolski rebuilt it. After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 it came under Austrian rule; it was under Russian rule from 1809 and returned to Austria in 1815. A railway linked it with Lemberg in 1870, and a Ukrainian gymnasium opened in 1898. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries it was the only urban locality in Galicia where ethnic Ukrainians outnumbered Poles.

It was proclaimed part of the West Ukrainian People's Republic on 11 November 1918 and became its temporary capital after Polish forces captured Lwów. Polish forces took it on 15 July 1919, and in the interwar period it was the capital of the Tarnopol Voivodeship. Soviet troops entered on 17 September 1939, and the city was incorporated into the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. After German occupation began on 2 July 1941, 10,000 Jews were killed in the city by July 1943 and another 6,000 were sent to the Belzec extermination camp. The Soviet offensive of 1944 almost completely destroyed it, and it was rebuilt in a Soviet style.
