Ternopil is the administrative centre of Ternopil Oblast and has been part of independent Ukraine since 1991. It is an important railway hub, and its light, food, electronics and construction industries grew under Soviet rule. Its universities include the West Ukrainian National University and the Ternopil Ivan Pul'uj National Technical University.
terracina: Terracina lies on the coast 56 km (35 mi) southeast of Rome, on the Via Appia, and the site has been occupied continuously since antiquity. It had strategic importance because the Volscian Hills reach the sea there, leaving no space for passage between them and the coast. The site also commands the Pontine Marshes, which Livy called a city surrounded by marshes, and it possessed a small harbour. The ancient sources give two names: the Latin Tarracina and the Volscian Anxur, the latter being the name of Jupiter as a youth, the tutelary god of the city.

Terracina joined the Etruscan League of twelve cities during the 600s BCE, and by 509 BCE it was under Roman supremacy, as the first treaty between Rome and Carthage reports. It was re-occupied by the Volsci, recaptured by the Romans in 406 BCE, lost in 402, recovered in 400 and finally secured by a colony of Roman citizens in 329 BCE. The Via Appia, built in 312 BCE, added to its importance. Under Trajan a cut was made in the rocks of the promontory to carry the road, and the port was built under Trajan and Antoninus Pius. The emperor Galba was born there in 3 BCE.

Terracina is mentioned in the Gothic War, and Theodoric is said to have had a palace there. It was sacked in 409 and 595, and later remained a Byzantine stronghold and became part of the Duchy of Naples. In 872 Pope John VIII brought it under the Holy See. In 1088 it was the seat of the first conclave held outside Rome, and in the 11th and 12th centuries it grew and became a free commune.

Malaria and raids by pirates from North Africa eroded the town in the 16th century. Pope Pius VI later began draining the marshes. The Concordat of 1818 between Pope Pius VII and Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies set its position on the border of the Papal States and the Kingdom of Naples. In 1934 it passed from the province of Rome to that of Latina. It suffered heavy damage in World War II, and afterwards a large new quarter, Borgo Marino, grew along the coast.
terracotta-army: Work on the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang began in 246 BCE, soon after he succeeded his father as King of Qin at the age of 13. The historian Sima Qian (145–90 BCE), writing about a century after the mausoleum was completed, said that the project eventually involved 700,000 conscripted workers. He described a burial with palaces, towers, officials and valuable objects, with the rivers of China simulated in mercury and the heavens on the ceiling. His account does not mention the terracotta figures. High levels of mercury later found in the soil of the tomb mound have lent support to it.

Later accounts say that the complex was looted by Xiang Yu, a contender for the throne after the emperor's death. Fire damage on figures in two of the pits, burnt roof rafters and the missing weapons have been taken as evidence of this looting and of a fire that brought the roof down on the figures.

The figures stand about 1.75 to 2 metres tall, the officers being taller, and differ in uniform and hairstyle according to rank. Scholars have identified ten base face forms, which were developed further so that each face looks different. Heads, arms, legs and torsos were made separately in workshops by government labourers and local craftsmen, then joined. The figures were painted with pigments including cinnabar, malachite and azurite, but the lacquer and colour flake off within minutes of exposure to dry air.

Pit 1, 230 metres long and 62 metres wide, holds the main army of more than 3,000 figures in eleven parallel corridors. Pit 2 has cavalry, infantry and chariots, and Pit 3 is a command post with high-ranking officers. Pit 4 is empty, perhaps left unfinished.

The army was found on 29 March 1974 by farmers digging a well about 1.5 kilometres east of the tomb mound: Yang Zhifa, his five brothers and a neighbour, Wang Puzhi. Archaeologists including Zhao Kangmin then investigated the site. Estimates from 2007 put the three main pits' contents at more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses, and 150 cavalry horses. The army is part of a necropolis covering about 98 square kilometres. The emperor's tomb itself appears to be a sealed space about 100 by 75 metres and remains unopened.

The naturalism of the figures has prompted debate. The art historian German Hafner suggested in 1986 a link with Hellenistic sculpture, while the site's chief archaeologist Zhang Weixing has said there is no substantial evidence for one. Few earlier figurines are known.
tertullian: Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus was a prolific author of the Roman province of Africa. Little reliable evidence about his life survives, and most of it comes from passing references in his own writings. He was well educated, and wrote at least three books in Koine Greek, none of which survives. Some sources describe him as Berber, and the linguist René Braun suggested a Punic origin; he called himself Poenicum inter Romanos, Punic among Romans. Jerome and Eusebius described him as a lawyer and a priest, but in his surviving writings he never calls himself ordained. His conversion to Christianity perhaps took place about 197 or 198, and he wrote that Christians are made, not born.

Thirty-one of his works survive, together with fragments of more, covering apologetics against paganism and Judaism, polemic, church discipline and morals. His Apologeticus, addressed to the Roman magistrates, defends Christians against pagan reproaches and demands a fair trial for them before they are condemned. In it he wrote that the blood of the Christians is seed. His five books against Marcion, written in 207 or 208, are the most comprehensive of his polemical works and are invaluable for understanding the early Christian view of Gnosticism.

In his treatise against Praxeas he used the words trinity, economy, persons and substance, though he did not state the later doctrine of the immanent Trinity, and his teaching that the Son is subordinate to the Father was later rejected by the Catholic Church. He attacked the use of Greek philosophy in Christian theology, asking what Athens has to do with Jerusalem, and urged Christians to avoid the theatre and the amphitheatre.

Around 207 Tertullian was attracted to the New Prophecy of Montanism. Most scholars today reject the claim that he left the mainstream church or was excommunicated, and the extent of his involvement is disputed. In the time of Augustine a group of Tertullianists still had a basilica in Carthage. Jerome says that Tertullian lived to old age, and Cyprian highly regarded him. Through his doctrinal works he became the teacher of Cyprian and the predecessor of Augustine, and he has been called the father of Latin Christianity. He was never canonised.
teruel: Teruel stands 915 metres above sea level in a remote, mountainous part of Aragon. Its climate is harsh, with wide daily variation in temperature, and its surroundings contain archaeological sites and rock outcrops with some of the oldest dinosaur remains of the Iberian Peninsula. The city is known for its cured ham and its pottery. Its isolation gave rise in 1999 to a campaign group with the slogan Teruel existe, Teruel exists, which pressed for greater recognition and investment in the town and the province.

The area was populated in the time of the Celtiberians, who called it Turboleta, and was later occupied by the Romans. Some authors hold that the site, specifically its Jewish quarter, was called Tirwal, from an Arabic word for tower. On 1 October 1171 King Alfonso II of Aragon captured Tirwal, threatened by the Almohad capture of Valencia and wanting to strengthen the southern border of his kingdom. That year he founded Teruel and granted it fueros and privileges to encourage settlement. A legend tells that the town's wise men found a favourable omen in a bull on a high place beneath a star, which explains the bull and star on the city's arms.

Teruel took part in the conquest of Valencia and in the War of the Two Peters against Castile, and in 1347 Pedro IV of Aragon granted it the title of city for its support at the Battle of Épila. Its Jewish and Mudéjar communities became important in the city's economic life. Many members of the Jewish community were killed in the persecutions of 1391, and others accepted Christianity to save their lives.

In the Spanish Civil War much of the city was destroyed. The Battle of Teruel, from December 1937 to February 1938, was one of the bloodiest of the war. The town changed hands several times, first falling to the Republicans and then being retaken by the Nationalists, after heavy artillery and aerial bombardment. The two sides suffered up to 140,000 casualties between them, and the Nationalists won a decisive victory.

Teruel is regarded as the town of Mudéjar because of its many buildings in that style, all part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Mudéjar Architecture of Aragon. Four churches belong to it, notably the cathedral. Other landmarks include the Torre de El Salvador, the Torre de San Martín, and El Torico, a small bull on a tall column in the main square. The church of San Pedro holds the mausoleum of Isabel de Segura and Diego de Marcilla, whose tragic love has inspired writers and an opera.
tetouan: Tétouan lies in the Martil Valley on the northern slope of a fertile valley, a few miles south of the Strait of Gibraltar and about 60 kilometres east-south-east of Tangier. It is one of the two major Moroccan ports on the Mediterranean, with its harbour at Martil, at the river's mouth. Mountains rise to the south and west, and the city sits in a belt of orchards growing oranges, almonds and pomegranates. A few miles outside it lies the ancient town of Tamuda, where Mauretanian settlements date to the 3rd century BCE and Phoenician and Roman artefacts have been found.

The Marinids built a casbah and mosque at Tétouan in the late 13th century, and in 1305 the sultan Abu Thabit Amir expanded and fortified the settlement as a base for attacks on Ceuta. The Castilians destroyed it in retaliation for piracy, and in 1436 the Portuguese commander of Ceuta sent a raiding party against it while it was recovering. The modern city dates from the late 15th century, when Ali al-Mandri, who had emigrated from Granada, rebuilt and fortified it. Muslim and Jewish refugees from Andalusia settled in northern Morocco, and Tétouan became a major centre of Andalusian civilisation. It is nicknamed the Daughter of Granada, and many families still keep keys to their old homes there.

From the 1530s Tétouan became one of the main centres of piracy in the western Mediterranean. In the 17th century the wealthy al-Naksis family governed it, until the Alaouite sultan Moulay Ismail took it at the end of the century. Spain took the city on 4 February 1860 under General Leopoldo O'Donnell, later made Duke of Tetuán, and evacuated it in May 1862. In 1913 it became the capital of the Spanish protectorate, governed by a Khalifa and a Spanish high commissioner, and remained so until 1956. The Spanish built new districts, the Ensanche, around a large circular plaza. During the protectorate Tétouan became a centre of Moroccan publishing and of the nationalist movement led by Abdelkhalek Torres, Abdessalam Bennuna and Mohammed Daoud.

The medina of Tétouan has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997, and since 2017 the city has belonged to the UNESCO Creative Cities Network for crafts and folk art. Its architecture is largely Andalusian, with carved and painted ceilings, tilework and houses with fountains. The city has seven gates and many Sufi zawiyas. A Sephardic Jewish community that spoke the Judaeo-Spanish known as Haketia once lived there. Most residents speak Arabic, and Spanish and French are also widely used.
tetrarchy: The first phase, sometimes called the diarchy, began when Diocletian made the general Maximian caesar in 285 and promoted him to augustus in 286. Diocletian took care of the east and Maximian of the west. In 293, thinking that civic and military problems needed more attention, Diocletian expanded the imperial college with Maximian's consent by appointing two caesares, one responsible to each augustus: Galerius and Constantius I.

The word tetrarchy, from the Greek for leadership of four people, was never applied in antiquity to Diocletian's college. It described independent portions of a kingdom, such as the tetrarchy of Judaea after the death of Herod the Great. Diocletian's arrangement was a college led by one supreme leader. The term entered scholarship in 1887 and became current only after Otto Seeck used it in 1897.

Diocletian and Maximian abdicated on 1 May 305, and Galerius and Constantius became augusti, with Valerius Severus and Maximinus Daza as new caesares. The system broke down quickly. When Constantius died in 306, his army proclaimed his son Constantine augustus. Maxentius, the son of Maximian, rebelled and defeated Severus, who was murdered in 307, and Maxentius and Maximian both declared themselves augusti. A conference at Carnuntum in 308 made Licinius augustus in the west, but Constantine and Maximinus refused to accept a superior, and both were recognised as augusti in 309.

Constantine forced Maximian's suicide in 310. Galerius died naturally in 311, Maxentius was defeated by Constantine at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312 and killed, and Maximinus killed himself at Tarsus in 313. Two rulers remained until Constantine defeated Licinius in 324 and became sole augustus. The fourfold division survived in the praetorian prefectures, and the idea of sharing imperial power recurred repeatedly.

The four tetrarchs based themselves in cities closer to the frontiers rather than in Rome, which stayed the nominal capital. Nicomedia was the capital of Diocletian, Sirmium of Galerius, Mediolanum (Milan) of Maximian and Augusta Treverorum (Trier) of Constantius. There was no precise regional division, and the Roman state was never split into four sub-empires. Each emperor was often in the field, delegating most administration to a praetorian prefect.

The public image of the four was carefully managed to suggest a united empire, and official portraits and coins show them with identical features. The system was meant to solve the problem of the third century, when an emperor could command on only one front. Under it Galerius crushed the Persian king Narseh in 298 and gained a treaty that kept peace for a generation, and Constantius defeated the British usurper Allectus.
tetum-language: In the fifteenth century, before the Portuguese arrived, Tetun spread through central and eastern Timor as a contact language under the Belunese-speaking Kingdom of Wehali, then the most powerful kingdom on the island. The Portuguese, present from about 1556, settled mostly in the west, and only in 1769, when the capital moved from Lifau to Dili, did they begin to promote Tetun as an inter-regional language. Timor was one of the few Portuguese colonies where a local language, not a form of Portuguese, became the lingua franca, because Portuguese rule was indirect, exercised through local kings who embraced Catholicism and became vassals of the King of Portugal.

After the Carnation Revolution in Portugal in 1974, Indonesia invaded East Timor and banned Portuguese, making Indonesian the sole official language. The Roman Catholic Church adopted Tetun as its liturgical language, making it a focus of cultural and national identity. When the United Nations Transitional Administration in East Timor took over in 1999, Tetun Dili was proclaimed the official language, and on independence in 2002 Tetun and Portuguese were both declared official.

Tetun is an Austronesian language, spoken in Timor-Leste and in Belu Regency and Malaka Regency in Indonesian West Timor. The linguist Geoffrey Hull distinguishes four dialects: Tetun Dili or Tetun Prasa, spoken in the capital and its surroundings; Tetun Terik, spoken on the south and southwestern coasts; Tetun Belu, spoken in a central strip of the island and split between Timor-Leste and West Timor, where it has no official status; and Nana'ek, spoken in the village of Metinaro.

Tetun Dili developed during colonial rule, with simpler grammar than other varieties and a heavily Portuguese vocabulary. Ethnologue and some researchers classify it as a Tetun-based creole, a position that is disputed. Without previous contact it is not immediately mutually intelligible with Tetun Terik.

Native words include liafuan, word, from lia, voice, and fuan, fruit, and Timór Lorosa'e, Timor of the rising sun, from loro, sun, and sa'e, to rise. Many words come from Portuguese, such as eskola, school, governu, government, and obrigadu, thanks, and others from Malay, such as uma, house, from rumah. Hybrid words add the Portuguese suffix -dór to a Tetun verb: han, to eat, gives handór, a glutton.

Plurals are not normally marked on nouns, and the word sira, they, can express them. Like other Austronesian languages, Tetun has two forms of we: ami, which excludes the person addressed, and ita, which includes them. Nouns of agents are formed with the suffix -na'in, so that hakerek, to write, gives hakerek-na'in, writer.
teutoburg-forest: The Teutoburg Forest is a long, narrow range of low forested hills of three ridges, in the German states of Lower Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia. It forms the northern edge of the German Central Uplands and extends from the eastern surroundings of Paderborn in the south to the western surroundings of Osnabrück in the north-west. South of Bielefeld a gap called the Bielefeld Pass divides it into the Northern Teutoburg Forest, two thirds of the range, and the Southern Teutoburg Forest, one third.

The oldest ridge, in the north-east, is Triassic limestone. Deciduous forest covers most of the ridges, and cereals are grown in parts of the valleys. The highest points are the Velmerstot (468 m) in the south and the Dörenberg (331 m) in the north. The river Ems rises at the western base of the southernmost part, and the range divides the Ems basin from the Weser basin. A hiking trail, the Hermannsweg, runs 156 km along it from Rheine to Leopoldstal.

Until the 17th century the hill ridge was officially called the Osning. It was first renamed the Teutoburg Forest in 1616, by the historian and geographer Philipp Clüver, in memory of the battle of 9 CE, and the name became common after Ferdinand of Fürstenberg used it in his history and had it printed on maps. The Roman historian Tacitus named the battle's location as the saltus Teutoburgiensis, a forest valley. Its exact site is disputed, and recent excavations suggest that at least the final stages took place further north-west, at Kalkriese, north of Osnabrück.

After the Napoleonic wars, in a period of national renaissance, German people came to see Arminius, also called Hermann the Cherusker, as an early figure of resistance to foreign rule and a symbol of national unity. The monumental statue known as the Hermannsdenkmal was raised on the hill of Grotenburg near Detmold, close to where the most popular theory of the time placed the battle. Emperor William I dedicated it in 1875. The old name Osning survived among local people, and the part of the ridge around the Ebberg near Bielefeld is still called by it.

Apart from a short area south of Osnabrück, the whole range lies in North Rhine-Westphalia. It is made up of two nature parks, the TERRA.vita Nature Park in the north-west and the Teutoburg Forest / Egge Hills Nature Park between Bielefeld and the river Diemel. Fighting took place in the forest at the very end of the Second World War. The composer Johannes Brahms liked to walk there while he stayed in Detmold.
teutones: The name Teutones derives from a Proto-Indo-European stem meaning people or tribe, with an ending common to both Celtic and Germanic tribal names. It can be read as Celtic or as pre-Germanic, and the personal names of their rulers show strong Celtic influence. The earliest classical writers counted the Teutones as Celts. Julius Caesar apparently was the first to draw a line between Celts and Germanic peoples, and later Strabo and Velleius Paterculus called them Germanic. Pliny placed them among the Ingaevones, related to the Cimbri and the Chauci.

Where they came from was uncertain even in antiquity. Plutarch wrote that nobody could tell what people they were or whence they had set out. Pytheas, as reported by Pliny, described the Teutones as neighbours of the island of Abalus, where amber washed ashore and was traded by them. Pomponius Mela placed them on the island of Codannovia in the Codanus Bay, usually read as Scandinavia in the Baltic. Stefan Zimmer notes that the Teutones and the Cimbri left traces in place names in Jutland.

The Teutones are known above all from the Cimbrian War against the Roman Republic. The Cimbri and Teutones won decisive victories over Roman armies at Noreia and, in 105 BCE, at Arausio, then divided their forces. Gaius Marius defeated them separately: the Teutones in 102 BCE at the Battle of Aquae Sextiae, near present-day Aix-en-Provence, and the Cimbri in 101 BCE. This ended the war.

Valerius Maximus and Florus report that the king of the Teutones, Teutobod, was taken in irons. They also say the surrender terms required three hundred married women to be handed over to the Romans as concubines and slaves. When the women learned of this, they begged to serve in the temples of Ceres and Venus instead. Refused, they killed their own children and then strangled one another during the night. Some surviving captives are said to have joined the rebelling gladiators in the Third Servile War of 73 to 71 BCE.

The tale of the Teutonic women passed into Roman legend as an example of Teutonic fury. In ninth-century monastic Latin texts the word Teuton began to refer to speakers of West Germanic languages, used as a learned alternative to the term theodiscus, meaning of the people. The adjective Teutonic has often been used since to mean Germanic.
teutonic-order: The fraternity that preceded the Order was formed by German merchants from Bremen and Lübeck during the siege of Acre, in the Third Crusade. In 1191 they took over a hospital in the city to care for the sick and began to call themselves the Hospital of St. Mary of the German House in Jerusalem. Pope Clement III approved it, and the Order came to play an important part in Outremer, controlling the port tolls of Acre.

In 1211 King Andrew II of Hungary granted the Order the district of Burzenland in Transylvania, to defend his south-eastern border against the Cumans. By 1220 the knights had built five castles, but the Hungarian nobility grew suspicious, and in 1225 Andrew expelled the Order.

In 1226 Duke Konrad I of Masovia asked the knights to subdue the pagan Old Prussians and gave them Chełmno Land as a base. Emperor Frederick II issued the Golden Bull of Rimini, granting the Order the conquest and possession of Prussia. After the fall of Acre in 1291 the Order moved its headquarters briefly to Venice, then to Marienburg, and turned its campaigns against the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania, joined each season by knights from England and France. It won victories at Strėva in 1348 and Rudau in 1370. In 1398 it conquered Gotland and drove out the Victual Brothers.

The Lithuanian ruler Jogaila was baptised in 1386, married Queen Jadwiga of Poland and became King of Poland. At Grunwald in 1410 Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen and 50 of the Order's 60 higher dignitaries died. Heinrich von Plauen held Marienburg, and the First Peace of Thorn in 1411 left the Order nearly all its land, though its reputation for invincibility was gone.

The Grand Master, elected by the general chapter, was the highest officer and until 1466 sovereign prince of Prussia, though in practice a first among equals. The Order had three national chapters, Prussia, Livonia and the Holy Roman Empire, each under a Landmeister. The smallest unit was the commandry, ruled by a Komtur, where knight-brothers, priest-brothers, sergeant-brothers and half-brothers, who worked in the economy and in healthcare, lived together as in a monastery. The knights wore a white surcoat with a black cross, granted by Pope Innocent III in 1205.
texas: Texas lies in the south-central United States. The Rio Grande forms its border with the Mexican states of Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, the Red River borders Oklahoma and Arkansas, and the Sabine River borders Louisiana. One classification divides the state, from south-east to west, into the Gulf Coastal Plains, the Interior Lowlands, the Great Plains and the Basin and Range Province of Far West Texas, which holds desert valleys and wooded mountain slopes.

The name comes from the Caddo word táy:shaʼ, meaning friend, which the Spanish applied, as Tejas or Texas, to the Caddo themselves, specifically the Hasinai Confederacy. In the 18th century Spanish rule called the area Nuevas Filipinas, or the province of the Tejas, and later the province of Texas. An alternative etymology advanced in the late 19th century connected the name with the Spanish teja, roof tile.

Before European contact Texas lay between the Southwestern and Plains cultural spheres, with the Ancestral Puebloans to the west, the Mississippian culture to the east and the civilizations of Mesoamerica to the south. The languages spoken included Caddoan, Atakapan, Athabaskan, Coahuiltecan and Uto-Aztecan, besides isolates such as Tonkawa. The agricultural, mound-building Caddo controlled much of the north-east, the Karankawa lived along the central coast, and Apache peoples lived throughout the interior. No one culture dominated the whole territory.

Spain was the first European country to claim and control Texas, followed by a brief French colonization. The territory became part of Mexico after its independence from Spain in 1821. Rising tensions between settlers and the Mexican government led to the Texas Revolution, which included the Battle of the Alamo, and to the independent Republic of Texas in 1836. In 1845 Texas joined the United States as the 28th state, which helped spark the Mexican-American War.

Texas remained a slave state until the American Civil War, in which it seceded from the Union and joined the Confederate States. After the war and the restoration of its representation in the federal government, it went through a long period of economic stagnation before substantial growth in the 20th century. The current Texas Constitution was adopted in 1876.

Austin is the state capital, and the largest metropolitan areas are the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex and Greater Houston. At the 2020 census Texas had 29,145,505 residents, the second-largest population of any state after California; it is also the second largest in area, after Alaska. Its nickname, the Lone Star State, refers to the single star on the flag of the Republic of Texas.
texas-revolution: The revolution followed a decade of political and cultural clashes between the Mexican government and the large and growing population of Anglo-American settlers in Texas, then part of the Mexican state of Coahuila y Tejas. The Mexican government had become more centralised and had stripped Texas of its autonomy, and curbed immigration from the United States and the holding of slaves as property. Mexico had abolished slavery in 1829 but made an exemption for Texas that was never written into the constitution. Slavery is not mentioned in the Texas Declaration of Independence, but the ownership of enslaved people mattered greatly to many settlers.

The uprising was part of a larger revolt in several provinces against the regime of President Miguel Barragán and General Santa Anna. The Mexican Congress passed the Tornel Decree, which declared that foreigners fighting Mexican troops would be treated as pirates.

Fighting began on 2 October 1835 at Gonzales, over a small cannon the army had lent the town. On 10 October about 125 volunteers, thirty of them Tejanos, stormed the presidio at Goliad, and Texian forces laid siege to Béxar. By mid-December the small Mexican garrisons had been defeated. The Consultation, meeting on 3 November, set up a provisional government under the Constitution of 1824 but did not declare independence, and its infighting left Texas with little effective government. A convention at Washington-on-the-Brazos declared independence on 2 March 1836.

Santa Anna entered Texas in mid-February 1836 with his Army of Operations. His troops defeated the garrison at the Alamo on 6 March and killed almost all its defenders. General José de Urrea won on the coast and executed most of those who surrendered at Goliad. Sam Houston, now commander of the army, withdrew while terrified civilians fled in the Runaway Scrape. On 21 April his army of about 900 men surprised Santa Anna's force of about 700 at the Battle of San Jacinto and routed it. Many Mexican soldiers who tried to surrender were killed.

Santa Anna was captured the next day. To save his life he ordered the remaining Mexican troops to retreat south of the Rio Grande, and he signed the Treaty of Velasco, which gave Texas its independence. Mexico refused to recognise the republic, because Santa Anna had signed as a prisoner, and intermittent conflict continued into the 1840s. The Republic of Texas was annexed by the United States in 1845 as the 28th state, which led directly to the Mexican–American War.
thai-national-anthem: About five days after the coup of June 1932, Luang Nithetkolakit revealed that he belonged to the People's Party and regretted that the party had no proper song for its success. He asked Phra Chenduriyang again, and this time the request came from the new power in Siam, so the musician reluctantly agreed. He completed the anthem on 6 July 1932 during a tram ride from Tha Tien to Bang Khun Phrom, arranging it for the Royal Siamese Navy Orchestra, and asked that his name not be revealed.

When the orchestra first played it at the Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall the following week, the newspaper Srikrung named him as composer. His commander, the Minister of the Palace, reprimanded him for making a national anthem on his own authority, and in October 1932 he was laid off from his post and re-entered it at half his former salary.

The conspirators of Khana Ratsadon asked Khun Wichitmatra to write words. His Phleng Chat Sayam had two stanzas of eight verses and had been printed by 29 August 1932. It was popular but never declared official, and it was banned because some lines spoke of seizing power. In 1934 the government held a competition for official lyrics. For a Western-style anthem the committee recommended Phra Chenduriyang's melody, with a revised version of Khun Wichitmatra's words and a second set by the runner-up, Chan Khamwilai. The Cabinet approved these on 20 August 1934.

The two sets made thirty-two lines in all, and most Thais preferred to sing only Khun Wichitmatra's. In 1939, when Siam became Thailand, a competition produced new lyrics by Luang Saranupraphan, cut from sixteen lines to eight and naming the new country. They were adopted on 10 December 1939.

Regulations of 1935 provided a full-length and a shortened performance of the anthem. Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram ordered the anthem played every day at 08:00 and 18:00 and told the public to stand in respect. Under his rule people who did not stand in silence could be fined up to 2,000 baht or jailed for up to a year; the law has since been abolished.

Today the morning and evening playings match the raising and lowering of the national flag at schools, workplaces and public buildings, and radio and television broadcast it twice a day. Pupils sing it at assembly each school day.
thailand: Thailand shares land borders with Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia and has coasts on the Gulf of Thailand and the Andaman Sea. It covers about 513,120 square kilometres, and the Gulf of Thailand covers 320,000 square kilometres. The north is the mountainous Thai highlands, where Doi Inthanon rises to 2,565 metres. The northeast, Isan, is the Khorat Plateau, bordered on the east by the Mekong. The centre is dominated by the flat Chao Phraya River valley, which runs into the Gulf of Thailand, and the south is the narrow Kra Isthmus widening into the Malay Peninsula.

The Chao Phraya and the Mekong are the indispensable watercourses of rural Thailand, and both are used for industrial-scale production of crops. The climate is shaped by the southwest and northeast monsoons, and most of the country has a tropical savanna climate.

Rice cultivation began around 2000 BCE, and the Ban Chiang site in the northeast is the earliest known centre of copper and bronze production in Southeast Asia, dating between 2000 and 1000 BCE. By the 6th century early multiethnic kingdoms had emerged, including the Mon principalities of Dvaravati and Hariphunchai, and in the 9th century the Khmer people established the Khmer Empire, centred in Angkor. Historians suggest the ancestors of the Thai people migrated from southern China and northern Vietnam between the 6th and 11th centuries, intermixing with Mon and Khmer populations.

King Ramkhamhaeng's reign (1279 to 1298) marked the inception of a unified Thai identity. After the destruction of Ayutthaya in 1767, King Taksin established the Thonburi Kingdom, and Rama I moved the capital to Bangkok in 1782. Siam was the only country in Southeast Asia to avoid European colonisation, though it ceded territory and trade rights through unequal treaties. The People's Party carried out a bloodless revolution on 24 June 1932, and the country was officially renamed Thailand on 24 June 1939.

Thailand has had 20 constitutions and charters since 1932, and all state that politics operate within a constitutional monarchy. The National Assembly has a 200-member Senate and a 500-member House of Representatives. The population is about 66 million, and Theravada Buddhism is central to modern Thai identity.
thales-of-miletus: Thales came from Miletus, a mercantile city at the mouth of the Maeander River in Ionia. The main source for the details of his life is the third-century CE writer Diogenes Laërtius, who wrote some eight centuries after Thales's death and drew on sources that often contained unreliable or even fabricated information. Herodotus called him a Phoenician by remote descent, and Diogenes names his parents as Examyas and Cleobulina, but other writers represent him as a genuine Milesian of distinguished family.

Later writers said that he visited Egypt, where he learned geometry, or Babylonia. Scholars dispute this, since such journeys were a commonplace attribution to philosophers by later writers explaining the origin of their mathematical knowledge.

Thales is counted among the Seven Sages of Greece, semi-traditional statesmen and founding figures, and Diogenes calls him the first of them. The Delphic maxim know thyself was attributed to him. Diogenes also tells of a gold tripod or bowl to be given to the wisest man, which passed round the sages and returned to Thales, who dedicated it to Apollo. According to Diogenes he advised the Milesians not to join the Lydians in a symmachia, a fighting together; when King Croesus was defeated by Cyrus the Great, Miletus was spared because it had taken no action.

Herodotus reported that Thales predicted a solar eclipse in 585 BCE. He also tells that Thales got the army of Croesus across the river Halys by digging a diversion upstream, though he himself finds the story doubtful.

Thales sought to explain natural phenomena by rational hypotheses that referred to natural processes, not to the will of gods and heroes. His best-known thesis, reported by Aristotle in the Metaphysics, is that the originating principle of nature, the arche, is a single material substance, water. Aristotle did not hold the view himself, though the attribution to Thales is generally accepted. Thales thought the Earth floats on water, and explained earthquakes as the Earth being rocked by waves.

Aristotle regarded him as the first natural philosopher, a view that most other writers did not adopt until eighteenth-century historians made it prominent. According to Aristotle he held that all things are full of gods, reasoning that lodestones and amber have souls because they cause movement. Thales is the namesake of Thales's theorem in geometry, and he was said to have calculated the heights of the pyramids and the distance of ships from the shore.
thane: Thane emerged as an urban area under the Shilahara dynasty, which ruled the North Konkan between 800 and 1265 CE. Its names in inscriptions include Srī-sthānaka, Sthānaka and Srī-sthāna. A Chinchani inscription of 1053 CE, issued by Vija-ranaka of the Modha family, states that brahmanas from Srī-sthāna settled at Samyana in his territory. A Shilahara inscription of 1094 CE calls Srī-sthānaka a velakula, a harbour that was an important centre for import and export. Early medieval Arab sources give the name as Thāna, and Ibn Battuta and Abulfeda knew it as Kukin Tana.

A Marathi chronicle, the Mahikavatichi Bakhar, written between the 15th and 17th centuries and of doubtful accuracy, tells that in the 12th century a general named Balkrishn-rao Somvanshi captured Thane from the Shilahara king Yashwant-rao. In the 13th century, according to the same text, Nagar-shah, the ruler of Gandevi, took the area, and it later passed to the Yadavas of Devagiri and back to Nagar-shah as a vassal of the Delhi Sultanate. It was then ruled in turn by local families, the Muzaffarids of Gujarat and the Portuguese.

In the 17th century the Thane area was contested between the Portuguese, the Mughals and the Marathas, and Shivaji captured it from the Mughals in 1675. The Portuguese regained control and began building a fort in 1734, but the Marathas captured the place in 1737. At the start of the First Anglo-Maratha War the East India Company occupied Salsette Island and Thana Fort; the island was recaptured by the forces of Haripant Phadke and Tukoji Holkar, but after the Treaty of Salbai of 1782 both the fort and Salsette were under British control.

Thane, spelled Thana until 1996, is a city in the state of Maharashtra in western India. It lies in the north-east of Salsette Island, neighbours Mumbai and belongs to the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. It is the headquarters of Thane district, and the 2011 census counted 1,886,941 inhabitants. Marathi is the main language, with Hindi widely understood, and some East Indian families in the Khatri ward still speak Portuguese. About 1,800 of India's Jews live in the city.

On 16 April 1853 a passenger train service was inaugurated between Bori Bunder in Bombay and Thane, a distance of 34 km, hauled by three locomotives named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan. When the line was extended to Kalyan in May 1854, the Thane viaducts, the first railway bridges, were built over Thane creek.
thanjavur: Thanjavur lies in the Cauvery delta, 340 km south-west of Chennai and 56 km east of Tiruchirappalli. The tributaries of the Cauvery, among them the Grand Anaicut canal, the Vadavaaru and the Vennaaru, flow through it. The plains beside the river have been cultivated from time immemorial, but most of the city and its surroundings lie in the New Delta, a dry upland tract that was brought under irrigation in the early 19th century. The district is known as the rice bowl of Tamil Nadu. Several explanations of the name are given, among them a Tamil phrase meaning the town where refugees entered and a legend of an Asura named Tanjan, slain on the site by Neelamegha Perumal, an incarnation of Vishnu.

Sangam-period Tamil records do not mention Thanjavur, though some scholars think the city existed then. The region was conquered by the Mutharayars in the sixth century, who ruled it until 849. The Cholas returned to prominence under Vijayalaya in about 850; he took Thanjavur from the Mutharayar king Elango Mutharayar and built a temple to the goddess Nisumbhasudani, and his son Aditya I consolidated the hold on the city. Thanjavur became the most important city of the Chola Empire and remained its capital until Gangaikonda Cholapuram emerged in about 1025. Rajaraja I, who reigned from 985 to 1014, built the Brihadeeswarar Temple there.

After the Cholas the city was ruled by the Mutharayars, the Pandyas, the Vijayanagar Empire, the Madurai Nayaks, the Thanjavur Nayaks and the Thanjavur Marathas. The Bhonsle family ruled the Thanjavur region from 1674 to 1855, and most of the Maratha kingdom was annexed by the British Empire in 1799. The Maratha palace, begun by the Nayaks, stayed in the family's hands. Thanjavur has been part of independent India since 1947.

Thanjavur is an important centre of religion, art and architecture in southern India. The Brihadeeswarar Temple, dedicated to Shiva and covered inside with wall paintings of the Chola and Nayak periods, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, and the Great Living Chola Temples around the city share that status. The historian Percy Brown called its construction a landmark in the evolution of building art in South India. The city is also the home of Tanjore painting, a style unique to the region, and the Saraswati Mahal Library dates from the end of the 16th century. Tamil is the widely spoken language, and Thanjavur Marathi and Saurashtra are also spoken.
thar-desert: The Thar Desert lies in the north-western part of the Indian subcontinent, across the border between India and Pakistan. About two thirds of it is in India, mostly in Rajasthan, with parts in Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab, and the remainder in the provinces of Sindh and Punjab in Pakistan. It is bordered by the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the north, west and northeast, by the Rann of Kutch to the south and by the Aravalli Range to the east. Sandy plains broken by low eroded hills rise to about 325 metres towards the Aravallis, and much of the desert is covered by sand dunes.

Most rain falls in the southwest monsoon from June to September. The Luni is the longest river of the desert. The 649-kilometre Indira Gandhi Canal, which carries water from the Indus system, is a major source of irrigation and drinking water, and rain is stored in reservoirs known as tobas, johads and taankas.

The region grew arid over a long time. During the Last Glacial Maximum, an ice sheet on the Tibetan Plateau meant that there was no monsoon over the subcontinent. Later the rise of the Aravallis changed the hydrography, and the Ghaggar-Hakra river system, which fed the region, no longer reached the sea. Beginning about 4,500 to 5,000 years ago the monsoons that fed it diminished further. The Indus Valley Civilisation had prospered along the river system, and as the Hakra dried to an intermittent river the urban Harappan civilisation declined into smaller agricultural communities.

Parts of the desert came under the Mauryan Empire by the third century BCE and the Gupta Empire in the 5th century CE. Mahmud of Ghazni annexed the region in the 11th century. Rajput states began to form in the late 7th century and later rose to prominence, and they resisted the Mughal Empire, which began with Babur's invasion, for over 200 years. The Marathas controlled most of the region in the 18th century, and in the 19th it came under British suzerainty as a number of princely states. The partition of India split the desert between India and Pakistan, with large-scale conflicts and mass migration across the new borders.

The Thari people, who speak a language of the Rajasthani family, are the natives of the region, and most live in small villages, many of them nomadic. Herding, limited agriculture and handicrafts support the economy. Desert National Park in Rajasthan covers 3,162 square kilometres, and Lal Suhanra in Pakistan is a UNESCO biosphere reserve. Natural gas was discovered in the Jaisalmer basin in 1988.
the-beatles: In November 1956 the 16-year-old John Lennon formed a skiffle group with friends from Quarry Bank High School for Boys in Liverpool, named the Quarrymen after the school song. Paul McCartney met Lennon on 6 July 1957 and joined shortly after, and in 1958 George Harrison, then 15, was enlisted as lead guitarist after playing Raunchy for Lennon on the upper deck of a Liverpool bus. Stuart Sutcliffe joined on bass in January 1960 and suggested the name Beatals, in tribute to Buddy Holly and the Crickets. By mid-August 1960 they were simply the Beatles.

The Beatles built their reputation playing clubs in Liverpool and in Hamburg, West Germany, from 1960. Ringo Starr officially joined in 1962. Manager Brian Epstein shaped them into a professional act, and the producer George Martin developed their recordings. After signing with EMI they had their first hit, Love Me Do, in late 1962. By early 1964 they were international stars, leading the British Invasion of the American pop market. They retired from live performance in 1966 and made more sophisticated albums, among them Revolver (1966) and Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967). In 1968 they founded Apple Corps. The band broke up in 1970.

Their arrival in the United States in 1964 is credited with beginning the album era. Young adults abroad name them among the people they most associate with British culture. In 1965 Queen Elizabeth II appointed the four members Members of the Order of the British Empire, and they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1988, their first year of eligibility.
the-canterbury-tales: The Canterbury Tales is an anthology of twenty-four stories, mostly in verse, written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer between 1387 and 1400. They are presented as part of a fictional storytelling contest among pilgrims travelling from London to the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral. The General Prologue introduces some 30 pilgrims, and Chaucer's stated plan was four stories from each, two on the way to Canterbury and two on the way back, about 120 in all. Most scholars think the work was incomplete at the end of his life. Chaucer began it during the years when he was Controller of Customs and Justice of the Peace from 1386 and Clerk of the King's Works from 1389.

Frame tales were an established genre, but Chaucer's collection differs from most in its intense variation. Most collections kept to a theme, usually a religious one, and even in the Decameron the storytellers stuck to the theme of the day. A pilgrimage brought together a diverse company, and the contest invites the reader to compare tales in many genres, from the Knight's Tale of chivalry to others in lower styles. Two tales, Sir Topas and The Tale of Melibee, are told by Chaucer himself, who travels with the pilgrims in his own story.

The tales reflect the controversies of the late 14th century: the Western Schism, Lollardy under John Wycliffe, the abuse of indulgences by pardoners, and the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. They are among the first English literary works to mention paper. Several characters are religious figures, so religion is a major theme, and the Knight's Tale examines chivalry, which was in decline in Chaucer's day, though scholars dispute whether it was meant to show its flaws.

No manuscript exists in Chaucer's own hand. There are 84 manuscripts and four incunabula editions, more than for any other vernacular English text except the Prick of Conscience. They vary in minor and major ways, and there is no agreement on a complete version or on Chaucer's intended order. Most modern editions divide the tales into ten Fragments, following the Ellesmere order, while Victorian editors used the nine Groups of F. J. Furnivall.

In the 15th century John Lydgate and Thomas Occleve praised Chaucer as the best English poet, and the Knight's Tale was the most respected. The incompleteness led medieval authors to add tales, such as the Tale of Beryn, to some manuscripts. The work may have helped popularise the English vernacular in literature, as against French or Latin. Shakespeare and John Fletcher based The Two Noble Kinsmen on the Knight's Tale, first performed in 1613 or 1614.
the-communist-manifesto: In spring 1847 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels joined the League of the Just, which became the League of Communists. At its first congress, held from 2 to 9 June, the League asked Engels to draft a statement of its programme. He wrote the Draft of a Communist Confession of Faith, a catechism of 22 questions, and in October produced the Principles of Communism, a longer one of 25 questions. Several scholars see the kernel of the Manifesto in this second text.

Marx delayed the work while lecturing on political economy and writing for the Deutsche-Brüsseler-Zeitung. In late January 1848 the League's Central Committee sent him an ultimatum demanding the manuscript by 1 February. The Manifesto was written over six to seven weeks, and only one page of draft is known to survive. Engels is credited as co-author, but the final text was penned by Marx; Engels wrote in 1883 that its basic thought belonged solely to Marx.

The Manifesto has a preamble and four sections. The preamble opens with the line about a spectre haunting Europe and urges communists to state their views openly. The first section, Bourgeois and Proletarians, sets out historical materialism: all earlier societies were marked by an exploiting minority and an exploited majority, and under capitalism the industrial working class, the proletariat, stands against the owners of the means of production, the bourgeoisie.

The authors argue that the bourgeoisie, by constantly revolutionising production, displaced feudal powers, and that in doing so it creates its own grave-diggers. In their view the proletariat will become conscious of its power and overthrow it, leading to a classless society. They also proposed ten measures for a society moving towards communism, which their 1872 preface called dated.

The pamphlet was published anonymously in late February 1848 in London, as a 23-page German text issued by the Communist Workers' Educational Association. Marx was expelled by the Belgian police on 4 March. The first English version, translated by Helen Macfarlane, appeared in November 1850 in George Julian Harney's Chartist paper The Red Republican, which also named the authors for the first time.

After years of obscurity the text revived in the early 1870s, through Marx's role in the First International, his support for the Paris Commune of 1871 and the treason trial of German Social Democratic leaders, where prosecutors read it into the record. A new German edition of 1872 first used the short title The Communist Manifesto. After the October Revolution of 1917 it became required reading for Leninist parties, and by its centenary in 1948 general publishers were printing it widely.
the-crystal-palace: The commission in charge of the Great Exhibition was established in January 1850, and the project was to be funded by public subscription. An executive building committee that included Isambard Kingdom Brunel and Robert Stephenson, chaired by William Cubitt, invited designs on 15 March 1850. The building had to be temporary, simple, cheap and quick to build, since the exhibition was already scheduled to open on 1 May 1851. The name may come from a piece by Douglas Jerrold in the satirical magazine Punch in July 1850, which spoke of a palace of very crystal.

Joseph Paxton's modular design was scaled around the size of the glass panes made by Chance Brothers of Smethwick, the largest then available, at 10 inches by 49 inches. Nearly the whole surface could therefore be glazed with identical panes, which cut cost and building time. More than 1,000 iron columns carried 2,224 trellis girders. Fox, Henderson and Co took possession of the site in July 1850, and more than 5,000 navvies worked on it. It was completed in thirty-nine weeks, with 293,000 panes of glass.

The Great Exhibition ran from 1 May to 15 October 1851, and Queen Victoria opened it. Its objects ranged from the Koh-i-Noor diamond to a hydraulic press and a fire engine. Prices were reduced so that working people could attend from 26 May. Over six million admissions were counted, and the surplus of £186,000 helped found the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Science Museum and the Natural History Museum in South Kensington.

A consortium of eight businessmen moved the building to Penge Place, at the top of Sydenham Hill, and rebuilt it from 1852 in a quite different, enlarged form. It stood there from June 1854. Its courts told the history of art, and the park held models of dinosaurs made by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins. The site also hosted the FA Cup Final from 1895 to 1914. In the First World War more than 125,000 men were trained there for the navy. The move cost far more than the original building, and the company never repaid its debt.

On the evening of 30 November 1936 an explosion in the women's cloakroom started a fire, and the Penge fire brigade was called. Eighty-nine fire engines and over 400 firemen attended, but within hours the Palace was destroyed. The fire spread quickly in high winds, helped by dry timber flooring and a large quantity of flammable material, and its glow was visible across eight counties.
the-gambia: The Gambia is the smallest country on the African mainland. Its borders mirror the meandering Gambia River, which flows through the middle of the country, and Senegal surrounds it on all sides except the 80 kilometres of Atlantic coastline in the west. It is less than 50 kilometres wide at its widest point, with an area of 11,295 square kilometres. The present boundaries were defined in 1889 after an agreement between the United Kingdom and France, though fixing the final borders took nearly 15 years. The river, known locally as the River, is navigable deep into the continent.

The name derives from the Mandinka term Kambra or Kambaa, meaning the Gambia River. Portuguese explorers adopted a variation of it, which was later anglicised. In 1964 Prime Minister Dawda Jawara asked that the name keep the definite article, in part to reduce confusion with the newly independent Zambia.

Arab traders gave the first written accounts of the area in the ninth and tenth centuries. Muslim merchants and scholars established communities in West African commercial centres and carried out trans-Saharan trade, exporting gold, ivory and people taken captive in raids and sold as slaves. At the beginning of the 14th century most of the present Gambia was part of the Mali Empire. The Portuguese reached the area by sea in the mid-15th century and began to dominate overseas trade.

In 1588 António, Prior of Crato, a claimant to the Portuguese throne, sold exclusive trade rights on the river to English merchants, and in 1618 King James I granted a charter to an English company. Between 1651 and 1661 parts of the Gambia, including St. Andrew's Island and Fort Jakob, were ruled by the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia under Prince Jacob Kettler, before being ceded to England in 1664.

Britain and France struggled for supremacy on the Senegal and Gambia rivers through the 18th century. The 1783 Treaty of Versailles gave Britain the Gambia River, but France kept an enclave at Albreda until it was ceded in 1856. The British established the military post of Bathurst, now Banjul, in 1816, and the Gambia gained independence on 18 February 1965.

The Gambia is the Republic of The Gambia, a republic since 1970, and its capital is Banjul, an island city once called Bathurst. English is the sole official language, and Mandinka is spoken as a first language by 38 per cent of the population. The Mandinka are the most numerous ethnic group. The river and its slave-trade history are the setting of Alex Haley's Roots.
the-great-game: Britain feared that Russian expansion to the south would threaten India, while Russia feared the spread of British interests into Central Asia. On one major view the rivalry began on 12 January 1830, when Lord Ellenborough, president of the Board of Control for India, told the governor-general, Lord William Bentinck, to open a trade route to the Emirate of Bukhara. Britain hoped to make Afghanistan a protectorate and to use the Ottoman Empire, Persia, Khiva and Bukhara as buffer states. The term Great Game was coined in 1840 by the British intelligence officer Captain Arthur Conolly and was popularised by Rudyard Kipling's novel Kim of 1901.

Britain annexed Sind in 1843 and fought the two Anglo-Sikh Wars, in 1845–1846 and 1848–1849, which brought the Punjab and the later North-West Frontier Province under its rule. After the Crimean War ended in 1856 with Russia's defeat, Alexander II of Russia waited some years and then expanded in two campaigns. Russia occupied Chimkent in 1864, Tashkent in 1865, Khokhand and Bukhara in 1866 and Samarkand in 1868, and Khiva in 1873.

Afghanistan was the main point of contact. In 1878 Russia sent a mission to Kabul uninvited; when Sher Ali Khan refused a British mission and turned back its envoy, the Second Anglo-Afghan War began, and 40,000 men invaded from British India in November 1878. The Treaty of Gandamak of 1879 and the accession of Abdur Rahman Khan left Afghanistan under British control of its foreign policy, with internal sovereignty, as a buffer. Persia was another field: Britain and Persia fought in 1856–1857 after a Persian assault on Herat.

The two powers never fought each other directly in the Great Game, and they also cooperated. Their agreement of 21 January 1873 treated Badakhshan and the Wakhan Corridor as Afghan, and the Afghan Boundary Commission followed the protocol of 10 September 1885. A frontier defined by the Pamir Boundary Commission in 1895 is the date many historians give for the end of the game. The Anglo-Russian Convention of August 1907 placed Afghanistan and southern Iran in the British sphere and Central Asia and northern Iran in the Russian sphere, and treated Tibet as neutral.

Historians do not agree on the dating. Edward Ingram places the beginning in 1832–1834 and the end in 1842, with the British withdrawal from Afghanistan, while Konstantin Penzev dates its start to Russia's victory over Persia. David X. Noack sees a later contest between Britain and the Soviet Union from 1919 to 1933.
the-hague: The Hague, in Dutch Den Haag, short for 's-Gravenhage, is the capital of the province of South Holland. It lies on the west coast facing the North Sea, and its coastal area includes the seaside resort of Scheveningen. The name comes from the Middle Dutch word hag(h)e, meaning hedge, enclosure or hunting ground, and first appeared in 1242. The fuller 's-Gravenhage, the count's enclosure, appeared in 1347 and refers to the Count of Holland. The municipal government adopted the shorter name in 1990.

The area belonged to the Roman province of Germania Inferior. Little is known of the city's origin, since no contemporary documents describe it, but it was founded by the last counts of the House of Holland. Floris IV presumably bought a court by the present Hofvijver in 1229 but died in a tournament in 1234. His son William II lived there, and after he was elected King of the Romans in 1248 he had builders turn the court into a royal palace, later called the Binnenhof. The Ridderzaal, or Knights' Hall, was completed under his son Floris V and still stands. From the 13th century the counts of Holland used The Hague as their administrative centre and residence.

In 1806, when the Kingdom of Holland was a puppet state of the First French Empire, Louis Bonaparte granted the settlement city rights. After Belgium separated in 1830, Amsterdam stayed the capital while the government remained in The Hague. When government grew more prominent after 1850 the city expanded quickly, with streets built for civil servants and for Dutchmen retiring from the administration of the Netherlands East Indies.

The Hague is the seat of the Dutch government, the States General, the Supreme Court and the Council of State, while Amsterdam is the official capital. The Ridderzaal is still used for political events such as the annual speech from the throne. Most foreign embassies in the Netherlands are in the city. It is home to the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court and the Permanent Court of Arbitration, and the Royal Library of the Netherlands is also there.
the-internationale: The title comes from the First International, the alliance of workers that held a congress in 1864. Pottier intended his text to be sung to the tune of La Marseillaise, and it was reputedly sung to that tune at his burial in November 1887. An earlier version, written in September 1870, marked the Third Republic declared after Prussia's defeat of the Second French Empire and honoured the First International. The text that endures is the one Pottier authorised for his Chants Révolutionnaires, published by his fellow Communard Jean Allemane in April 1887.

The melody was composed in 1888 by Pierre De Geyter for the choir La Lyre des Travailleurs of the French Workers' Party in his hometown of Lille. He had been commissioned by Gustave Delory, the future mayor of Lille, who had received the text from a young socialist teacher, Charles Gros. Pottier's lyrics contain one-liners that became slogans, and others such as Ni Dieu, ni César, ni tribun, meaning neither God, nor Caesar, nor tribune, were already familiar in the workers' movement.

The Second International adopted the song as its official anthem, and it became a standard of the socialist movement from the late nineteenth century. The first English version has been attributed to Pottier himself, and the first US translation was made by Charles Hope Kerr, who heard it in Lille in 1894. By the time of the International Socialist Congress in Copenhagen in 1910 versions existed in 18 languages. Arkady Kots made the first Russian translation in 1902, and after the Bolshevik Revolution its future tenses were rewritten in the present. Qu Qiubai made a new Chinese translation in 1923, and the song was played at the close of the Chinese Communist Party's third National Congress that year.

In the Soviet Union it was the national anthem until it was replaced by the State Anthem of the USSR; Arturo Toscanini's orchestration of it was broadcast in 1943 for the anniversary of the October Revolution. In South Africa communists, unionists and activists of all races sang it until the Communist Party was suppressed from 1950.

Pierre De Geyter's authorship was obscured. To protect his job as a woodcarver, the first leaflets gave only the French form of his name, Degeyter, and a second edition named his brother Adolphe as the composer. Pierre lost a lawsuit over this in 1914 and was legally recognised as the author only in 1922. Adolphe died in 1916, leaving a note explaining the fraud. Pierre De Geyter died in 1932, and the music is now in the public domain.
the-knight-in-the-panthers-skin: The poem was written during the Golden Age of the Kingdom of Georgia, in the reign of Queen Tamar, who had been enthroned by her father, King George III of Georgia. Tamar expanded the kingdom to its historical maximum, repulsed invasions and set up protectorates over many Muslim and Christian lands. Georgian trading caravans reached Ayyubid Egypt, the Kievan Rus and the Byzantine Empire.

Shota Rustaveli, born in the Meskhetian village of Rustavi, was close to the queen and possibly served as her treasurer. In the prologue he says he wrote the poem to praise Tamar, whom he calls a king. The historian Stephen H. Rapp sees it as an expression of the Iranian epic tradition rather than of Byzantine literature, and Rustaveli calls it a Persian tale translated into Georgian. It runs to over 1,600 quatrains in the shairi verse form.

The story is set in the invented lands of Arabia and India. Avtandil, commander of the armies of King Rostevan of Arabia, is asked by the king's daughter Tinatin to find a mysterious knight in a panther's skin within three years. After two years and nine months he finds Tariel, son of King Saridan, living in a cave. Tariel had fallen in love with Nestan-Darejan, daughter of King Pharsadan, who was promised to another suitor. At her request he killed the suitor, and she was set adrift on the sea.

Avtandil swears friendship to Tariel and sets out again to find Nestan-Darejan. In the city of Gulansharo, Patman tells him that Nestan was abducted by Kaji, the demon king. Avtandil, Tariel and Nuradin-Phridon go to the land of Kaji with three hundred men and free her. Avtandil marries Tinatin in Arabia, Tariel marries Nestan in India, and the three friends reign in their own realms.

The poem celebrates friendship, loyalty and courtly love, and condemns forced marriage and slavery. Readers see Nestan-Darejan as an allegory of Tamar and the settings as colourful stand-ins for the Georgian kingdom.

Until the early 20th century a copy of the poem was part of the dowry of every bride. Its moral framework is Christian, though the poem contains no prayers and no references to Christ, and it refers to the Quran to show that most characters are Muslim. Because Rustaveli presents God as a universal force, the Georgian Orthodox Church in the past destroyed copies, believing him to be a Muslim.

Interest abroad began in 1802 with a Russian translation of the first stanza. Marie-Félicité Brosset made a partial French translation in 1828, and Marjory Wardrop published the first English translation in 1912. The poem has been translated into dozens of languages, and Lyn Coffin's English version of 2015 keeps the shairi form.
the-last-supper-leonardo: The painting measures 460 by 880 centimetres and covers an end wall of the dining hall of the convent. Ludovico Sforza planned to remodel the church as a family mausoleum and commissioned the work to decorate its wall; the lunettes above it carry Sforza coats of arms. On the opposite wall is the Crucifixion fresco by Giovanni Donato da Montorfano, to which Leonardo added figures of the Sforza family in tempera. These have deteriorated in much the same way.

Leonardo did not work continuously, and the start date is uncertain because the convent's archives for the period were destroyed. A document of 1497 indicates that the painting was nearly complete. A prior who complained about the delay was told, according to the report, that if Leonardo could not find the right face for Judas he would use the prior's features.

The scene follows the Gospel of John, at the moment after Jesus announces that one of the apostles will betray him. The twelve react in four groups of three, with Jesus at the centre. Judas, in shadow, clutches a small bag and tips over a salt cellar, and Peter holds a knife. Leonardo seats all the diners on one side of the table, so that none has his back to the viewer, and leaves Judas among them rather than apart. The perspective lines meet at Jesus's turned right cheek.

The apostles were named from an unsigned mid-sixteenth-century fresco copy; before that only Judas, Peter, John and Jesus had been identified with certainty. Two early copies attributed to Leonardo's assistants survive, one by Giampietrino in London and one by Cesare da Sesto in Ponte Capriasca, Switzerland.

The damage began early. By 1556 Giorgio Vasari described the work as a muddle of blots, and in 1652 a doorway was cut through its lower centre and later bricked up. Restorations were attempted by Michelangelo Bellotti in 1726 and Giuseppe Mazza in 1770, and Stefano Barezzi damaged the central section in 1821 when he tried to remove it from the wall. In 1796 French troops used the refectory as an armoury and stable, and on 15 August 1943 Allied bombing struck the room, though sandbags protected the wall.

From 1978 to 1999 Pinin Brambilla Barcilon led a major restoration, and the painting was returned to display on 28 May 1999 in a sealed, climate-controlled room. Its changes of colour and tone drew criticism, notably from the art historian James Beck. Since Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code (2003), some writers have claimed that the figure beside Jesus is Mary Magdalene, but art historians hold that it is John.
the-merchant-of-venice: The play is believed to have been written between 1596 and 1598. Francis Meres mentioned it in 1598, and its first edition of 1600 says it had been performed divers times. A reference to the ship the Andrew is thought to allude to the Spanish ship St. Andrew, captured by the English at Cádiz in 1596. James Roberts entered it in the Register of the Stationers Company on 22 July 1598, and Thomas Heyes published the first quarto in 1600. That edition is regarded as accurate and is the basis of the text in the 1623 First Folio.

A merchant forfeiting a deadly bond after standing surety for a friend was a common tale in late 16th-century England. The test of the suitors, the rescue from the pound of flesh by the friend's new wife disguised as a lawyer, and her demand for a betrothal ring appear in Il Pecorone by Giovanni Fiorentino, published in Milan in 1558. The story of the three caskets is in the Gesta Romanorum, probably compiled at the end of the 13th century.

Bassanio, a young Venetian who has squandered his estate, wishes to woo Portia, the wealthy heiress of Belmont, and needs 3,000 ducats. His friend Antonio, a merchant, has no ready cash because his ships are at sea, so Bassanio turns to the Jewish moneylender Shylock, and Antonio guarantees the loan. Though the First Folio classes the play as a comedy, it is remembered mostly for its dramatic scenes and for Shylock's demand for a pound of flesh. It holds two well-known speeches: Shylock's Hath not a Jew eyes? and Portia's on the quality of mercy.

Critics disagree over whether the play is antisemitic. Harold Bloom argued in 1998 that it is profoundly so, and others point to Shylock's plea for the rights of all who suffer discrimination. English Jews had been expelled under Edward I in 1290 and could not return until 1656, and in Venice Jews had to live in a ghetto and wear a coloured hat in public.

The earliest recorded performance was at the court of King James in the spring of 1605. In 1701 George Granville's adaptation, The Jew of Venice, played the role of Shylock comically and was acted for about forty years. Charles Macklin returned to the original text in 1741. According to the actor Jacob Adler, the tradition of a sympathetic Shylock began with Edmund Kean in the first half of the 19th century, and Henry Irving's proud Shylock of 1879 was called the summit of his career. Adler himself played the part in Yiddish in New York. Operas based on the play include Reynaldo Hahn's Le marchand de Venise, first performed in Paris on 25 March 1935.
the-prince: Machiavelli's letters show that a version, with the Latin title De Principatibus, Of Principalities, was being written in 1513, the year after the Medici regained control of Florence and a few months after Machiavelli's arrest, torture and banishment by the incoming Medici regime. He discussed it for a long time with his friend Francesco Vettori, whom he wanted to commend it to the Medici. It was originally intended for Giuliano di Lorenzo de' Medici, and after Giuliano died in 1516 it was dedicated to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici. William Connell views its writing as a lengthy process of revision from 1513 to 1515. No manuscript in Machiavelli's own hand survives.

Machiavelli says that the book holds the knowledge of the actions of great men, drawn from his own political experience as well as from reading. It begins by describing the kinds of state, using the word stato for all forms of supreme political power, whether republican or princely. It treats new princedoms, either wholly new or added to an older state, and ecclesiastical principalities, using the Borgia family as a nearly successful example. He argues that the two essential foundations of any state are sound laws and strong military forces, and that a prince should have his own arms and avoid mercenaries.

Machiavelli holds that a prince should make war his chief study, since being disarmed makes you despised, and that it is wiser to take a side than to be neutral. In the last chapters he argues that fortune governs only half of our actions, and that the princes who rise highest take risks and adapt to changing circumstances.

The printed version appeared in 1532, five years after Machiavelli's death, with the permission of the Medici pope Clement VII, although controversy had surrounded his writings since the work first circulated in manuscript. About fifteen editions of The Prince and nineteen of the Discourses on Livy were in circulation before Paul IV placed them on the Index in 1559. Interpreters differ: some read it as satire, as Garrett Mattingly did, and Rousseau held that Machiavelli, by choosing Cesare Borgia as his hero, aimed to expose tyranny. The treatise gave rise to the word Machiavellian.
the-second-sex: Volume One, Facts and Myths, asks what a woman is. Beauvoir compares the physiology of men and women and concludes that values cannot be based on physiology, so that the facts of biology must be read in their ontological, economic and social context. She rejects the views of Sigmund Freud, Alfred Adler and Friedrich Engels, and traces the history of women's condition from ancient Greece and Rome through Christianity, courtly love, the Napoleonic Code and the Industrial Revolution to trade unions, birth control and women's suffrage. She argues that women's historical insignificance, not an inferiority, has doomed them to inferiority, and she examines the myths about women in writers such as Henry de Montherlant, D. H. Lawrence, Paul Claudel, André Breton and Stendhal.

Volume Two, Lived Experience, follows a woman's life. A girl is taught to be a woman, her feminine destiny is imposed on her by society, and she has no innate maternal instinct. Beauvoir then describes puberty, sexual relations, marriage, motherhood, the work of married women, prostitution and old age. She calls marriage an institution that almost always destroys woman and argues that abortion is not an issue of morality. She concludes that women must work for their own liberation and looks to a future of equality in which men and women affirm their brotherhood.

The book was condemned by the Vatican and remained on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum until the Index itself was abolished in 1966. A Spanish translation printed in Argentina was banned in Francoist Spain in 1955, and Spanish feminists smuggled in copies. Beauvoir recalled in a 1974 interview that Camus was furious and that professors threw the book across the room, partly because she had spoken about female sexuality. The sex researcher Alfred Kinsey thought it interesting as literature but of no value to science.

Its attack on psychoanalysis helped inspire later feminist arguments, including Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique, Kate Millett's Sexual Politics and Germaine Greer's The Female Eunuch. Camille Paglia calls it the supreme work of modern feminism. Judith Butler reads the line One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman as separating sex from gender, a reading contested by Toril Moi and Nancy Bauer. Critics have also charged Beauvoir with an unconscious misogyny and with writing from a middle-class standpoint.

The 1953 English translation by H. M. Parshley, which cut great swaths of the text and mistranslated its philosophical vocabulary, was widely judged poor. Beauvoir asked for a more faithful one in a 1985 interview, and a complete translation by Constance Borde and Sheila Malovany-Chevallier appeared in November 2009.
the-sorrows-of-young-werther: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, aged 24, wrote the novel in five and a half weeks between January and March 1774, and it appeared anonymously; a revised edition followed in 1787. It drew on real triangular relationships. In the summer of 1772 Goethe fell in love at Wetzlar with Charlotte Buff, who was engaged to Christian Kestner, and then with Maximiliane von La Roche, who married Peter Anton Brentano in January 1774. A further source was Karl Wilhelm Jerusalem, a 25-year-old lawyer known to Goethe's circle, who suffered a similar impossible love for an engaged countess and killed himself on the night of 29 or 30 October 1772 with a pistol borrowed from Kestner.

The book is presented as letters written by Werther, a sensitive young artist, mostly to his friend Wilhelm, with some details supplied by an unidentified editor. He stays in the fictional village of Wahlheim, based on Garbenheim near Wetzlar, and meets Charlotte, who cares for her siblings after their mother's death. He loves her although he knew before meeting her that she was engaged to Albert, eleven years her senior. He befriends them both, leaves for Weimar, where he is turned away from a gathering of the aristocracy because he is not a nobleman, and returns to find them married.

Charlotte tells him to visit less often and suggests that it is only the impossibility of possessing her that makes his desire so strong. Werther, who had made pessimistic remarks about life even before meeting her, resolves to take his own life. He asks Albert for his pistols on the pretext of a journey, and Charlotte hands them over at Albert's command. The novel ends with Werther's death and burial.

The Sorrows of Young Werther was an immediate international bestseller, perhaps the first in literary history. It gave rise to Werther Fever: young men across Europe dressed as Werther does in the novel, and prints, decorated Meissen porcelain and a perfume were sold. Napoleon Bonaparte admired it and carried it on his campaign in Egypt. It is a main novel of the Sturm und Drang period and influenced later Romanticism. Some readers were reported to have copied Werther's suicide, which is known as the Werther effect, though the biographer Rüdiger Safranski calls this a persistent rumour. Leipzig banned the novel in 1775, and Denmark and Italy banned it too.

Goethe later distanced himself from the book and regretted the fame it brought him. Friedrich Nicolai wrote a satire with a happy ending, and Goethe attacked him for it in verse. Jules Massenet adapted the novel as the opera Werther in 1892.
the-star-spangled-banner: The words come from a poem called the Defence of Fort M'Henry, which Francis Scott Key wrote after he witnessed the British Royal Navy's bombardment of Fort McHenry during the Battle of Baltimore in the War of 1812. He was inspired by the large American flag, with 15 stars and 15 stripes, that flew over the fort after the battle. Key gave the poem to his brother-in-law Joseph H. Nicholson, who saw that the words fit a popular melody, The Anacreontic Song, by the English composer John Stafford Smith, written for the Anacreontic Society, a gentlemen's club of amateur musicians in London.

Nicholson took the poem to a printer in Baltimore, who anonymously made the first known broadside on 17 September; two copies survive. On 20 September the Baltimore Patriot and The American both printed it with the note Tune: Anacreon in Heaven, and it was in the end printed in 17 newspapers from Georgia to New Hampshire.
