Thomas Carr of Baltimore then published words and music together as The Star Spangled Banner; his arrangement introduced the raised fourth that became the standard departure from the earlier tune. The first public performance came in October, when the actor Ferdinand Durang sang it at Captain McCauley's tavern.

Bands played the song at public events such as Independence Day celebrations through the 19th century. The United States Navy adopted it officially in 1889, and in 1916 President Woodrow Wilson ordered it played at military and other appropriate occasions. Congress passed a joint resolution making it the national anthem on 3 March 1931, which President Herbert Hoover signed into law.

Although the poem has four stanzas, usually only the first is performed. The melody has a range of a twelfth, which makes it difficult for nonprofessional singers. Most performances follow a 1918 arrangement by Walter Damrosch and John Philip Sousa. Translations appeared as immigrant communities grew, among them a German version in 1861, probably to encourage German-American service in the Union forces, and later Hebrew, Yiddish, Irish, Navajo, Cherokee and Samoan versions. At the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City the athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos each raised a black-gloved fist while the anthem played at their medal ceremony, a gesture Smith described as a human rights salute.
the-tale-of-genji: The tale is said to have been written by the noblewoman and lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu at the peak of the Heian period. She lived when the Fujiwara clan was at the height of its power and Fujiwara no Michinaga was regent in all but name, and she is believed to have shaped the character of Genji partly on her experience of him. The tale may have been written chapter by chapter and delivered to aristocratic women of the court. How much of it Murasaki wrote has been debated for centuries. Her own diary mentions the tale in 1008, and the author of the Sarashina Nikki recorded in 1021 her joy at acquiring a complete copy of more than fifty chapters.

The first section, chapters 1 to 33, follows the early life and love affairs of Hikaru Genji, son of an emperor and a low-ranking concubine, whom the emperor removes from the succession for political reasons by giving him the surname Minamoto. The second, chapters 34 to 41, tells of his old age and death, and the last, chapters 42 to 54, turns to his grandson Niou and supposed son Kaoru. Of some four hundred characters, almost none is named. They are called by function, rank or relation, such as Minister of the Left, which court manners made necessary.

The language is Heian court Japanese, in kana rather than the kanji used for more prestigious writing, and it needs specialised study. The tale ends abruptly. Arthur Waley thought it finished, Ivan Morris thought later chapters were lost, and Edward Seidensticker thought Murasaki simply wrote as long as she could.

The original manuscript no longer exists, but about 300 later copies differ from one another. In the thirteenth century Minamoto no Chikayuki and Fujiwara Teika each edited and revised the text, and Teika's more conservative version is thought to represent the original better. A twelfth-century picture scroll, the Genji Monogatari Emaki, is the earliest surviving Japanese picture scroll, though only about 15 per cent of it remains. Tosa Mitsuoki painted scenes in Heian style in the seventeenth century, and ukiyo-e prints of the Edo period also took the tale as a subject.

A century after its completion it was already hard to read without notes. The poet Akiko Yosano turned it into modern Japanese in the early twentieth century. Suematsu Kencho made the first, incomplete English translation in 1882, and Arthur Waley's version appeared from 1925 to 1933.
the-tale-of-igors-campaign: The poem describes the failed raid of 1185 by Igor Svyatoslavich, Prince of Novgorod-Seversk, on the Polovtsians, the name Rus' sources give to the Cumans, who lived along the lower Don. Other figures of the Rus' world appear, among them the bard Boyan and the princes Vseslav of Polotsk, Yaroslav Osmomysl of Halych and Vsevolod the Big Nest of Suzdal. The author appeals to the warring princes of the Rus' to unite against the constant threat from the Turkic East. Igor's campaign is also recorded in the Kievan Chronicle of about 1200.

The text shows Christianity and the old Slavic religion side by side. Igor's wife Yaroslavna calls on the forces of nature from the walls of Putyvl, and Christian motifs stand beside depersonalised pagan gods. Its main themes are patriotism, the power of nature and the homeland. Scholars have compared it with the Song of Roland and the Song of the Nibelungs, but it differs from these in its many vivid descriptions of nature.

The only manuscript, claimed to date from the 15th century, was found in 1795 in the library of the Transfiguration Monastery in Yaroslavl. Its superior, Joel Bykovsky, sold it to the landowner Aleksei Musin-Pushkin as part of a collection of ten texts. Musin-Pushkin made a transcription for Catherine the Great in 1795 or 1796 and published the poem in 1800 with the paleographers Alexei Malinovsky and Nikolai Bantysh-Kamensky. The manuscript was reported to have burned in the Moscow fire of 1812 with Musin-Pushkin's library. Vladimir Nabokov translated it into English in 1960, and Dmitry Likhachev prepared the standard Soviet edition.

After the manuscript was lost, doubts arose about its authenticity, partly because contemporary fabrications such as the Songs of Ossian were known. The current scholarly consensus holds it to be a work of the late 12th century, perhaps composed orally and written down in the 13th. Edward L. Keenan has argued that Josef Dobrovský forged it, but Andrey Zaliznyak concluded in 2004 that forgery is virtually impossible, noting that birch bark documents found in Novgorod showed that puzzling words of the poem were common speech in the 12th century.

The publication caused a stir in Russian literary circles because the poem was the earliest Slavonic writing without any element of Church Slavonic. Alexander Borodin adapted the story as the opera Prince Igor, first performed in 1890, which became one of the classics of Russian theatre. The poem also became a subject of politics: in the Soviet Union, attempts to question its authenticity were condemned.
the-troubles: The roots of the conflict lie in the Plantation of Ulster of 1609, when Scottish and English settlers were given land taken from the native Irish, and in later conflicts between Catholics and Protestants. As Home Rule drew near in 1912, unionists led by Edward Carson signed the Ulster Covenant and formed the Ulster Volunteer Force. Unionists and loyalists, mostly Ulster Protestants, wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom, while nationalists and republicans, mostly Catholics, wanted a united Ireland. It was not a religious war, though the division ran along those lines.

Writers disagree on the start of the Troubles, proposing the formation of the modern Ulster Volunteer Force in 1966, the civil rights march in Derry on 5 October 1968, or the deployment of British troops on 14 August 1969. Tensions grew during a campaign by the Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association against discrimination against the Catholic minority. The government tried to suppress the protests, the Royal Ulster Constabulary was criticised for sectarianism and brutality, and loyalists opposed the campaign. The riots of August 1969 brought British troops, in what became the Army's longest operation, and peace walls were built to separate communities.

Catholic support for the Army fell after Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, when British paratroopers shot dead thirteen unarmed men at an anti-internment rally in Derry. The violence included bombings and shootings by the Provisional IRA, the INLA and loyalist groups such as the UVF and UDA, as well as killings by state forces, collusion, riots and the creation of no-go areas. In 1981 ten republican prisoners died on hunger strike, and the first, Bobby Sands, had been elected to Parliament. Republican and loyalist ceasefires were declared in 1994, and the IRA ended its own with the Docklands bombing in London on 9 February 1996.

Talks between the main parties led to the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, which restored self-government to Northern Ireland on the basis of power-sharing and provided for consent, civil and political rights, police reform, paramilitary disarmament and the early release of prisoners. An executive with the four main parties, Sinn Féin among them, was formed in 1999, and the Royal Ulster Constabulary became the Police Service of Northern Ireland.

More than 3,500 people died. About 52% were civilians, 32% members of the British security forces and 16% members of paramilitary groups. Republican paramilitaries were responsible for about 60% of deaths, loyalists for 30% and the security forces for 10%.
the-wealth-of-nations: The Wealth of Nations was published in two volumes on 9 March 1776, during the Scottish Enlightenment. It was the product of seventeen years of notes and earlier studies, and took Smith some ten years to write. It drew on the conversation of economists of the time, such as Nicholas Magens, about conditions at the beginning of the Industrial Revolution. In the 18th century much of the world economy was dominated by European feudal and mercantilist institutions, with hereditary privilege, guilds, colonial trading monopolies and protective tariffs. Smith offered a reformed economic theory to replace the mercantilist and physiocratic theories.

Book I holds that the division of labour caused a greater increase in production than any other factor, and that it arises from humans' propensity to barter and is limited by the extent of the market. Book II treats stock and capital, and Book III the different progress of opulence in different nations, in which Smith argues that capital is directed first to agriculture, then to manufactures and last to foreign commerce.

Book IV attacks mercantilism, in particular protectionist tariffs and the idea that large reserves of precious metals are necessary for a country's success. Smith rejected the view that wealth came from zero-sum competition between states. He argued that individuals pursuing their own interest often promote that of society, using the metaphor of an invisible hand, which appears only once in the book. He also criticised slavery, rent-seeking by landlords, primogeniture, public debt and military spending for imperial purposes, and favoured public education, a judiciary and a standing army. Book V sets out four maxims of taxation: proportionality, transparency, convenience and efficiency, and Smith called a land value tax most reasonable.

The first edition sold out in six months. The printer William Strahan wrote that Hume thought it required too much thought to be as popular as Edward Gibbon's history, and Gibbon praised it as an extensive science in a single book. In 1791 James Madison cited it in Congress against a national bank, and Thomas Jefferson called it the best book on money and commerce, unless Say's Political Economy could be had. It was translated into French, German and Spanish in the late 18th century, and the Spanish Inquisition banned the French translation.

The book did not at once transform policy, but it became one of the most influential of modern times. Karl Marx called it the true Bible of the classical political economy of the 18th century, and Marxian economics developed as a critique of the tradition it established. Modern scholars stress that Smith used the invisible hand sparingly, acknowledged the dangers of monopolies and supported some state intervention.
theatre: Modern Western theatre comes in large measure from the theatre of ancient Greece, from which it takes technical terms, classification into genres and many themes, stock characters and plot elements. Western theatre originated in the city-state of Athens, as part of a wider culture of performance that included festivals, religious rituals, law, athletics, music and poetry. Attendance at the City Dionysia was an important part of citizenship. The Greeks also developed dramatic criticism and theatre architecture.

According to Aristotle, the first theoretician of theatre, its origins lie in festivals honouring Dionysus. Greek drama consisted of tragedy, comedy and the satyr play. Athenian tragedy emerged in the sixth century BCE and flowered in the fifth. Playwrights at the City Dionysia presented a tetralogy, usually three tragedies and one satyr play. Official records begin in 501 BCE, when the satyr play was introduced. Of more than a thousand tragedies performed in the fifth century BCE only 32 survive, with complete texts by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides.

Theatre is a collaborative art that uses live performers, usually actors, to present a real or imagined event before a live audience in a specific place, often a stage. The word comes from the Ancient Greek théatron, a place for viewing. Greek performances took place in semi-circular auditoria cut into hillsides, seating 10,000 to 20,000 people, with a dancing floor called the orchestra and a scene building called the skene. The actors, always men, wore masks and each might play several parts. Modern musical theatre emerged from comic opera, variety, vaudeville and music hall in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Theatre has been part of human culture for more than 2,500 years and has produced many theories. Aristotle's Poetics, from about 335 BCE, is the earliest surviving example and has influenced theories ever since. He held that tragedy has six parts, in order of importance plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle. Konstantin Stanislavski treated theatre as an art autonomous from literature, and his system of actor training spread across Europe and the United States.
thebes-greece: Excavations in and around Thebes have revealed a Mycenaean settlement, cist graves holding weapons and ivory, and clay tablets in Linear B, which show its importance in the Bronze Age. The Cadmea, the central citadel, shows signs of destruction towards the end of the Mycenaean era, and much of the site was abandoned. Thebes was the setting of myths about Cadmus, Oedipus, Dionysus and Heracles, and the Iliad calls it Seven-Gated Thebes to distinguish it from the city in Egypt. In 480 to 479 BCE a contingent of 400 Thebans stood at Thermopylae, but the governing aristocracy then joined Xerxes I and fought for him at Plataea, and the victorious Greeks took away the city's presidency of the Boeotian League.

Thebes was a firm ally of Sparta in the Peloponnesian War, but it broke with Sparta afterwards. A Spartan force seized the Cadmea in 382 BCE; three years later the garrison was expelled and a democratic constitution replaced the oligarchy. The army trained and led by Epaminondas and Pelopidas, which included the Sacred Band of Thebes, defeated the Spartans at Leuctra in 371 BCE. Thebes then led a large coalition into Peloponnesus and crippled Sparta, partly by freeing many helots. Its predominance was short, and after Epaminondas died at Mantinea in 362 BCE it fell back to a secondary power.

Thebes and Athens lost the Battle of Chaeronea to Philip II of Macedon in 338 BCE. After an unsuccessful revolt in 335 BCE, Alexander the Great and his Greek allies destroyed the city, except, according to tradition, the house of Pindar and the temples, divided its territory among other Boeotian cities and sold its people into slavery. Ancient writers treat this as excessive. Cassander re-established Thebes in 315 BCE, but it never regained its prominence, and Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged it in 293 and 292 BCE.

Thebes came under Roman rule after the Boeotian League was dissolved in 146 BCE, and in the late 7th century Justinian II made it the capital of the Theme of Hellas. By the middle of the 12th century it was the biggest producer of silks in the Byzantine Empire, until the Normans of Sicily plundered it in 1147 and took craftsmen to Palermo. The city conquered by the Fourth Crusade in 1205 is today the largest city of Boeotia in Central Greece. It has an archaeological museum, remains of the Cadmea and the church of Luke the Evangelist, which holds the saint's tomb and relics.
themistocles: Themistocles was born in the Attic deme of Phrearrhii, the son of Neocles, whom Plutarch calls no very conspicuous man at Athens. His mother's name was either Euterpe or Abrotonum, and her origin is given variously as Halicarnassus, Thrace or Acarnania. Plutarch indicates that because of her background he was something of an outsider. He grew up after Cleisthenes had set up the Athenian democracy, which opened power to men like him. He moved to the Ceramicus, a down-market part of Athens, and courted the poor, and he was the first in Athens to practise law as a preparation for public life.

Elected Archon Eponymous in 493 BCE, he began the building of a new port at Piraeus, which had three natural harbours and could be easily fortified. Naval power depended on the common citizens as rowers, so the policy also strengthened ordinary Athenians. In 483 BCE he persuaded the Athenians to build a fleet of 200 triremes. At the congress of Greek states in 481 BCE the other naval powers refused to let Athens command the fleet, and the Spartan Eurybiades took the command, although Herodotus is clear that Themistocles commanded in all but name.

Later he grew arrogant and made enemies. The Spartans promoted Cimon, son of Miltiades, as a rival, and he lost favour by building a sanctuary of Artemis Aristoboulē, meaning of good counsel, near his home. In 472 or 471 BCE he was ostracised. The Spartans then tried to implicate him in the treason of their general Pausanias. He fled, found sanctuary with Alexander I of Macedon at Pydna, and sailed to Asia Minor.

Thucydides has his ship land at Ephesus, while Plutarch has it dock at Cyme. Themistocles sought service with Artaxerxes I and became governor of Magnesia, perhaps the first ruler to issue coins with his own portrait. According to Thucydides he died at Magnesia in 459 BCE, aged 65, of natural causes, although rumour held that he poisoned himself rather than make war on Athens.

He died with his reputation in tatters, but Pericles rehabilitated it in the 450s BCE, and by the time of Herodotus he was again seen as a hero. Plutarch calls him the man most instrumental in achieving the salvation of Greece. His naval policy lay behind the Delian League and the later Athenian Empire.
theodor-herzl: Theodor Herzl was born on 2 May 1860 on Dohány utca in the Jewish quarter of Pest, then in the Kingdom of Hungary, to Jeanette and Jakob Herzl, German-speaking, assimilated Jews of the Neolog tradition. His father was a highly successful businessman. After a brief legal career in Vienna he became the Paris correspondent of the Viennese newspaper Neue Freie Presse. He also wrote comedies and dramas, among them Das Neue Ghetto of 1898, his only play with Jewish characters. On 25 June 1889 he married Julie Naschauer; the marriage was unhappy, although three children were born to it.

In Paris Herzl followed the Dreyfus affair, in which the Jewish army captain Alfred Dreyfus was falsely convicted of spying for Germany. Herzl said that the case turned him into a Zionist, though some modern scholars think he may have exaggerated its influence. Convinced that anti-Jewish sentiment made assimilation impossible, he published the pamphlet Der Judenstaat on 14 February 1896 in Leipzig and Vienna.

In 1897 Herzl founded the Zionist newspaper Die Welt in Vienna and convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel, where he was elected president of the Zionist Organization, a position he held until his death. He met Wilhelm II on 29 October 1898 near Mikveh Israel and again in Jerusalem, and proposed to Abdul Hamid II that Zionism could improve the sultan's reputation and finances in exchange for Jewish settlement in Palestine. Through Joseph Chamberlain he negotiated for a charter at Al 'Arish in Sinai, which the Earl of Cromer blocked as impractical. At the Sixth Zionist Congress in 1903 he presented the Uganda Scheme, which met strong opposition and was rejected.

Herzl died of cardiac sclerosis on 3 July 1904 at Edlach in Reichenau an der Rax, Lower Austria, at the age of 44. His will asked for the poorest-class funeral without speeches, yet some six thousand people followed the hearse. He was first buried in the Döbling district of Vienna, and in 1949 his remains were taken to Israel and buried on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, which is named after him. He is mentioned in the Israeli Declaration of Independence and is known in Hebrew as Chozeh HaMedinah, the Visionary of the State. Herzl Day is an Israeli national holiday.
theodora-wife-of-justinian-i: Much of Theodora's early life, including the date and place of her birth, is uncertain, and later sources propose Syria, Cyprus, Paphlagonia and Alexandria; modern scholars think she was most likely raised in Constantinople. Her father, Acacius, kept bears for the Green faction of the Hippodrome. After his death her mother remarried, and when the Greens refused to give the family his post, the Blue faction gave it to them. She worked as an actress, and later travelled to North Africa as the concubine of Hecebolus, governor of the Libyan Pentapolis.

The chief source for this period is the Secret History of Procopius, which some modern scholars regard as slanderous and exaggerated, though David Potter writes that behind its inventions there lies the semblance of fact. Justinian could not marry an actress under the law of Constantine's time; after the death of Empress Euphemia in 524, Emperor Justin issued an edict allowing it.

Theodora was crowned augusta when Justinian became emperor in 527. Justinian called her his partner in his deliberations in a law of 535, and the Secret History says she sat in state councils. She helped bring down the praetorian prefect John the Cappadocian in 541, and Procopius alleges that she ordered the murder of the Ostrogothic queen Amalasuintha, a claim that a surviving letter of King Theodahad appears to support. In 528 the couple ordered the brothels closed, and she founded a convent called the Metanoia for former prostitutes, though Procopius describes the women as confined there.

During the Nika riots of January 532 the rioters proclaimed Hypatius, nephew of Emperor Anastasius I, as emperor, and Justinian's officials prepared to flee. According to Procopius, Theodora told the council that flight was wrong and that royal purple was the noblest shroud. Scholars such as J. A. S. Evans think the speech is dramatised and reflects palace discussions rather than her literal words. Justinian's troops attacked the crowd in the Hippodrome and killed over 30,000 rebels.

Theodora supported the Miaphysites against her husband's Chalcedonian position, though Procopius and Evagrius Scholasticus suggested that the two only pretended to disagree. She founded a monastery at Sykae and sheltered Miaphysite leaders in the palace. Her opposition to Pope Silverius ended with his exile and starvation, and Vigilius was appointed in his place. She died on 28 June 548, probably of cancer, and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles. Mosaics in the Basilica of San Vitale at Ravenna, completed in 547, show her in imperial dress, and the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox Churches commemorate her as a saint on 14 November.
theodore-roosevelt: Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was born at 28 East 20th Street in Manhattan on 27 October 1858, the son of the businessman Theodore Roosevelt Sr. and Martha Stewart Bulloch. A sickly child with debilitating asthma, he overcame his health problems through vigorous exercise, which he called the strenuous life. He was homeschooled, solid in geography and bright in history, biology, French and German, but weak in mathematics and the classical languages. He entered Harvard University in September 1876, and his father's sudden death in 1878 devastated him. His book The Naval War of 1812, published in 1882, remains a standard study of the war.

In 1881 Roosevelt won election to the New York State Assembly. He lost the 1886 race for mayor of New York City, finishing third, and served on the United States Civil Service Commission from 1889 to 1895, fighting the spoilsmen. Appointed Assistant Secretary of the Navy in 1897, he called for a build-up of naval strength. When the Spanish–American War began in 1898 he resigned to form the Rough Riders with Colonel Leonard Wood, and returning a war hero he won the New York governorship by just 1 per cent.

Chosen as William McKinley's running mate in 1900, he became president when McKinley, shot by the anarchist Leon Czolgosz, died on 14 September 1901. He was elected to a full term in 1904 and, keeping his pledge not to run again, secured the 1908 nomination for William Howard Taft. After failing to win the Republican nomination in 1912 he founded the Bull Moose Party, and the split let the Democrat Woodrow Wilson win. He then led an expedition to the Amazon basin, where he nearly died of tropical disease. His offer to lead volunteers to France in the First World War was rejected, and he died on 6 January 1919.

Roosevelt's Square Deal had three main goals: conservation of natural resources, control of corporations and consumer protection. In 1902 he opposed the merger that created the Northern Securities Company, challenging the banker J. P. Morgan, and he sought a larger regulatory role for the federal government in place of 19th-century laissez-faire. Henry Kissinger's analysis holds that he was the first president to hold that the United States had a duty to make its power felt globally. His Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine held that the United States had to police the Western Hemisphere, lest European powers intervene there. He also made the White House the daily centre of news, and is credited with inventing the presidential press briefing.
theodoric-i: Theodoric succeeded King Wallia in 418. The Romans had ordered Wallia to move his people from Iberia to Gaul, and Theodoric completed their settlement in Gallia Aquitania II, Novempopulana and Gallia Narbonensis, then used the declining power of the Roman Empire to extend his territory southwards. After the death of Emperor Honorius and the usurpation of Joannes in 423, he tried to take the road junction of Arelate, but the general Aëtius, assisted by the Huns, saved the city. The Visigoths made a treaty and received Gallic noblemen as hostages. The later Emperor Avitus visited Theodoric, lived at his court and taught his sons.

In 436 the Franks were plundering Cologne and Trier, and Theodoric saw a chance to take Narbo Martius and reach the Mediterranean. The commander Litorius, with the help of the Huns, drove the Visigoths back to Tolosa, but Theodoric won the decisive battle there, and Litorius died of his injuries in Gothic captivity. Avitus then offered a peace treaty, which Theodoric accepted, and the Romans perhaps recognised the sovereignty of the Visigothic state at this time.

Relations with the Vandals turned hostile after Huneric, son of the Vandal ruler Geiseric, accused Theodoric's daughter, his wife, of plotting to kill him and in 444 had her mutilated and sent home. Theodoric then married another daughter to the Suevic king Rechiar in February 449, and Rechiar, with Visigothic troops, devastated the country around Caesaraugusta and took Ilerda by guile.

When Attila invaded Gaul, Avitus arranged an alliance between Theodoric and his long-standing enemy Aëtius. Theodoric joined with his whole army and his sons Thorismund and Theodoric. The allies relieved the city of Aurelianorum in June 451 and followed the Huns to the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains near Troyes, where Theodoric commanded the right wing. His forces contributed decisively to the Roman victory, but he was killed. Jordanes gives two accounts: that he was thrown from his horse and trampled, or that the Ostrogoth Andag killed him with a spear. His body was found the next day, and according to Gothic tradition his warriors buried him on the field. Thorismund was elected king at once.
Three of his sons ruled in turn and died violently: Thorismund was murdered in 453 by Theodoric II, who was murdered in 466 by Euric. Euric ruled until his death in 484.
theodoric-the-great: Theodoric, also called the Amal, was born around 454, at about the time the Ostrogoths defeated the Huns after Attila's death. His father Theodemir belonged to the Amal dynasty and his mother Ereleuva was the king's concubine. The Ostrogoths were settled in Pannonia, south of the Danube. In 461, when Theodoric was seven or eight, he was taken as a hostage to Constantinople to secure compliance with a treaty Theodemir had made with the emperor Leo I, which also provided for a yearly payment of gold. There he was well educated.

He returned to Pannonia around 470 and was recognised as king in 471. The emperor Zeno made him commander of the Eastern Roman forces in 483 and consul in 484, but Theodoric remained in constant hostilities with the emperor and often raided East Roman territory.

In 487 Theodoric blockaded Constantinople, occupying suburbs and cutting off its water, though he seems never to have intended to take the city. Zeno was also in difficulty with Odoacer, the king of Italy, and in 488 or 489 ordered Theodoric to overthrow him. Theodoric moved towards Italy in the autumn of 488 and won the battles of Isonzo and Verona in 489. He won the Battle of the Adda River on 11 August 490. He besieged Odoacer in Ravenna until 2 February 493, when a treaty made them joint rulers. Theodoric entered Ravenna on 5 March, and at a banquet on 15 March he killed Odoacer and had his most loyal followers slaughtered.

As ruler of Italy he upheld Roman legal administration and learning and promoted a major building programme. He repaired Ravenna's aqueduct, built himself a palace there, and restored the walls of Rome, for which the Senate erected a gilded statue of him. He was an Arian, and in his last years his relations with his Catholic Roman subjects and the emperor Justin I worsened. The philosopher Boethius, his magister officiorum from 522, was put to death in 524, and Pope John I died in 526.

Theodoric died in Ravenna on 30 August 526 and was succeeded by his grandson Athalaric, with Athalaric's mother Amalasuintha as regent. The union of the Gothic realms collapsed after his death, and the later campaigns of the emperor Justinian ended his kingdom. Historians differ on the nature of his rule. Traditionalists call him a Germanic king who imitated Roman customs, while others, citing his use of the title princeps, regard him as a Western Roman emperor in all but name. In medieval German legend he lives on as Dietrich von Bern.
theodosius-ii: Theodosius II was born on 10 April 401, the only son of Emperor Arcadius and Aelia Eudoxia. His father proclaimed him co-augustus on 10 January 402, at nine months, the youngest to bear the imperial title up to then. When Arcadius died on 1 May 408, the seven-year-old boy became sole emperor of the Eastern half of the empire. The praetorian prefect Anthemius governed at first, and the Theodosian walls of Constantinople were built under his supervision. In 414 his older sister Pulcheria, who had vowed perpetual virginity, was proclaimed augusta and acted as his guardian. In June 421 he married Aelia Eudocia, a woman of Athenian origin.

When the Western emperor Honorius died in 423 and Joannes was proclaimed in his place, Theodosius made war on him in 424 and installed Valentinian III in the West on 23 October 425. In 425 he founded the University of Constantinople, with 31 chairs, 15 in Latin and 16 in Greek. In 429 he appointed a commission to collect the laws since Constantine I; a second commission completed the Codex Theodosianus, published in 438 and later a basis for Justinian I's Corpus Juris Civilis.

Against the Huns he paid 350 pounds of gold a year from 424, doubled to 700 pounds in 439 with the rise of Attila and Bleda. After the Huns sacked the middle Danube cities in 441 and defeated Roman armies in 447, a peace brought an annual tribute of 2,100 pounds of gold. Theodosius also made war on the Sasanian Empire in 421 to 422, which ended in stalemate.

He frequently tried to settle disputes about the nature of Christ. He appointed Nestorius archbishop of Constantinople in 428 and called the First Council of Ephesus in 431, which condemned Nestorius. The Second Council of Ephesus in 449 restored Eutyches and deposed Flavian, and Pope Leo I called it the robber synod; the Council of Chalcedon reversed it after the emperor's death.

Theodosius died on 28 July 450 after falling from his horse, and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles. Pulcheria married Marcian, who became emperor. Ancient and modern historians often see Theodosius as pushed around by his sister, his wife and the eunuch Chrysaphius, whose influence on foreign policy towards the Huns and on the pro-Monophysite line was resented by Pulcheria.
theogony: The Theogony is written in the epic dialect of Ancient Greek and contains 1,022 lines. It is a large-scale synthesis of many local Greek traditions about the gods, arranged as a narrative of how they came to be and how they secured permanent control of the cosmos. It is the first known Greek mythical cosmogony. In form it is a hymn invoking Zeus and the Muses, and it developed from the hymnic preludes with which a rhapsode began a performance at poetic competitions. Its written form was established in the 6th century BCE.

The universe begins as Chaos, a dark void. Gaia (Earth), Tartarus and Eros (Desire) then arise, and from Chaos come Erebus (Darkness) and Nyx (Night). Gaia bears Uranus (Sky), the mountains and Pontus (Sea). Uranus and Gaia produce the twelve Titans, the three Cyclopes and the three Hundred-Handers, whom Uranus hides away inside Gaia. At her urging the youngest Titan, Cronus, castrates his father with an adamantine sickle and takes supreme command.

Cronus is told that one of his children will overthrow him, so he swallows each child Rhea bears. Rhea hides Zeus on Crete and gives Cronus a stone wrapped in baby's clothes. Grown, Zeus forces Cronus to disgorge the others, and the Titanomachy follows. In its tenth year Zeus frees the Hundred-Handers, who help him win, and the Titans are thrown into Tartarus. Zeus then defeats the monster Typhon, is elected king of the gods and swallows his first wife, Metis, so that no son of hers can overthrow him.

The poem also gives long genealogies of the gods and their descendants, and tells how Prometheus tricked Zeus over the division of a sacrificial ox, stole fire in a fennel stalk and was chained to a cliff, where an eagle fed on his liver until Heracles freed him.

The decipherment of Hittite texts, notably the Kingship in Heaven text first presented in 1946, showed in Kumarbi an Anatolian parallel to the conflict of Uranus and Cronus. Some scholars hold that Near Eastern traditions such as the Babylonian Dynasty of Dunnum reached Hesiod as lingering traces from the Mycenaean period rather than through contacts in his own time.

Its account of Chaos as the origin influenced the first Greek philosophers, who sought a first principle (arche) of all things. John Milton regarded the poem as inspired by Satan, in line with early Christian writers such as Justin Martyr. The earliest surviving manuscripts date from the end of the 13th century, and about 64 are known from 1600 or earlier.
theophilos-emperor: Theophilos was born in late 812 or early 813, the son of Emperor Michael II and Thekla and the godson of Emperor Leo V the Armenian. Michael crowned him co-emperor in 821. Unlike his father, he received an extensive education, from the grammarian John Hylilas, and was a great admirer of music and art. On 5 June 830, aged seventeen, he married Theodora, and the couple had seven children, among them the future Emperor Michael III.

Theophilos became sole emperor on 2 October 829 and issued an edict against the veneration of icons in 832. He saw himself as a champion of justice. At his accession he faced war with the Arabs on two fronts: Palermo fell to them in 831 after a year-long siege, and the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun invaded Cappadocia. After destroying an Abbasid raiding army at Charsianon in 831, Theophilos held a triumph, but the retaliation cost the Byzantines the fortress of Loulon and the city of Tyana.

In 837 he led an army of 70,000 men into Mesopotamia, but in 838 Caliph al-Mu'tasim invaded Anatolia. Theophilos was defeated on 21 July 838 at the Battle of Anzen, and Amorion, the ancestral home of his dynasty, fell on 12 or 15 August 838 after holding out for fifty-five days. Around 839 or 840 he sought allies against the Abbasids and sent an embassy to the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba. He also gave refuge to Khurramite refugees under the Persian Theophobos, a convert who became one of his generals.

Theophilos was a keen builder. With John the Grammarian he built the palace of Bryas in imitation of Arab palaces, and he decorated the Magnaura hall in Constantinople with a throne and mechanical lions and birds, according to Liudprand of Cremona. He repaired the Walls of Constantinople, and his name appears in their inscriptions more often than any other emperor's.

Theophilos died on 20 January 842. In his last illness he suspected that Theophobos would attempt a coup, and after the emperor's death his leading officers executed Theophobos. His widow Theodora ruled until 856 and defended his reputation, which softened the condemnation of his memory, although later sources that favoured icons remained critical. He was remembered as a just ruler, and the Timarion shows him as one of the judges in the Netherworld.
theory-of-relativity: Albert Einstein published special relativity in 1905, building on results of Albert A. Michelson, Hendrik Lorentz, Henri Poincaré and others, with later work by Max Planck, Hermann Minkowski and others. He developed general relativity between 1907 and 1915, with contributions from many others after 1915, and its final form was published in 1916. The name comes from the expression 'relative theory' used by Planck in 1906, who stressed how the theory uses the principle of relativity. Much of the background lay in attempts to detect the luminiferous aether, the hypothetical medium thought to carry light waves. The Michelson-Morley experiment, performed in 1881 and again in 1887, found no aether wind.

Special relativity is a theory of the structure of spacetime, introduced in Einstein's 1905 paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies. It rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same for all observers in any inertial frame, and the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers regardless of the motion of the source. Its consequences include the relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, in which moving clocks tick more slowly, length contraction, a finite maximum speed, and the equivalence of mass and energy, E = mc2.

General relativity is a theory of gravitation. It began with the equivalence principle, under which accelerated motion and rest in a gravitational field are physically identical, so that free fall is inertial motion. Einstein proposed that spacetime is curved, and after discussion with the mathematician Marcel Grossmann he formulated the theory in Riemannian geometry. In 1915 he devised the Einstein field equations, which relate the curvature of spacetime to the mass, energy and momentum within it. Its consequences include gravitational time dilation, the precession of orbits, as observed in the orbit of Mercury, and the bending of light.

By the 1920s the physics community understood and accepted special relativity, and it became a necessary tool in atomic physics, nuclear physics and quantum mechanics. General relativity at first seemed less useful, since its assertions were mostly on an astronomical scale and its mathematics was difficult. Around 1960 it became central to physics and astronomy, as discoveries such as quasars (1963), the microwave background radiation (1965), pulsars (1967) and the first black hole candidates (1981) were explained by it. The theory superseded a 200-year-old mechanics created chiefly by Isaac Newton, and predicted neutron stars, black holes and gravitational waves.
thermae-himeraeae: The site has been populated since prehistoric times. Its documented history begins after the second Battle of Himera in 409 BCE, when the older neighbouring town of Himera was completely destroyed by the Carthaginian army under Hannibal Mago. Survivors moved to a site then called Thermae, today Termini, which became Himera's successor. The new town took its name from the hot springs for which it was known, whose discovery legend connected with the wanderings of Hercules. It quickly became a considerable town, though it stayed under Carthaginian rule.

In 260 BCE a body of Roman troops encamped nearby was attacked by Hamilcar and defeated with heavy loss. Before the First Punic War ended in 241 BCE the Romans besieged and took Thermae, but treated it with unusual favour: Cicero reports that they allowed the Thermitani to govern their city and territory by their own laws as a reward for steady fidelity. In his time it was a flourishing place with considerable trade, and he praised its citizens' taste for art, noting that Scipio had restored statues to them after the conquest of Carthage.

Thermae seems to have become a colony in the time of Augustus. Few accounts survive of later periods, but its name appears in Ptolemy and the Itineraries, and the aqueduct and other remains suggest that it continued through the Roman Empire. After the fall of the Roman Empire it declined, though it remained a bishopric until the 12th century.

From the Middle Ages to the early 19th century it was a major centre for the collection and shipping of grain, stored and taxed in a government warehouse complex, the caricatore regio. This made it one of the major ports of Sicily, with trade links to Genoa, Pisa and Venice. The closing of the caricatore in the 19th century brought a profound economic crisis that lasted until the end of the 20th century.

Termini Imerese is a town of the Metropolitan City of Palermo, about 33 km from Palermo. Its Roman remains include the largest and best preserved aqueduct bridge on the island and an amphitheatre probably of the Augustan age, built into houses. The Greek ruins of Himera lie within the comune's borders, and hot waters have flowed in the thermal baths in the old town since the Roman age.
thermometer: Records of the early history are sparse and conflicting, which makes it hard to pinpoint the invention of the thermometer to one person or date. Because of the many parallel developments and gradual improvements, it is best viewed as an evolving technology rather than a single invention. Philo of Byzantium described an experiment with a tube dipped in liquid and joined to an air-tight hollow sphere. When the air in the sphere was heated by a candle or the sun, bubbles escaped into the vessel; as it cooled, liquid was drawn up the tube.

Hero of Alexandria gave a more elaborate version of the same principle in his Pneumatics, in which heated and cooled air moved water. Translations of the work reached Italy in the late 16th century, and Galileo Galilei had read it by 1594. Robert Fludd used a translation of Philo's experiment around 1617 as the basis for his air thermometer.

A thermometer has two essential elements: a sensor in which something changes with temperature, such as the bulb of a mercury-in-glass instrument, and a way of turning that change into a number, such as a marked scale or a digital readout. W. E. K. Middleton argued that a meter must have a scale or its equivalent, so that a thermometer is simply a thermoscope with a scale, and that the invention of the thermoscope remains far more obscure.

Readings from two thermometers can be compared only if they follow an agreed scale. Traditionally a scale was put on a liquid-in-glass thermometer in three stages: the instrument was placed in a stirred mixture of pure ice and water and the level marked, then in a steam bath at standard atmospheric pressure and marked again, and the distance between the marks was divided into equal parts. The most recent official scale is the International Temperature Scale of 1990.

Fahrenheit proposed his temperature scale in 1724. René Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur invented an alcohol thermometer and a scale in 1730, which proved less reliable than Fahrenheit's mercury instrument. Celsius's scale of 1742 placed zero at the boiling point of water and 100 at the freezing point, the reverse of the scale that now bears his name.

Herman Boerhaave was the first physician to use thermometer measurements in clinical practice. In 1866 Sir Thomas Clifford Allbutt invented a clinical thermometer that gave a body temperature in five minutes instead of twenty. Traditional thermometers did not keep their reading once moved; registering thermometers hold the highest or lowest temperature reached until reset, and electronic ones increasingly provide a digital display or feed a computer.
theseus: In the myth Aegeus, king of Athens, was childless and consulted the Oracle of Delphi, whose cryptic reply he did not understand. His host Pittheus, king of Troezen, understood it and gave him his daughter Aethra. Following Athena's instructions in a dream, Aethra also waded to the island of Sphairia and was possessed there by Poseidon, so that Theseus had both divine and mortal parentage. Before leaving, Aegeus buried his sandals and sword under a huge rock, to be taken by his son when he was strong enough to move it as proof of his royal birth.

Theseus was raised in Troezen. When he grew up he moved the rock and set out for Athens. He chose the dangerous land route round the Saronic Gulf rather than the sea, and defeated a series of bandits on the way: Periphetes, Sinis, the Crommyonian Sow, Sciron, Cercyon and Procrustes, who was cut to fit his own beds. Scholars believe that Theseus, if he lived, may have lived in the Late Bronze Age, or perhaps as a king in the 8th or 9th century BCE.

In Athens Medea, then Aegeus's consort, recognised Theseus and tried to have him killed by sending him to capture the Marathonian Bull. When he returned, she tried to poison him, but Aegeus recognised the sandals and sword and knocked the cup from his hands. Theseus then defeated the Pallantides, the sons of Pallas, who plotted against him as rivals for the throne. He is credited with the synoikismos, the union of Attica under Athenian rule.

Minos of Crete required Athens to send seven youths and seven maidens as tribute to the Minotaur, which lived in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus. Theseus took the place of one of the youths, promising his father to hoist a white sail if successful. Minos's daughter Ariadne gave him a ball of thread, and he killed the Minotaur and escaped. He abandoned Ariadne on Naxos, where Dionysus found and married her, and forgot the white sail. Aegeus, thinking his son dead, threw himself into the sea. In Euripides's version Theseus cursed his own son Hippolytus after Phaedra's false accusation.

In one account Lycomedes of Skyros threw Theseus off a cliff after Theseus had lost popularity in Athens. In 475 BCE, following an oracle, Cimon of Athens conquered Skyros and identified a coffin holding a large corpse with a bronze spearhead and a sword as Theseus's remains, which were reburied in Athens. The Athenians preserved the thirty-oared ship in which Theseus returned from Crete, replacing its planks as they decayed, and sent it each year to Delos in honour of Apollo; philosophers asked whether it remained the same ship, the Ship of Theseus paradox.
thessaloniki: Thessaloniki stands on the Thermaic Gulf, at the northwest corner of the Aegean Sea, bounded on the west by the delta of the Axios and on the southeast by Mount Chortiatis. It lies 502 kilometres north of Athens. Under the Roman Empire the Via Egnatia carried trade between Rome and Byzantium through the city and linked the empire with Asia, notably the Silk Road.

Cassander of Macedon founded the city around 315 BCE, on or near the ancient town of Therma, and named it after his wife Thessalonike, a half-sister of Alexander the Great. Under the kingdom of Macedonia it kept its own autonomy and became the most important city in Macedonia, though Pella remained the capital. In the Byzantine Empire it was the second city after Constantinople in wealth and size, with 150,000 inhabitants in the mid-12th century, until it passed to Venetian control in 1423.

Sultan Murad II captured and sacked the city in 1430; contemporary reports estimated that about one-fifth of its population was enslaved. Under Ottoman rule it was one of the empire's most important trading hubs, and Sephardic Jews arriving from Spain made its Jewish community mostly Sephardic. The city passed to the Kingdom of Greece on 8 November 1912. In 1917 a great fire destroyed much of the centre, and planners including Thomas Mawson and Ernest Hébrard rebuilt it on a plan of axes, diagonal streets and monumental squares.

Thessaloniki is the second-largest city of Greece and the capital of the region of Central Macedonia. The municipality had 319,045 inhabitants in 2021 and the metropolitan area 1,006,112. Its Paleochristian and Byzantine monuments form a World Heritage Site, and the Ano Poli, the old town that escaped the fire, is also heritage-listed. The Roman forum, found by accident in the 1960s, is among its sites. Aristotle University, founded in 1926, is the largest university in Greece.
thimphu: Thimphu lies in the western central part of Bhutan, in the narrow, linear valley of the Wang Chhu, also called the Thimphu River, which flows out into India as the Raidāk. The city extends north and south along the west bank and stands between 2,248 and 2,648 metres above sea level, making it the highest capital in Asia. The surrounding hills range from 2,000 to 3,800 metres, and the two altitude zones, warm temperate and cold temperate, decide the vegetation of the valley. At its southern end the Lungten Zampa bridge connects the east and west banks of the river. The city has no airport of its own and relies on Paro, about 52 kilometres away by road.

Before 1960 Thimphu was a group of hamlets scattered across the valley, among them Motithang, Changangkha, Changlimithang, Langchupakha and Taba. In 1885 a battle at what is now the Changlimithang sports ground ended in a decisive victory that opened the way for Ugyen Wangchuck, the first King of Bhutan, to control virtually the whole country. Under the Wangchuck dynasty the country enjoyed peace and progress under reformist monarchs. The third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, abolished serfdom, redistributed land and reformed taxation and the executive, legislative and judicial systems.

The capital was moved from the ancient capital of Punakha to Thimphu, and in 1961 Thimphu was officially declared the capital of the Kingdom of Bhutan by Jigme Dorji Wangchuck. It was then a hamlet of a few houses built around the Tashichho Dzong. It was only after roads were built in the 1960s, and the country opened to the outside world following the coronation of the fourth king, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, that the city grew rapidly. India provided financial and other assistance.

Thimphu is the capital and largest city of Bhutan and the seat of most important political institutions, including the National Assembly and the embassies. Dechencholing Palace, the official residence of the King, lies to the north of the city. Vajrayana Buddhism is the state religion, and the chief abbot, the Je Khenpo, spends six months of the year in the Tashichho Dzong in Thimphu and six months in Punakha. The Tshechu festival, held in September or October, features mask dances in the courtyards of the dzong. Other landmarks include the Memorial Chorten, Changangkha Lhakhang, founded in the 13th century, and the National Institute of Zorig Chusum, which teaches the thirteen traditional arts and crafts of Bhutan.
third-crusade: After the fall of Edessa in 1144 and the failure of the Second Crusade, Nur al-Din of the Zengid dynasty united Aleppo, Mosul and later Damascus, and reduced the Crusader states. His nephew Saladin became vizier of Egypt in 1169 and, after Nur al-Din's death in 1174, took Syria for himself, defeating the Zengids at the Battle of the Horns of Hama in 1175. Raids by Reynald of Châtillon on caravans gave Saladin a pretext to move against the Franks. News of the loss of Jerusalem reached the West in the autumn of 1187, and within ten days of the death of Pope Urban III, his successor Gregory VIII proclaimed a new crusade.

Emperor Frederick Barbarossa took the cross at Strasbourg and put the Jews of Germany under his protection, since the earlier crusades had brought violence against them in Germany. He set out from Regensburg on 11 May 1189 and led his army through Hungary and the Balkans, where relations with the Byzantine emperor Isaac were strained. In Anatolia the army defeated Turkish forces at Iconium on 18 May 1190, but Frederick drowned while crossing a river on 10 June 1190, and most of his troops returned home.

Henry II of England and Philip II of France ended their war in January 1188 and both took the cross; each imposed a Saladin tithe. Henry died on 6 July 1189 and Richard I took his place. The crusaders besieged Acre, where Saladin's forces in turn besieged them, and disease killed Queen Sibylla of Jerusalem in 1190. Philip left the Holy Land in August 1191. Richard won the Battle of Arsuf on 7 September 1191 and took Jaffa. In the winter he advanced to within 12 miles of Jerusalem but turned back because of bad weather and fear of being trapped. Saladin retook Jaffa in July 1192.

The crusade kept the Crusader states from collapse, and the capture of Cyprus strengthened them, but it failed to retake Jerusalem. Historians have called it a success, a failure or hardly justified by its cost. Neither side was satisfied, though trade flourished along the Mediterranean coast. The failure inspired the Fourth Crusade of 1202 to 1204, and Europeans regained the city only briefly, in the Sixth Crusade in 1229.

On 2 September 1192 Richard and Saladin agreed the Treaty of Jaffa. Muslims kept Jerusalem, but unarmed Christian pilgrims and merchants could visit it. The Christians kept a narrow strip of coast from Tyre to Jaffa, with Ramla and Lydda to be divided, and a three-year truce was agreed. Richard left on 9 October 1192 because of threats to his rule in Europe.
third-dynasty-of-ur: The Akkadian Empire was destroyed in the middle of the 22nd century BCE in circumstances that are not well known, with the Gutians seeming to be the main actors, and Lower Mesopotamia broke into kingdoms centred on cities such as Uruk and Lagash. Utu-hegal of Uruk defeated the Guti king Tirigan but was dethroned after about eight years by court notables led by Ur-Namma, the governor of Ur, who was probably his brother. Ur-Namma (c. 2112 to 2094 BCE) took the title King of Sumer and Akkad, restored cities, sanctuaries and irrigation canals, and issued a law code that presented him as a just king.

His son Shulgi (c. 2094 to 2047 BCE) reigned for about half the dynasty's duration. His campaigns reached the Upper Tigris, the western Zagros and Elam, and he made marriage alliances with kingdoms on the Iranian plateau and with Mari. He was deified, and a literature glorifying him was written. The fall is poorly understood, but Ibbi-Sin held on for about twenty years while controlling only a small part of the empire, after Ishbi-Erra seceded at Isin amid food shortages and revolts. A coalition of Elamite troops from Anshan and Shimashki dealt the fatal blow around 2004 BCE.

The state was a patrimonial system, a hierarchy of households with the royal household at the top, in which all resources belonged to the king and his family. The king, whose power rested on the support of the god Enlil of Nippur, headed the administration and army and appointed high officials. The administration was centralised and bureaucratic, and the vast majority of surviving documents from the period are administrative.

The economy was redistributive. Dependent workers, men and women, were organised in troops and paid in rations of barley, wool and other goods. Textile workshops were the most important, with some 6,000 workers in the province of Girsu under a single office. About 250 trial reports survive, and the Code of Ur-Nammu, known from fragmentary late copies, is the earliest law collection of its kind. Sumerian was the language of administration and literature, and Shulgi sponsored a scribal school, the e2-dubba.

The fall of Ur was a turning point, and a new era, the Old Babylonian period, began. The dynasties of Isin and Larsa that followed claimed its heritage, took up the titles of its kings and wrote lamentations on the fall of Ur, Uruk, Nippur and Eridu, which presented the fall as a divine decision and legitimised the new rulers. Hymns to Ur-Namma and Shulgi continued to be copied in schools. The dynasty never equalled the prestige of the kings of Akkad in tradition, perhaps because its conquests were less impressive.
thirty-years-war: The Reformation had led to the Schmalkaldic War between Protestants and Catholics within the Holy Roman Empire. The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 tried to prevent a recurrence by designating states as Lutheran or Catholic according to the religion of their ruler. It was undermined by the spread of Protestantism, particularly Calvinism, into Catholic areas, and by the fragmented structure of the empire, which had some 300 imperial estates and an Imperial Diet that met rarely. In 1608 Frederick IV, Elector Palatine formed the Protestant Union, and in 1609 Maximilian of Bavaria established the rival Catholic League.

In May 1618 Protestant nobles led by Count Thurn threw two of the Catholic Ferdinand's representatives and their secretary from the windows of Prague Castle, an episode known as the Third Defenestration of Prague. All three survived. Bohemia became the first battleground, and fighting then expanded into the Palatinate, drawing in the Dutch Republic and Spain, and later Christian IV of Denmark. In 1630 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Pomerania with nearly 18,000 troops. His line formations and light artillery defeated the army of Tilly at Breitenfeld in September 1631.

The period from 1618 to 1635 was chiefly a civil war within the empire and largely ended with the Peace of Prague. France then entered the war in alliance with Sweden, and the empire became one theatre in a wider struggle against the Habsburgs of Austria and Spain. Related conflicts included revolts in Portugal and Catalonia in 1640, backed by France. Field armies averaged 13,000 to 20,000 men, and the forces deployed by both sides in Germany peaked at 250,000 in 1632.

The Peace of Westphalia consisted of three agreements: the Peace of Münster between Spain and the Dutch Republic, signed on 30 January 1648, the Treaty of Osnabrück between the empire and Sweden, and the Treaty of Münster between the empire and France. Talks had begun in 1642, with 109 delegations attending at one time or another. The settlement confirmed Dutch independence from Spain and reconfirmed the liberties of the German states, ending Habsburg attempts to turn the empire into a centralised state.

Estimates of the dead range from 4.5 to 8 million, most of them civilians and most after Sweden entered the war in 1630; claims of 12 million are no longer considered realistic. Collapse of local government produced landless peasants and rebellions, and witch-hunts began in Franconia in 1626, with over 900 people executed in the Bishopric of Würzburg by 1631. Historians count the war part of the General Crisis of the mid-17th century, and one lesson drawn was the need for permanent state armies.
thomas-aquinas: Thomas Aquinas was most likely born around 1225 in the family castle of Roccasecca, near Aquino, then controlled by the Kingdom of Sicily. His father, Landulf VI of Aquino, was a knight in the service of Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, and his mother was Theodora Galluccio, Countess of Teano. He was the youngest of nine children, and the family intended him to follow his uncle Sinibald into the abbacy of Monte Cassino, where he began his education at five.

In 1239 his parents enrolled him at the studium generale in Naples, where he was presumably introduced to Aristotle, Averroes and Maimonides. At nineteen he resolved to join the Dominican Order, which did not please his family: on his way to Rome his brothers seized him and brought him back to his parents.

Although he wrote actively for only about two decades, Thomas wrote over eight million words. His best-known work is the unfinished Summa Theologiae (1265 to 1274), alongside the Disputed Questions on Truth (1256 to 1259), the Summa contra Gentiles (1259 to 1265) and commentaries on Scripture and on Aristotle.

Thomas treated theology as a science whose data are Scripture and the tradition of the Church, and held that faith and reason, distinct but related, are both necessary for true knowledge of God. He held that rational thinking and the study of nature, like revelation, are valid ways to understand truths about God. His central thought was that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. He never considered himself a philosopher, and he often cites Aristotle simply as the Philosopher.

Thomas died on 7 March 1274. Dante asserts that he died by poisoning, on the order of Charles of Anjou, but the account of one of his friends gives no hint of foul play. In 1277 Étienne Tempier, bishop of Paris, issued a condemnation listing 219 propositions, twenty of them Thomistic, which severely damaged Thomas's reputation for many years. On 18 July 1323 Pope John XXII, seated in Avignon, pronounced him a saint, and his remains were moved to the Church of the Jacobins in Toulouse on 28 January 1369.
thomas-becket: Becket was born at Cheapside in London, on 21 December, the feast day of Thomas the Apostle. His parents were Gilbert and Matilda Beket, both of Norman descent. Gilbert began as a merchant and later lived on the rents of London properties and served as the city's sheriff. At the age of ten Becket was sent to Merton Priory in Surrey, and he later attended a grammar school in London. When his father suffered financial reverses he worked as a clerk, and later he entered the household of Archbishop Theobald of Bec.

Theobald sent him on missions to Rome and to Bologna and Auxerre to study canon law, and in 1154 made him Archdeacon of Canterbury. As chancellor he enforced the king's traditional revenues, including those owed by churches. After Theobald's death Becket was confirmed as archbishop on 23 May 1162, ordained priest on 2 June and consecrated the next day. He resigned the chancellorship and sought to recover and extend the rights of the archbishopric, to the king's displeasure.

At Clarendon Palace on 30 January 1164 Henry presented sixteen constitutions to limit clerical independence and weaken connections with Rome. All the clergy agreed except Becket, who still refused to sign. Summoned to Northampton Castle on 8 October 1164 to answer charges of contempt of royal authority and malfeasance as chancellor, he was convicted and fled to the Continent. Louis VII of France protected him. He spent nearly two years at the Cistercian abbey of Pontigny, until Henry's threats against the order sent him to Sens. Pope Alexander III favoured diplomacy, and in 1170 Henry offered a compromise that allowed Becket to return.

In 1170 the Archbishop of York crowned the heir, Henry the Young King, which breached Canterbury's privilege, and Becket excommunicated those involved. Henry II is said to have spoken words that his men took as a wish to have Becket killed, and the exact wording is in doubt. Four knights, Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy and Richard le Breton, came to Canterbury on 29 December 1170 and killed Becket in the cathedral. The eyewitness Edward Grim, who was wounded, left an account.

Veneration began across Europe at once, and Alexander III canonised him on 21 February 1173. On 12 July 1174 Henry did public penance at his tomb. In 1220 his bones were moved to a gold-plated shrine in the Trinity Chapel, which Henry VIII destroyed in 1538. Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is set among pilgrims travelling to it.
thomas-cromwell: Cromwell is thought to have been born around 1485 in Putney, then a village in Surrey. His father, Walter, was an ambitious yeoman landowner who worked as a sheep farmer and fuller, and also ran a tavern and a brewery.

Around the start of the 16th century Cromwell left his family and crossed to continental Europe, allegedly after time in prison, and later admitted to Archbishop Thomas Cranmer that he had been a ruffian in his youth. Accounts of his years in France, Italy and the Low Countries are problematic. By 1520 he was established in London mercantile and legal circles, and in 1523 he obtained a seat in the House of Commons.

Cromwell secured a seat for Taunton in November 1529 and was reported to be in favour with the King. He joined the Privy Council late in 1530. By the autumn of 1531 he had taken control of the supervision of Henry VIII's legal and parliamentary affairs. In April 1534 Henry confirmed him as principal secretary and chief minister, a position he had held for some time in all but name. He enforced the Act of Succession, and when Sir Thomas More and John Fisher refused the oath, both were imprisoned and within a month executed.

In July 1536 he became Lord Privy Seal and Baron Cromwell of Wimbledon. He orchestrated the Dissolution of the Monasteries. He also secured the licence for the Matthew's Bible and obliged every church to own a Bible by 1538, and the Great Bible followed in 1539. Scholars generally agree that he was a Protestant with a Lutheran mindset. His injunctions for the Ten Articles of 1536 provoked the Pilgrimage of Grace.

Cromwell arranged the King's marriage to Anne of Cleves, which took place on 6 January 1540 and was not consummated. Henry made him Earl of Essex on 18 April 1540, but his conservative opponents, notably the Duke of Norfolk, used the King's anger as their opportunity. Cromwell was arraigned under an act of attainder and executed for treason and heresy on Tower Hill on 28 July 1540.

Until the 1950s historians discounted his role. Geoffrey Elton then presented him as the central figure of a Tudor revolution in government, and later historians agree on his importance if not on that term. Diarmaid MacCulloch credits him with guiding the early careers of William Cecil and Nicholas Bacon.
thomas-hobbes: Thomas Hobbes was born in Westport, now part of Malmesbury in Wiltshire. He later reported that his mother, hearing of the coming invasion of the Spanish Armada, gave birth prematurely: "my mother gave birth to twins: myself and fear." His father, also Thomas, was vicar of Charlton and Westport; according to the biographer John Aubrey he was uneducated and disesteemed learning. After a fight with local clergy outside his church he was forced to leave, and the family was left in the care of his older brother Francis, a wealthy glove manufacturer. Hobbes graduated from the University of Cambridge in 1608.

Hobbes became a tutor to the Cavendish family, and in 1636 he visited Galileo Galilei in Florence, then under house arrest. He later joined the philosophical groups in Paris gathered by Marin Mersenne. Back in England in 1637, he had written The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic by the end of the Short Parliament in 1640; it circulated only in manuscript until a pirated edition about ten years later.

When the English Civil War began in August 1642 and the royalist cause declined from mid-1644, many royalists came to Paris, and their company renewed his political interests. From 1647 until 1648 he was mathematical instructor to Charles, Prince of Wales. The exiled royalists led him to write Leviathan, which compares the state to a monster composed of men, created under pressure of human needs and dissolved by civil strife arising from human passions.

In Leviathan Hobbes begins from a mechanistic understanding of human beings and asks what life would be like without government, a state of nature in which each person has a right to everything. This, he argues, would lead to a war of all against all, with life "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." In 1658 he published De Homine, completing the system he had planned more than nineteen years before. After the Restoration, his former pupil Charles II granted him a pension of £100. Hobbes died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick Hall, aged 91, and was interred at Ault Hucknall in Derbyshire.
thomas-jefferson: Thomas Jefferson was born on 13 April 1743 (2 April, Old Style) at the family's Shadwell Plantation in the Colony of Virginia, the third of ten children. His father, Peter Jefferson, was a planter and surveyor, and his mother was Jane Randolph. He was born into a slave-owning family and remained a slave owner all his life. He was admitted to the Virginia bar in 1767.

Between 1769 and 1775 Jefferson represented Albemarle County in the Virginia House of Burgesses. In 1769 he wrote and sponsored legislation giving masters of slaves discretion to emancipate them; it met strong opposition. Elected to the Second Continental Congress in 1775, he was named to the Committee of Five with John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman. Adams persuaded the committee to choose Jefferson to write the Declaration of Independence, which Congress passed in 1776. Jefferson drafted it largely alone.

In 1784 he joined Franklin and Adams in Paris and then succeeded Franklin as Minister to France, serving five years. President George Washington appointed him the first Secretary of State, and he clashed with Alexander Hamilton over the national debt and the site of the capital, settled by the Compromise of 1790 in favour of the Potomac River. With James Madison he founded the Democratic-Republican Party in 1792. He lost to John Adams in 1796, by 71 votes to 68, and became vice president, then won the presidency in 1800 and was sworn in on 4 March 1801.

As president he defended American shipping against the Barbary pirates and British trade policies, acquired the Louisiana Territory, which doubled the nation's size, and reduced military forces and spending. His second term brought the trial of Aaron Burr and, in 1807, the Embargo Act. In 1819 he founded the University of Virginia, designed its buildings and was its first rector from 1825.

Jefferson followed the ideals of John Locke, Francis Bacon and Isaac Newton. He regarded the independent yeoman as the ideal of republican virtue, distrusted cities and financiers, and favoured decentralised government. He wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and pressed for a wall of separation between church and state. His views became known as Jeffersonian democracy. From 1768 he built Monticello in the Palladian style, with the help of local masons and carpenters and of his slaves. Historians acknowledge his lifelong ownership of large numbers of slaves but differ on his views of slavery.
thomas-more: Thomas More was born in the City of London on 7 February 1478, the second of six children of Sir John More, a successful lawyer and later a judge, and his wife Agnes. He was educated at St. Anthony's School and from 1490 to 1492 served John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor, as a household page. According to his friend Desiderius Erasmus, he once seriously considered becoming a monk, and between 1503 and 1504 he lived near the Carthusian monastery outside the walls of London. He chose to remain a layman, was elected to Parliament in 1504 and married Joanna Colt the following year.

In 1504 More was elected to Parliament for Great Yarmouth, and from 1510 he represented London. Between 1512 and 1519 he worked on a History of King Richard III, which he never finished. Utopia, a frame narrative in Latin, was published by Erasmus at Leuven in 1516; More is a character in it, discussing modern ills in Antwerp with the traveller Raphael Hythlodaeus, who describes the island of Utopia. After the fall of Wolsey, More became Lord Chancellor in 1529. Heresy was the most time-consuming issue of his chancellorship. He saw the Reformation as a threat to the unity of church and society, and he denied stories of torture of Protestants in his Apologia of 1533. Modern commentators remain divided over his campaign against Protestantism.

In 1533 More refused to attend the coronation of Anne Boleyn, and he was later imprisoned in the Tower of London, where he wrote A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation. At his trial on 1 July 1535 he argued that his silence on the new statutes could be taken as consent. He was executed on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535, declaring that he died the king's good servant, and God's first. He was beatified in 1886 and canonised in 1935, and in 1980 the Church of England added him to its calendar of Reformation martyrs.
thomas-paine: Thomas Paine was the son of Joseph Pain, a tenant farmer and stay-maker, and Frances Pain, born Cocke. His father was a Quaker and his mother an Anglican. He attended Thetford Grammar School from 1744 to 1749 and at 13 was apprenticed to his father. At 19 he served as a privateer aboard the King of Prussia, and in 1759 he became a master staymaker in Sandwich, Kent. He married Mary Lambert that year, but his business collapsed, and she and their child died in early labour at Margate. He was using the spelling Paine by 1769, while living in Lewes, Sussex.

Paine barely survived the voyage to Philadelphia, where typhoid fever killed five passengers, and in March 1775 he became editor of the Pennsylvania Magazine. Common Sense appeared on 10 January 1776, signed by an Englishman. He estimated that it sold 100,000 copies in three months, though some historians dispute such figures. Benjamin Rush suggested the title, since Paine had called it Plain Truth.

Rights of Man, a tract of some 90,000 words answering Edmund Burke, appeared on 13 March 1791. Its second part proposed state support for the poor, public education and pensions for workers from the age of 50. Agrarian Justice argued that landed property had robbed most people of a natural inheritance, and proposed a national fund paying fifteen pounds to each person at the age of twenty-one. In The Age of Reason he wrote that he believed in one God and in no church. He was also an abolitionist, and Rush later credited him with a Pennsylvania Magazine article against slavery.

Paine stayed in France until 1802 and returned to the United States at Thomas Jefferson's invitation, to find himself disliked by the devout and by the Federalists. He died on 8 June 1809 at 59 Grove Street in Greenwich Village, aged 72. The Quakers refused to bury him in their graveyard, so he was buried on his farm at New Rochelle. In 1819 William Cobbett dug up the bones to give him a reburial in England that never took place, and they were later lost. His writings gave radical societies in England and Wales in the early 1790s a boost to their confidence. A marble column raised in New Rochelle in 1839 is the oldest memorial to him.
thomas-the-apostle: The name Thomas comes from the Aramaic Tʾōmā, meaning the twin, and the Greek equivalent Didymos is also used in the New Testament. Early Syrian traditions give his full name as Judas Thomas. In the Gospel of John he speaks twice: when Lazarus has died he says, Let us also go, that we may die with him, and later he asks how the disciples can know the way. He is best known as doubting Thomas, because he doubted the resurrection of Jesus until he saw the places where the wounds still appeared fresh, and then confessed his faith with the words My Lord and my God.

The earliest tradition about his mission is that his allotted field was Parthia, a statement of Origen preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea. Churches of the Middle East and southern Asia also name Thomas as their first evangelist. According to the traditional accounts of the Saint Thomas Christians of India, he landed at Muziris on the coast of the Chera kingdom, in present-day Kerala, in 52 CE, and founded seven communities there; historians still dispute the visit. Frykenberg, a historian of religion, notes that whatever the doubtful historicity of such traditions, there can be little doubt as to their great antiquity.

The main source is the apocryphal Acts of Thomas, written about 180–230, which most Christian churches regard as apocryphal or even heretical. The two centuries between the apostle's life and the work cast doubt on its authenticity. It tells that a king was angered when Thomas converted a queen and others of his household.

According to Syrian Christian tradition, Thomas was killed with a spear at St. Thomas Mount in Chennai on 21 December 72 and buried at Mylapore. Ephrem the Syrian, whose hymns are the earliest known record of his death, states that he was killed in India and that his relics were taken to Edessa; tradition says the greater part of them was sent there in 232. In 1258 some relics were brought to Ortona in Italy.

The San Thome Church at Mylapore, said to stand at his tomb, was built in 1523 by Portuguese missionaries. The feast of Saint Thomas was entered in the Roman calendar in the 9th century on 21 December and moved to 3 July in 1969, which is also observed by Indian Christians as Indian Christians' Day. The name Thomas remains popular among the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala.
thoth: The Egyptian name of Thoth, written ḏḥwty, may derive from ḏḥw, said to be the oldest known name for the ibis, with an ending marking him as having the ibis's attributes, so that it would mean he who is like the ibis. The Greek form Thoth is more common than the Egyptological rendering Djehuti. Thoth was a moon god. The moon allowed time to be measured at night without the sun, and its phases organised much of the rituals and events of Egyptian society, civil and religious. He therefore came to be seen as a god of wisdom, magic and the measurement and regulation of events and time, and as the secretary and counsellor of Ra.

Thoth was most often shown as a man with the head of an ibis, sometimes wearing a lunar disk on a crescent moon, or as a baboon, or as the ibis itself. Scholars suggest the curve of the ibis's beak was seen as the crescent moon. As Aani, an ape in the underworld, he reported when the scales weighing the heart of the dead against the feather of Maat were exactly even. His feminine counterpart is Seshat, and his wife is Ma'at; with Ma'at he stood beside Ra on the solar barque. He was regarded as the scribe of the gods and the inventor of writing and hieroglyphs, and Egyptian scribes worshipped him, keeping a picture of him in their offices.

In myth Plutarch credits him with the 365-day calendar.
