When the year had only 360 days and the goddess Nut could bear no children, Thoth gambled with the moon for one seventy-second of its light and won five days, on which Osiris, Set, Isis, Horus and Nephthys were born. In the central Osiris myth he gives Isis the words to restore her husband, and after the battle between Horus and Set he offers counsel.

His chief temple was at Hermopolis, called Khemenu in Egyptian, and in the Late Period his cult gained prominence as Khmun also became the capital. Millions of dead ibis were mummified and buried in his honour. The temple was mostly destroyed before the Christian era, and its large pronaos, standing in 1826, was demolished by the mid-19th century and used as fill for the foundation of a sugar factory. The Greeks identified him with Hermes, and his title Thrice Great, trismégistos in Greek, gave the combined figure Hermes Trismegistus.
three-kingdoms-of-korea: The Three Kingdoms were founded after the fall of Wiman Joseon and gradually conquered and absorbed many small states and confederacies. After Gojoseon fell, the Han dynasty set up four commanderies in the north-west of the peninsula and in present Liaoning. Three fell quickly to the Samhan, and Goguryeo destroyed the last in 313. The three polities made the transition from walled-town states to full state-level societies between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. The main sources are the Korean histories Samguk sagi and Samguk yusa and the Eastern Barbarians section of the Book of Wei. The Book of Sui records that the customs, laws and clothes of the three kingdoms were generally identical.

Goguryeo arose on the Yalu River and was the largest of the three, holding the north of the peninsula, the Liaodong Peninsula and Manchuria. It was at its height in the 5th century under King Gwanggaeto the Great and his son King Jangsu. Paekche, founded as a member of the Mahan confederacy, controlled most of the western peninsula at its peak in the 4th century and was a maritime power that passed Chinese characters, metallurgy, ceramics, architecture and Buddhism to ancient Japan. Under pressure from Goguryeo it moved its capital south to Ungjin in the late 5th century and later to Sabi.

According to Korean records Silla, in the south-east, began in 57 BCE as a unification of the Jinhan city-states, though other evidence suggests it was the last of the three to build a centralised government. It was the smallest and weakest, but it made pacts with stronger neighbours, took the name Silla in 503 and annexed the Kaya confederacy in the first half of the 6th century. Buddhism became its official religion in 528, after Goguryeo adopted it in 372.
Silla allied with Tang China. Paekche was conquered in 660 and Goguryeo in 668. Silla then drove the Tang forces out of the peninsula and occupied the lands south of Pyongyang.

Silla's unification of the peninsula in the 7th century was the first in Korean history. It was later divided into the Later Three Kingdoms and annexed by Goryeo, a state that revived Goguryeo. The name Samhan, used since the 7th century for the three kingdoms, came to mean Korea as a whole, and the Han in the names Daehan Jeguk and Daehan Minguk refers to it. The Samguk sagi and Samguk yusa, whose titles use the name Three Kingdoms, should not be confused with the Three Kingdoms of China.
thrissur: Thrissur is the headquarters of Thrissur district in central Kerala, 284 km north-west of the state capital, Thiruvananthapuram. The city is built around a hillock of 65 acres, Thekkinkadu Maidanam, which holds the Vadakkumnathan temple. From the hillock the land flattens into the Thrissur-Ponnani Kole Wetlands, which act as a natural drainage for the city. The name is a shortened form of the Malayalam Thirusshivaperoor, the city of the sacred Lord Shiva, after the temple's presiding deity. The English form Trichur was the official name until 1990. In ancient times it was also called Vrishabhadripuram.

Numerous prehistoric megaliths and dolmens show that the area was inhabited from at least 1000 BCE to 500 CE. It was once a point of contact for Assyrians, Greeks, Persians, Arabs, Romans, Portuguese, Dutch and English, and Christianity, Islam and Judaism are believed to have entered the subcontinent through Thrissur and its surroundings. In the 16th century the Portuguese had naval influence in much of Kerala, and in the early 17th century the Dutch took their place as the main naval power. With Dutch help the royal family of Cochin recaptured Thrissur from the Zamorin of Calicut in 1710.

Thrissur rose to importance when Maharaja Sakthan Thampuran ascended the throne of Cochin and made it his capital. He invited Syrian Christian families and Brahmins from neighbouring areas, and the city became a financial and commercial hub of South India. Hyder Ali, the Sultan of Mysore, conquered it in 1750–60 and made it a tributary of Mysore.

Sakthan Thampuran's successor, Rama Varma X, signed a treaty with the East India Company that made Cochin a British protectorate. Mahatma Gandhi visited the city in 1927 and 1934 to promote civil disobedience. R. K. Shanmukham Chetty, Diwan of Cochin from 1935 to 1941, built the Thrissur Town Hall and other civic buildings. Thrissur district was formed on 1 July 1949, with its headquarters in the city.

Thrissur is known as the cultural capital of Kerala. Its Thrissur Pooram, held at the Vadakkumnathan temple in April or May, is one of the largest temple festivals in the state, with a large gathering of people and elephants lasting thirty-six hours. The city is a centre of banking, gold jewellery and Ayurvedic drugs, and it holds the Kerala Sangeetha Nadaka Academy, Kerala Lalithakala Akademi and Kerala Sahitya Academy. The Our Lady of Dolours Basilica is the largest church in India.
thucydides: Little is known of Thucydides's life, and the most reliable information comes from his own History. He identifies himself as an Athenian, gives his father's name as Olorus and names his deme as Halimous. He fought in the war, survived the Plague of Athens, which killed Pericles and many other Athenians, and records that he owned gold mines at Scapte Hyle in Thrace, opposite the island of Thasos. A story that as a boy he heard Herodotus lecture and wept with joy is disputed and most likely comes from a later account.

Because of his influence in the Thracian region, Thucydides was sent as a general to Thasos in 424 BCE. In the winter of 424 to 423 BCE the Spartan general Brasidas attacked Amphipolis, half a day's sail to the west, and the Athenian commander there, Eucles, sent to Thucydides for help. Brasidas, aware of Thucydides's influence with the people of Amphipolis, offered moderate terms, and the city surrendered before Thucydides arrived. Its fall caused consternation in Athens and was blamed on him, although he claimed he had been unable to reach it in time. He was exiled.

Later sources on his life are less reliable. Pausanias says a law passed by Oenobius allowed him to return to Athens after the war ended in 404 BCE and that he was murdered on the way, while Plutarch preserves a tradition that he was murdered at Scapte Hyle and that his remains were brought to Athens. Many doubt the first account, and the evidence suggests he may have lived as late as 397 BCE or slightly later.

Thucydides began to write the History of the Peloponnesian War at the outbreak of the war in 431 BCE, believing it of unmatched importance, and intended it as a possession for all time. It breaks off in the middle of 411 BCE, after the Athenian defeat at Syracuse, so it does not cover the last seven years of the war. The division into eight books was probably made after his death by scholars of Alexandria. He values eyewitness testimony, consulted written documents and interviewed participants, and unlike Herodotus he does not acknowledge divine intervention in human affairs.

He admired Pericles and disliked the demagogues who followed him, such as Cleon and Hyperbolus, but his account is generally even-handed, and he does not minimise the effect of his own failure at Amphipolis. Scholars have seen in him the influence of the Sophists and of Hippocratic medical writing, and the Melian dialogue and his version of Pericles's Funeral Oration are widely studied. Historians such as Jacqueline de Romilly have stressed his concern with Athenian imperialism, and others have read him as a tragedian in the tradition of Homer.
thurgau: Thurgau is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation, in Eastern Switzerland, with its capital at Frauenfeld. It is named after the river Thur and is bounded to the north by Lake Constance, with the High Rhine forming part of the border in the northwest. The name Thurgovia was historically used for a larger area that took in much of the modern canton of St. Gallen, the Appenzell lands and the eastern parts of the canton of Zurich.

In the Neolithic period the land was inhabited by the Pfyn culture, named after Pfyn on Lake Constance. In Roman times it belonged to the province of Raetia until 450, when the Alemanni settled; Roman settlements included Ad Fines (Pfyn), Arbor Felix and Tasgetium. In the sixth century Thurgovia became a Gau of Francia as part of Alamannia, and it passed to the Duchy of Swabia in the early 10th century. Its most important early medieval cities were Konstanz, seat of the bishop, and St. Gallen, home of the Abbey of Saint Gall.

The dukes of Zähringen and the counts of Kyburg took over much of the land in the High Middle Ages. Zurich left Thurgau in 1218, and when the Kyburg dynasty became extinct in 1264 the House of Habsburg took over its lands. In 1460 the Old Swiss Confederacy, allied with ten freed bailiwicks of the former Toggenburg, seized the territory from the Habsburgs, and it became a subject territory of seven cantons: Zurich, Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug and Glarus.

In 1524 local peasants occupied the cloister of Ittingen, driving out the monks. Between 1526 and 1531 most of the population adopted the Reformed faith from Zurich, but Zurich's defeat in the Second War of Kappel in 1531 ended Reformed predominance, and the First Peace of Kappel protected both faiths. Zurich briefly occupied the region in the First War of Villmergen in 1656. Thurgau became a canton in 1798 under the Helvetic Republic and a member of the Confederation in 1803 under the Act of Mediation.

The canton has five districts and 282,909 inhabitants in December 2020, and is mostly German speaking. Its current constitution dates from 1987. Thurgau is known for apples and pears, many of them grown for cider, and for wine from the Thur valley.
thuringia: Thuringia is a landlocked state in the middle of Germany, bordered by Bavaria, Hesse, Lower Saxony, Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt. It has been called the green heart of Germany since the late 19th century because of its broad, dense forest, and most of it lies in the drainage basin of the Saale, a left-bank tributary of the Elbe. The Thuringian Basin is the driest part of Germany, with only 400 to 500 mm of rain a year. The natural vegetation is beech forest, though centuries of settlement mean that most plains are cleared for farming and most forests are planted with spruce and pine.

The name derives from the Germanic tribe of the Thuringii, who emerged during the Migration Period. Their origin is largely unknown: an older theory made them successors of the Hermunduri, which later research rejected, and other historians argue that they were allies of the Huns. They were first mentioned around 400, when they were known for their excellent horses. The first documented duke of Thuringia was a local noble, Radulf I, appointed by King Dagobert I in the early 630s. He secured the borders on the Saale against Slavic incursions, but in 641 or 642 rebelled against Dagobert's successor Sigebert III and declared himself king of Thuringia.

In the Middle Ages the Saale marked the border between Germanic and Slavic territories, and the movement of eastward settlement assimilated the Slavic population between the 11th and 13th centuries. Thuringia generally accepted the Protestant Reformation, and Roman Catholicism was suppressed as early as 1520. The German Peasants' War of 1525 destroyed many churches and monasteries, and Thomas Müntzer was active among the Anabaptists of Mühlhausen. Catholicism survived within the modern borders only in the Eichsfeld, ruled by the Archbishop of Mainz, and in and near Erfurt.

The modern state was established in 1920 under the Weimar Republic by merging the Ernestine duchies; only Saxe-Coburg voted to join Bavaria instead, and Weimar became the capital. After the Second World War Thuringia lay in the Soviet occupation zone, became part of the German Democratic Republic in 1949, and was dissolved in 1952 into the districts of Erfurt, Suhl and Gera. It was re-established in 1990 after reunification. The Free State of Thuringia has about 2.1 million inhabitants, and its capital and largest city is Erfurt. The Wartburg castle, Classical Weimar and Bauhaus Weimar are UNESCO World Heritage Site listings, and the University of Jena was founded in 1558.
thutmose-iii: Thutmose III was the son of Thutmose II by a secondary wife, Iset. His father's Great Royal Wife was Hatshepsut. When his father died he was too young to rule, and estimates of his age range from two to 13 years. Hatshepsut became his regent and eventually declared herself pharaoh, though she never denied kingship to Thutmose III. For the first 22 years of his reign he was therefore a junior co-regent while she held the senior place. When he was old enough and had shown his capacity, Hatshepsut appointed him to head her armies, and he became sole ruler after her death around 1458 BCE.

The dating of the reign depends on the chronology used. The Low Chronology gives 1479 to 1425 BCE, the convention in academic circles since the 1960s, while some scholars prefer 1504 to 1450 BCE. The length of the reign is known to the day from the tomb of the commander Amenemheb, who records his death in the 54th regnal year, corresponding to 11 March 1425 BCE.

Thutmose III conducted at least 16 campaigns in 20 years, recorded in the Annals inscribed on the walls of the temple of Amun at Karnak. The first led to the Battle of Megiddo. In his eighth campaign, in Year 33, he carried boats overland, crossed the Euphrates and attacked Mitanni, setting up a stele beside the one his grandfather Thutmose I had raised. To prevent rebellion in Syria he took hostages from the noble families of its cities. His last campaign, in Year 50, reached the fourth cataract of the Nile in Nubia. The Egyptologist James Breasted called him the Napoleon of Egypt.

He built more than 50 temples and gave Karnak more attention than any other site, adding Pylon VI, a wall around the central sanctuary and a jubilee hall in an early basilica style. Some of Hatshepsut's monuments were defaced after her death. Earlier scholars read this as vengeance and an erasure of her memory by Thutmose III, an interpretation presented as a theory.

Two years before his death, after the death of his firstborn son Amenemhat, Thutmose III appointed Amenhotep II as junior co-regent and successor. His tomb, KV34, was found in the Valley of the Kings by Victor Loret in 1898. His mummy was discovered in the Deir el-Bahari Cache in 1881, along with those of other pharaohs of the 18th and 19th Dynasty.
tian-shan: The Tian Shan, also known as the Tengri Tagh or Tengir-Too, is a large system of mountain ranges in Central Asia. It lies north and west of the Taklamakan Desert and directly north of the Tarim Basin, and straddles the border regions of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Xinjiang in northwest China. In the south it connects with the Pamir Mountains, and to the north and east it meets the Altai Mountains of Mongolia. It forms part of the Himalayan orogenic belt, produced by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates in the Cenozoic era. Its highest peak, Jengish Chokusu, rises to 7,439 metres, and its lowest point is the Turpan Depression, 154 metres below sea level.

One of the earliest references to the mountains may be the Xiongnu word Qilian, which the Tang commentator Yan Shigu said meant sky or heaven. Sima Qian mentioned Qilian in the Records of the Grand Historian in connection with the homeland of the Yuezhi, and the term is believed to refer to the Tian Shan rather than the Qilian Mountains about 1,500 km further east. The lower, forested Alatau ranges in the northern Tian Shan are home to Turkic-speaking pastoral tribes. In Tengrism the mountains are sacred, and Khan Tengri, the second-highest peak, means Lord of the Spirits.

Around 950 CE Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam, which marked a major turning point in the spread of Islam among the Turkic peoples of the region. The tulip is said to have originated in the Tian Shan and to have reached Turkey along the Silk Road, and the strain of Y. pestis that caused the Black Death may have originated there too. The Russian explorer Peter Semenov documented the range extensively in the 1850s and later changed his family name to refer to the mountains.

During the last ice age a plateau glacier covered the plateau between the Kokshaal-Tau and the Terskey Alatau, and glaciers flowed north into Lake Issyk Kul. The glaciation occupied about 118,000 square kilometres. The mountains hold forests of Schrenk's spruce above 2,000 metres, and the lower slopes have natural forests of wild walnuts and apples. The eastern portion in Xinjiang was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2013 and the western portion in Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in 2016.
tianjin: Tianjin lies on the west coast of the Bohai Gulf, surrounded by Hebei Province on every side except the sea, with Beijing about 120 kilometres to the northwest. Its main urban area stands along the Hai River, which connects to the Yellow and Yangtze rivers by the Grand Canal. The land was formed between 900 and 1300 CE by sediments from rivers entering the sea at the Bohai Gulf. The name, written 天津, means the ford of the emperor, and its origin is disputed; the most common theory holds that the Yongle Emperor of the Ming bestowed it after crossing the Gu River on his way south to overthrow his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor.

The Grand Canal, running from Hangzhou to the Beijing and Tianjin region by 609 CE, carried southern grain north and helped the area's development. Tianjin appears increasingly in records under the Song dynasty and gained importance under the Yuan as a storage place for goods and grain. Under the Ming it was a garrison town and shipping station, and the walled city was built in 1404. By the 17th century it was a centre of commerce.

In the Second Opium War the British and French captured the Taku forts near Tianjin in May 1858, and the Treaty of Tientsin signed that June opened the city to foreign trade; the Xianfeng Emperor ratified the treaties in 1860. Between 1895 and 1900 Japan, Germany, Russia and other powers joined Britain and France in establishing self-contained concessions, each with its own prisons, schools, barracks and hospitals, which left churches and thousands of villas. During the Boxer Rebellion the city was the seat of the Tianjin Provisional Government.

Tianjin fell to Japan on 30 July 1937, though the Japanese generally respected the foreign concessions until 1941. In June 1939 the Japanese army blockaded the British concession in the Tientsin Incident. In the Pingjin Campaign of the Chinese Civil War the city was taken after 29 hours of fighting, and the Chinese Communist Party held it from 15 January 1949.

Tianjin is a provincial-level municipality of China with 13,866,009 people at the 2020 census, and the largest coastal city of northern China. Its seaport remains the gateway to Beijing, and some European-style buildings of the concessions are preserved.
tiber-river: The Tiber is the third-longest river in Italy and the longest in central Italy. It rises at Mount Fumaiolo in the Apennine Mountains in Emilia-Romagna and flows 406 km through Tuscany, Umbria and Lazio, where the River Aniene joins it, to the Tyrrhenian Sea between Ostia and Fiumicino. Its mouth has advanced by about 3 km since Roman times, which left the ancient port of Ostia Antica 6 km inland. The name is probably pre-Latin and may be Italic in origin; the same root appears in the Latin name Tiberius.

According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BCE on the banks of the Tiber, about 25 km from the sea. Tiber Island was the site of an important ford and was later bridged. Legend says the twins Romulus and Remus were abandoned on the river's waters and rescued by the she-wolf Lupa. The river marked the boundary between the Etruscans to the west, the Sabines to the east and the Latins to the south.

The Tiber was critically important to Roman trade, since ships could reach as far as 100 km upriver. During the Punic Wars of the third century BCE the harbour at Ostia became a key naval base, and it later became Rome's most important port, receiving wheat, olive oil and wine from around the Mediterranean. The Romans linked the river to a sewer system, the Cloaca Maxima. Heavy sedimentation made Ostia difficult to maintain, so Claudius and Trajan established a new port at Fiumicino in the first century CE; both ports were eventually abandoned because of silting.

The Tiber was long known for floods; the Campus Martius, a flood plain, regularly flooded to a depth of about 2 m, and on 15 September 1557 the river rose 19 m above sea level and more than 1,000 people died. High stone embankments, begun in 1876, now confine it within the city. Ancient bridges survive in part, such as the Ponte Milvio and the Ponte Sant'Angelo, and in whole, as the Pons Fabricius. Because the river is identified with Rome, the phrase crossing the Tiber has become shorthand for converting to Roman Catholicism.
tiberius: Tiberius was born in Rome on 16 November 42 BCE to Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia Drusilla, both of the patrician gens Claudia. In 39 BCE Livia divorced Nero and married Octavian, later Augustus. At the age of nine Tiberius delivered the eulogy for his biological father, and in 29 BCE he rode beside Octavian's triumphal chariot after the victory over Antony and Cleopatra at Actium. He entered politics at eighteen as quaestor, with the right to stand for praetor and consul five years before the legal age.

In 20 BCE Tiberius went east to join Augustus, and either Augustus or Tiberius, or both, recovered the standards that Parthia had taken from Roman armies. He then led a force into Armenia. His conquests of Pannonia, Dalmatia, Raetia and, for a time, parts of Germania helped lay the foundations of the empire's northern frontier. In 6 BCE he was granted tribunician power and control in the East, then withdrew from politics and retired to Rhodes, for reasons that are unclear.

The deaths of Lucius Caesar in 2 CE and Gaius Caesar in 4 CE left Augustus no other choice. Tiberius was adopted as full son and heir on 26 June 4 CE, and had to adopt his nephew Germanicus. At Augustus's death in 14 CE he became princeps at 55.

Tiberius refused the title Pater Patriae and the Civic Crown, which the Senate took as insult rather than modesty, and his relations with it were difficult. He was nevertheless an effective administrator. Germanicus died in 19 CE and Tiberius's son Drusus in 23 CE, after which Tiberius grew reclusive. When he withdrew from Rome in 26 CE the praetorian prefect Sejanus was left in charge of the state, and Tiberius had him executed for treason in 31 CE. Tiberius died at Misenum on 16 March 37 CE, and his grand-nephew Caligula succeeded him. The treasury held nearly 3 billion sesterces at his death.
tiberius-gracchus: Tiberius belonged to the Roman aristocracy from birth. His father, also named Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, was consul in 177 and 163 BCE and censor in 169 BCE. His mother, Cornelia, was a daughter of the general Scipio Africanus, and his sister Sempronia married Scipio Aemilianus. Cornelia brought up the children after her husband's death. Tiberius served under Scipio Aemilianus in the Third Punic War from 147 BCE and, according to Plutarch, was among the first to scale the walls of Carthage.

In 137 BCE Tiberius was quaestor to the consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus in Hispania Citerior during the Numantine War. Mancinus's army was surrounded, and Tiberius negotiated a treaty with the Numantines, helped by the influence his father had gained in the region. The senate rejected it as humiliating and sent Mancinus back to the Numantines stripped and bound. A proposal to send Tiberius in chains as well was defeated, but his political future was damaged.

Elected plebeian tribune for 133 BCE, he proposed the Lex Sempronia agraria. He believed an earlier law had limited the public land any person could hold to about 120 hectares, a limit largely ignored, and he proposed enforcing it and passing the surplus to poor citizens. The reform drew strong support from the rural plebs and from some senators, including his father-in-law Appius Claudius Pulcher, but wealthy holders of public land opposed it. When the tribune Marcus Octavius vetoed the bill, Tiberius had him removed from office, an unconstitutional step. He then proposed using the bequest of Attalus III of Pergamum to fund the land commission, which broke the senate's prerogatives over finance and foreign policy, and his enemies accused him of seeking royal power.

Tiberius then sought a second consecutive tribunate, which broke Roman constitutional norms. At the elections his followers occupied the Capitoline hill. The pontifex maximus Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio asked the consul Publius Mucius Scaevola to use force, and when Scaevola refused, Nasica called on all who wanted the community safe to follow him and led a mob to the assembly. Tiberius and his supporters did not fight back; they were killed with stones, chairs and other blunt weapons, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber.

The land law was not repealed. Its commission, which included his brother Gaius Gracchus, went on working, and the surviving boundary stones show distributions across southern Italy of some 1.3 million jugera. Historians see the killing as the start of a cycle of violence: before it, domestic strife in the middle republic had basically never ended in violent death. Modern scholars treat 133 BCE as the traditional beginning of the Republic's crisis, while noting that the idea of earlier calm between rich and poor is at best a nostalgic fiction.
tibet: Tibet covers much of the Tibetan Plateau and is the homeland of the Tibetans. It is the highest region on Earth, with an average elevation of 4,380 m, and its southern edge in the Himalayas includes Mount Everest at 8,848 m. Several major rivers rise on the plateau, among them the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Indus, the Mekong, the Ganges and the Salween. Cultural Tibet is divided into Amdo in the northeast, Kham in the southeast, and Ü-Tsang with Ngari in the centre and west.

In the 7th century the Yarlung dynasty of central Tibet expanded into neighbouring regions such as Zhangzhung and Amdo, and by the 9th century the Tibetan Empire stretched from the Tarim Basin and the Pamirs in the west to Yunnan and Bengal in the southeast. After the empire dissolved, the region divided among principalities and tribal groups. Under the Mongol Yuan dynasty the Sakya lama kept a degree of autonomy as political authority, while an appointed administrator, the dpon-chen, held administrative and military power.

Between 1346 and 1354 Tai Situ Changchub Gyaltsen overthrew the Sakya and founded the Phagmodrupa dynasty, and the disciples of Je Tsongkhapa founded the Gelug school and the monasteries of Ganden, Drepung and Sera near Lhasa. In 1578 Altan Khan of the Tümed Mongols gave the Gelug lama Sonam Gyatso the title Dalai Lama. The 5th Dalai Lama (1617–1682), helped by Güshi Khan of the Khoshut Khanate, defeated the Kagyu and Jonang sects and the Tsangpa prince, and his government, the Ganden Phodrang, ruled the heartland.

Qing rule began with an expedition in 1720 that expelled the invading Dzungars. Amdo came under Qing control in 1724 and eastern Kham was joined to neighbouring Chinese provinces in 1728. The Qing sent resident commissioners called Ambans to Lhasa, and after a riot in 1750 in which the Ambans and many Han Chinese and Manchus were killed, they restored the Dalai Lama as ruler while giving the Ambans a larger part in Tibetan affairs.

Lhasa is the traditional capital, and the Potala Palace and Norbulingka, former residences of the Dalai Lama, are World Heritage Sites there. China governs most of the historical area as the Tibet Autonomous Region and as autonomous prefectures within Gansu, Sichuan, Qinghai and Yunnan. Tibetan Buddhism is the main religion and shapes the region's art, music and festivals; Bön is the indigenous religion.
tibetans: Tibetan tradition holds that the Tibetan people descend from the monkey Pha Trelgen Changchup Sempa and the rock ogress Ma Drag Sinmo. Genetic studies trace their roots to a deep East Asian lineage representing the indigenous population of the Tibetan plateau from about 40,000 to 30,000 years ago, joined within the last 10,000 years by Neolithic farmers from the Yellow River, who are associated with the spread of the Sino-Tibetan languages. Modern Tibetans are thought to derive up to 20 per cent of their ancestry from the Paleolithic plateau population and most of the rest from Yellow River farmers. Most Tibeto-Burman speakers of south-west China are thought to descend from the ancient Qiang people.

Tibetans carry more than 30 genetic factors suited to high altitude, among them a variant of the EPAS1 gene, which regulates the body's production of haemoglobin. Researchers describe its spread over the past 5,000 years as possibly one of the fastest genetic changes observed in humans.

Most Tibetans practise Tibetan Buddhism, and a significant minority follow the indigenous Bon religion. According to legend the 28th king, Thothori Nyantsen, dreamed of a sacred treasure falling from heaven, holding a Buddhist sutra, but Buddhism did not take root until the reign of Songtsen Gampo, who married two Buddhist princesses, Bhrikuti of Nepal and Wencheng of China. It gained popularity when Padmasambhāva visited Tibet at the invitation of the 38th king, Trisong Deutson. Tibetan Buddhists walk clockwise around stupas and mani stones and chant Om mani padme hum, while followers of Bon walk in the opposite direction.

Tibetan art is deeply religious. Thangka paintings, a blend of Indian scroll painting with Nepalese and Kashmiri painting, appeared around the 8th century. Lhamo, the folk opera of dances, chants and songs, is traditionally said to have been founded in the 14th century by Thang Tong Gyalpo, a lama and bridge-builder. Traditional medicine draws on up to two thousand plants, and the physician Yuthog Yontan Gonpo of the 8th century is credited with the Four Medical Tantras. The Potala Palace, once the residence of the Dalai Lama, is regarded as the most important example of Tibetan architecture.

The 2010 Chinese census counted 6,282,187 Tibetans, of whom 2,716,388 lived in the Tibet Autonomous Region, with large numbers in Sichuan, Qinghai, Gansu and Yunnan. Communities live also in India, Nepal and Bhutan, and nearly 100,000 Tibetans have lived in exile in India since 1959, many of them at Dharamshala and Bylakuppe.
ticino: Ticino is a canton unlike the others, since it lies almost entirely south of the Alps and has no natural access to the Swiss Plateau. It borders Valais, Uri and the Grisons along the crest of the Gotthard Massif and adjacent ranges, and shares international borders with Italy. Apart from small areas in the north and south, it lies in the basin of the Ticino, a tributary of the Po, from which it takes its name. It is traditionally divided into the Sopraceneri and the Sottoceneri, north and south of Monte Ceneri. The climate, influenced by the Mediterranean and sheltered by the Alps, is warmer and wetter than in the rest of Switzerland, and German-speaking Swiss call the canton the Sonnenstube, the sun porch.

During the Bronze and Iron Ages the land was settled by the Lepontii, a Celtic tribe. Probably around the time of Augustus it became part of the Roman Empire. After the fall of the Western Empire it was ruled by the Ostrogoths, the Lombards and the Franks. Around 1100 it was the centre of a struggle between the free communes of Milan and Como, and in the 14th century it was acquired by the Visconti, Dukes of Milan. The Swiss Confederates then conquered the valleys south of the Alps in three separate conquests, in the last transalpine campaigns of the Old Swiss Confederacy.

Leventina was a subject of Uri until 1798. In that year the Helvetic Republic joined it with the condominiums of Bellinzona, Riviera and Blenio as the canton of Bellinzona, while Locarno, Lugano, Mendrisio and Vallemaggia formed the canton of Lugano. The Act of Mediation of 1803 combined the two into the canton of Ticino, which joined the restored Swiss Confederation. The former condominiums and Leventina became its eight districts, which still exist. The current constitution derives from a draft approved on 18 August 1801 and was itself approved on 14 December 1997.

Cantonal identity was forged in the 19th century, partly through intellectuals such as Stefano Franscini and Carlo Cattaneo. Because of its position the canton has depended on routes over the Gotthard, a strategic pass since the 13th century. The Gotthard Rail Tunnel, 15 kilometres long, opened in 1882, the Gotthard Road Tunnel in 1980 and the Gotthard Base Tunnel on 1 June 2016.

Ticino is the only canton in which Italian is the sole official language, and its capital is Bellinzona; Lugano is the largest city, and Locarno another notable centre. Its official name is the Republic and Canton of Ticino, a style it shares with Geneva, Neuchâtel and Jura. Four World Heritage Sites lie in it, among them the Three Castles of Bellinzona and Monte San Giorgio. It was the birthplace of the architect Francesco Borromini.
ticino-river: The Ticino is the most important perennial left-bank tributary of the Po, about 248 km long, and it gave its name to the Swiss canton through which its upper part flows. It is one of the four major rivers that rise in the Gotthard region, with the Rhône, Reuss and Rhine. It begins in the Val Bedretto, on the border between the cantons of Valais and Ticino just below the Nufenen Pass, where glaciers and many torrents feed it. Its name may have meant the runner, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to run or flow.

From Val Bedretto it flows north-east to Airolo, where the southern portals of the Gotthard Railway Tunnel and Gotthard Road Tunnel lie, then south-east through the Valle Leventina, with two narrow gorges. At Biasca it receives the Brenno, and near Bellinzona the Moesa. It crosses the flat Piano di Magadino, built from its own sediments over ten thousand years, and enters Lake Maggiore at 193 metres, the lowest point of Switzerland. It leaves the lake at Sesto Calende, passes about 20 km east of Milan and joins the Po a few kilometres below Pavia.

The Gallic leader Bellovesus, known only from tradition, was said to have defeated the Etruscans by the Ticino in about 600 BCE. The river gave its name to the Battle of Ticinus, fought in November 218 BCE between the Carthaginian forces of Hannibal and the Romans under Publius Cornelius Scipio; it was the first battle of the Second Punic War.

In the Middle Ages Pavia, first capital of the Kingdom of the Lombards and then of the kingdom of Italy, was a hub of communications and trade between Venice and the Po valley thanks to the Ticino. Its covered bridge, the ponte Coperto, was until the 19th century the only brick bridge across the river between Lake Maggiore and the Po.

The Visconti built a wooden bridge at Vigevano in the early 14th century, which the Pavia fleet burned in 1315 and again in 1356, after Luchino Visconti had rebuilt it; it was never rebuilt. For much of the later Middle Ages and the early modern period the river lay in the Duchy of Milan, but the upper part as far as Bellinzona fell to the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1500, and as far as the shores of Lake Maggiore in 1513, as a result of the Swiss campaigns in the Italian Wars.

The stretch between Lake Maggiore and the confluence with the Po is the Parco naturale lombardo della Valle del Ticino, a nature reserve included by UNESCO in its World Network of Biosphere Reserves. Towns on the river or its lake include Bellinzona and Locarno in Switzerland and Stresa, Vigevano and Pavia in Italy.
tienen: Tienen, called Tirlemont in French, is a city and municipality in the province of Flemish Brabant in Flanders, Belgium. The municipality includes the town itself and Bost, Goetsenhoven, Hakendover, Kumtich, Oorbeek, Oplinter, Sint-Margriete-Houtem and Vissenaken. It covers 71.77 square kilometres. Tienen was a Roman settlement and trade centre with roads to other important places. In the early Middle Ages the town was probably ruled by an old German family, Thienen.

During the Franco-Spanish War of 1635 to 1659 Tienen belonged to the Spanish Netherlands, and a combined Franco-Dutch army captured it in May 1635. The town was sacked in one of the most serious atrocities of the Dutch Revolt. Over 200 civilians were killed and many buildings, including Catholic churches and monasteries, were damaged. The episode ended Dutch hopes of winning over the largely Catholic population of the Southern Netherlands. After the Treaty of Utrecht of 1714 the town was incorporated into the Austrian Netherlands.

German forces occupied Tienen in the First World War after breaking through the Belgian defensive lines. Sixty houses were destroyed and 152 damaged, and about 100 soldiers and civilians from the town died.

In the later world war the town was an important railway junction. The Allies bombed it in April 1944, and on 25 May 1944 a larger raid killed 13 civilians and injured 40. The bombs largely missed their intended targets, the bridges and the railway, and hit over 200 houses. The Dean of Rochette died in the confession booth after refusing to leave. The Allies liberated the town on 7 September 1944. The war cost the lives of 80 inhabitants, and 549 houses were destroyed.

Tienen is the centre of Belgian sugar production, and its large sugar refinery stands on the eastern edge of the town. A summer rock festival, Suikerrock, takes place there. The Sint-Germanus Church dates from the 12th century, and its belfry is part of the UNESCO listing of the Belfries of Belgium and France. The principal church, Onze-Lieve-Vrouw-ten-Poel, was begun in the 12th century and enlarged in the 15th, and remains unfinished. Tienen railway station is the oldest in Belgium still in use. The mystic Beatrijs of Nazareth (1200 to 1268) was born in the town.
tiglath-pileser-i: Tiglath-Pileser I, in Akkadian Tukultī-apil-Ešarra, meaning my trust is in the son of Ešarra, was the son of Ashur-resh-ishi I. Under him Assyria confirmed its position as the leading power of the Ancient Near East, which it largely kept for the next five hundred years. According to Georges Roux he was one of the two or three great Assyrian monarchs since the days of Shamshi-Adad I. His first campaign, in 1112 BCE, was against the Mushku, whom the sources call Phrygians, who had occupied districts held by Assyria on the Upper Euphrates. He then overran Commagene and Cappadocia and drove the Hittites from the Hurrian province of Subartu.

Later campaigns reached the mountains south of Lake Van and received the submission of Malatia. In his fifth year he attacked Comana in Cappadocia and placed an account of his victories, engraved on copper plates, in a fortress he built to secure his conquests in Cilicia. He campaigned against the Arameans in the Levant and secured the high road to the Mediterranean by taking the Hittite town of Pitru. At Arvad he sailed out and killed a nāhiru, a sea-horse, which A. Leo Oppenheim translates as a narwhal.

Tiglath-Pileser called himself the unrivalled king of the universe and king of the four quarters. He stressed the brutality of his conquests and was the first Assyrian king to take hostages, sometimes children, as a political instrument against conquered peoples. He restored the temple of the gods Ashur and Adad in the capital Assur and is believed to have been one of the first kings to commission parks and botanical gardens with foreign trees and plants from across his lands.

His inscriptions were written on eight-sided prisms and on tablets. One prism lays out his campaigns year by year and is considered one of the first preserved annals in the world. It states: Altogether I conquered 42 lands and their rulers, from the other side of the Lower Zab to the other side of the Euphrates, to the people of Hatti and the Upper Sea in the west, from my accession year to my fifth regnal year. Returning from campaigns, he set up statues of animals he had met or hunted at the gates of Ashur.

The latter part of his reign appears to have been a time of retrenchment, as Aramaean tribesmen pressed on his realm. He died in 1076 BCE and was succeeded by his son Asharid-apal-Ekur. His sons Ashur-bel-kala and Shamshi-Adad IV later ruled as well.
tigranes-the-great: Tigranes belonged to the Artaxiad dynasty and was either the son or the nephew of King Artavasdes I. Around 120 BCE the Parthian king Mithridates II invaded Armenia, and Tigranes was given to the Parthians as a hostage. He lived at Ctesiphon, where he was schooled in Parthian culture and language, until about 96 or 95 BCE, when Mithridates released him and appointed him king. Babylonian astronomical diaries for 95 BCE mention him as crown prince of Armenia. He ceded an area called the seventy valleys to Mithridates II and remained a Parthian vassal until the late 80s BCE.

Tigranes set out to build a centralised empire and first consolidated his power in Armenia, where the nakharars held great influence. He deposed Artanes, the last king of Sophene, and allied with Mithridates VI of Pontus by marrying his daughter Cleopatra. Between 88 and 85 BCE he retook Adiabene, Gordyene and Media Atropatene.

In 83 BCE, after strife over the Syrian throne, the Syrians chose him as protector of their kingdom and offered him the crown. He then conquered Phoenicia and Cilicia and ended the last remnants of the Seleucid kingdom. His empire stretched from the Pontic Alps to Mesopotamia and from the Caspian Sea to the Mediterranean, and he took the title King of Kings. Many inhabitants of conquered cities were moved to his new capital, Tigranocerta, which was noted for its Hellenistic architecture.

Mithridates VI took refuge at his court after confronting Rome, and Tigranes refused the demand of the Roman commander Lucullus to expel him. Lucullus defeated Tigranes at the Battle of Tigranocerta on 6 October 69 BCE and again at Artaxata in 68 BCE. When Pompey was sent in 66 BCE, helped by Tigranes' son Tigranes the Younger, Tigranes surrendered. Pompey let him keep the heartland of Armenia as a buffer state, removed his conquests and took 6,000 talents of silver.

Tigranes ruled Armenia as a client king of Rome until his death around 55 BCE, aged 85. His successor was his youngest son, Artavasdes II. His court blended Iranian and Hellenistic influences, he took the title Philhellene, and his silver coinage minted at Antioch has been called the finest struck by an Armenian monarch. Armenian tradition ranks him first among its kings, and Movses Khorenatsi called him the most powerful, intelligent and valiant of them. Roman sources marginalised him, and modern historians differ: René Grousset praised him, while Robert H. Hewsen found his short-lived empire not especially significant and noted the forced deportations of his subjects.
tigris: The Tigris is about 1,750 kilometres long. It rises in the Taurus Mountains of eastern Turkey and flows for 400 kilometres through south-eastern Turkey before forming part of the border between Syria and Turkey. Its tributaries include the Great and Little Zab. Near its confluence with the Euphrates it splits into several channels that feed the marshes, and the main channel joins the Euphrates near al-Qurnah to form the Shatt al-Arab.

Ancient writers such as Pliny held that the two rivers once had separate outlets to the sea. The Tigris has long been a transport route in a largely desert country: shallow-draft vessels can reach Baghdad, while rafts were needed downstream from Mosul. It has also been prone to floods after the April melting of snow in the Turkish mountains.

The name comes through Latin Tigris and Greek Tígris from Old Persian Tigrā, which came from Akkadian Idiglat and Sumerian Idigna. The Sumerian name can be read as the swift river, in contrast to the Euphrates, which flowed more slowly and deposited more silt. In ancient times many of the great cities of Mesopotamia stood on or near the Tigris and drew water from it to irrigate the civilisation of the Sumerians; the city of Lagash was irrigated from the river by a canal dug around 2900 BCE.

In Sumerian mythology the god Enki created the Tigris by filling it with flowing water. In the Book of Genesis it is the third of the four rivers branching from the river that issues out of Eden. The Mandaeans use the river for baptism, and the river appeared on the coat of arms of Iraq from 1932 to 1959.
timbuktu: Timbuktu stands on the southern edge of the Sahara, about 15 to 20 kilometres north of the main channel of the Niger. It is surrounded by sand dunes, and its streets are covered in sand. The port of Kabara lies 8 kilometres to the south. The town's wealth and very existence depended on its place as the southern end of a trans-Saharan trade route.

The one good now routinely carried across the desert is rock salt, cut in slabs at Taoudenni, 664 kilometres to the north. Until the second half of the 20th century large caravans of several thousand camels took three weeks each way. The climate is a hot desert one, with most rain between June and September.

Timbuktu began as a seasonal settlement and became permanent early in the 12th century. After the visit by Mansa Musa around 1325 it flourished on the trade in salt, gold and ivory, and Mansa Musa recruited scholars from across the Islamic world. In the first half of the 15th century the Tuareg held the city for a short period, until the Songhai Empire absorbed it in 1468. A Moroccan army defeated the Songhai in 1591 and made Timbuktu its capital; the invaders formed a ruling class, the Arma, who after 1612 were virtually independent of Morocco.

The French took over Mali in 1893, and colonial rule lasted until 1960. Leo Africanus, born in Granada in 1485 and educated in Fes, visited the city and wrote an account in Italian that gave Europeans most of what they knew of Africa for centuries.

Timbuktu is the capital of the Tombouctou Region of Mali. It has three notable mosques: Djinguereber, built in 1327 under Mansa Musa, Sankoré, built in the 14th or 15th century, and Sidi Yahya, founded in 1400 and completed in 1440. In December 1988 the World Heritage Committee inscribed parts of its historic centre. The city was a world centre of Islamic learning from the 13th to the 17th century, and hundreds of thousands of manuscripts were gathered there, hidden in cellars or buried to survive the decline; libraries in Timbuktu held up to 700,000 in 2003.
timgad: Timgad lies in the Aurès Mountains of Algeria, about 35 km east of Batna, at roughly 1,000 metres above sea level. Its full name was Colonia Marciana Ulpia Traiana Thamugadi. Trajan named it for his mother Marcia, his eldest sister Ulpia Marciana and his father Marcus Ulpius Traianus, while Thamugadi is the Berber name of the site, the plural of Tamgut, meaning peak or summit. It has been nicknamed the Pompeii of North Africa.

Trajan founded the city as a colony in about 100 CE, intended chiefly as a Roman bastion against the Berbers of the nearby Aurès Mountains, and it was populated largely by Roman veterans and colonists. After a peaceful early existence it became a centre of Christian activity from the 3rd century and a Donatist centre in the 4th, when its bishop Optatus became spokesman for the Donatist movement.

The Vandals sacked the city in the 5th century, and Berber tribes from the Aurès destroyed it at the end of that century. In 539 the Byzantine general Solomon retook and rebuilt it during the Moorish wars. It was no longer inhabited by the 8th century. The Scottish explorer James Bruce reached the ruins on 12 December 1765, probably the first European to see them in centuries. French colonists took control of the site in 1881 and excavated it systematically until 1960.

The ruins are one of the best surviving examples of the Roman grid plan. The decumanus maximus, running east to west, and the cardo, running north to south, were lined with a Corinthian colonnade. Built to hold about 15,000 people, the city outgrew its plan and spread beyond the grid. The Arch of Trajan, a 12-metre triumphal arch of sandstone, stands at the west end of the decumanus.

A theatre of 3,500 seats is in good condition and is used for contemporary productions. Other buildings include four baths, a basilica and a Capitoline temple dedicated to Jupiter, of about the same dimensions as the Pantheon in Rome. The library, a gift of Julius Quintianus Flavius Rogatianus, probably dates from the late 3rd or the 4th century and could have held about 3,000 scrolls. UNESCO inscribed Timgad as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
timisoara: Timișoara lies on the Bega River, the southernmost tributary of the Tisza, in the south-eastern part of the Pannonian Basin. Archaeological remains show farmers, hunters and artisans living in the fertile lands between the Mureș, the Tisza and the Danube by 4000 BCE. The Bega was canalized, and a navigable canal was built along it between 1728 and 1760. The Hungarian name Temesvár was first recorded as Temeswar in 1315 and refers to a castle on the Timiș River; the Romanian and German forms derive from it.

The city is first officially mentioned in 1212 as a royal fortress, though some historians date its first documentary mention to 1266, when the heir apparent Stephen V of Hungary donated part of a fortress built by his father, Béla IV. After Tatar destruction in the 13th century it was rebuilt under Charles I of Hungary, who ordered stone walls and a royal palace in 1307 and moved the royal seat there from Buda between 1316 and 1323.

After the defeat at Mohács in 1526 the Banat was contested between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans. On 22 July 1552 an army led by Kara Ahmed Pasha took the city and made it the capital of the Temeşvar Eyalet; the local commander István Losonczy and other Christians were massacred on 27 July as they tried to escape. In 1716 Prince Eugene of Savoy besieged it for 48 days, and bombardment destroyed much of the city. By the Treaty of Passarowitz (1718) the Banat of Temeswar became a possession of the Habsburg crown under military rule until 1751. From 1848 to 1860 the city was the capital of the Serbian Vojvodina.

Under Austria-Hungary the city grew quickly and its industries included breweries, an iron foundry and a match factory. On 1 November 1918 the Banat Republic was proclaimed briefly. Serbian forces held the city until 1919, and the Treaty of Trianon of 4 June 1920 ceded it to Romania, whose King Ferdinand I made it a university centre that year.

Timișoara is the capital of Timiș County and the main economic and cultural centre of western Romania, with 250,849 inhabitants at the 2021 census. Romanian is the official language; German, Hungarian and Serbian communities remain, and the city has the largest German population in Romania. It was the first city in the Habsburg monarchy with street lighting, in 1760, and the first in Europe lit by electric street lamps, in 1884. It is nicknamed Little Vienna and the City of Roses.
timur: Timur was born in Transoxiana near the city of Kesh, now Shahrisabz in Uzbekistan, about 80 kilometres south of Samarkand, then part of the Chagatai Khanate. He belonged to the Barlas, a Turkicized Mongol confederation. His name, Temur, means iron in Chagatai, his mother tongue. Timurid histories trace his descent in the male line from Tumbinai Khan, an ancestor of Genghis Khan, but no written evidence from his own lifetime links him directly to Genghis Khan. By about 1360 he had become a military leader whose troops were mostly Turkic tribesmen, and he campaigned in Transoxiana with the Khan of the Chagatai Khanate.

Timur reduced the Chagatai khans to figureheads and ruled in their name. Because he was not a descendant of Genghis Khan, Mongol tradition denied him the title of khan, so he used the title of amir and set up a puppet khan, Suyurghatmish. His first campaigns took Khwarazm and Urgench, and in 1383 he began his conquest of Persia. When Herat did not surrender he reduced it to rubble and massacred most of its citizens.

In 1398 Timur invaded the Indian subcontinent, where the Tughlaq dynasty's Delhi Sultanate had declined and most provincial governors had asserted their independence. He crossed the Indus on 30 September 1398 with a force of 90,000 and sacked Tulamba, massacring its inhabitants. Before the battle for Delhi on 17 December 1398 he slaughtered some 100,000 captives, fearing that they might revolt. In the following years he fought the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I and the Mamluk sultan of Egypt, Nasir-ad-Din Faraj, and had Ming envoys detained. Scholars estimate that his campaigns caused the deaths of millions.

In December 1404 Timur began a winter campaign against Ming China. He fell ill beyond the Syr Daria and died at Farab on 17 or 18 February 1405. He had outlived two chosen heirs, his son Jahangir and his grandson Muhammad Sultan, and on his deathbed named Muhammad Sultan's brother Pir Muhammad. A civil war among his descendants followed, and his youngest son Shah Rukh took the throne only in 1409.

His legacy is mixed. Central Asia flourished under him, while Baghdad, Damascus, Delhi and other cities were sacked and their people massacred. He keeps a positive image in Muslim Central Asia and is vilified in Arabia, Iraq, Persia and India. Two Zafarnamas written under Timurid patronage present him favourably, while the Arabic chronicle of Ahmad ibn Arabshah is far less so.
timurid-empire: Timur belonged to the Barlas tribe, a Mongol group of the Chagatai ulus that had become Turkified in language and culture. He saw himself as the restorer of the Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan. Because he could not claim descent from Genghis, he married a Genghisid princess, Saray Mulk Khanum, and took the title Gurkani, meaning son-in-law. He took Samarkand in 1366 and Balkh in 1369, and was recognised as ruler of the region in 1370. He acted officially in the name of the Chagatai khan, but in practice Timur chose the khans, who became puppet rulers.

From 1380 Timur campaigned westwards against the successor states of the Ilkhanate. He removed the Kartids from Herat, captured Isfahan in 1387, drove the Muzaffarids from Shiraz and expelled the Jalayirids from Baghdad. In 1394–1395 he defeated Tokhtamysh, khan of the Golden Horde, after a campaign in Georgia, and enforced his sovereignty in the Caucasus. The costs of his conquests included the deaths of possibly 17 million people.

Timur gave the main governorships to his sons and grandsons. After his death in 1405 the dynasty fell into disputes and civil wars, and many governors became independent. Samarkand and Herat became the centres of the Timurid Renaissance under Shahrukh Mirza (1405–1447) and his son Ulugh Beg (1447–1449), and Herat flowered again under Husayn Bayqara (1469–1506). Meanwhile the Timurid habit of partitioning the realm weakened it. The Aq Qoyunlu took most of Iran, and the Safavid Empire under Shah Ismail I soon took Persia, the Caucasus and Mesopotamia. The Uzbeks under Shaybani Khan overran the central Asian principalities and founded the Khanate of Bukhara.

Babur, a Timurid prince exiled from Fergana, set up a base at Kabul in 1504 and invaded the Delhi Sultanate in 1526. The Mughal dynasty he founded was directly inherited from the Timurids, and the last nominal Mughal rule was abolished by the British after the Indian Rebellion of 1857.

The Timurid era combined Turco-Mongol origins with Persian high culture. The military was at first almost wholly Turco-Mongolian, while the administration was Persian, and Persian became the official language, with Chaghatay as the family's home language. The golden age of Persian painting began under the Timurids, with Chinese influence. Their architecture favoured large buildings, double-shelled domes and rich tile decoration, as at the Gur-i Amir Mausoleum and the Bibi-Khanym Mosque in Samarkand. Gawhar Shad was its most important patron in the 15th century. Its style passed to the Safavids, the Mughals and early Ottoman builders.
tin: Tin is a chemical element with the symbol Sn, from the Latin stannum, and atomic number 50. It is a soft, silvery-white, malleable metal that can be cut with little force, and a bent bar of tin makes a crackling sound known as the tin cry, caused by the twinning of its crystals. It resists corrosion from water. It does not occur as the native element but is extracted from ores, chiefly cassiterite, the only commercially important source, which is almost always associated with granite.

The word tin is shared among the Germanic languages and traces back to a reconstructed Proto-Germanic form; cognates include German Zinn, Swedish tenn and Dutch tin. The Latin name stannum or stagnum originally meant an alloy of silver and lead, and came to mean tin in the fourth century. The earlier Latin word was plumbum candidum, or white lead. The origin of stannum is unknown and may be pre-Indo-European.

Tin extraction and use can be dated to the beginnings of the Bronze Age around 3000 BCE. The earliest bronze objects had a tin or arsenic content of under 2 per cent and are believed to be the result of unintentional alloying. Adding a second metal to copper increases its hardness, lowers its melting temperature and gives a more fluid melt, which allowed the more complex shapes cast in closed moulds of the Bronze Age.

Arsenical bronze appears first in the Near East, where arsenic is commonly found with copper ore, but its health risks were quickly realised, and the quest for sources of the much less hazardous tin began early in the Bronze Age. This created a demand for rare tin and a trade network linking distant sources of tin to the markets of Bronze Age cultures. The first tin alloy used on a large scale was bronze, of one eighth tin and seven eighths copper; after 600 BCE pure metallic tin was produced. Pewter, an alloy of 85 to 90 per cent tin, has been used for flatware since the Bronze Age.
tirana: Tirana lies on the Plain of Tirana in the centre of Albania, between Mount Dajti to the east, hills to the south and a valley to the north that overlooks the Adriatic Sea. Its average altitude is about 110 metres. The Tiranë and Lanë rivers flow through the city. Dajti National Park lies on the mountain above it, with forests of pine, oak and beech, and the city's mountains are a popular retreat in winter, when snow often covers them although the city itself rarely receives it.

The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with the earliest recognised reference at the Cave of Pëllumbas, of the Palaeolithic period. Illyrians were its first population and most likely formed the core of the Illyrian kingdom of the Taulantii. After the Illyrian Wars the Romans integrated the area into their empire. The oldest surviving find from that period is a Roman house of the 3rd century, later turned into a church with a mosaic floor. A castle, possibly known as Tirkan, was built by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian I and was restored by Ahmed Pasha Toptani in the 18th century.

Tirana appears in Venetian documents of the 1350s and in 1418. The first Ottoman land registrations of 1431–32 record 60 inhabited areas with nearly 2,028 houses and 7,300 inhabitants. In 1510 Marin Barleti, in his biography of Skanderbeg, called it a small village, distinguishing Little Tirana from Great Tirana. The town was founded in 1614 by the Ottoman Albanian nobleman Sylejman Pasha Bargjini, who built the Old Mosque, a small commercial centre and a hammam. Some sources describe a bazaar with watermills already existing before 1614. In the 16th century craftsmen made silk and cotton fabrics, leather, ceramics and metal artefacts. The Et'hem Bey Mosque was completed in 1821.

The city was fairly unimportant until the 20th century, when the Congress of Lushnjë proclaimed it the capital of Albania following the Albanian Declaration of Independence of 1912. Its present appearance was shaped by two totalitarian regimes: Mussolini's, whose architects Florestano Di Fausto and Armando Brasini designed the ministry buildings, and Enver Hoxha's afterwards. The population tenfolded between 1820 and 1955, and it grew faster after the fall of communism.

Tirana is the capital and largest city of Albania and seat of its government, parliament and highest courts. The centre from the University of Tirana's Mother Teresa Square to Skanderbeg Square was declared a protected cultural area in 2000. The 2023 census counted 598,176 residents in the municipality. The airport is named after Mother Teresa.
togo: Togo is a small tropical country of 56,785 square kilometres, less than 115 kilometres wide between Ghana and Benin. It extends north from the Gulf of Guinea, where its coast is 56 kilometres long and consists of lagoons with sandy beaches, to the border with Burkina Faso. The south has a savannah and woodland plateau reaching a coastal plain with lagoons and marshes, the centre is hilly, and the north is rolling savannah. The highest mountain is Mont Agou at 986 metres, and the longest river is the Mono, at 400 kilometres.

The name Togo means 'by the water' or 'behind the sea', from the Ewe words to, 'water', and go, 'shore'. It originally referred only to the town of Togo, now Togoville, and the Germans later extended it to the whole country.

Archaeological finds indicate that societies in the area could produce pottery and process iron. Between the 11th and 16th centuries the Ewe entered the area from the west, and the Mina and Gun from the east, and most settled on the coast. The Atlantic slave trade began in the 16th century. For the next two hundred years the coastal region was a trading centre for Europeans in search of slaves, which earned Togo and the surrounding region the name the Slave Coast.

In 1884 a paper was forcibly signed at Togoville with King Mlapa III, whereby Germany claimed a protectorate over a stretch of coast and gradually extended its control inland. In 1905 this became the German colony of Togoland. The local population was forced to work, to cultivate cotton, coffee and cocoa, and to pay taxes, and a railway and the port of Lomé were built for export.

Britain and France invaded in August 1914, and German forces surrendered on 26 August. The territory was partitioned into British and French zones, which on 20 July 1922 became League of Nations mandates. French Togoland became an autonomous republic in 1956, and British Togoland voted to join the Gold Coast, as part of Ghana, in 1957. Togo became independent from France in 1960.

Togo is the Togolese Republic, with its capital, Lomé, on the Gulf of Guinea. French is the official language, and Kabiye and Ewe are national languages. The population is about 8 million, with some 40 ethnic groups, of which the Ewe in the south are the most numerous. Culture draws on Ewe and Mina traditions in the south, including the creator god Mawu and the vodun, and on Kabye and Tem traditions in the north, including the Evala wrestling initiation rite.
tokelau: Tokelau consists of three tropical coral atolls, Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo, with a combined land area of about 10 square kilometres, between latitudes 8 and 10 degrees south, about midway between Hawaii and New Zealand and some 500 kilometres north of Samoa. The highest point is just 5 metres above sea level, and the islands lie in the Pacific tropical cyclone belt. Swains Island (Olohega), culturally and geographically part of the same archipelago, has been under United States control since about 1900 and is administered as part of American Samoa. The name is a Tokelauan word meaning north wind; European explorers called the group the Union Islands, and it was shortened to Tokelau on 9 December 1976.

Archaeological evidence indicates that the atolls were settled about 1,000 years ago from Samoa. The three atolls functioned separately in politics while keeping social and linguistic cohesion, governed by chiefly clans, with occasional wars between atolls as well as intermarriage; Fakaofo held some dominion over Atafu and Nukunonu. Life was subsistence-based, relying mainly on fish and coconut.

Commodore John Byron sighted Atafu on 24 June 1765, and Captain Edward Edwards visited it in June 1791 in search of the Bounty mutineers. In 1877 an Order in Council placed the islands under United Kingdom protection, and in June 1889 Commander C. F. Oldham of HMS Egeria raised the Union Flag on each atoll. They were annexed on 29 February 1916 and included in the Gilbert Islands. They were placed under the Governor-General of New Zealand in 1925, and New Zealand took over administration on 11 February 1926, though sovereignty remained with the United Kingdom.

Tokelau is a dependent territory of New Zealand, whose King is its head of state, and both governments call it a nation. About 2,500 people live there, and some 94 per cent speak Tokelauan as their first language. Since 1993 the territory has elected its own head of government, the Ulu-o-Tokelau, a post that rotates among the faipule of the three atolls, and the basis of its system is the Tokelau Islands Act 1948. Tokelauans have twice narrowly failed to reach the two-thirds majority needed for further self-determination.
tomsk: Tomsk stands on the Tom River, from which the city takes its name. The river's name may derive from the Ket word toom, meaning river, from the Russian tyomny, meaning dark, or from the Turco-Mongol tom, meaning great. The climate is humid continental, barely escaping a subarctic classification, with severe and lengthy winters; the lowest recorded temperature was −55 °C in January 1931.

The fortress of 1604 followed a request from Toian, the Tatar duke of the Eushta Tatars, for the tsar's protection against the Yenisei Kyrgyz and the Oirats. Boris Godunov sent 200 Cossacks under Vasily Fomich Tyrkov and Gavriil Ivanovich Pisemsky, and Toian ceded the land. In 1804 Tomsk became the seat of the Tomsk Governorate, and gold was found in 1830. In the mid-19th century one fifth of its residents were exiles. When the Trans-Siberian Railway of the 1890s bypassed the city, growth shifted south and Novosibirsk in time surpassed it.

Tomsk then built its name on education. Tomsk Polytechnic University was founded in 1896 and opened in 1900, and by World War II every twelfth resident was a student. After 1917 Tomsk became a notable centre of the White movement, led among others by Anatoly Pepelyayev and Maria Bochkareva. Factories moved there from 1941, which led to the creation of Tomsk Oblast. In the Cold War it was a closed city, and in 1949 the secret settlement of Tomsk-7, home to the Soviet Union's first industrial-scale nuclear power station, was founded nearby; it was renamed Seversk in 1992.

Tomsk is the administrative centre of Tomsk Oblast in Russia, with 556,478 inhabitants at the 2021 census. It has six universities with over 100,000 students, among them Tomsk State University, the oldest university in Siberia. The city is known for the intricate gingerbread decoration of its traditional wooden houses, though their number is falling through redevelopment and fire.
toronto: Toronto stands on a harbour on the north-western shore of Lake Ontario, on a broad sloping plateau interspersed with rivers, deep ravines and urban forest. The city covers 631 square kilometres and has a 46-kilometre waterfront. The Toronto Islands and Port Lands extend into the lake and shelter the harbour south of downtown. The name was recorded in many spellings. The early form Taronto referred to the Narrows between Lake Simcoe and Lake Couchiching, which the Mohawk called tkaronto, meaning where there are trees standing in the water, a name recorded as early as 1615 by Samuel de Champlain.

Indigenous peoples have inhabited the area for more than 10,000 years. The Wendat, an Iroquoian-speaking agricultural people, farmed it for centuries before European contact, until the Haudenosaunee invaded and massacred them between 1648 and 1650. By the 1660s the Haudenosaunee had two villages in what is now Toronto, Ganatsekwyagon on the Rouge River and Teiaiagon on the Humber River. By 1701 the Mississaugas, an Anishinaabe-speaking people from northern Ontario, had displaced them at the end of the Beaver Wars. A portage route from Lake Ontario to Lake Huron, the Toronto Carrying-Place Trail, led to the wide use of the name.

French traders founded Fort Rouillé in 1750 but abandoned it in 1759 during the Seven Years' War. The British defeated the French and their Indigenous allies, and in 1763 the area became part of the colony of Quebec. After the broadly disputed Toronto Purchase, in which the Mississaugas surrendered the area to the British Crown, the British established the town of York in 1793 and later made it the capital of Upper Canada.

During the War of 1812 York was the site of the Battle of York, which caused heavy damage and a two-week occupation by American troops. It was renamed and incorporated as the City of Toronto in 1834. In 1867, at Canadian Confederation, it became the capital of the province of Ontario. The city grew beyond its original limits by annexation and amalgamation, reaching its present area in 1998. The completion of the St. Lawrence Seaway in 1959 gave ships access to the Great Lakes from the Atlantic.

Toronto is the capital of Ontario and the most populous city in Canada, with 2,794,356 people at the 2021 census. About half of its residents were born outside Canada, over 200 ethnic origins are represented, and more than 160 languages are spoken. It is governed by a mayor and a unicameral city council of 25 councillors. It is Canada's largest financial centre and the home of the Toronto Stock Exchange, and of institutions such as the National Ballet of Canada, the Canadian Opera Company and the Toronto Symphony Orchestra.
torshavn: The Viking settlers of the 9th century held their parliaments, called tings, at neutral and uninhabited places so that no location favoured anyone. The main ting met on the flat rocks of Tinganes, the peninsula that divides the harbour in two, which was the most central place in the islands although no settlement stood there. The Færeyinga Saga says the ting of the Faroese was on Streymoy at the harbour called Tórshavn. A market grew beside the ting and gradually became a permanent trading area, and Tórshavn was never a distinct farming community like other Faroese villages.

In 1271 the Norwegian Crown set up a royal trade monopoly at Tórshavn, with two ships sailing regularly from Bergen with salt, timber and cereal. Officials of the Norwegian and then Danish administration made their home there. Around 1580 Magnus Heinason built the small fort of Skansin at the north end of the harbour, and in 1584 the town had 101 inhabitants. From 1655 to 1709 the von Gabel family held the islands and the monopoly, a period known as Gablatíðin, when islanders complained of unjust treatment and fixed prices. A gunpowder explosion burned Tinganes in 1673, and smallpox in 1709 killed about 250 of some 300 inhabitants.

The town began to develop in the later 18th century, while Niels Ryberg ran the trade monopoly. From 1768 he carried on an entrepot trade, mostly smuggling to England, and he was the first to think of profiting from fishing, with salted cod and herring. Tórshavn Cathedral was first built in 1788 and partly rebuilt in 1865.

On 30 March 1808, during the Anglo-Danish Gunboat War, HMS Clio entered the harbour and the fort at Skansin surrendered without firing a shot. The trade monopoly was abolished in 1856, opening the islands to free trade and putting Tórshavn at the centre of a changed economy. Its town council was founded in 1866, and in 1909 it became a market town with the same charter as Danish ones.

Tórshavn is the capital and largest town of the Faroe Islands, on the east coast of Streymoy, with 14,223 inhabitants in 2024 and 22,444 in the greater urban area. Mountains rise to the northwest and southwest, separated by the Sandá River. It is the seat of the Faroese self-rule government, part of which still sits on Tinganes, and of the Løgting. Since 1990 it has been the seat of the Bishop of the Faroe Islands.
toulon: Toulon lies on the French Riviera at the eastern end of the Gulf of Lion, in the historical region of Provence. Greek colonists from Phocaea founded trading depots along this coast from about the 7th century BCE, and the Ligurians settled the area from the 4th century BCE. After the Romans defeated the Ligurians, a settlement named Telo Martius arose on the site of the city. It became one of the two principal Roman centres for the purple dye used in imperial robes, made from the murex sea snail.

Toulon was Christianized in the 5th century, and its first cathedral was built then. Pirates and Saracens attacked the town often as Roman power crumbled. Provence became part of France in 1486, and in 1494 Charles VIII of France began a military port at the harbour to make France a Mediterranean sea power. In 1524 Francis I completed the Tour Royale at the harbour entrance, but its commander sold it to an imperial commander and Toulon surrendered. In the winter of 1543 the fleet of the Ottoman admiral Barbarossa occupied the town, whose residents were made to leave, under the Franco-Ottoman alliance.

Toulon resisted a siege by the Imperial Army under Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy and Prince Eugene in 1707. In 1720 plague from Marseille killed about 13,000 people, half the population. In 1793 the city joined the Federalist revolts against the First Republic and handed itself and its fleet to the British; Republican forces forced them out, and the town was briefly renamed Port-la-Montagne. From 1803 to 1805 a fleet under Horatio Nelson blockaded the port. In 1849 Georges Eugène Haussmann, then prefect of the Var, laid out the street plan of the city centre. On 27 November 1942 French naval officers scuttled the fleet based there, after German forces occupied southern France, and Allied bombing the following November destroyed much of the port.

Toulon is the prefecture of the Var department and has 179,116 inhabitants in 2023, with a metropolitan area of 591,135. It is the third most populous French city on the Mediterranean, after Marseille and Nice. Its military port is the chief naval centre of France's Mediterranean coast, and the city also has shipbuilding, fishing, winemaking and several manufacturing industries. The University of Toulon opened in 1979.
toulouse: Toulouse lies on the banks of the Garonne, 150 kilometres from the Mediterranean Sea, 230 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean and 680 kilometres from Paris, on the axis of communication between the two seas. The Garonne valley has been a central point for trade between the Pyrenees, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic since at least the Iron Age. The historical name of the city, Tolosa, and that of its inhabitants, the Tolosates, first recorded in the 2nd century BCE, is of unknown meaning or origin, and has been connected with the Gaulish Volcae Tectosages and, by others, with a root meaning little hill.

Charlemagne created the county of Toulouse in 778 to guard the border of Muslim Spain. The disintegration of the kingdom of Aquitaine and the weakness of royal power in the following centuries led to the de facto independence of the county. The treaty of 1229 made Toulouse subordinate to the kingdom of France, and when Joan of Toulouse and her husband Alphonse of Poitiers died without heirs in 1271 the city had no count and was annexed to the royal domain. Royal officers settled in the city, trade and crafts grew, and in 1298 King Philip the Fair eased the ennobling of the capitouls, whose annually renewed council was increasingly made up of rich merchants.

The University of Toulouse was founded in 1229. In the 16th century the woad trade brought merchants of international stature to the city, and the Parlement of Toulouse made it the judicial capital of much of the south of France.

On 10 April 1814 Wellington's Hispanic-British troops fought the French under Marshal Soult at the Battle of Toulouse, four days after Napoleon's surrender, though neither army yet knew of it; it was the last Franco-British battle on French territory. In the First World War the city, sheltered from attack, gained chemical industries and aviation workshops, which began its aeronautical tradition and gave rise to the airmail company Aéropostale.

Toulouse is the prefecture of the Haute-Garonne department and of the Occitania region, with 514,819 inhabitants within its municipal boundaries in 2023. Its architecture of pinkish terracotta brick has earned it the name La Ville rose. The Basilica of Saint-Sernin, the largest remaining Romanesque building in Europe, and the former hospital Hôtel-Dieu Saint-Jacques are World Heritage Sites for their place on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela, as is the Canal du Midi, which begins in the city. Toulouse is the centre of the European aerospace industry, with the headquarters of Airbus, and its rugby club, Stade Toulousain, is among the most successful in Europe.
tours: In Gallic times Tours was an important crossing of the Loire. It became part of the Roman Empire in the 1st century and was named Caesarodunum, meaning hill of Caesar; by the 4th century the name had changed from Turones to Civitas Turonum and then Tours, and the Tours Amphitheatre was built. Around 380 to 388 it became a metropolis of the Roman province of Lugdunum, dominating Maine, Brittany and the Loire Valley. Its bishop Saint Martin, who shared his coat with a naked beggar at Amiens, made the city a major centre of the medieval West on the pilgrimage route to Santiago de Compostela.

In the 6th century Gregory of Tours, author of the Ten Books of History, restored a cathedral destroyed by fire in 561, and Saint Martin's monastery received patronage from the Frankish king Clovis I. In the 9th century Alcuin of York, a book collector and abbot of Marmoutier Abbey, made the city a heart of the Carolingian Renaissance. In 732 Abdul Rahman Al Ghafiqi's army from Al-Andalus, having advanced 500 km into France, was stopped by Charles Martel at the Battle of Tours. Tours repelled a Viking attack by Haesten in 845, but the Vikings sacked it in 852.
