Medieval Tours had two competing centres: the City in the east, with the cathedral and the castle of the Counts of Tours, and in the west Châteauneuf around the Abbey of Saint Martin, which became the economic centre after its enclosure around 918. The two were joined in the 14th century. Touraine was disputed between the counts of Blois and Anjou, and Anjou won in the 11th century.

Under Louis XI, who lived at the castle of Montils, Tours was the capital of France, and he introduced the silk industry, which still survives. The kings and court stayed in Touraine until the 16th century, and the Renaissance left the private mansions and châteaux of the Loire. Protestants were imprisoned by the aldermen in the Wars of Religion, which prevented their massacre.

Tours is the largest city of Centre-Val de Loire and the prefecture of Indre-et-Loire, with 138,668 inhabitants in 2022. From 10 to 13 June 1940 it was the temporary seat of the French government, and German incendiary bombs then burned part of the city centre from 20 to 22 June. Its historical centre is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
trabzon: The city stands on the Black Sea coast of north-eastern Turkey, on a table-like central hill between the Zağnos (İskeleboz) and Kuzgun streams. The Greek name Trapezous refers to this hill, since the word τράπεζα meant table in Ancient Greek. Before the Greek colony was founded the area was dominated by Colchian and Chaldian tribes, and Greek authors later mentioned the Macrones and the Chalybes as native peoples. The Pontic Mountains rise behind the coast, and the province's total area is 4,685 square kilometres.

The city was founded in 756 BCE as Trapezous by Greeks from Miletus. It was added to the Achaemenid Empire by Cyrus the Great, later belonged to the Kingdom of Pontus, which challenged Rome until 68 BCE, and then passed to the Roman and Byzantine empires. In the time of Justinian I it served as an important base in his Persian Wars, and an inscription above its eastern gate recorded the rebuilding of the walls at his expense after an earthquake. Its university, the Pandidakterion, was re-established before the 7th century and drew students from Armenia as well.

The Empire of Trebizond formed after a Georgian expedition into Chaldia, commanded by Alexios Komnenos a few weeks before the sack of Constantinople in 1204. It was the longest surviving of the Byzantine successor states. Byzantine writers connected with the Lascaris and later the Palaiologos regarded its rulers as not true emperors. The last emperor, David, surrendered the city to Sultan Mehmed II in 1461, and Mehmed sent many Turkish settlers into the area, though the Greek, Laz and Armenian communities remained.

Under the Ottomans the city was a sanjak centre and then part of several provinces. Ottoman tax books of 1523 show that about 85 percent of the population was Christian, mostly Greek, with an Armenian community making up thirteen percent of adult men. In July 1915, during the Armenian genocide, most adult male Armenians of the city were marched south in five convoys and never seen again.

Trabzon is the capital of Trabzon Province and the second largest city and port on the Black Sea coast of Turkey. Its Byzantine Hagia Sophia, now a mosque, is probably its most important sight. From 1683 to 1921 the Phrontisterion of Trapezous, a teachers' college, operated here and helped spread Greek education across the region; its 1902 building survives. Karadeniz Technical University is in the city, and the horon is the dance of the area.
tractor: The word tractor comes from the Latin trahere, to pull, and the earliest recorded use for an engine or vehicle that pulls wagons or ploughs dates from 1896, from the earlier term traction motor of 1859. The first powered farm machines of the early 19th century were portable steam engines on wheels that drove other machinery through a flexible belt. Richard Trevithick designed a semi-portable barn engine in 1812 to drive a corn threshing machine, and William Tuxford of Boston, Lincolnshire, invented a truly portable engine in 1839.

The first gasoline tractors were built in Illinois by John Charter in 1889, combining single-cylinder Otto engines with a Rumely steam engine chassis. John Froelich built another in Clayton County, Iowa, in 1892 and started the Waterloo Gasoline Engine Company, but the venture failed and he was out of business by 1895.

A tractor is designed to deliver high tractive effort at slow speeds, for hauling a trailer or machinery. The earliest, called standard tractors, were meant almost only for ploughing and harrowing, which were difficult tasks for people and draft animals. Implements were first attached by a drawbar, a steel bar to which the implement's hitch was pinned, so the tractor could be used for other tasks daily. Harry Ferguson later developed the three-point hitch, which lets hydraulics raise and lower the equipment. From the 1910s to the 1950s farm mechanics in the United States often converted automobiles, especially Ford Model Ts, into tractors, and dozens of firms sold conversion kits.

Economic historians have called the farm tractor one of the most revolutionary technological innovations in the history of modern agriculture, which vastly increased farm power, raised productivity and reshaped the rural landscape. Adoption met resistance. There were 500 gas tractors in the United States in 1910 and nearly 5,000 in 1920, when 3.6 per cent of American farms had one. The share reached 13.5 per cent by the end of the 1920s and rose to 40 per cent during the Great Depression. By 1935 nearly a million tractors were in use in the United States, against 15,000 in Germany. In the 1910s and 1920s the Nebraska tests, run by the University of Nebraska, helped farmers see through marketing claims.
trajan: Trajan was born Marcus Ulpius Traianus at Italica, a Roman colony in Hispania Baetica, near present-day Seville, to a family that came from Tuder in Umbria. His father, of the same name, was a general and distinguished senator who governed Syria in 76 and 77, when Trajan served there as a tribune. In 89 Trajan, commanding a legion in Hispania Tarraconensis, supported Domitian against a revolt on the Rhine led by Antonius Saturninus. He then governed Germania and Pannonia. The elderly and childless Nerva was unpopular with the army, and in the summer of 97 he named Trajan his adoptive son and successor. Some contemporary sources hint that the adoption was imposed on him.

Trajan's entry into Rome in 99 was understated. He gave the people a gift of money but halved the donative to the troops. By showing reluctance to hold power he built a consensus in the Senate, and Pliny the Younger praised him as a ruler who governed by example rather than fear. The Senate gave him the title optimus princeps. He rebuilt the Circus Maximus in stone by 103 and, with the architect Apollodorus of Damascus, built a great bridge over the Danube. He also formalised the alimenta, which supported orphans and poor children in Italy from Dacian war booty, estate taxes and gifts.

In letters to Pliny about the Christians of Pontus he ruled that anonymous denunciations were not to be accepted, though those who admitted the faith and refused to recant were to be executed. He overcame the Dacian king Decebalus, annexed the Nabataean kingdom after Rabbel II's death in 106, and from 113 fought Parthia over Armenia. A Jewish uprising in the eastern provinces in 116 and 117 forced him to withdraw his army.

Trajan fell ill early in 117, sailed for Italy and died at Selinus shortly before 11 August. Tradition places his ashes in the small chamber at the base of Trajan's Column. Dio reports that his wife Pompeia Plotina secured Hadrian's succession by hiding his death until a document of adoption was signed, a story that may rest on rumour. Ancient sources on Trajan are unanimously positive, and in the fourth century emperors were hailed as more fortunate than Augustus and better than Trajan.
transylvania: Transylvania is a historical region in Central Europe, bounded on the east and south by the Carpathian Mountains and on the west by the Apuseni Mountains. Its core is the Transylvanian Plateau, 300 to 500 metres high, drained by the Mureș, Someș, Criș and Olt rivers. The name first appears in a Medieval Latin document of the Kingdom of Hungary in 1078 as ultra silvam, meaning beyond the forest. The German name Siebenbürgen refers to the seven cities of the Transylvanian Saxons.

The first known people of the territory were the Agathyrsi, followed by the Celtic La Tène culture from the 4th century BCE and the Dacian tribes, who were united under King Burebista. Trajan's wars created Roman Dacia in 106, and Emperor Aurelian withdrew the legions south of the Lower Danube in 275. The Goths, Huns, Gepids and Avars then held the region in turn, and the First Bulgarian Empire expanded into its south in the 9th century. Hungarian tribes conquered it in the late 9th century, and King Stephen I of Hungary brought it into the Kingdom of Hungary in 1002. Saxon colonists settled in the 12th and 13th centuries.

Historians disagree about the early population. The theory of Daco-Roman continuity holds that Romanians lived there without interruption, while its opponents point to the lack of written, archaeological and linguistic evidence. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the region belonged to the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom, from which the Principality of Transylvania emerged in 1570 under the Treaty of Speyer. For most of the 16th and 17th centuries it was a vassal of the Ottoman Empire, with dual Ottoman and Habsburg suzerainty. In 1848 the Hungarian government proclaimed union with Transylvania, but the Compromise of 1867 reincorporated it into the Kingdom of Hungary within the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

The National Assembly of Romanians from Transylvania proclaimed union with Romania on 1 December 1918, and the Treaty of Trianon confirmed new borders in 1920. Over a million Hungarians remained on the Romanian side, mainly in the Székely Land. Northern Transylvania returned to Hungary in 1940 under the Second Vienna Award and to Romania after the Second World War. Its fortified churches, the old town of Sighișoara, the Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains and Roșia Montană are World Heritage Sites. Bram Stoker's 1897 novel Dracula made the region a byword for vampires in popular culture.
treaty-of-ghilajharighat: The Treaty of Asurar Ali of 1639 fixed the limit between Ahom and Mughal interests at the Barnadi river on the north bank of the Brahmaputra and the Asurar Ali on the south. During the Mughal war of succession of 1658–1659 Pran Narayan, king of Koch Bihar, attacked the Mughal faujdar at Guwahati. The Ahoms refused a Koch offer to partition Kamrup, drove the Koches out and took the whole valley up to the Sankosh River.

Aurangzeb made Mir Jumla II subahdar of Bengal. He annexed Koch Bihar in December 1661, recovered Guwahati on 5 February 1662 and occupied Garhgaon on 17 March. The rains from April turned the country to marsh and brought food shortage and cholera to the camps, while the Ahoms waged the guerrilla warfare devised by Atan Burhagohain. When the rains ended the Mughals recovered and the king withdrew to Namrup. The Ahom commander-in-chief, Baduli Phukan, defected at the end of November, and Mir Jumla, by then ill, reached Tipam by 18 December with a worn-out army eager to go home.

Atan Burhagohain persuaded the king that further fighting was futile and sent four emissaries offering tribute if the Mughals left Assam. Mir Jumla, who had refused everything short of unconditional surrender, took the opening and left the bargaining to Dilir Khan. The terms are pieced together from Persian and Assamese sources that do not fully agree.

The king accepted Mughal vassalage; his daughter Ramani Gabharu went to the imperial harem with a dowry of 20,000 tolas of gold and 120,000 of silver. The indemnity was 300,000 tolas of silver within a year and 90 elephants in instalments, the annual tribute 20 elephants. Four sons of leading nobles were to be hostages. The ceded land ran from Guwahati to the Bharali River on the north bank and to the Kolong River on the south.

The princess left on 5 January 1663 with the gold, silver and part of the elephants, and Mir Jumla ordered the retreat from Tipam on 10 January. He died on board on 31 March 1663. Jayadhwaj Singha founded a new capital at Bakata and died in November 1663; his cousin succeeded as Chakradhar Singha. Neither king could accept tributary status, and the terms were only partly fulfilled. The treaty was the root of the later conflicts, which ended with the Mughal defeat at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671 and, after the Battle of Itakhuli in 1682, the end of Mughal interests in the Brahmaputra valley.
treaty-of-versailles: The armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the fighting but left the peace to be settled. It took six months of Allied negotiations at the Paris Peace Conference to conclude a treaty. Talks between the Allies began on 18 January 1919 at the French Foreign Ministry on the Quai d'Orsay, with 70 delegates from 27 nations.

The victors wanted different things. France had lost 1.3 million soldiers and had its industrial north-east devastated, and Clemenceau sought security by weakening Germany. British opinion favoured a just peace in which Germany paid reparations. President Woodrow Wilson, whose Fourteen Points of 8 January 1918 had called for a League of Nations and self-determination, hoped for a peace of reconciliation. The result was a compromise that satisfied none of them.

The treaty was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Palace of Versailles, five years to the day after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Germany lost 65,000 km2 of territory and 7 million people. Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, the Saar coalfield passed to France with the territory under League of Nations control for 15 years, and Eupen-Malmedy went to Belgium. Germany's colonies became League of Nations mandates, and its concessions in Shandong were given to Japan.

The army was limited to 100,000 men, conscription was abolished and the General Staff was dissolved. Allied troops were to occupy the Rhineland for up to fifteen years. Article 231, the so-called War Guilt clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage of the war, and a Reparation Commission was to fix the sum. The Covenant of the League of Nations formed Part I of the treaty.

Germany protested that it was excluded from the talks. The government of Philipp Scheidemann resigned rather than sign, and Gustav Bauer's government signed after an Allied ultimatum threatening an invasion across the Rhine. The United States Senate never ratified the treaty, and the United States made a separate peace with Germany.

In 1921 the Reparation Commission set Germany's share at 50 billion gold marks, later reduced by the Dawes Plan and the Young Plan. The last Allied troops left the Rhineland on 30 June 1930. Critics such as John Maynard Keynes thought the treaty too harsh, while Marshal Ferdinand Foch thought it too lenient, and historians still disagree about its effects. Resentment of the treaty, together with the stab-in-the-back myth, was exploited by Adolf Hitler, and the treaty has been cited as a cause of the Second World War.
trento: Trento stands on the Adige river, on the river route to Bolzano and the low Alpine passes of the Brenner and the Reschen Pass. It is the capital of the autonomous province of Trento, or Trentino, in the region of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol, and has 119,359 inhabitants. The city centre lies just under 200 metres above sea level, while the municipality reaches 2,000 metres at Monte Bondone. Before the river was diverted in the mid-nineteenth century the Adige ran through the centre of the town and was a navigable commercial route in the Alps. Its old course is now covered by Via Torre Vanga, Via Torre Verde and Via Alessandro Manzoni.

The origins of Trento are uncertain. Some scholars hold that it was a Rhaetian settlement, though the Adige area was influenced by neighbours including the Veneti, the Etruscans and the Gauls. Other theories say the Gauls founded the city in the fourth century BCE. A late-Roman basilica lies beneath the later cathedral, which can be seen in an underground crypt. The Castello del Buonconsiglio was the seat of the Prince-Bishops of Trento, and the Council of Trent was held in the city in the sixteenth century. It was part of Austria and then of Austria-Hungary before Italy annexed it in 1919.

The railway station opened in 1859 on the Brenner line from Verona to Innsbruck, the main rail link between Italy and Germany. The Teatro Sociale was built in 1819. The University of Trento was founded in 1962 as a Higher University Institute of Social Sciences.

Much of the Late Medieval and Renaissance centre has been restored to its pastel colours and wooden balconies. Part of the medieval walls and a circular tower can be seen in Piazza Fiera. The Romanesque-Gothic Cathedral of Saint Vigilius dates from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and the Piazza Duomo beside it has frescoed Renaissance buildings and the Late Baroque Fountain of Neptune of 1767 to 1768. The Tridentine Diocesan Museum, in the Palazzo Pretorio, shows the artistic treasures of the diocese and the influence of the council on the city. Since 2011 Trento has belonged to the Euroregion Tyrol-South Tyrol-Trentino.
trier: Trier lies in a hollow midway along the Moselle valley, between low vine-covered hills in the west of Rhineland-Palatinate, near the border with Luxembourg, which is some 15 kilometres away. Most of the city is on the east bank of the river. Wooded and vineyard-covered slopes stretch up to the Hunsrück plateau in the south and the Eifel in the north. The city lies within the Moselle wine region.

The Celtic tribe of the Treveri settled the area in the last pre-Christian centuries. The Romans subdued them in the 1st century BCE and founded Augusta Treverorum around 16 BCE. From 293 to 395 the city was one of the residences of the Western Roman emperor, and in the 4th century it was one of the largest cities of the empire, with some 75,000 people and perhaps as many as 100,000. The Porta Nigra dates from this age. Emperor Constantine the Great exiled Athanasius of Alexandria to Trier in 336, and Saint Ambrose was born there. The Franks seized the city in 459.

In 870 Trier became part of Eastern Francia, which developed into the Holy Roman Empire. Relics of Saint Matthias began widespread pilgrimages, and the archbishops grew powerful. The University of Trier was founded in 1473. The Trier witch trials of 1581 to 1593 reached the city itself in 1587 and led to the deaths of about 368 people. France annexed Trier in 1794 and dissolved the electoral archbishopric, and after 1815 it passed to Prussia. Karl Marx was born there in 1818.

Trier is a city of about 110,000 on the Moselle, and several Roman and medieval monuments are a World Heritage Site. They include the Porta Nigra, the best-preserved Roman city gate north of the Alps, the Aula Palatina, the throne hall of Constantine, now a Protestant church, a Roman bridge of the 2nd century still used by traffic, and the largest Roman baths north of the Alps. Trier Cathedral houses the Holy Tunic, one of a number of garments claimed to be the robe Jesus wore when he died.
trieste: Trieste lies at the head of the Gulf of Trieste, on a narrow strip of Italian territory between the sea and Slovenia, which is about 8 km to the east. Most of the city is built on a hillside at the foot of an escarpment that drops from the Karst Plateau towards the sea. The city lies where the Italian region, the Balkan Peninsula and central Europe meet. Its deep-water port is a maritime gateway for northern Italy, Germany, Austria and Central Europe.

The site has been inhabited since the second millennium BCE. The Veneti seem to have given the town its name, Tergeste, from a word for market. It became part of the Roman Republic in 177 BCE during the Second Istrian War. It belonged to the Habsburg monarchy from 1382 until 1918. Venice occupied it in 1508, but the Habsburg Empire recovered it a little over a year later. In 1719 Emperor Charles VI made it a free port, and the reign of Maria Theresa began a very prosperous era.

French troops occupied Trieste in 1797, 1805 and 1809, and from 1809 to 1813 it was part of the Illyrian Provinces, which interrupted its free port status and its autonomy. In the 19th century it was the most important seaport of the Habsburg monarchy and the fourth largest city of Austria-Hungary. James Joyce lived there between 1904 and 1915, working on Dubliners and Ulysses. Italy annexed Trieste at the end of the First World War. In 1947 it was declared the Free Territory of Trieste under United Nations protection, divided into Zones A and B along the Morgan Line; the Free Territory lasted until 1954.

Trieste is the capital and largest city of the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Half the city was built in the Austro-Hungarian period, giving it some of the architecture of Vienna. Its sights include Miramare Castle, built between 1856 and 1860 for Archduke Maximilian, the Roman theatre, and the cathedral of St Justus. Piazza Unità d'Italia is the largest seafront square in Europe.
trigonometry: The word comes from the Ancient Greek trigonon, "triangle", and metron, "measure". Sumerian astronomers studied angle measure, dividing the circle into 360 degrees. They and the later Babylonians studied the ratios of the sides of similar triangles and found some of their properties, but did not make a systematic method for finding the sides and angles of triangles. The ancient Nubians used a similar method. In the 3rd century BCE Hellenistic mathematicians such as Euclid and Archimedes studied chords and inscribed angles in circles and proved theorems equivalent to modern trigonometric formulae, though they presented them geometrically rather than algebraically.

Hipparchus of Nicaea gave the first tables of chords in 140 BCE, and in the 2nd century CE Ptolemy constructed detailed tables in Book 1 of his Almagest. Ptolemy's treatise stayed in use for calculations in astronomy for the next 1,200 years in the Byzantine, Islamic and later Western European worlds.

Trigonometry relates the angles of a right triangle to the ratios of its side lengths. The sine is the ratio of the side opposite the angle to the hypotenuse, the cosine the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, and the tangent the ratio of the opposite to the adjacent side. Their reciprocals are the cosecant, secant and cotangent. With the laws of sines and cosines one can find the remaining sides and angles of any triangle once enough of them are known. Spherical trigonometry applies the same ideas to triangles on a sphere, and was long used to locate the sun, moon and stars and to predict eclipses.

The modern definition of the sine is first attested in the Surya Siddhanta, and Aryabhata documented its properties in the 5th century CE. Medieval Islamic mathematicians translated and expanded Greek and Indian works. Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi made the first table of cotangents in 830 CE, and by the 10th century Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani used all six functions, with sine tables in steps of a quarter of a degree.

Nasir al-Din al-Tusi was the first to treat trigonometry as a discipline independent of astronomy, and in the 14th century Madhava of Sangamagrama developed infinite series for sine, cosine and arctangent. Knowledge reached Western Europe through Latin translations of the Almagest and the works of al-Battani and al-Tusi. Regiomontanus wrote De Triangulis in the 15th century, and Copernicus devoted two chapters of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium to the basics. Bartholomaeus Pitiscus first used the word trigonometry in his Trigonometria of 1595, and Gemma Frisius described the method of triangulation still used in surveying.
tripura: Tripura is a landlocked state of about 10,491 square kilometres, bordered by Assam and Mizoram and by Bangladesh, and one of the Seven Sister States of North East India. Five ranges of hills, Baramura, Atharamura, Longtharai, Shakhan and the Jampui Hills, run from north to south with valleys between them, while Agartala stands on a plain in the west. The highest point is Betling Shib, at 939 metres. The climate is tropical savanna, with heavy monsoon rain from May to September, and more than half of the land is forest.

The Mahabharata, the Puranas and the Edicts of Ashoka are said to mention Tripura, and the Mahabharata names the region Kirat Desh, though it is unclear whether that land matched the modern state. The Twipra Kingdom ruled the area for centuries, but when its dynasty began is not documented. The Rajmala, a chronicle first written in the 15th century, lists 179 kings down to Krishna Kishore Manikya, who reigned from 1830 to 1850, but it is not a reliable source. The name is linked to the goddess Tripura Sundari, whose temple at Udaipur is one of the 51 Shakta pithas.

After 1947 Tippera district in the plains became part of East Pakistan, while Hill Tippera stayed under a regency council until 1949. On 9 September 1949 the Maharani Regent signed the Tripura Merger Agreement, making Tripura a Part C state of India. Partition cut it off: the road distance from Kolkata to Agartala grew from under 350 kilometres to 1,700. In 1947–51 an estimated 610,000 Bengali refugees entered, a number almost equal to the state's whole population, and about 1.038 million more came during the war of 1971.

Agartala is the capital and largest city. The official languages are Bengali, Kokborok and English. The 2011 census counted 3,671,032 people, and in 2001 Bengalis were almost 65 per cent of them, with 19 scheduled tribes, of which the Kokborok-speaking Tripuris are the largest. Most of the land belongs to the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council. The sculptures at Unakoti, Pilak and Devtamura show a fusion of organised and indigenous religious art.
trondheim: Trondheim lies on the south shore of Trondheim Fjord, at the mouth of the river Nidelva, with an excellent and sheltered harbour. In the Middle Ages the river was deep enough for most boats, but in the mid-17th century an avalanche of mud and stones made it less navigable and partly ruined the harbour. Despite its northerly latitude it has a mild climate. Around the summer solstice the nights are light enough that no outdoor lighting is needed between 23 May and 19 July, while at the winter solstice the sun stands only slightly more than 3 degrees above the horizon at midday.

The settlement was founded in 997 as a trading post by the Viking king Olav Tryggvason, who named it Kaupangen, meaning market place. Shortly afterwards it came to be called Nidaros, the outlet of the river Nid. The district around it, Trondheim, meant the home of the Trønder people, and Trøndelag the law area of the Trønder. The city served as the king's seat and was the capital of Norway until 1217. From 1152 to 1537 it was the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Nidaros; it then became, and has remained, the seat of the Lutheran Diocese of Nidaros.

Nidaros Cathedral, begun in 1070, is the most important Gothic monument in Norway and was Northern Europe's most important Christian pilgrimage site in the Middle Ages, with routes leading to it from Oslo and from the Jämtland and Värmland regions of Sweden. Sverre Sigurdsson built the fortification Sverresborg in 1182 and 1183; it was burned in 1188 and had been restored by 1197. Kristiansten Fortress, built from 1681 to 1684, repelled invading Swedes in 1718 and was decommissioned in 1816. During the German occupation of Norway in the Second World War the city held a submarine base for the 13th U-boat Flotilla, and Vollan District Jail was used for prisoners of war and political prisoners.

Trondheim is a city and municipality in Trøndelag county, the third most populous municipality in Norway. It was incorporated as a city on 1 January 1838, and its present municipality was formed in 1964 by merger with four neighbouring municipalities, and enlarged again in 2020. The Norwegian University of Science and Technology and the research foundation SINTEF have their headquarters there, and the cathedral stands beside the Archbishop's Palace in the city centre.
troy: The archaeological site of Troy consists of the hill of Hisarlık and the fields below it to the south. The hill is a tell, formed of strata holding the remains of more than three millennia of occupation. Nine main layers are identified, numbered with Roman numerals from Troy I, the earliest, to Troy IX, the latest, with sublayers marked by letters such as VIIa and VIIb. Relative dates come from comparing artefacts with those from other sites, and precise absolute dates are not always possible because radiocarbon dating has limited accuracy.

Troy I was founded around 3000 BCE beside a shallow lagoon and was notable for massive limestone fortifications. Troy II, built around 2550 BCE, was twice the size, with a lower town and a citadel divided into two precincts; its Megaron IIA is the biggest known building of its kind in the Aegean and Anatolian region. Troy VI–VII was a major Late Bronze Age city with a steep citadel and a sprawling lower town, in contact with Mycenaean Greece. Hittite records name a city of Wilusa, usually identified with it, though not all scholars regard the identification as firmly established. Sublayers VIh and VIIa show possible signs of violent destruction and are candidates for the setting of the later myths.

Troy VIII grew from about 700 BCE, when Greek immigrants began building, and lasted into the Roman era. Herodotus says that Xerxes sacrificed 1,000 cattle at the sanctuary of Athena Ilias on his march towards Greece. Ilion was destroyed in 85 BCE after an eleven-day siege by the Roman general Fimbria, then rebuilt after Sulla bestowed benefactions on it, and its new civic calendar took 85 BCE as its first year. Earthquakes around 500 CE devastated the city, and from the 4th century until the Byzantine era Ilion was the seat of a Christian bishop.

Interest in the site began with travellers who mistook Alexandria Troas for Troy. Charles Maclaren was the first to identify Hisarlık with confidence, in 1822, and Frank Calvert surveyed it in 1865. Heinrich Schliemann secured permission to excavate in 1868 and began his trench in April 1870; Wilhelm Dörpfeld, Carl Blegen and, from 1988 to 2005, Manfred Korfmann continued the work, the last revealing the lower city. Schliemann proposed Troy II as the city of legend, though later research showed it predates the Mycenaean era by several hundred years. The relationship between myth and reality remains unclear. The Turkish government created a Historical National Park at Troy in 1996, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.
tubingen: Tübingen is a traditional university city in central Baden-Württemberg, 30 kilometres south of Stuttgart. It grew around the base of the fortress Schloss Hohentübingen and of the St. George's Collegiate Church, on both sides of the Neckar and Ammer rivers. The Neckar flows east through the city, just south of the medieval old town. To the north lies the Schönbuch, a densely wooded nature park, and the Swabian Alb rises to the south-east. The Schlossberg and the Österberg stand in the city centre, and large parts of the city are hilly.

The area was probably first settled in the 12th millennium BCE. The Romans left traces in 85 CE, when they built a limes frontier wall at the Neckar in confrontation with the Alamanni. Records of the castle of Hohentübingen go back to 1078, when Henry IV, King of Germany, besieged it. In the middle of the 12th century the Counts of Zollern were raised to Imperial Counts Palatine, with their seat at Tübingen. By 1231 it was a civitas, which meant the Crown recognised its civil liberties, a market and a court system.

In the later 13th century the town gained Augustinian and Franciscan monasteries and a Latin school, today's Uhland-Gymnasium. In 1342 the town and castle passed to the Counts of Württemberg. The clock tower of the Collegiate Church was begun in 1411. The Jewish community, centred on the Judengasse below the Rathaus, was expelled in 1477, the year the university was founded.

The university, Eberhard Karl University, is one of the oldest north of the Alps. In the 19th century it was associated with the German-patriotic student Burschenschaften, whose large fraternity houses remain a feature of the town. It was associated with the rise of National Socialism in the years between the world wars. Among those linked with the town are Philip Melanchthon, the astronomer Johannes Kepler, and Wilhelm Schickard, professor of Hebrew and astronomy and inventor of a mechanical calculator. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel and Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling studied there, and Friedrich Hölderlin studied, lived and died in the town, as did the theologian Ferdinand Christian Baur.

Tübingen survived the Second World War with its historic fabric almost wholly intact, and its old town, with crooked cobblestone lanes, half-timbered houses and the Rathaus on the central market, is one of the few Altstädte in Germany that is completely intact. Students make up almost a third of its 90,000 residents. After the 1960s the city expanded on the high ground to the north, and later into the Loretto and French Quarter on land that French military bases had left. It is the capital of a district and of an administrative region, and the university is its largest employer.
tukoji-rao-holkar-iii: Tukoji was born on 26 November 1890, the son of Shivajirao Holkar, Maharaja of Indore, and Maharani Sita Bai. His father abdicated on 31 January 1903, and as the new maharaja was only thirteen a council of regency governed until he came of age. He was educated at the Daly College in Indore and at Dehradun. On 6 November 1911 he was invested with ruling powers, and in the same year he attended the coronation of King George V in London.

As ruler he founded two orders, the Order of Merit of Holkar in February 1914 and the Order of Ahilyabai Holkar on 22 November 1920. In the New Year Honours of 1918 he was made a Knight Grand Commander of the Order of the Star of India.

In January 1925 Mumtaz Begum, a courtesan and one of his mistresses, left his harem after what she described as repressive conditions and the death of her daughter, which she blamed on palace nurses. While performing in Bombay she met Abdul Bawla, a 25-year-old Memon businessman, who was threatened several times and told to send her back, and refused. On 12 January a group of assassins attacked the couple at Malabar Hill. Bawla was shot in the head and killed; Mumtaz Begum survived with a wound to the face after British officers who were nearby intervened.

She testified against nine accused, among them men of the maharaja's household. The court sentenced three men to death and three to life imprisonment. One of the latter, General Anandrao Gangram Phanse of the Indore army, escaped the death penalty after being represented by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. The court did not formally hold Tukoji responsible, but under British pressure he abdicated on 26 February 1926 and left Indore.

After his abdication he lived mainly in France. He had married three times. His senior wife, Chandravati Gawade, whom he married on 16 March 1895 when both were small children, stayed in Indore and brought up their son, the new maharaja. His second wife, Indira Talcherkar, married in 1913, also remained there and became a patron of historical research bodies such as the Rajwade Historical Research Institute.

In 1928 he married Nancy Anne Miller, who before the wedding embraced Hinduism, was received into the Dhangar community and took the name Sharmista Devi Holkar; they had four daughters. The Bawla case inspired a film of 1925, Kulin Kanta, and two books. Tukoji died in Paris on 21 May 1978, leaving one son and six daughters.
tunisia: Tunisia lies on the Mediterranean coast of north-west Africa, bordered by Algeria to the west and south-west and Libya to the south-east. It covers 163,610 square kilometres and has a coastline of about 1,300 kilometres. The Dorsal, the eastern extension of the Atlas Mountains, crosses the country north-eastward; north of it lies the Tell, a region of low hills and plains. The Sahel, a coastal plain on the east, is among the world's premier areas of olive cultivation, and much of the south is semi-arid and desert. Tunis, the capital, stands on a hill slope above the lake of Tunis.

Tunisia was inhabited by Berber tribes at the beginning of recorded history. Phoenicians began settling the coast from as early as the 12th century BCE, at Bizerte and Utica. Carthage, founded in the 9th century BCE, became the dominant power in the western Mediterranean after wars with the Greek city-states of Sicily. According to the Greek writer Timaeus of Tauromenium, Dido of Tyre founded it in 814 BCE, though this is regarded as legend. Its people worshipped Baal and Tanit. After the Second Punic War, in which Hannibal invaded Italy, Carthage was a client state of Rome until it was conquered in 146 BCE and made the province of Africa.

Arab Muslims conquered Tunisia in the 7th century CE, and the migration of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym tribes in the 11th and 12th centuries accelerated the process, and by about the 15th century the region was almost completely Arabised. The Ottoman Empire took control in 1546 and held it until the French conquest of 1881. Tunisia became independent as the Tunisian Republic in 1956.

The Tunisian Revolution of 2011 overthrew President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali after 24 years in power and set off the wider Arab Spring. A new constitution was adopted on 26 January 2014, and a constitutional referendum in 2022 made it a unitary presidential republic.

The population is 12.1 million, the vast majority Arab and Muslim. Arabic is the official language, and French serves as an administrative and educational language without official status. The European Union is the first trading partner: Tunisia signed an Association Agreement with it in July 1995, the first Mediterranean country to do so.
turin: Turin lies in north-western Italy, mainly on the western bank of the River Po, surrounded on the west and north by the Alps and on the east by a high hill that continues the hills of Monferrato. Four major rivers pass through it: the Po and its tributaries the Dora Riparia, the Stura di Lanzo and the Sangone.

The Taurini, a Celto-Ligurian Alpine people, occupied the upper valley of the Po. In 218 BCE Hannibal, allied with their enemies the Insubres, took their chief town, Taurasia, after a three-day siege. In the 1st century BCE the Romans founded Augusta Taurinorum, a town of about 5,000 inhabitants within high walls; its Porta Palatina is still preserved. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the town was held by the Heruli, Ostrogoths and Lombards, and passed to the Franks under Charlemagne in 773. The Counts of Savoy gained control after the marriage of Adelaide of Susa to Otto, son of Humbert Biancamano, and when the city was annexed to the Duchy of Savoy at the end of the 13th century it had 20,000 inhabitants.

Emmanuel Philibert, nicknamed Iron Head, made Turin the capital of the Duchy of Savoy in 1563. The French Empire annexed it with the rest of Piedmont in 1802, and in 1814 the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia was restored with Turin as its capital. That kingdom led the struggle for the unification of Italy, and Turin was the political and intellectual centre of the Risorgimento. It became the capital of the new Kingdom of Italy in 1861; the capital moved to Florence in 1865 and to Rome after the conquest of the Papal States in 1870.

Turin is the capital of Piedmont and is sometimes called the cradle of Italian liberty. Its architecture is predominantly Baroque, and part of the historical centre is inscribed in the World Heritage List as the Residences of the Royal House of Savoy. It is the base of Fiat, Lancia and Alfa Romeo, and hosted the 2006 Winter Olympics.
turkey: Turkey, officially the Republic of Türkiye, lies mainly in Anatolia, which makes up 97% of its surface, with a smaller part called East Thrace in Southeast Europe. Together they cover 783,562 square kilometres, and the Turkish straits and the Sea of Marmara run between them. The inland Anatolian Plateau grows more rugged towards the east, where Mount Ararat, the highest point at 5,137 metres, and Lake Van, the largest lake, are found. The Euphrates, the Tigris and the Aras rise in the east, and the country is divided into seven major regions.

The area has been inhabited by modern humans since the late Paleolithic and holds some of the oldest Neolithic sites, among them Göbekli Tepe, close to 12,000 years old, and Çatalhöyük. Written records begin with clay tablets of about 2000 BCE from Kültepe, which belonged to an Assyrian trade colony. The Hittite kingdom, with its capital at Hattusa, lasted approximately between 1700 and 1200 BCE, and Phrygia was established around 750 BCE. Alexander the Great's conquests brought Hellenization, followed by Romanization under the Roman and Byzantine empires.

The Seljuk Turks began migrating into Anatolia in the 11th century. The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum ruled until the Mongol invasion of 1243, after which Turkish principalities emerged. From 1299 the Ottomans united them, and Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453. The Ottoman state entered World War I in 1914, and its government committed genocides against its Armenian, Greek and Assyrian subjects. After defeat came the Turkish War of Independence, the abolition of the sultanate and the Treaty of Lausanne. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first president, proclaimed the Republic on 29 October 1923.

Turkey has more than 86 million people. Most are ethnic Turks, and Kurds are the largest minority, with estimates ranging from 12 to 20% of the population because census figures have not recorded ethnicity since 1965. Ankara is the capital and Istanbul the largest city. The country is a presidential republic under the constitution approved by referendum in 1982, with a 600-member Parliament and 81 provinces.
turku: Turku lies at the mouth of the Aura River in the south-western corner of Finland and covers both banks. The eastern bank, where Turku Cathedral stands, is the older and original centre; the western side, with Turku Castle, is the newer part. South-western Finland stayed below sea level for a long time after the Ice Age, and tectonic uplift turned the region from an outlying archipelago into a shoreline between about 3000 and 2000 BCE. In the Iron Age it was densely populated, and the word Finland once referred only to the area round Turku, which is why the province is called Finland Proper.

The Finnish name Turku is related to the word torg, meaning market. Pope Gregory IX mentioned the town of Aboa in his bull of 1229, and that year is now used as the founding year of the city. By the pope's permission of 23 January 1229 the episcopal seat was moved from Nousiainen to Koroinen, near the present centre. Because no reliable document records the founding, it has also been suggested that the city was founded in the 1280s or 1290s by the joint initiative of the king, the bishop and the Dominican Convent of Saint Olaf. Turku was the most important city in Finland under Swedish rule.

After the Finnish War, Sweden ceded Finland to Russia at the Treaty of Fredrikshamn in 1809, and the Russians entered Turku in October 1809 without resistance. Turku became the capital of the Grand Duchy of Finland but lost the status in 1812, when Emperor Alexander I decided to move the capital to Helsinki. After the last great fire, in 1827, most government institutions were moved to Helsinki together with the Royal Academy of Turku, founded in 1640, which later became the University of Helsinki.

Turku is the oldest city in Finland and the regional capital of Southwest Finland, with about 210,000 inhabitants. It is officially bilingual in Finnish and Swedish. The Swedish-language Åbo Akademi was founded there in 1918 and the Finnish-language University of Turku two years later. Its port runs ferries to Stockholm and Mariehamn.
tutankhamun: Tutankhamun was born in the reign of Akhenaten, during the Amarna Period. His original name, Tutankhaten or Tutankhuaten, meant living image of Aten, reflecting the shift to Atenism that characterised Akhenaten's reign. When he became king he married Ankhesenpaaten, one of Akhenaten's daughters, who later changed her name to Ankhesenamun. They had two daughters who died at or soon after birth and were buried with him in his tomb.

Tutankhamun became pharaoh between 8 and 9 years of age, after the short reigns of Akhenaten's successors Smenkhkare and Neferneferuaten, and he took the throne name Nebkheperure. At the start of his reign the court was still at Amarna and the Aten was still acknowledged, but his court was trying to reconcile Atenism with the traditional religion. Activity at Amarna decreased during the first four years, and given the king's age the reversals of Akhenaten's policies must have been instigated by his advisors. His restorations of cults were recorded on the Restoration Stela.

He sought to restore diplomatic relations with other kingdoms, in particular with the Mitanni, and battles with Nubians and Asiatics were recorded in his mortuary temple at Thebes, both as Egyptian victories. He was one of the few pharaohs worshipped as a deity during their lifetime, as temples in Nubia and stelae at Karnak indicate. There are no surviving records of the circumstances of his death. Hawass and his team postulate that it resulted from a leg fracture, perhaps from a fall, combined with a severe malarial infection.

Tutankhamun's two known children were stillborn or died shortly after birth, and his death left no immediate heir. Ay, who performs the opening of the mouth ritual for him on the burial chamber wall, became pharaoh, and Horemheb, commander-in-chief of his armed forces, succeeded Ay. Horemheb completed the restoration of the traditional religion and had his own name inscribed on monuments that Tutankhamun had commissioned.

His tomb was unusually small for his status, and its entrance was lost under debris from later tombs and workers' houses. Howard Carter found it in 1922, with the patronage of George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon. It is the only royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings found in near-intact condition, with 5,398 items, among them a solid gold coffin, a face mask, thrones, bows and trumpets, and Carter took ten years to catalogue them. Rumours of a curse of the pharaohs followed the death of Carnarvon on 5 April 1923. In 1962 the Louvre held an exhibition of the treasures that drew 1.2 million visitors.
tuva: Tuva lies at the geographical centre of Asia in southern Siberia, and its capital, Kyzyl, stands near the geographic centre of the continent. The republic is a mountain basin about 600 metres above sea level, encircled by the Sayan and Tannu-Ola ranges, and mountains and hills cover over 80 per cent of its territory. Its highest point is Mongun-Tayga, at 3,970 metres. There are over 8,000 rivers, including the upper course of the Yenisei. It borders Mongolia to the south.

The territory was controlled by a succession of powers, among them the Xiongnu, the Rouran Khaganate, the Tang dynasty, the Mongol Empire and the Yuan dynasty. From 1758 to 1911 Tuva was part of China's Qing dynasty, administered through Outer Mongolia. During the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 a separatist movement formed among the Tuvans, and on 17 April 1914 Tuva became a Russian protectorate as Uryankhay Krai. In 1918 and 1919 it was occupied by the White Russian troops of Alexander Kolchak, later by China, until the Bolsheviks expelled the Chinese in 1921.

On 14 August 1921 the Bolsheviks established the Tuvan People's Republic, popularly called Tannu-Tuva, formally independent between the World Wars. Its capital was renamed Kyzyl, meaning red, in 1926. A coup of 1929, carried out by five young Tuvans trained in Moscow, replaced Chairman Donduk Kuular, and Buddhist and Mongol influences were then curtailed. The Soviet Union annexed Tuva in 1944, with the approval of its Little Khural but without a referendum. Tuva signed the treaty creating the Russian Federation on 31 March 1992.

The Republic of Tyva is a republic of the Russian Federation, with 336,651 inhabitants at the 2021 census, more than a third of them in Kyzyl. Tuvans make up most of the population and speak the Tuvan language, a Turkic language. Tuvan and Russian are both official. Tuvan throat singing, in which the singer produces a fundamental tone and an overtone together, is a defining tradition. Tibetan Buddhism, first met in the 13th and 14th centuries, coexists with shamanism, which is preserved as part of traditional culture.
tycho-brahe: Tycho was born Tyge Ottesen Brahe on 14 December 1546 at his family's seat at Knutstorp in Scania, then Danish, the oldest of twelve siblings. He was heir to several of Denmark's most influential noble families, and both his grandfathers and all his great-grandfathers had served on the king's Privy Council. In 1566 he went to study at the University of Rostock. On 29 December of that year he lost part of his nose in a sword duel with his third cousin Manderup Parsberg, after a drunken quarrel over who was the better mathematician, and he wore a prosthetic nose for the rest of his life. His family had expected him to enter politics or law but supported his choice of the sciences.

Tycho devoted himself to more accurate instruments, enlarging the sextant and the quadrant, and mounted them underground on the bedrock once he realised that wind and the movement of buildings affected them. King Frederick II granted him an estate on Hven and money to build Uraniborg, the first large observatory in Christian Europe. In De nova stella of 1573 he refuted the Aristotelian belief in an unchanging celestial realm, and he showed that comets were not atmospheric phenomena. He could not reconcile Copernican heliocentrism with Aristotelian physics, so he devised a system in which the Sun and Moon orbit the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun.

After Frederick's death in 1588 Tycho's influence at court declined, and in 1597 he was forced by the new king to leave Denmark. He was invited to Prague, where he became imperial astronomer and built an observatory at Benátky nad Jizerou.

Tycho fell ill after a banquet in Prague and died eleven days later, on 24 October 1601, aged 54. Before dying he urged Johannes Kepler to finish the Rudolphine Tables using Tycho's own planetary system. Kepler used Tycho's records of the motion of Mars to deduce his laws of planetary motion. Tycho's planetary model was soon discredited, but his observations were an essential contribution to the Scientific Revolution. Danish scholarship often depicted him as a mediocre scholar and a traitor to the nation, but from the second half of the 20th century scholars reassessed his significance.
tyrrhenian-sea: The Tyrrhenian Sea lies off the western coast of Italy. The islands of Corsica and Sardinia bound it on the west, the Italian Peninsula, in the regions of Tuscany, Lazio, Campania, Basilicata and Calabria, on the north and east, and Sicily on the south. Its maximum depth is 3,785 metres. The International Hydrographic Organization defines its limits by lines across the Strait of Messina, from Sicily to Sardinia, across the Strait of Bonifacio and along the north from Cape Corse in Corsica to the Italian coast. The sea contains smaller islands such as Capri, Elba, Ischia and Ustica, and the eight Aeolian Islands lie in its southern part, north of Sicily.

It lies near the meeting of the African and Eurasian plates, and mountain chains and active volcanoes such as Mount Marsili are found in its depths. It is a back-arc basin that formed during the Neogene as the Calabrian slab rolled back towards the south-east. Episodes of fast and slow retreat formed first the Vavilov basin and then the Marsili basin, which are separated by an undersea ridge, the Issel Bridge. The same process gave rise to submarine volcanoes and to the active volcano Mount Stromboli.

The name derives from the Greek name for the Etruscans. Hesiod, in the 8th century BCE, first mentions them, describing them as living in central Italy alongside the Latins. The Etruscans lived along the coast of modern Tuscany, Latium and Campania, and they called the water the Sea of the Etruscans. In Greek mythology the cliffs above the sea were believed to house the four winds kept by Aeolus: the Mistral from the Rhône valley, the Libeccio from the southwest, and the Sirocco and Ostro from the south.

The main Italian ports on the sea are Naples, Palermo, Civitavecchia, Salerno, Trapani and Gioia Tauro, and Bastia lies on Corsica. The maritime facilities called the port of Rome are at Civitavecchia, about 68 kilometres north-west of the city, since Rome itself has no port. Its islands include Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, the Tuscan Archipelago, the Pontine Islands, Procida and the Aeolian Islands.
